TO MY WIFE

PREFACE 

The very great increase in governmental activities, national, state, and local, in the last two decades has given the study and the teaching of administration a new impetus, a new meaning. 

In consequence there has been widespread technological and professional progress in the American administrative service and there has developed a considerable professional and technical literature in a wide variety of administrative fields. In the preparation of this book the author has sought to interpret the written materials in relation to administrative practices, to bring the researcher and the practitioner together. The book is, in short, the cumulative product of several years of teaching experience combined with administrative contacts. It is hoped that it has captured a certain flavor of realism-glimpses here and there of the wheels of administration in motion. 

I am deeply grateful to my colleague, Robert E. Ahrens, for his assistance in the preparation of this manuscript. In addition to editing the entire work, he is responsible for a great deal of the legal research that has gone into the chapters on administrative law. I also gratefully acknowledge my indebtedness to the following persons who have given generously of their time in reading and criticizing parts of the manuscript: Clifford N.

PUBLIC ADMINISTRATION

CHAPTER I  

The prevailing political philosophy in the United States during the early nineteenth century accentuated the theory that any citizen, notwithstanding his training and ability, was capable of efficiently discharging the duties of public office. 

Equally prevalent was the belief that any one had an indefeasible right to be employed in the science and art of government. The functions of government were few in the simple social order which then existed. The electorate did not expect any administrative officer, national, state, or local, to possess any particular qualifications or to have had any specialized training. The professions and occupations in the public service as well as in the field of industry and private endeavor were not highly specialized. The industrial revolution was in the embryo and the agrarian mode of life predominated over the urban. A professional police force did not appear until about the middle of the century, while government engineers were self-trained surveyors.¹ The only professional group of considerable size engaged in public administration was composed of lawyers who had meager training, inasmuch as the modern law school was just coming into existence. The influence of the laissez-faire theories of the eighteenth century tended to restrict governmental functions and activities. The 1 2

fear of bureaucracy, together with the attitude of the average person toward competency in the public service, conspired against the introduction of the expert administrator and the technician into public administration. 

The result was a lack of emphasis on, if not an actual hostility and unsympathetic attitude toward, technical administrative processes. The effect of the elective system with regard to the chief administrative positions in state, county, and municipality, was to place a premium on mediocrity. This adversely influenced any tendency there might have been to improve administrative methods. America was so preoccupied with the pioneering and development of the unsettled lands of a continent, that it would not consider any but the outstanding political issues connected therewith. There was no interest in establishing a budget system when the federal treasury contained a surplus, as was usual except during and following the Civil War. It required a $25,000,000,000 World War debt to force the budget issue, and the assassination of a President by a disappointed office seeker to initiate the modern civil service movement.5 The scientific approach toward administration as a governmental problem was virtually non-existent prior to the dawn of the present century. 

By the beginning of the twentieth century, the industrial revolution had produced a new society based upon the division of labor into specialized tasks. This inexorable trend of events had its effect on government-it spelled the doom of the commonplace that the man on the street is qualified to perform every governmental employment. Gradually the public service was forced to call upon the expert who alone was competent to struggle with the complexity of modern administration. The resulting absorption of professional and technical personnel into the public service; the pressure of organized groups for more

This new public administration is evidenced in the comparatively recent emergence of the private bureaus of municipal research, the employment of trained investigators by taxpayers' associations, and the inevitable absorption of the technician into the government itself. Let us take particular fields for purposes of illustration. An Atlantic seaboard state desiring to secure some trained civil service examiners, announced the open competitive test as far west as California. The City of Oakland wanted a city manager and eventually employed an experienced and well-trained man at a substantial salary. 

He had served six other cities in that capacity during a westward trek from Niagara Falls over a period of almost twenty years. The financial planning for the City of Los Angeles is now performed by a bureau of technicians composed largely of young college men. They are chosen by open competitive examination and their tenure is under civil service protection." 

The legal work for Los Angeles County is carried on by a group of recent graduates of accredited law schools who were chosen by civil service examination. When the head of the 

Accounting Division of the Los Angeles County Auditor's Office died, his placed was filled by competitive examination. The successful applicant was a certified public accountant who had been chief auditor in the city controller's office for several years. Technology and Government 

These recent professional additions to the personnel of government are the products of the growth of technology in an industrial age.

The health department must have a bacteriologist who, of course, is not to be found among the workers of the old machine. Modern criminal investigation demands the services of a chemist, and only a specialist with the best training can solve present-day police problems. The health officer requests budget provision for trained veterinaries to serve as meat inspectors. Thus, the demand of government for technicians and technologists in a myriad of specialized fields becomes almost endless. 10 So far, mention has been made of those employed in the fields of technology not peculiar to government. The twentieth century, however, has produced for the public service its own unique technical problems. While a few members of the embryo profession of city planners may obtain employment with large-scale real estate developers, the group as a whole must depend on public work for support. The same may be said of sanitary engineers, doctors of public health," budget investigators, public personnel technicians, and scientific crime investigators. These and many others must either work for the government directly or for various governments intermittently on a consulting basis. Their daily work is based upon a skill and body of knowledge which is not a part of the equipment of the average man. That is achieved only through training and experience. In other words, modern government finds that the equalitarian doctrine of the nineteenth century must give way to personnel possessing special attainments-technicians and technologists. 

The terms "technical" and "technological" are derived from 10 Harvard University has announced a special course for the training of city planners.

"Technique is the manner of artistic execution, the performance or method of manipulation in any art, but as to just how inclusive this definition should be regarded is a question." 12

The word technologie was recognized by the French Academy in 1835. A more recent dictionary sets forth the information that it constitutes an Explication des procédés, des termes spéciaux à un art, â une science.13 The following chapters will attempt to describe a technique and technology of public administration, which is both a science and an art of the everyday operations of government.¹¹

One of the most significant developments in the professionalization of the public service is found in the establishment of national secretariats of a number of organizations of public officials at 850 East 58th Street, Chicago, near the University of Chicago campus. In addition to several new organizations one will find there the following which have been familiar to students of public administration for some time: the International City Managers' Association, the American Legislators' Association, the American Municipal Association, and the Governmental Research Association. The Public Admin istration Clearing House fosters co-operation and co-ordination between these and other organizations and institutions in the field. The Public Administration Service publishes monographs on subjects of interest to administrators and offers a professional and technical consulting service to those who may require it. While these institutions are not to be regarded as integral parts of the University of Chicago, there is afforded an extremely happy contact between administrative and academic viewpoints.' 18 The previous reference to a technology and technique of public administration is not intended to create the impression that a fool-proof answer to every administrative problem has been worked out with mathematical precision. Far from it—the contemporary pioneers of the new public administration are frequently very humble regarding the state of development of their particular technical processes. The better type of personnel administrator is far from satisfied with his tests. 

Traffic experts have seldom made the basic factual studies essential to solving a city's traffic ills, and criminologists are far from sure as to how to handle prisoners. In each of these

No costly and wasteful administrative process is sacrosanct because it is intermingled with an emotional patriotic appeal, or because it had the stamp of approval of the ox-cart days. Administrative institutions and practices must bear up under the white light of exhaustive examination, observation, and inquiry on the part of trained and experienced observers. The scientific approach, not the rule-of-thumb, characterizes the methodology of the new public administration.

Politics and Administration 

The average reader will experience a certain skepticism while reading the foregoing pages. He will be unable to reconcile the picture of a competent, technical, and professional public service with the contemporary political scene in his community. The friends and advocates of the new public administration are not blind to the ways of politics, for they have too often come in contact with its worst manifestations. Moreover, they are too intelligent and experienced to give even passing consideration to its elimination. Instead, politics is regarded as an inevitable and necessary part of the process of government. It must, however, be controlled and confined to its proper sphere which is the determination, crystallization, and declaration of the will of the community. Administration, on the other hand, is the carrying into effect of this will once it has been made clear by political processes.19 From these premises, therefore, is derived the keystone of the new public administration-the conclusion that politics should stick to its policy-determining sphere and leave administration to apply its own technical processes free from the blight of political meddling. 20 

19 F. J. Goodnow, Politics and Administration (The Macmillan Co., 

1900), p. 18. 

20 This is coming to pass in school_administration through the growing power of the superintendent. J. B. Edmonson, "Recent Achievements in 

School Administration," Public Management (August, 1930), Vol. XII, No. 8, pp. 429-433.

ΙΟ [Ch. I 

Let no apostle of political realism think that advocates of such a separation of powers are unaware of its doctrinaire pitfalls. They do not advocate that it be embalmed into constitutional breakwaters designed to stand for centuries, as was the classical threefold division into legislative, executive, and judicial functions. The desire is merely to establish a rule of action which will automatically determine, in most cases, whether a given matter is properly of legislative or administrative competence." There is no denial that in a considerable number of instances questions of policy will be closely intermingled with administrative action. Such a situation will be much more aggravated in some fields of activity than others. 

The dividing line between policy and administration is much easier to ascertain in a fire department than in a police department, in a recorder's office than in a district attorney's office, and in public works than in poor relief. 

Politics and administration cannot always be separated and isolated. The realization of this fact should not, however, vitiate the basic soundness of a gentleman's agreement, growing out of tradition, that one will not encroach upon the other in a meddlesome manner. There can be little doubt that just this thing is coming to pass. Thus, in 1931, Manager C. A. 

Dykstra 22 was able to say: "I can testify that for one city in the United States it has been possible to maintain the nice balance between administrative duties and the determination of public policy." He also stated that "To date no member of the city council with which I work has come to me with a candidate to be appointed, a contract to be signed, or an award to be made. As a city manager I have been free from political distinction. Thus there is an Organization of Will as evidenced by the Board of Directors, an Organization of Thought in the staff and research agencies, and an Organization of Performance in the line workers. H. The success to be attained in this direction will depend largely upon the extent to which partisan politics is kept out of administration, and upon the assurance of tenure given to technical and expert personnel. This will entail just as great an obligation for the administrative personnel to abstain from political controversy as for the political officers to keep hands off administration. It is not always possible for a city manager to refrain from defending his administration in the public forum.23 However, the more he can avoid the heat of election campaigns the better it will be for him and his profession. 

Partisanship is gradually being eliminated from administration.24 

This is evident from such examples as exist in the mayor and council cities of Detroit and Los Angeles; in the County of Los 

Angeles where the charter virtually compels civil service for department chiefs and lesser employees; in the personnel administration of such states as Wisconsin, New Jersey, and California; and in the increasing number of permanent directors of federal bureaus. If the reader is not convinced, he need but compare Mr. Dykstra's statement of present conditions in Cincinnati with Lincoln Steffens' description of the same scene some thirty years before.25

To secure the proper equilibrium between politics and administration it will be necessary to have a working arrangement between political officers and administrative officers.

The desired situation is best illustrated by the relationship between the highest civil service officers and ministers in Great Britain. Civil servants reared and educated in the Tory tra-

Less than a hundred offices in a service numbering thousands are vacated by a change in government, and these are purely political in nature and openly stamped as such. In the United States two steps in this direction are necessary: first, a forthright and open acknowledgment that some offices are political and others administrative; and, second, a resulting reduction of the offices whose duties are purely administrative but in which appointment and tenure are yet subject to political vicissitudes. In other words, we need a rapid expansion of the merit system, both upward and outward, in most jurisdictions. The following distinctions between political and administrative officers are offered in the hope that they may indicate where the merit system should begin, and where it should end.

Influenced by technological data gleaned from study and research It would be folly to say that administrative officers should have absolutely no hand in the formulation of policy. They may legitimately participate in this process in several ways, the most important of which is probably in the presentation of studies, surveys, and reports with conclusions and recommendations. Here the staff officer is acting merely as a factfinder, drawing his policy recommendations from the facts as revealed. There is a point in the dissemination of this information beyond which the administrator should not pass, but just where the dividing line between politics and administra-

Ch. 1] 

tion should be drawn is not always clear. Some city managers feel that they are justified in campaigning for bond issues. 

Others feel that this is an activity for lay citizens and council members only. The permanent official may legitimately influence policy through his rightful position as servant of the governing legislative body. The superintendent of schools and city manager are in this position. A representative of the 

Bureau of Budget and Efficiency of the City of Los Angeles is always present at council meetings and takes a prominent part in the deliberations of the finance committee which is probably the most powerful policy group in the city. The unpreparedness of the amateur in political office to cope with matters demanding technical information and training forces him to rely upon the advice of permanent officials. Thus the sheer pressure of circumstances in the modern state compels the politician to defer to the expert. It is in this field of counsel and advice that the expert has a proper influence on policy. 

A similar place of influence is not accorded him in the public forum or on the campaign platform.

The new public administration rises above petty provincialism. It does not object to confining the choice of clerks, stenographers, and unskilled workers to local residents, nor does it seriously question the advisability of purchasing from local vendors where they substantially meet the offers of outside competitors on an open market. This new administration, however, does favor making a selection of certain officials from applicants representing a large geographical area, as is the case with reference to choosing superintendents of schools. 

This class of public officials includes city managers, police chiefs, fire chiefs, health officers, and other technical and supervising personnel. This will both widen the opportunities for professional careers and counteract bureaucratic self-esteem and stagnation in local organizations. The objections always raised are that the newcomer will not be familiar with "local conditions" and that local residents are being deprived of employment. The answer to the former is that in most branches differences in "local conditions" are due to politics, and that the problems of administration are so essentially identical ir

[Ch. I 

most places that the experienced administrator will be able to adjust himself to his new environment in a relatively short time.20 The latter objection is based on "spoils" psychology and as such is unworthy of consideration. Moreover, it may be said that no community will suffer by the addition of one more high-class family, that the newcomer immediately becomes a local resident and taxpayer, and that local residents are permitted to compete for similar positions elsewhere. Further, there is no objection to selecting a local man if his calibre compares favorably with others. 

Analogy with Private Management The new public administration is constantly on the alert to adapt to governmental needs the best devices which are. used in private management. It is increasingly evident, however, that in certain respects government operates under environment, circumstances, and restraints unknown to private business. Suppose a city has too few policemen and too many engineers. A private corporation would be able to correct an analogous situation in a few weeks at most, but in a city it takes years. If a corporation fails to make a profit, a change in management may result. The current movement toward the establishment of administrative standards and measurements is a frank acknowledgment that something will have to be devised for public management to take the place of the profit and loss statement in private enterprise. Public administration will always have to give greater consideration to the humane and welfare aspects of technical problems than private business has done in the past. It must by its very nature have a social concept of efficiency rather than that of scientific management relative to the productivity of the individual plant or person.

It must use both, but one must be tempered by the other. The normal operation of a department of public works, for instance, should attempt to achieve the utmost production at competitive cost. During the last three 

26 C. F. Cahalane confirms this view in "The Need for and Benefits to be 

Derived from Police Training." International Assn. of Chiefs of Police, Proceedings Thirty-sixth Convention, Atlanta, Georgia (1929), pp. 87, 91–92.

Ch. 1] 

years, however, citizen clamor has forced upon public works departments programs of "made work" for purposes of unemployment relief, which were decidedly not productive in the ordinary acceptance of that term.27 A government cannot be operated like the Standard Oil Company, but it can use its own adaptation of private management's better methods. 

The chief function of government in the past has been to render intangible services upon which it was difficult to place a monetary value. These services were rendered in a monopolized field where the stimulus and measuring stick of competition were lacking. For this reason it was difficult to say whether a given governmental department was operated efficiently or not. Hence, governmental management has had to depart from the efficiency criteria of private management at this point. It cannot use the profit and loss statement to judge the effectiveness of public health work, police protection, and recreation services. To answer this need public management is just beginning to develop a management technique of its own. It will eagerly avail itself of all that private experience has to offer. The profit and loss statement, however, can never be its sole, or even its chief, guide. 

Other important differences between public administration and private management lie in structure and control. Stockholder votes are ordinarily cast in large blocks by proxies in the hands of the management itself, and votes are based on ownership. On the other hand, every citizen has one vote irrespective of his material possessions in the commonwealth. 

While there is some analogy as to the relationship existing between boards of directors and management, and between a city council and a city manager, the independence of the executive from the legislature has been the rule in the United States. 

The relationship between management and personnel also presents contrasts. Public personnel is to a varying extent its own employer, and if well organized it can bring to bear pressure which will materially limit public management's freedom of "W. action. This is true, if at all, to a much more limited extent in private enterprise.

There is a popular conviction that ethical standards are higher in business than in government, that "politics" corrupt public administration while business administration is comparatively free from such sinister influences. But the view expressed by John T. Flynn that, "the average politician is a rank amateur in the gentle art of graft compared with his brother in the field of business" 28 is shared by many careful observers; and the investigations, prosecutions, and convictions, in the post-war years, of persons prominent in the fields of business and banking call for a revision of the popular theory that business operates on a higher ethical plane than does the government. 

Furthermore, there is something to be said for Lincoln Steffens' charge that it is business itself which corrupts our cities.29 

However, the professional and technical personnel of the new public administration is bringing into government a growing group of incorruptible public officials. It is worthy of note that there have been no charges of malfeasance against any city manager in almost thirty years of experience. American graft has been carried on by politicians rather than by the professional element in government. The gradual assumption of its rightful rôle by administration is having the salutary effect of removing the "apple" 30 from politics and thus giving a less corruptible personnel a chance to operate free from the clamor of privilege seekers. The scientific approach makes politics unattractive to corruptionists by eliminating the spoils. 31 The progress of the new public administration is beset with numerous obstacles and hazards. Chief among them is the well-intentioned citizen who wants the other fellow to be regulated, but who schemes to have himself made an exception. 

This person is absolutely sincere in agreeing that there should be administrative regulation of traffic, but he tries every possible

One of the most persistent bars to the achievement of sound administrative practice is the legislator who prostitutes administration to curry favor among his constituents. Thus Congress devotes valuable time to debating the merits of a claim for $160 resulting from the death of a cow which drank Geological Survey paint,33 councilmen spend immense sums to place traffic signals at corners where they are not needed, and state legislators dissipate their energies setting the salaries of county officers.

Those in charge of administration themselves may unwittingly perform acts inimical to the highest administrative achievement. The political executive comes into office burdened with many obligations and promises, the fulfillment of which he would frequently like to avoid. Inevitably this causes a period of uncertainty and readjustment during which the cause of good administration must suffer. On the whole, however, our mayors, governors, and presidents have been better friends of good administration than have the legislatures. They have been so intimately connected with its day by day functioning that they have realized its weaknesses, frequently because of their own inability to achieve results due to faulty administrative organization. The state reorganization movements have been led by Governors Lowden in Illinois, Smith in New 

York, Young in California, and Byrd in Virginia. Nevertheless, many a lesser governor and mayor has violated good administrative precepts to insure political preferment.

There will be a persistent struggle to advance class interests at the expense of the general good, and isolation from popular control may lead to the arbitrary exercise of authority. In the United States, however, administration has suffered more from political amateurism than from bureaucracy. The advocates of the new public administration feel that bureaucracy, while a menace, can be counteracted by certain designated popular checks. This subject will be further discussed in the chapter on external controls. 34 The new public administration has profound respect for law as an instrument for achieving social ends, but it is decidedly unfriendly toward that concept of law which makes men worship the rules of the past long after the social needs have changed. 

By its very nature law must lag behind social progress. The lawyer must look to the past for his legal precedents, but in doing so he frequently develops an undue reverence for outworn social institutions. The twentieth century social scientist feels, therefore, that the lawyer should not have the predominant part in moulding political and social thought. The lawyer too frequently asks, "Is such action legal?" The administrator, on the other hand, asks, "Is it sound policy?" For this reason the eighteenth century legalistic approach to government must give way to the realistic scientific method. 

The new public administration is impatient with blind obeisance to technical legal rules, which, at least to its followers, serve only to hinder social progress. Those who believe in a wide degree of personal liberty in all fields of endeavor have expressed apprehension lest the recent growth of administrative powers become an arbitrary despot injecting government into every possible human activity. Such a view fails to grasp the real function of administration. Let us set up the hypothesis of pure anarchy wherein a race of supermen would be able to harmonize their differences without government. In such a society the streets would still have to be swept, the paving repaired, fires put out, sewage disposed of, and pure water supplied. Hence, administration would be necessary if all of the coercive activities of government were abolished. Furthermore, where the new public administration has entered the field of coercion it has done so to give greater liberty to a thousand while restricting the liberty of one or two. If workmen injured in an industrial accident recovered damages in one out of eight cases under the common law and in eight out of ten under the new administrative control, it can hardly be truthfully stated that liberty has been curtailed. If life insurance companies are forced to maintain with a state insurance commissioner sufficient reserve to cover payment of claims, is liberty restricted? The growth of the administrative branch of government is not a sinister enemy of freedom. It is merely a manifestation of a greater movement-society working through government to solve the collective problems of a technological age.

PART I ORGANIZATION

CHAPTER II EVOLUTION OF ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION 

Colonial experience created in the American people an abiding trust in popular assemblies, combined with a deep-seated fear of executive power.

In their conflicts with royal authority the popular branch of the legislature had been the champion of colonial rights, while the colonial governors had naturally tended to stand by the king when controversial issues presented themselves. The result was that while the first state constitutions provided for a governor, they practically left him bereft of all power. The lines of administrative authority ran from the legislature or from the people to elective officials. The municipal government of that same era carried over the colonial form of borough organization in which the mayor was a little more, at least administratively, than a slightly exalted councilman. 

Municipal administration was non-technical, in a modern sense, and very much restricted in its scope, while administrative powers resided for the most part in the legislative body. 

These weak types of administrative organization answered the purpose very well as long as two conditions prevailed. In the first place, the country was predominantly agricultural and the services demanded of government were meager, thus permitting amateur administrators to function satisfactorily. In the second place, the process of government was in the hands of a more or less closed corporation composed of the wealthy, land owners, and the aristocracy. This was so because of the property-holding and tax-paying qualifications for voters and office holders. During the first half of the nineteenth century, however, both of these situations were altered. The industrial revolution began its transformation of a rural society into one which is today predominantly urban and industrial, and the property 25

[Pt. I 

ORGANIZATION 

and tax restrictions on participation in government were removed. 

The industrial revolution so altered the social and economic basis of American society as to call for a vast growth in the functions of government. As population increases in density more governmental regulation is necessary. A farmer located a half-mile from his nearest neighbor may dig a cesspool without causing any particular harm to society, but if a city dweller does likewise he may pollute the water supply of scores of others. A frontiersman may, with social impunity, allow his garbage to rot on the prairie, but disastrous consequences would result from similar action on the part of urbanites. There are many living today who can remember the first street car in their city, the first electric street light, the first sanitary sewer, the first pavement, the first automobile, the coming of the railroad, and the first telephone. Practically all of these events have taken place in the last half century for most American communities. 

Their coming has transformed the problem of public administration from that of ministering to the meager wants of a rural eighteenth century society to that of satisfying the twentieth century urban dweller's insatiable appetite for ever-increasing services. The history of administrative organization from 

1850 onward has been characterized by an unplanned experimentation, almost a groping, which has sought to bridge this gap. 

At about the same time that the social and economic basis of government began to change, its political aspects were greatly altered by the popularizing forces of the Jeffersonian and Jacksonian movements. Those without property or income were allowed to vote and hold office. The tide of agrarian democracy created a host of elective administrative offices which were to be filled by popular vote for short terms and rotated among the populace. This would keep rascals from causing excessive damage by staying in too long, and it would give all a sporting chance at the blessings and emoluments of public office. Qualifications were a matter of minor importance, the processes of administration being deemed so simple that any ordinary citizen could master them without difficulty.

Ch. 2] 

The United States embraced extreme democratic ideas and practices just before government started to become increasingly intricate, with resulting friction at many points. The story of the capture of administration by venal political machines, "porkbarrel" politicians, and plundering Tweeds, together with the amateurish blundering of well-intentioned but unqualified officials, is familiar to students of government. Administrative services were added with no effort to correlate and co-ordinate each with the other or with some central official or agency, such as the governor or mayor. Many activities would be placed under independent boards with overlapping terms, subject to no administrative control other than the letter of the law contained in constitution, charter or statute. Some states had from one to two hundred of these independent administrative agencies. 

From the mid-century on, the cities experimented with various types of boards in an effort to discover some machinery that would harmonize the ills of a democracy with a new machine civilization.

While the offices of governor and mayor had been steadily gaining prestige and power, the effort to secure effective administration through centralizing administrative authority in those officials did not achieve momentum until the last decade of the nineteenth century. In 1899 the National Municipal League introduced its municipal program, sometimes referred to as the first model charter. While its recommendations covered a wide field of reform, most significant was the clause which boldly made the mayor the actual head of administration with power to appoint and control his subordinates. Referring to this program in 1908, Mr. Fairlie could say that "the legislation of the past ten years shows a distinct advance in the adoption of these principles." 2 The League transferred its advocacy successively to the commission and council-manager form of charter, each of which concentrates administrative authority in a

The philosophy of the reorganization movement was probably best crystallized in the reports of the New York Bureau of 

Municipal Research to the New York Constitutional Convention of 1915.

It conceived the governor as the central agency of administration, standing at the apex of a hierarchy over which he has broad powers of control. Although this constitution. was rejected at the polls, its basic ideas were carried into effect by constitutional amendment a decade later under Governor Smith. In 1917, under the influence of Governor Lowden, Illinois adopted an administrative code embodying thoroughgoing integration. From that time on the integration movement achieved a momentum which has brought much in the way of concrete adoptions, resulting in reorganization and consolidation in more than a score of states. At the same time the executive budget movement grew by leaps and bounds. More than four hundred cities came under the operation of council-manager government, and new charters in Detroit, San Francisco, Denver, Buffalo, New York, and numerous other cities concentrated more administrative authority in the hands of the mayor. This placing of power in the hands of a single executive officer is the outstanding tendency of contemporary administrative reform.

In practice these units are still largely under loose, disjointed, and uncorrelated administrative organization, with many elective officers who are independent of each other as well as of any central co-ordinating authority. It is extremely difficult to generalize by way of classifying existing organizations into categories. Nevertheless, it may be stated that there are five general types of organization into which most cities and states can be classified. These are: the weak executive type, the strong executive type, the no-executive type, the commission plan, and the council-manager plan. 

The Weak Executive Type 

The weak executive form of organization possesses a mayor or governor elected by the people for a term of two or four years, and with little actual summary control over the administrative agencies. These latter are largely independent of each other and of any one else. The only supervision over those who are elected consists of recall at the polls or judicial action, and neither of these controls are administrative. They are legal and political in nature. In those areas not permitting the recall, even the popular remedy must wait until the next election. To say that an administrative agency is responsible to the people is to utter a platitude. Furthermore, a chief executive will apply to the courts for writs to force officers into line only in extreme emergencies. Such action by the executive will frequently place himself on trial before public opinion more than those against whom the action is directed. The result is that those officers who are elected by the people often direct their efforts toward perpetuating their tenure rather than perfecting the processes of administration.

Where the governor or the mayor is given authority to appoint certain administrative officials, he must usually consult the senate or a council for approval. Most close students of administration regard this practice as vicious, because it forces the chief administrative officer to make compromise political appointments which often are much worse than those he would have made if such approval were not required. His power of

Ch. 2] 

controlling these appointees, from the administrative standpoint, is impaired because he does not have a free hand in directing their work, owing to fear of alienating their political friends and because the law makes removal difficult in a large number of jurisdictions.

The chief executive is deprived, of course, of any administrative supervision over those officers appointed by the legislature, of which there are many in the smaller cities operating under a mayor and council charter. Under this organization an outstanding personality can achieve a high degree of political and civic leadership, as did Governors Johnson, Hughes, and La Follette, and as did such mayors as Tom Johnson and Brand Whitlock. However, public management in the true sense is impossible under such arrangements. This is true because the

should not be undertaken at all. Administrative organization approaches chaos. There is no effective central planning and control of administration, and co-ordination is usually lacking. 

The legislative body is generally averse to changing this state of affairs because it is jealous of its own detailed control over administration, which it would inevitably have to relax or lose if the governor or mayor were made chief administrative officer in fact. The majority of American states and cities probably can be classified yet as belonging to this category, although the mayor and governor are gaining rapidly in strength, and practically one out of every five cities having populations over 10,000 has a city manager.

The Strong Executive Type 

Under the strong executive type, administrative authority is centralized in the hands of a political executive who appoints the heads of departments without council confirmation, and who may remove them without restrictions. Lines of authority run from the bottom upward and inward, converging in the hands of the mayor or governor. Activities are departmentalized on a uni-functional basis as nearly as possible. The administrative personnel becomes administratively responsible to the political executive who can be held politically responsible for his acts. 

More recent proposals have sought to interpose an appointive chief administrative officer between the mayor or governor and the department heads, after a principle similar to that exemplified by the British permanent undersecretaries, hoping thereby to minimize the evil effects of political changes. By combining power and responsibility in a single person responsible to the electorate, the strong executive organization aims to bring political leadership out in the open instead of leaving it in the hands

This type of administrative organization exists in theory in such cities as New York, Boston,¹¹ and Denver; and, with certain mitigations, in such recent charters as those of Buffalo and San Francisco. It has been embodied in recent years in varying degrees in the reorganizations of state governments in California, Illinois, New York, Ohio, Tennessee, Virginia, and others.12

The integration idea has probably received its most thoroughgoing trial in the four-hundred and some odd cities which have adopted the council-manager plan of municipal government. 

Because it involves a little different principle than the strong mayor form, it has been given separate treatment later in this chapter. 

The No-Executive Organization 

The types of administrative organization considered thus far have had some kind of executive or chief administrative officer, in one case with only nominal authority, and in the other with considerable actual directing power. However, most American counties, and a number of smaller cities, have no single executive authority with even nominal powers. Executive authority is divided between an elective board and a number of elective officers. In the smaller cities, as in California municipalities of the fifth and sixth class, the chairman of the elective board may be designated as mayor, but his administrative responsibilities. are no greater than those of his colleagues. The board divides. itself into committees on the chief functional divisions of administration, which, while having no more legal authority than ordinarily possessed by legislative committees, in practice exercise considerable control over administration. The elective officers derive their powers from statute or charter and, therefore, are not subject to any other administrative control.13

Commission Cities 

Coming into existence on the Galveston tidal wave of 1900, commission government enjoyed a great vogue and secured widespread adoption during the decade ending about 1915. It combined legislative and administrative functions into three, five, or seven elective commissioners who acted collectively as the city council and individually as heads of administrative departments. 

The initial popularity of the scheme was probably largely due to the fact that it was frequently adopted on the wave of a civic renaissance and attracted a high class citizenry to its support. 

The inherent weaknesses of the idea soon became apparent, however. In the first place, combining the political function with the direction of administration in the absence of a tradition

[Pt. I 

ORGANIZATION 

of permanent administration, proved an unhappy union in many instances. Administrative action, in its details, frequently became a matter of controversy before the commission, which in turn led to official animosities causing certain commissioners to combine in cliques against others. The result was that the supervising administrative personnel became composed of puppets who capitulated to the political exigencies of the commissioners. Further, as is usual under political control of administration, the fear of the man on the job of political removal created a certain formalism which deprived departments of that 

ELECTORATE COMMISSIONERS ACT COLLECTIVELY AS CITY COUNCIL ACT INDIVIDUALLY AS DEPARTMENT HEADS Figure 4. Commission Form of City Organization elasticity and freedom of action which is so vital to effective management. The meddling of political amateurs in the field of the technician led the latter to surrender his command and become an automaton who responds mechanically to the commissioner's will. Good administration cannot develop under such conditions.

In the second place, commission government did not bring the centralization of power and responsibility which it promised. 

Instead of the much needed executive budget, the sine qua non of effective administration, it offered the opportunity for legislative treasury raids free from administrative checks. Furthermore, five men can be as effective as a mob when it comes to agreeing on administrative policy. Political dickering led to agreements whereby one commissioner would agree to refrain

Ch. 2] 

from voting adversely on matters concerning the departments under another, for a reciprocal consideration. The result was lack of co-ordination and centralized planning. While this plan of municipal government is still working well in many small and medium sized cities, the crest of its wave of popularity passed almost twenty years ago.

Council-Manager Organization 

Approximately 425 American cities now operate under the council-manager plan of municipal government.¹ This most recent American contribution to the field of charter experi-

Its members must refrain from interfering in the realm of administration proper, leaving the manager a free hand in such "Nolting, Municipal Year Book, 1934, pp. 90, 93.

matters as the appointment of his subordinates, as well as that whole field commonly understood as belonging to management. 

Some charters even go so far as to prohibit councilmen from even suggesting prospective employees to the manager. A good city manager is supposed to resist all attempts of council members to interfere in the field of administration. He should resign rather than work under conditions which subject him to excessive councilmanic meddling in what is considered properly to be his own sphere.16 If the council is not pleased with the conduct of administration it should seek to correct the situation. without petty interference, and if this fails it can always bring about the removal or resignation of the manager. 

Because city managers are expected to be professional and experienced administrators, their selection is not confined to local candidates. Some of the newer charters are even going so far as to require that the manager shall have had experience as city manager or assistant manager. The objective is to secure the best qualified man available at the salary which can be paid, regardless of whether he lives in Maine or Florida, and irrespective of campaign contributions or party activity. Of course this admirable theory does not always work out in practice, for managers are frequently chosen on a basis having little to do with sheer merit. Nevertheless, much progress is being made in this direction." The city managers are gradually constituting themselves into the most professionally conscious group in the field of general administration. Indeed, the city manager movement offers more hope for the future of effective administration than any other phenomenon on the current American scene. 

Federal Administrative Organization 

National administration has always been much more integrated than that of states and cities by virtue of the fact that the principal officers have been largely subject to presidential 16 See discussion by leading managers in City Manager Yearbook, 1932, pp. 109-132.

While Congress has frequently sought to retain detailed control over the departments, and while early constitutional decisions tended toward a concept of executive power denying presidential supremacy in the field of administration,18 the President is nevertheless becoming in fact as well as in law the chief administrative officer of the United States. This tendency has been accelerated since the war by such events as the Budget and Accounting Act of 1921;19 the Myers decision (1926), which enables him to defy the Senate in removal;20 and recent Congressional delegation of carte blanche authority to reorganize specific administrative units." 21 The citizen is accustomed to regard national administration chiefly in terms of the cabinet, which is composed of the heads of the ten great departments nominated by the President and affirmed by the Senate. The administrative agencies under members of the cabinet are quite properly regarded as being under presidential administrative control or direction. To recapitulate, the administrative services of the national government may be divided into five different categories: (1) the departments over which the President has considerable administrative control because of being placed in charge of their functions by the Constitution, that is, the Departments of State, Navy, and War; (2) the other departments, over which Congress has at one time or another exercised considerable control, but which are now thoroughly under presidential direction by virtue of statutes, judicial decisions, and the accumulation of practice and tradition; (3) agencies under the President's direct control but not represented in the cabinet, such as, the Veterans' Administration; (4) independent agencies such as the Interstate 

Commerce Commission; and (5) several agencies predominantly administered by Congress, such as the Government 

Printing Office. 

A distinction is made between the executive and administrative powers of the President. When he is seeing that the laws are enforced he is acting as an executive, but when he is directing the actual fulfillment of that for which the law calls he is performing an administrative act. Thus the executive function is said to be essentially political, having to do with the formulation of policies, while the administrative function is concerned with putting these policies into effect.23 In American public law administrative authority has its source in the legislature and not in the chief executive. Congress has set up administrative agencies directly responsible to itself and not to the President. 

However, Congress cannot deprive the President of the power to direct such agencies by virtue of his constitutional power "to take care that the laws be faithfully executed." The federal 

22 A chart of the federal administrative structure as of December 1, 1930, is contained in Beard, American Government and Politics (6th ed.), p. 212. 

23 W. F. Willoughby, An Introduction to the Study of the Government of 

Modern States (The Century Co., 1919), pp. 231–232; Willoughby, Principles of Public Administration, pp. 9–51.

Ch. 2] 4I 

courts have held that the Congress could give the power of appointment of postmasters to the Postmaster-General, and that the President, while having the power to see that the Postmaster- General obeyed the laws and performed the duties prescribed by law, could not direct how he was to perform the acts so prescribed. 24

The distinction between his executive and administrative power is amply demonstrated by the situation relative to appointments and removals. The Constitution states that the President shall appoint specified officers with the advice and consent of the Senate, but that Congress may provide that "inferior officers" may be appointed by the President alone, by the courts of law, or by heads of departments. It has never been exactly determined just what constitutes inferior officers, but theoretically Congress could provide for the means of appointing a larger part of the administration by agencies other than the President. It could further provide that these officers report directly to Congress, in which case the President would have executive power over them, but not administrative power. In practice, however, Congress has delegated to the President the power to appoint all important administrative officers, and the courts have held that the power to remove all such officers is incidental to the power to appoint.25 Thus, while the distinction between executive and administrative "power" is becoming less apparent, there may continue to exist a distinction between executive and administrative "functions" for some time to come.

The liberal interpretation of the removal power has given the President so much authority to direct the methods of administrative operation, if he so chooses, that he is the chief administrative officer in fact. His own personal inclination and the limitations of physical capacity may, however, tend toward his exercising only the executive function and leaving the administrative function to others. Our administrative establishment has never been sufficiently co-ordinated so that one could desig-

The President has always been acknowledged to possess control over the Departments of State, War, and Navy, which have at times been referred to as "Presidential Departments." The reason for this is that the President is specifically charged in the Constitution with the executive functions pertaining to these departments, which makes him Commander-in-Chief of the Army and Navy and gives him the power to negotiate treaties and appoint ambassadors, other public ministers, and consuls.26 

On the other hand, the enumerated powers granted by the Constitution to the national government were specifically given to Congress,27 and that body has continued to retain in theory, and largely in fact, the administrative control that goes with such a grant of authority. In spite of this fact, however, the President has acquired by statute and usage an increasing administrative importance. This was accelerated by the Myers decision which seemed to give him an unfettered removal power. 

The more recent Humphrey case seems to limit such removal power as applied to certain independent agencies.28

While the ten great departments have been organized on the hierarchical basis into bureaus and divisions with lines of authority converging in the President, functions and activities have not been departmentalized on any very rational basis. Mr.

House Committee on Expenditures in the Executive Departments has been actively interested in reorganization, and has held hearings on and sponsored several bills to this end. Those which have been enacted into law include the transfer of prohibition from the Treasury to the Department of Justice, and the concentration of veterans' activities in the new Veteran's Administration. Early in 1932 the committee held hearings on proposals to reorganize the civil service and public works activities. During the same year the President requested authority to effect, through administrative orders, economies designed to balance the budget. An outline of proposals indicated a plan of reorganization based on principles quite in line with the major premises set forth in the following chapters. 

There will be a natural curiosity to know what has happened to federal administrative organization under President Franklin 

D. Roosevelt's "New Deal" program. On March 3, 1933,

The most significant development from the standpoint of management has not been brought to common notice, however. 

This is the integration of control of departmental expenditure in agencies directly responsible to the President. The spending agencies are held down to monthly allotments approved by the Director of the Budget. Through a central system of budgetary accounts kept in the Treasury Department, the Director of the Budget is able to maintain a check on expenditure by means of reports made by the spending agencies four times per month. All governmental purchasing and stores are under the newly created Director of Procurement in the Treasury Department. All disbursing officers are now controlled by a Chief 

Disbursing Officer, also in the Treasury Department.32 If these developments are pursued properly they can form the basis for making the President more nearly a normal chief administrator than he has yet achieved. Discussion thus far has been directed entirely to the normal rather than emergency or recovery administrative services. 

The National Industrial Recovery Act of June 16, 1933, gave the President widespread discretionary powers to set up new administrative services, and to use existing officers and agencies to accomplish the purposes of the statute.33 Owing to the fact that these administrative agencies are undergoing more or less constant change it is not profitable to deal with them further than to note their relation to the ordinary or normal structure. 

While the Adminstrator for Industrial Recovery is administratively responsible directly to the President, the recovery program is co-ordinated with a number of the normal administrative services. The various boards connected with the NRA have several cabinet and other officials serving both as chairmen and as members. The Secretary of the Interior is the actual admin-

Thus, while there have been many additions to the category of so-called independent federal agencies, the general effect has been decidedly in the direction of concentrating administrative authority in the hands of the President. Admitting that this augmented presidential authority may be partially transitory in the person of Franklin D. Roosevelt, the net result of the statutory enactments must, nevertheless, leave some larger residue of power in the hands of any future chief executive. The integration of expenditure control alone is so thoroughly a common sense move that its effects are bound to be noticeable for decades to come.

Government-Owned Corporations 

One of the noteworthy features of the New Deal is the increased utilization of government corporations in the various recovery projects. There is nothing new in the use of such corporations as agencies for carrying on a governmental or public purpose. The East India Company, while owned and controlled by private shareholders, was largely a public and governmental instrumentality in practice. The same may be said of the Hudson Bay Company, which for many years exercised governmental powers over Arctic America. Beginning during the World War, the United States has experimented with a corporate entity that is owned and controlled entirely by the government. For purposes of illustration, the organization, purposes, and activities of the United States Shipping Board 

Emergency Fleet Corporation will be described. 

An act of 1916 created the United States Shipping Board, "A list of the recovery agencies with the participating officials is contained in Congressional Directory, 73d Congress, 2d Session, beginning January 3, 1934 (Government Printing Office, 1933), pp. 363-373. Office, 1935).

primarily for the purpose of stimulating American shipbuilding as well as to meet the shipping shortage emergency of the war. After the declaration of war in 1917, the Board organ ized the United States Shipping Board Emergency Fleet Cor poration with a capital of fifty million dollars and incorporated it in the District of Columbia. In pursuance of emergency war powers, it proceeded to build billions of dollars worth of ships, the total cost of which was seven times that of the Panama Canal. The corporation was headed by a board of trustees identical in membership with the shipping board, and Mr. 

Edward N. Hurley was both president of the board of trustees and chairman of the shipping board. The latter agency held and voted the stock of the corporation. This was the first time that the national government had ever delegated a great business enterprise to a corporation. It established an operating division which managed the actual shipment process. This activity was continued after the war when the corporation found itself the possessor of surplus shipping capacity. About 1925 it began a policy of liquidating its operating facilities to private concerns.  Federal Surplus Relief Corporation. The Reconstruction 

Finance Corporation is managed by a board of directors consisting of the Secretary of the Treasury and six others appointed by the President, not more than four of whom are members of the same political party. It was incorporated by direct act of Congress which has altered and extended its powers from time to time. It loans upon security to banks, insurance companies, governmental agencies, and federal relief units. It has the power to borrow on its own notes and debentures, but so far all of its offerings have been taken by the Treasury Department. Its object was to aid financial recovery by supplying cash to liquidate frozen assets in private hands, loans to governmental units for public works and to finance relief projects. 

The Tennessee Valley Authority is a non-stock corporation under a board of three directors appointed by the President. 

It has all of the ordinary powers of a corporation. Its funds are supplied by congressional appropriation, and it has a limited bonding authority. It has taken over the Muscle Shoals property and has undertaken a vast project of industrial and economic transformation. The Federal Housing Corporation was incorporated under the laws of Delaware by Harold L. Ickes, Frances Perkins, and Robert D. Kohn (Director of the Housing Division of the Public Works Administration), acting as indi viduals instead of in their official capacities. Each holds one share of stock of no par value in trust for the United States. 

The stock cannot be transferred except to some one authorized by the President, the Administrator of Public Works, or some other designated official. The corporation receives its funds from the RFC and PWA. It was incorporated under the laws of Delaware rather than under the laws of the District of Columbia because broader powers are permissible under the former than under the latter.

What are the advantages of carrying on these federal projects by corporations instead of under the ordinary bureau or departmental type of organization? In the first place, there is greater freedom from congressional politics. There is also greater flexibility in administrative matters. Each corporation has its own accounting, personnel, and control agencies, being largely

[Pt. I 

ORGANIZATION 

free from the housekeeping control of the general government.37 

Thus the corporate form of organization provides means of cutting through red tape and getting around legal restrictions that might tend to interfere with action. It is sometimes said that it will permit a management environment more nearly approximating that of private operations than ordinary governmental organization.38 But most important of all, it provides a vehicle for speedy and effective action in the face of emergency, a means of getting things done. As such the governmentowned corporation is probably here to stay, a major development of permanent significance in the field of public administration.39

CHAPTER III  

The controversy over the importance of organization structure is unending. One side claims that high-class personnel will overcome structural defects, the other that good men will be thwarted in their best efforts by faulty organization. Experience in the public field tends decidedly to confirm the latter viewpoint. There is no question but that a high-class chief administrative officer generously endowed with diplomatic traits can do much to secure adequate standards of operation in those administrative agencies which the charter has removed from his control. On the other hand, case after case can be cited where independent administrative officers have seriously embarrassed governors, mayors, and managers, to the detriment of effective operation. Frequently they have done this for no reason other than the furthering of their own selfish interests. 

Even a casual contact with such situations must convince the careful student that organization structure is of prime impor- Granting that exceptional executives can secure results under adverse conditions, there is still the consideration that they must do so through indirect methods which consume time and energy better spent elsewhere. A realistic approach must force the conclusion, moreover, that administrators will rarely be supermen. Hence, organization must be geared, not to the exceptional manager, but to ability which may at times descend toward the mediocre. Such being the case, no structural aids to good management should be overlooked.

It should not be concluded from the foregoing that organization is a fetish to be worshipped for its own sake, for quite the contrary is the case. Just as belittling the importance of structure may hinder administrative achievement, so may blind obeisance to the letter of the model organization chart fail to take cognizance of unusual situations. Organization should 50

Ch. 51 

1 be constantly evolving, making salutary changes. The transfer of an unusually large number of activities to a strong department head might justifiably violate the dictates of proper functionalization. Hence, the conclusions of the following pages relative to organization practice are not inviolable dogmas, nor are they superficial generalizations to be disregarded with impunity. They constitute guides whose judicious observance will materially aid in attaining a high order of administrative accomplishment. 

Figure 6. A Hierarchy 

The predominant trend in organization is toward greater integration-the arrangement of lines of authority so that they converge in some single individual or agency responsible for all administrative activity. This is variously known as the hierarchical or strong executive type, shown in its pure line form in Figure 6. Fixed and definite lines of responsibility place definite authority in the hands of the president, governor, mayor, or manager. Underneath and directly responsible to him are department heads, who in turn act through bureau chiefs to whom the heads of divisions are accountable. These direct lines of authority descend indefinitely to superintendents, super-

The organization chart resembles a pyramid with the chief administrative officer at the apex and the most remote subordinates at the base.

It has been customary to say that activities should be distributed among departments on the basis of general purpose or functions. This means that all police activities rightfully belong in the police department, all the fire activities in the fire department, and all finance activities in the department of finance. This functionalization may be carried to an absurd extreme, however. Recent trends in industry tend to make each departmental unit as nearly a complete and self-contained organization as practical considerations of cost allow.5 Hence, it may not be advisable to create separate departments which have charge of all statistics, all drafting, and all typing. A department head who is rendering services directly to the public should not, as a general rule, be deprived of the control of services that are essential to the complete and effective execution of the main object or purpose. But those departmental services which are common to all branches, such as accounting, stores, and personnel, may and should be supervised by some central agency. Another exception to the pure functionalization principle may be made where groups having similar community objectives differ vastly in their techniques, sources of knowledge, or professional background. For instance, it has recently been suggested that the general purpose of a police department is so A. E. Buck, Administrative Consolidation in State Governments (National

The engineering aspects of traffic control might very well be placed elsewhere than in the police department. In other words, departmentalization by function can never be accomplished with the precision of the slide rule. This does not mean, however, that there is justification in so many exceptions as to vitiate all semblance of functionalization. 

Staff and Line

The idea of a staff organization is said to have originated in the old Prussian army. Staff officers were relieved of command of troops and assigned to the making of war plans, including the whole range of military activities from the details of equipment to formulating campaign action years in advance of hostilities. The distinguishing feature of the pure staff officer was that he could not issue orders. He could merely make recommendations to those in command, namely, the line officers, whose order was necessary in making staff findings effective. The tendency in the United States is to use the term "staff" with a somewhat different connotation than the Prussians gave to it. There are few agencies, either in business or government, which are pure staff. There are many which are predominantly staff but which have certain control authority necessitating the issuance of orders or commands. Thus, the 

Federal Bureau of the Budget acts normally in an advisory capacity to the President, but it does possess certain control over the monthly apportionments of the spending agencies. One of the truest examples of a pure staff agency in government is the Bureau of Budget and Efficiency of the City of Los Angeles,¹ which has no legal authority to issue binding orders.¹¹ 10 American business practice tends toward separating activities and functions, rather than positions or agencies on the basis

Thus, every line officer is said to be part staff, and there is no pure line or pure staff officer except the president at the top, who is pure line.12 Frequently the central control offices, such as the purchasing agent, comptroller, and treasurer, are referred to as staff agencies. There is no question but that one of their major functions is the furnishing of information and advice to the chief administrative officer, yet their essential purpose is so a matter of control that it is questionable practice to refer to them as staff agencies. Mr. Willoughby's terminology, "bureaus of general administration," is much happier, especially in view of the fact that they are endowed with considerable power to issue orders binding on the departments. 

Figure 7. Line Type of Organization 

Both thought and action on this subject will be much more clear-cut in nature if one bears in mind that a staff activity is merely inquisitive and advisory in nature, while a line activity is one of action and command. Further, in practice it is unusual to find any given officer or bureau that is pure line or pure staff, although a distinction can generally be made upon the ground that this agency is essentially staff and that essentially line. 

It is customary to distinguish between the pure line, the pure staff, and the line and staff organization.13 The distinctive characteristic of the line type of control lies in the fact that authority may be traced in an unbroken channel from the chief administrative officer direct to the most remote subordinate. 

This type of organization is well suited to small units where

quick changes in command may be necessary. As the organization grows larger, however, certain defects show up. The chief administrative officer, who has to know everything and direct everything, is so burdened with routine operations that he is unable to spend time on planning. Co-ordination becomes more difficult because the burden rests on one man. 

It is rarely possible to secure executives with wide enough experience and sufficient general ability to cover all of the requirements, with the result that hasty decisions and snap judgments become the rule.¹ The chief is frequently a self-styled "man of action" with scant regard for thought processes. The result is that "rule-of-thumb" predominates. Sooner or later there will occur friction and difficulty which could have been avoided by earlier introduction of the staff element.

Staff and Line Organization 

The staff and line organization, as the name implies, sets up two types of subdivisions, the functions of one of which is essentially staff, the other essentially line. The former has only advisory authority, while the latter has the power of order and command applied directly toward the consummation of the job which the agency as a whole is designed to accomplish. 

From the chart in Figure 8 it will be seen that there are no channels of authority running directly from the staff agencies to the line. All staff determinations must go back to the chief administrative officer who gives them force through his orders to the line. Sometimes the staff is so thoroughly in the confidence of the management that its determinations become law for the organization with only his nominal approval. In such cases the staff agency comes very close to becoming actually line, although the relationship is still potentially staff. Authority to act has, in effect, been delegated to the staff. 

The chief administrative officer need not be the only official to have staff agencies. There is no reason why department heads, and if the organization is large enough, bureau chiefs, should not have their staff. Thus each line executive is freed

Various considerations are urged in favor of this type of organization. In the first place, it has been said that the man on the job, including those in command, become obsessed with their routine. It becomes such a part of them that in time they refuse to question it, innovations are anathema, and suggestions for changes leading to improvement are resented.

Central Control Agencies 

15 It has already been indicated that agencies with exclusively staff functions are comparatively rare in American governmental practice. Much more important are certain central agencies with mixed line and staff functions which have a considerable power of control over all departments. They combine research, planning, control, and service. Thus, the auditor of 

Los Angeles County carries on considerable research and planning in the field of cost accounting; controls the accounting and pre-audits the expenditure of all departments; and furnishes various reporting services to both the public and administrative units. Many private organizations, as well as governmental units, are centralizing the control of automotive transportation in a general control agency. Central control is based upon the premise that there are two types of departmental activities: one group which is common to all departments, and one which is distinctive to a particular department. 

Mr. Willoughby has struck upon happy terminology in describing the two general categories of activities engaged in by all departments.16 Each administrative unit must do just so much housekeeping, the conduct of which is not dependent upon the specialized technology or professional background of individual organization units. The police department must have the floors scrubbed, but it is not necessary that policemen do it;

the health department must maintain accounting records, but a doctor is not required for the task; the county home needs potatoes, but a central purchasing agency can procure them cheaper than could the cook. These activities common to all departments are known as institutional or housekeeping activities, and are commonly subjected to a considerable degree of central control and supervision. 

Functional activities, on the other hand, are those based primarily on the specialized technology and professional background peculiar to a given organization unit. Examples would be finger-printing in the police department, clinical service in the health department, the preparation of legal briefs by the city attorney, and street repair in the department of public works. 

Functional activities, because of their specialized nature, are commonly subjected to less central control and supervision than housekeeping or institutional activities. 

The most familiar type of central control agency is concerned with financial administration. The comptroller supervises departmental accounts and pre-audits departmental purchase orders. The treasurer supervises departmental receipts of money and pays for departmental expenditures. The purchasing agent procures equipment and supplies, and operates a store for all departments. The personnel director certifies eligible lists and checks payrolls for each organization unit. Generally, these officers are independent of each other, but the tendency is toward uniting them in a department of finance or a bureau of administration. The excessive cost of automotive transportation is leading cities to place the preponderance of equipment under a central bureau either for operation or control, and sometimes for both.17 Janitor and custodian service is frequently in the hands of a central officer in order to have unified control over the maintenance of buildings and grounds. 

In America some tendencies are at work toward calling these central control units staff agencies. While they do not, at least in theory, conform to the original concept of staff func- 17
