There is no particular evil in calling a comptroller or a purchasing agent a staff officer. Indeed, valid theoretical considerations may be advanced in favor of just such nomenclature on the ground that the coercive authority which they exercise is a delegated authority, and that their every act is merely advisory in nature. It may be said that originally the purchasing agent was to make recommendations to his line chief, who made the actual purchases. However, as the line chief became absorbed in other duties, and as he gained confidence in his staff officers, he delegated authority to the purchasing agent to place orders direct. Whether this theoretical justification be needed or not, the fact remains that the duties of the financial officers are so largely in an advisory capacity to line administrators that we are not minded to oppose their designation as staff, if professional practice continues to develop in that direction. 

The current trend is in favor of placing the staff and control officers in a single unit to be known variously as the Bureau of 

General Administration,18 Bureau of General Fiscal Adminis tration, or Department of Finance. This agency would be directly under the chief administrative officer, under whose direction it would supervise and control the housekeeping activities in each department. For this purpose it would have contact with another bureau of administration in each department. 

The members of this latter unit would be directly responsible to their department head and would be integral parts of their respective departments, but they would be subject to the supervision and control of the central bureau of administration in many important respects. (See Figure 9.)

Central control agencies prevent extravagance and waste by eliminating overlapping departmental personnel. One instance is central purchasing, which is cheaper than departmental purchasing. They permit departments to devote their major attention to those purposes for which they were organized by placing control of routine housekeeping tasks in the hands of other agencies. does a fairly good job. Many departments will feel that they can do better recruiting for themselves than a personnel agency can do for them. Others will desire to carry on their own purchasing, and still others will resent the fact that central preaudit prevents them from making certain purchases even though a deficit would be created thereby. These, and countless other irritations arising from outside invasion of what departments regard matters for their own determination, give rise to considerable resentment at times. This is probably inevitable. 

Nevertheless, the advantages of central control of housekeeping activities are so great that departmental self-assertion must give way to the general good.

It has been contended that integration, with housekeeping activities under a central control agency, will tend to weaken. departmental responsibility and initiative. The question of devolving responsibility is tied up too closely with the personal characteristics of individual administrators to permit of effective generalization. Some chief administrative officers will achieve their utmost effectiveness by holding a tight rein over departmental details, while others will devolve a great deal of authority upon their subordinates. The better city managers seem inclined toward the view that they should protect themselves against dealing with any problem that can be solved or decided upon within the departments.19 Experience has shown that some department heads can be trusted with authority more than others, and devolution will come naturally to the former. Central control will not hinder such devolution. It should actually aid it by establishing standards of performance which improve the service. The effectiveness of the health service is not injured by requiring the sanitary inspectors to keep their cars overnight in the city hall garage instead of taking the family riding at public expense. The effectiveness of the service is not impaired by having all departments procure typewriter ribbons through the central purchasing agent at a saving of 30 per

Is Integration Advisable? 

This chapter has thus far attempted to describe the main thesis of the advocates of integration. This is understood to include hierarchical lines of authority, functional distribution. of activities among a small number of departments, distinction between staff and line activities, and central control of housekeeping services. While the general tenor of these pages has revealed the author's leaning toward the integrated plan of organization, it would be only fair to state that there is far from unanimity on this point.20 Integration is generally favored by teachers of political science, professional administrators, and the members of governmental research agencies. On the other hand, it is opposed by professionals in the field of public welfare, public education, and large elements of the lay citizenry. 

The advocates and opponents of integration are trying to reach the same ends, but, owing to opposite approaches and fundamental misunderstanding, they work at cross purposes. 

Both fear the crooked machine politician, and each has a means of eliminating him which is the antithesis of the other's proposal. The one wants to bring political leadership out into the open where it can be called to account for its misdeeds by combining power with responsibility. The political scientist is, by and large, convinced that "invisible government" by bosses and 20 "Authoritative control from above has much to recommend it in business, in terms of dollars and cents. It is by no means so certain that concentrated power, on the state level, of such governmental functions as highway administration and the management of schools would yield the same good results.

CHAPTER IV  

The layman in government has been disposed to solve an annoying administrative problem by placing it under a board or commission. The professional element in the public service, on the other hand, has become increasingly distrustful of the wholesale use of these plural-headed administrative units. The following pages will attempt to lay down principles which will aid in determining whether a given activity should be placed under a board or single head. While certain authorities recognize a distinction between a board and a commission, the difference is not essential to our discussion. The terms will be used here interchangeably as being synonymous. 

The Pro and Con of Boards 

It is said that boards give an opportunity for administration to secure the advice and services of the best lay competence in the community at little or no cost to the taxpayer. This tends to promote intelligent citizen co-operation and develop a sense of civic responsibility by enabling wider citizen participation in government. By providing that board terms shall overlap, that the terms of members shall expire at different times, a holdover of personnel will work toward a continuity of policy at times when political change is in the air. Boards have grown up in welfare and educational activity in response to demands that these activities be freed from the political taint of the general government, and in many instances the disinclination of city councils to give these agencies what they considered adequate financial support has led to giving them their own taxing power. 

It is furthermore maintained that commissions offer an opportunity for representing differing phases of opinion in the community, such as nationality and religious groups on a school 66

Ch. 4] 

board. Underneath citizen reliance on boards and commissions is that intangible but omnipresent American distrust of one-man authority, the feeling that several citizens will be less corruptible and less inclined to be arbitrary and officious than the single head. 

Students of political science and large numbers of professional administrators have come to realize that board administration in practice has fallen far short of fulfilling these lofty objectives. The most potent cause of this failure is that board organization defies at the outset that fundamental basis of good government—the distinction between politics and administration. Into those departments whose work is almost entirely technical and routine, is injected the lay and amateur element in the form of board members. In Great Britain, where administration is supervised by committees of the city council, this has caused no great difficulty because the layman has not seen fit to hamper the professional through petty interference in administrative matters. In the United States, however, the ordinary board appointee regards it as his prerogative and duty to control the minute details of administrative routine.¹ He frequently regards himself as so competent to do so that he resents well-intentioned advice on the part of members of the technical staff whose professional qualifications and experience are beyond question. This leads to demoralization of the staff through fear of the politically minded board member, and it makes the directing personnel mere sycophantic automatons, or errand boys, to the board.

Occasionally, an exceptional department manager or director will be endowed with such a keen insight into human nature that he will be able to "handle" his board, that is, keep it in its proper sphere without letting the members become conscious of it. This need not come about as the result of any sinister design or calculated plotting. It is simply the desirable and natural outcome where a confident and competent administrator has a board which respects him and is willing to be led by his tactful suggestions. Under these conditions, board administra-

tion will work without appreciable friction, but in the United States neither board nor technical directorship has commanded the quality of personnel essential to achieve this relationship. 

Thus, the ideal of the highly competent leading citizen giving generously of his time to his city or state with only nominal compensation has proved largely a phantom in practice. Without denying scattered exceptions, it would be quite within the facts to state that the personnel on boards and commissions has been, in many cases, rather mediocre if not actually inferior. 

In making these appointments, governors and mayors have been concerned with either repaying political debts or in securing "safe" individuals who could be controlled. They are seldom skilled in the technical background of the function of which the board is in charge. Mr. Willoughby is of the opinion that the commission system has worked out much better for national administration than for the states and cities.2 

The board system aggravates the disintegration and lack of responsible directorship which is so characteristic of our state and local administration. If anything goes wrong, it is impossible to fix responsibility. Action is slowed down, and proper decisions are delayed or vitiated by compromise. In many cases the technical director is made to understand that desired changes are not to be attempted because of the peculiar interest of certain board members. Subordinates curry favor with commissioners in order to thwart the manager's worthy efforts to improve administration. Plural leadership makes for inaction, dissension, lack of teamwork, and lack of control in general. The governor or mayor is unable to maintain the executive control over administration which the electorate expects of him, because his political future depends on the proper manipulation of commission personnel. Even though he may sincerely desire to obey all of the dictates of sound administrative practice, he is frequently thwarted at the outset by having to deal with politically-minded boards. 

2 W. F. Willoughby, Principles of Public Administration (Johns Hopkins 

Press, 1927), pp. 123-127. See R. B. Fosdick, American Police Systems (Century Co., 1920), pp. 103-107; and W. E. Mosher and F. G. Crawford, Public Utility Regulation (Harper & Bros., 1933), pp. 54–66.

 Proper Use of Boards 

The foregoing paragraphs perhaps lead the reader to wonder whether there is ever any justification for the use of boards, and the answer is that they do have their proper place. Where the administrative activity gives rise to seemingly irreconcilable differences of opinion in the community, it may be desirable to permit opposing groups to sit on a board to satisfy the wish to protect their interests. School boards often answer this purpose in communities where racial, religious, and nationality interests are accentuated. In discussing which commissions should be retained and which abolished in the City of Los Angeles, the author has expressed the opinion that the water and power commission should be retained as long as municipal ownership is a political issue. The board is needed to settle policy matters concerning the expansion of the power facilities around which all of the controversy centers. If the question at issue were only the management of the water system, a single general manager under the mayor would be practicable and desirable. This justification for boards should not be carried too far, however, for it is possible to rationalize one's self into a state of mind which recognizes a controversial issue in almost any administrative activity.

Boards are considered to be desirable, at least at times, in those administrative activities where the technology or techniques are not sufficiently settled to be generally accepted by the lay public. Again the example is the school board, one of the functions of which is to act as a brake on the enthusiasm of professional educators for innovations on which the school patrons, whether rightfully or wrongfully, are unwilling to place their stamp of approval. This interference of the laity may be justified on the grounds that the schools are conspicuously connected with American family life, yet it is not unthinkable that the educational technique of the future will so win public approval as to eliminate the board entirely. This exceptional justification for a board should not be used to sanction their wholesale introduction into fields where they are not desirable.

[Pt. I 

ORGANIZATION 

It is quite generally agreed that boards may be used in those administrative activities requiring deliberation and the determination of policy. This is very closely associated with the justification, above, where there is a seemingly irreconcilable difference of opinion in the community, yet there are many boards which deliberate on matters not the basis of violent community controversy. Such is the case normally with a civil service. commission hearing appeals of dismissed employees; the California State Board of Control in making rules for the settlement of claims against the state; and the Federal Board of Tax 

Appeals in reviewing Treasury decisions on revenue matters. 

In these cases the boards are acting in either a quasi-legislative capacity, meaning that they are making rules of a combined legislative and administrative nature; or in a quasi-judicial capacity, meaning that they are acting much the same as a court of law in pronouncing a decision in a controversy involving administrative officials themselves, or between them and citizens. While practice favors giving such power to a board, there the countless examples of single officials exercising quasilegislative and quasi-judicial authority with seeming satisfaction to those affected.

The opinion is fast becoming unanimous that board control is ill-fitted for those branches of the service demanding quick decisions and immediate action, where delay or deliberation would seriously impair the possibility of effective operation. 

Fire and police administration falls into this category, as does public health. While the American Public Health Association still recommends a board of health, there is a tendency to relieve it of administrative powers in the larger cities. Mr. McCombs of the National Institute of Public Administration, on the other hand, favors the entire abolition of the board. He cites the 

Iowa case where the clerk of the board called up the members individually to secure authority to establish a quarantine, the Supreme Court later invalidating a quarantine effected under such procedure. Mr. McCombs states that emergencies "are The nature of quasi-legislative and quasi-judicial power is treated much more in detail in a later chapter. 

I. V. Hiscock (Ed.), Community Health Organization (The Common wealth Fund, New York, 1932), pp. 27–31.

Ch. 4] 

995 constantly arising in public health service, which if met adequately, must be met immediately. It is well-nigh impossible for a board of health to foresee all of these emergency situations or always to be promptly available to take formal action when emergencies arise. Los Angeles County has a single health officer instead of a board of health. Health administration of some of the smaller cities there is performed by the county on contract. In 1930 and 1931, two of these municipalities received national first awards in their class.

Boards tend to become less necessary in those fields where technology and procedure have become well developed and accepted by the public. The board of health constitutes an excellent example. Fifty years ago public health procedure was not a matter of well-settled agreement, so it was thought advisable to have a meeting of the best minds in the community to deliberate and devise the best known means of combating disease. Today, however, public health technique is so well developed, and has won such popular approval, that the board can very well be eliminated. Fire departments also have a well-settled technology, which is the primary reason for their being comparatively free from politics. The National Board of Fire Underwriters forces cities to adopt its ideas of what constitutes the best mode of fire fighting and fire prevention, the penalty for failure to do so being higher insurance rates. 

It can be stated with a fair degree of accuracy that, as technology and technique become more highly developed in a given field, politics tends to disappear; hence, the need for the board diminishes at the same time.

The single head is necessary in those activities which require discipline of a semi-military type. Included in this group, perhaps, would be police, fire, prison administration, highway patrol, and all peace officer activity. Here effectiveness is dependent on firm, decisive, and unified command. The hesitance, "buck-passing," and delay so frequently present under board control tends toward demoralization which undermines morale.

If the captain of a police district knows that the chief is merely a figurehead, and that real power lies in the hands of the chairman of the police commission, who is the lodge brother and lifelong friend of the captain, is it not quite possible that the chief's control at that district might become considerably undermined?

Those activities which consist almost entirely of routine and which involve the exercise of practically no discretion, should be headed by a single officer. Examples are the office of county recorder, the city clerk, and the custodian of public grounds and buildings. Here a board would be mere extra baggage, an encumbrance, as it so often proves in practice.

Types of Boards or Commissions The Administrative Board 

The administrative board is the department head for an organization unit of a government. While examples are to be found practically all over the United States, one of the best illustrations of their use is presented by the Los Angeles city charter where each of the principal departments is headed by a commission composed of five citizens, the term of one of which ends each year. In spite of the fact that a general manager stands between the commission and the rest of the staff, the charter specifically provides that the use of the term “department head" shall be interpreted as meaning the commission

Ch. 4] 

where such an agency exists. Members of the commission are appointed by the mayor with the affirmation of the council, and the consent of the latter body must likewise be secured for removal by the mayor. Students and a growing number of administrators and lay observers feel that the functioning of these commissions has produced working examples of the objections to boards outlined in the forepart of this chapter.7 

The Regulative Commission 

The regulative commissions, while not entirely innovations of the last quarter-century, have nevertheless come into widespread use during that period in answer to the need for some means of attempting to correct economic and social abuses growing out of the industrial revolution, urban life and the machine age. They are endowed by constitution and statute with authority to regulate private persons and property in the interest of the general well-being, and are given quasi-judicial and quasilegislative functions thought to be necessary to achieve that objective. Familiar examples are state public utilities commissions, industrial accident boards, the Interstate Commerce Commission, the Federal Trade Commission, and the Federal Communications Commission. Because their work is largely deliberative involving the use of judgment based on discretion, the board type of organization is thought to be justified. The system of overlapping terms is designed to secure a continuity of policy and independence of action not obtainable through single individuals placed in the departmental hierarchy. The regulative commission has its proper place and seems destined to become a more important governmental organ if the regulative functions of government continue to expand at the present ratio.

Boards Tied in to Hierarchy 

In reorganization schemes it was frequently found advisable, if not politic, to retain administrative commissions, but to tie 'As a matter of fact, almost a whole paragraph on this subject has been taken from an unpublished manuscript by a well-known city official whose name is not mentioned for reasons of policy.

them into the hierarchical administrative structure with greatly reduced powers, usually entirely quasi-judicial and quasi-legislative in nature. In these cases, administration was placed in the hands of an officer located directly in the responsible hierarchy and not responsible to the board. Two excellent examples are supplied by the State Department of Finance in California.

The Act of 1929 created, under the director of finance, a division of organization and personnel to which it transferred the administrative functions formerly exercised by the civil service commission. This left the latter with very much impaired authority, apparently almost entirely quasi-judicial in nature. 

A similar change was made in Wisconsin the same year." In fact, one may venture that the civil service commission, if not doomed, is at least destined to lose its administrative functions to agencies responsible to the chief administrative officer. The 

California Department of Finance took over most of the administrative functions of the Board of Control which was retained for the sole purpose of making rules for allowing claims against the state and hearing appeals from administrative decisions arising under such rules. This use of a board for quasijudicial and quasi-legislative matters, administration remaining within the hierarchy, is legitimate and frequently desirable. 

Frequently, moreover, it constitutes a sop to the die-hard advocates of board administration. It has been suggested that these boards be called "administrative courts."

Permanent Advisory Boards 

Recent council-manager charters have frequently provided that the manager may at his discretion appoint advisory boards composed of citizens to confer and give advice relative to the activities of specific administrative departments. The American lay citizen has not been content to serve on a government commission without attempting to take hold of the levers and manipulate the entire machine. In the course of a recent inquiry among California city managers, the writer found that practically none had made use of the permanent advisory committee even in those cases where the charter specifically permitted their appointment. With some exceptions, the feeling seemed to be that such committees would "cause complications," tend "to assume powers and prerogatives not vested in them by legal enactment," and slow up business through added machinery. 

Practically every manager, however, expressed confidence in, and told of, satisfactory experience with temporary citizen advisory groups organized to study a specific problem, bring in a report, and disband after its purpose had been accomplished. 

The foregoing should not be interpreted to discourage any projected use of advisory boards. It merely seeks to advise caution with them until we can witness the record of greater experimentation. In the meantime, some agreement should be reached as to just what limitations should be placed on the meaning of the term "advisory," for some recent usage tends to confuse advisory boards with those exercising quasi-judicial and quasi-legislative powers, described immediately above.13 There is strong reason to believe that the term does not justify such a connotation, and that further confusion of this nature will tend to justify the apprehensions of those who believe advisory committees would become political dictators to administrative departments.

These committees could, if confined to their proper sphere, offer an avenue into the public service for meritorious industrial, professional, commercial, and civic leaders without the necessity of exposing them to the humiliations and indignities of politics. 

There would thus be made available to city, state, county, or nation the type of person who never would adopt the customary legerdemain of the political class. The type of person to be attracted would be the successful technical expert, industrial manager, financier, or philanthropist-persons who shun cheap publicity and mob adulation, and individuals who automatically recoil from the shams that cloud many political campaigns. 

13 See Report of the Waterbury Charter Commission, pp. 859, 945.

Ch. 4] 

People of this type have much to offer administration as distinct from politics, and they would be more than willing to offer a part of their time to their city, state, or nation if they could do so without running for some elective office, and if they could deal with professional administrators instead of spoils politicians. 

The entire project will depend, however, on the quality of personnel; mediocrity, so characteristic of board appointments in the past, will but perpetuate the evils of yesterday. Indeed, one might question whether advisory councils are not proper instrumentalities of a rather higher state of political development than most communities have yet achieved. 

Ex-Officio Boards 

It is the practice in some states to create ex-officio boards composed of the highest state officers such as treasurer, secretary of state, and auditor. In one case there are ten such boards. 

It is not here intended to lay down the rule that there should never be any ex-officio commissions, but service on three or four by a single department head cannot help but make serious inroads on time needed for departmental matters. It will usually be found that such types of organization constitute an accumulation of makeshifts. The legislature is at a loss to know what to do with a certain function. It is under pressure to keep down taxes and prevent the "growth of bureaucracy." What could be easier than to lump it off onto existing officials sitting as a board? It is quite proper to create ex-officio co-ordination committees for advisory purposes only, but many of the functions of these agencies are purely administrative. As such they could much better be articulated into the framework of an administrative department. Such was the case of the federal personnel classification board made up of representatives of the bureau of the budget, the civil service commission, and the bureau of efficiency.14 Good personnel practice labels classifica-

The Bipartisan Board 

Bipartisan boards composed of members belonging to the two leading political parties are sometimes set up with a view toward eliminating politics. The idea seems to be that if both parties are represented neither one will be able to accomplish its direct political designs, the check thus provided tending to subdue partisan interests and place emphasis on achieving the best possible administration. In local governments such arrangements are sometimes found in civil service commissions and police boards, while in the national government both major parties are represented on the Civil Service Commission, the Interstate Commerce Commission, the Shipping Board, the Federal Trade Commission, and the Federal Reserve Board. 

Bipartisan boards have failed to eliminate politics in local administration, police commissions constituting an excellent example. There the grip of politics was actually strengthened, for the result was a pooling of interests and spoils by the representatives of both parties on the board.15 Instead of having effective administration at heart, they distributed the plums according to a gentlemen's agreement. 

On the other hand, the bipartisan commissions have been relatively more successful in federal administration. Among the reasons advanced for this is that the commissions of the national government are not charged with the administration of a specific department; their duties are of a regulatory and research nature. Thus they are confined within limits which restrain them from interfering in administration on a wholesale scale. Furthermore, some feel that the federal service is better protected against political pressure through civil service laws and regulations than are most states and cities,¹º although some 15 R. B. Fosdick, American Police Systems (The Century Co., 1920), p. 106.

observers would question the superiority of the federal personnel system to those of the better states and cities. Is not the prominence of federal appointments, together with the possible scandal to be aroused by a bad choice, more responsible for the success of federal commissions than any question of the nature of their functions? Partisanship in administration is to be condemned wherever found. Where it insists on creeping in, it is logical to ask whether administration is not erroneously charged with a task which should be transferred back to the political branch.

The Clamor for Boards 

Special interest groups have frequently insisted on placing certain activities under independent boards in order to insure that they would be directed by technically qualified and sympathetic persons instead of suffering from the blighting incompetence of political appointment. Moreover, they have frequently been able to give these boards independent taxing power to insure financial support that city councils had not been previously willing to give. Such functions have included schools, libraries, parks, hospitals, and eleemosynary institutions of various kinds. The political situation is such in many American cities and states that it would be inadvisable to tie the schools in with the general government. Nevertheless, many of these functions could just as well be administered by single heads and should be placed under the budgeting control of the city just as rapidly as cities and states are able to make their houses clean enough to receive them. Until the housekeeping practice of the general government achieves a level of freedom from political interference at least equal to that now possessed by school, library, and park boards, it is advisable to retain the latter. In many cities this standard of administrative competence has been achieved and the consolidation of independent boards and commissions should proceed.

The social welfare group is particularly apprehensive of the integration movement," and there is no denying that such appre-

hensions have frequently been well grounded in experience. 

Members of this group have seen institutions built up to a high state of efficiency after years of painstaking struggle, only to have this labor overthrown at a single stroke by a spoils removal and mediocre appointment. Is it any wonder that they immediately clamor for a board independent of political control? The political scientist is entirely sympathetic toward these aspirations. He would figuratively spend his last farthing and breathe his final breath to end political interference in administration. His experience with boards has not convinced him, however, that they constitute the proper medium for accomplishing this purpose. This is due to the fact that he has seen the most rampant machine politics control municipal administration through police commissions, boards of public works, building commissions, finance commissions, and even civil service commissions.

Special interest groups, such as education, social welfare, libraries, parks and recreation, have found that more than semioccasionally there will be placed on their commissions highminded and influential lay leaders. These leading citizens will protect them from political inroads and force the financial support essential to a minimum program. A recent study has shown, moreover, that board supervision of municipal lighting plants in small cities has produced greater freedom from political interference, and hence better operating conditions, than where the plant was under the mayor or (and) council.18 It is difficult for the public administration group among the political scientists to permit the prejudices against boards—and the writer admits that he, at least, has such prejudices-to belittle these arguments which others have found in favor of boards. 

Perhaps there is a common ground which can reconcile the pro and anti-board forces.

The one and only significant argument which the experience of special interest groups has produced in favor of boards is that they assure freedom from political interference. This, in turn, is said to lead toward continuity of policy. The political scientist wonders whether similar objectives could not be achieved even more effectively by working toward the enforcement of high professional standards through a rigorous merit system of personnel administration. It is realized that the term "civil service" does not have a fortunate meaning among some special interest groups, but they should be made to understand that the highest technical achievements in public personnel administration frequently have little in common with "civil service" as practiced. In most advanced states and communities, the social welfare group could rally sufficient support from philanthropic citizens and influential humanitarians to demand the observance of professional personnel standards. Instead of abetting the mutual enemy by belittling "civil service❞—which has frequently deserved past calumny-they could demand that the director of public welfare and all of his subordinates be chosen by competitive examination and guaranteed a tenure conditioned only upon performance and behavior.¹ By abolishing the chief argument in favor of boards, this step would take the board question out of the realm of controversy. 

The truth of this conclusion seems to be demonstrated in those municipalities where city managers have been permitted to function as they are intended to function. Thus, in the study referred to above, finding in favor of board supervision of light plants in municipalities with mayor and council charters, it was also concluded that there is absolutely no need for such a board where the appointment and supervision of the superintendent is placed in the hands of a city manager.20 There is also the statement attributed to the field agents of the Family Welfare Association of America that recent family relief activities under a city manager in Fort Worth have shown more thorough investigating methods and case work than formerly when the same

work was done by private agencies.21 Such instances demonstrate that boards do not constitute the only means of thwarting political interference.

The clamor for boards as bulwarks against political sabotage is frequently a subtle shield for special interest groups to secure departmental freedom from central co-ordination activities. In other words, much of the clamor for independent boards with their own taxing powers and budgets comes from organized and vested minority interests. These groups resent as unwarranted interference with their internal affairs, such co-ordination devices as central budgeting, accounting control, purchasing, and supervision by a central personnel office. To the argument that these mediums make for economy in government they reply that the American fetish for technical efficiency makes for speed rather than quality.22 This is the inevitable resistance of the specialist against any form of control from outside or above. 

It prevails in private management as well as in the public field, the difference being that special interest groups in government can fortify their position of smug independence through legal provisions pushed through by organized minority pressure movements.

This desire for freedom from central budgeting and co-ordination on the part of the education and welfare groups was well merited in the days when public management was characterized by political "grab and pork" influence, resulting in the virtual starvation of these services. Many a splendid library, park, or recreation system would probably never have reached its present development without its own friendly board and independent budget. We are wondering, however, whether public appreciation of these activities has not reached the point where they can safely be subjected to budgeting by a central agency on the basis of their merits. Experience seems to indicate that this practice leads to better business methods without injuring service. Those interested in a humanitarian attitude toward

This brings us to the point of departure in the previous chapter. It will be remembered that we were discussing the desirability and possible dangers of integration, but had to digress in order to consider the vexed question of boards and commissions. 

The preceding paragraph has indicated that the social welfare people have not been happy under integration because proper safeguards were not erected against spoils politics. This experience demonstrates that integration can very well be an instrument of political machination as well as a tool of effective public management. The difficulty in the early reorganizations has been that the structure of integration has been absorbed without its spirit and minus controls. The integration movement of the future must give more consideration to external controls which will thwart political domination of the hierarchy, while at the same time counteracting bureaucratic tendencies. 

There is some evidence that the early advocates of integration in the New York Bureau of Municipal Research had these controls more in mind than is indicated by later reorganization schemes. 

Chapter VII indicates the types of external control that should accompany integration. Probably, development in that direction will serve to settle the board controversy by placating advocates of the plural-headed system.

CHAPTER V STATE CONTROL OF LOCAL ADMINISTRATION 

Political science terminology makes a distinction between integration and centralization. Integration means gathering into the hands of a single person or body all of the administrative authority for a given unit-a city, a county, or a state. 

Centralization, on the other hand, has to do with the extension of state control over local administration. Centralization is the antithesis of home rule as generally understood. Integration refers to but a single level of government. Centralization deals with the relationship between two levels of government: nation and state, or state and local. Integration can exist without centralization, and the reverse is also true. This chapter will endeavor to treat the relationships between upper and lower levels of administration, chiefly the relations of the state to the city and county.

Federalism 

Types of Relationships 

A federal relationship exists when the powers of government are divided between a central government and local area. Each is prevented by a fundamental law, which neither can change of its own accord, from encroaching upon the sphere assigned to the other. Thus, the relation of the forty-eight commonwealths to the national government under the Constitution of the United States is federal. The central government has certain enumerated powers and the states have all other powers not denied them in the Constitution or given exclusively to the national government. Neither can in general encroach upon the sphere granted to the other. Thus, the national government

was presumed to be unable to enact a national prohibition law until the creation of the Eighteenth Amendment, and a state cannot levy a tax on imports. The relation of the city or county to the state is ordinarily not federal. In those states having constitutional home rule, a situation approaching federalism may arise if the courts adopt a liberal attitude in construing cases involving the boundary between what are local affairs and those of general state interest. In most of our 

American states, however, the city is the creature of the legislature which has tried to control municipal corporations by minute regulations contained in elaborate statutes. That a system of administrative control of local areas can be established in spite of strict federal arrangements, will be demonstrated in a later section on federal grants-in-aid to the states. 

Centralized Administration 

A centralized administration is one in which the local officers are appointed by, and subject to, the orders of the central government. In other words, local administration is incorporated in, and becomes an integral part of, the central organization. 

This is the situation in France for all except the communes, and they are under a system of administrative control so all-inclusive as practically to constitute centralized administration. The great administrative areas known as departments are under prefects who are national officers appointed by and responsible to the Minister of the Interior, a member of the national government in Paris. As far as the department is concerned in its relation to the central government, there is centralized administration. The cities or communes, however, are more largely administered by officers of their own choice. They are thus under administrative control. Therefore, centralized admin-

Legislative Control 

The normal relationship between the state and local administration in the past has been one of legislative control. The state legislature passes laws regulating local administration, sometimes in considerable detail. Thus, in some states the salaries of municipal officers are set by the legislature, in some cases each county or city being dealt with individually. Legislative control is a by-product of the American distrust of executive power. The legislature seeks to control city administration by giving detailed instructions in advance. The scope of

[Pt. I

the city's authority is defined in detail, and a municipal corporation has no power unless specifically granted in the law. This tends to strait-jacket the administrator. He fears to take a step which seems desirable, yet the legality of which is not

THE STATE LAW.) COUNTY ELECTORATE (ELECTS THE SHERIFF) SHERIFF (ADMINISTERS THE DEPARTMENT SUBJECT TO STATE LAW AS MADE AND INTERPRETED.) Figure 11. Legislative Control entirely apparent. That discretion which becomes essential to administration in a technical age is largely lacking because of this system.

Legislative control has the further defect that no state administrative agency is set up to see that local governments obey the laws enacted to control the conduct of their affairs. Frequently there is great laxity and lack of uniformity in the way cities and counties live up to the laws affecting administration. 

Under a system of pure legislative control, the only means of forcing compliance with such statutory requirements is an action. before a court of law.

Judicial Control 

Judicial control is not separable from legislative control; it is merely a remedy or series of remedies available for the purpose of causing the wish of the legislature to be followed. A statute might require cities to install sanitary sewers but provide no administrative means of enforcing action. 

A taxpayer might try to secure from the courts a writ of mandamus requiring such action. A taxpayer might believe that a county board of supervisors was issuing bonds contrary to law. He could apply to the courts for an injunction barring such action. 

One accused of crime might be held incommunicado. His remedy would be to secure a hearing upon a writ of habeas corpus. A comptroller might be accused of illegally approving requisitions upon the public treasury; he might be made to stand criminal trial. Many states have statutes permitting the removal of public officials after trial by the courts for misfeasance, malfeasance, or nonfeasance of office. All of these are extraordinary remedies which should be a part of the law of the land under all circumstances. It is maintained, however, that this type of judicial control is not sufficiently direct and summary to constitute the normal means of insuring fair, honest, and efficient administration. Things ordinarily have to be in a rather terrible condition before any one will resort to the courts.

Where this is not the case, a court action will constitute a deliberate annoyance of good officials for the sake of securing advantage to special interest. The ordinary, normal controls should be administrative and not either legislative or judicial.º 

Administrative Control 

In other words, it is believed that state control of local administration should be in the hands of state administrative officers who are given general directions coupled with a great deal of discretion. Under administrative control the city and county officials are selected locally, but they are subject to considerable On the general question of judicial control, see J. A. Fairlie, “Judicial and

Under certain circumstances, they may take positive steps to see that laxity in local office is corrected. Administrative control is not one of direct management of local affairs by the state. It

Administrative Control is rather a relationship of guidance, counsel, and advice. In other words, the state administrative authorities try to aid the cities in achieving effective administration. In doing so their method is one of co-operation and mutual consultation. Coercion comes into use only in those rare circumstances where recalcitrant local officials persist in unlawful abuses.

Administrative control usually begins with a rather innocuous or toothless procedure. Thus the statutes of some states, such as California and Iowa, require cities to make an annual report of their financial operations to the state controller or auditor. The state officers have practically no control over municipal finances as far as this report is concerned, so the re-

STATE CONTROL OF LOCAL ADMINISTRATION 

91 port may be said to have merely a moral effect. Inspection by state officials constitutes another moral threat over local laxity. 

In several states, municipal finances are audited by state agencies. These auditors usually have no authority to disallow items or to order correction of irregularities, but they do render reports setting forth the results of their audits. State agencies are frequently authorized to render advice to municipal authorities, an example being technical consultation on sanitary problems given to local health officers. These types of control constitute embryo developments. At first, all forms of control which threaten coercion by the state are feared. This apprehension is responsible for these first controls being innocuous. 

As the abuses which they were designed to remedy continue, however, something more drastic must be done. Instead of mere publicity given to municipal finances in a state report, a state agency is charged with prescribing accounting procedure and holding the cities to it. Instead of merely rendering advice, the state sanitary engineer sets standards and approves or rejects plans for a sewage disposal plant. By means of grantsin-aid, the cities subject themselves to a considerable amount of state supervision in return for state money. In emergencies the state may enter the county or city and actually take over administration until danger has passed. In certain cases, state agencies may remove local officers who function improperly." In 

New York, New Jersey, and Massachusetts, the central state personnel agency either has supervision over the local personnel activities or certifies the local civil service eligible lists itself. 

The selection of certain county officers by the state, usually the governor, is more common in New England and along the Atlantic seaboard. The essential point is that state control is at first rather spineless, but, as administration becomes more intricate and technical, more vigorous means are established to bring local administration in line with good practice.

It is well to bear in mind, moreover, that school administration is generally thought to be maintained on a higher basis than other branches of local government. One may well ponder whether this may be due in part to state maintenance, through administrative agencies, of minimum standards by local boards. 

Recently there has been a tendency to establish staff agencies to furnish technical advice to cities, as well as to accumulate statistics and perform specific services. State bureaus of criminal identification aid the cities in criminal investigations. 

State universities offer training courses for firemen, police, and meter readers. These same institutions conduct researches on which are based bulletins of information of value to specific technical branches of administration. The State of Pennsylvania has erected in its Department of Internal Affairs a Bureau of Municipalities. Among its many functions are the gathering and publishing of statistics, the installation of accounting systems, the rendering of advice helpful to the improvement of administration in general, and the preparation of plans. It is claimed that the better class of municipal officials would welcome and appreciate this study, and would no doubt cooperate willingly in providing the material for determining standards and costs of service. It is the duty of the state to promote the collection and distribution of this kind of information through a competent financial research agency.12

Many states authorize their cities to unite in a semi-official state organization, frequently known as a state league of municipalities. Support of a permanent staff and regular league functions is largely provided by membership fees paid from municipal funds. Membership is ordinarily entirely voluntary, seldom if ever including all cities in the state. At an annual meeting matters of policy are decided and officers are elected. 

Usually the program is arranged so as to provide education and training in matters of municipal interest. While the functions of leagues vary from state to state, practically all of them attempt to maintain a clearing office on legal matters and administrative practice. As a result, they are frequently able to furnish valuable advice to their members. In their early stages, the leagues were largely under the control of mayors and councilmen who were more interested in influencing legislation at the state capital than technical administrative problems. In recent years, however, the administrative officers have had a larger say in league affairs with the result that league staffs have become more interested in administrative research and training programs. Leagues of municipalities usually have a strong "home rule" complex which leads them to oppose many attempts to expand state administrative control.13 If a league's day-by-day work is in the hands of a competent staff which is not politically minded, a league can accomplish much of the 12 The Commission to Investigate County and Municipal Taxation and

Hardly anywhere in the nation has there been a discussion of local taxation in which the so-called Indiana plan has not been advocated as a panacea. The Indiana law provides that ten taxpayers may petition the State Board of Tax Commissioners to review either a local tax levy or a local bond issue. 

The Board has the power after hearing to affirm or reduce either a tax levy or a bond issue. The Board has no initiative of its own in the matter. It must await action upon petition of ten taxpayers. The official report of the Board claims that up to 

1932 it had handled 1,230 appeals on tax levies and had ordered a total reduction of $21,172,544.14 From March 11, 1919 to 

October 1, 1931, bond issues were approved to the extent of approximately forty millions, whereas thirty millions were disapproved.15 It is obvious that this mere statement of reductions should not be taken as complete evidence of the efficacy of the plan. The recent period of depression brought out much controversy on this point.16 We shall not enter into the merits of the situation here.

Administrative Control and Home Rule 

Efforts to expand administrative control are usually opposed by local officials, as evidenced by the reference above to the home rule complex of at least some state leagues of municipalities. It seems that they would much prefer taking their chances at getting what they desire from state legislatures than to giving state administrative authorities any supervisory authority over cities. When the smaller municipalities, which frequently dominate leagues of municipalities, refer to "home rule," they do not mean the constitutional home rule familiar to the student

17 of municipal government. They frequently mean freedom from the interference of state administrative authority. They are not so conscious of the legislative domination which students have decried for decades. According to American law, municipalities have been subject to a rather minute and rigorous legislative control. This has been slightly relaxed, to be sure, in those states where the courts have liberally interpreted constitutional home rule provisions. On the whole, however, local government has been a football of legislative log-rolling. 

Home rule, at best, has been more or less of an unrealized fetish. At the same time, opposition to the expansion of a reasonable type of administrative control comes largely from a lack of understanding. A greater consciousness of the fact that so-called home rule in practice is only a phantom lure would end much blind worship. It should also be understood that the cry of home rule is frequently raised as a smoke screen to protect officials who have vested interests in the status quo. 

The reader should not infer from these statements that the writer is opposed to municipal home rule. He simply feels that this ideal has not been achieved by past state legislative control of cities. He would like to see some experimentation with wider contacts between local and state administrative branches dealing with similar subject matter. 

A salutary step in this direction would be the "Co-operative home rule" plan proposed by the New Jersey Commission to 

Investigate County and Municipal Taxation and Expenditures. 

This body suggested that a middle course would be desirable. 

A contact for each major governmental service with the appropriate state agency would be provided. It is claimed that this is neither new nor novel, for such contacts have existed in many fields for a long time, and with perfectly happy results. 

The cooperative aspects of these contacts should be stressed. 

State and local agencies have heretofore operated too much as mutually exclusive, and sometimes as actually hostile organizations. The idea of inspection and criticism by an external, higher authority is not inherently inimical to a vigorous local 17 At least this is so of cities under the general law in California with which the author is most familiar.

administration, as has been demonstrated by the comparative success of the educational system. As a feature of this relationship, the state agencies should be prepared to supply, as requested, technical advice and assistance to smaller localities, on a cost basis, thus saving these places substantial sums now paid to private consultants. The advisory relationship could be broadened through cooperative advisory committees or councils composed of local and state representatives, reinforced as occasion required by citizen members and by outside experts.18 

The reasonableness of this New Jersey view is attested by what can occur when extreme legislative control leads to local laxity. Becoming alarmed at the rapidly mounting local tax levies and bonded debts, North Carolina, in 1931, took an extreme swing toward centralization. In the field of highways and education, the change went beyond the moderation of state administrative control well on toward actual state administration of those functions.19 In the realm of finance there was established a Local Government Commission composed of three state officers ex officio and six appointed by the governor to hold office at his pleasure. One of the latter is designated by the governor as director of local government. This Commission is given control over all local bond issues. This control is not merely perfunctory. It goes into such vital matters as necessity, adequacy to accomplish purpose, its effect on the tax situation, and the condition of sinking funds. Bonds not approved by the Commission can be issued only after a favorable vote at an election. Sales of local bonds are made by the Commission at the state capitol. The Commission also exercises a stringent supervision over the investment of local sinking funds. 

The director is authorized to appoint a special administrator of finance to take over as virtual receiver the financial operations of any unit which defaults on its bonds. There is adequate

Such is the extreme to which state centralization may go when popular indignation becomes aroused. Moderation of extreme home rule ideas would probably have avoided such a long swing of the pendulum.

Administrative control can occasionally be secured through grants-in-aid. Through this medium the central agency offers a local government a grant of money for a specific purpose with the proviso that it must be spent in accordance with stated limitations. These latter may be purely nominal or they may be quite stringent. In the latter case, the central agency assumes a wide degree of administrative control over local administration. The federal government grants such aid to the states in such fields as forestry, highways, and vocational education. To secure federal aid in forest fire prevention the state must submit a plan for approval and then submit to inspection and advice. Federal aid to state highways involved a much more thoroughgoing control. Each project must be approved by the 

Bureau of Public Roads of the Department of Agriculture as to route, nature of construction, type of paving, grades, and estimated cost. Federal authorities must approve the letting of contracts and will release no federal funds until the job is certified by an inspector from the Bureau of Public Roads. 

There is continued federal inspection each year as long as the road lasts. This may act as a control of highway maintenance through refusals to grant future construction aid where roads are poorly cared for.21 

Many people fear federal aid. They say that it upsets the balance of power between nation and state, and that it is remov-

Centralization Trends 

The depression of the nineteen thirties has accentuated the movement toward state control over local government and federal control over the states. By the winter of 1932-1933, the federal authorities had capitulated to the realization that unemployment relief is a national problem rather than one for local governments to solve unaided. The result was an entirely new set of relationships between the national authorities in Washington on the one hand, and states, counties, and cities on the other. The administrative relationships involved in this situation have been a matter of experimentation with frequent readjustments, a complete picture of which has not been presented at the time this is written. In some cases, federal money is being dispensed by local agencies with little direct federal supervision, while elsewhere the national officers have virtually taken over local relief bodily. The national government is in the field with its own relief agencies even where local bodies continue to handle the bulk of unemployment cases. The entire list of New Deal laws tends to augment vastly the sphere of control in which the state was formerly considered to have paramount or exclusive authority. 

22 James M. Beck, Our Wonderland of Bureaucracy (The Macmillan Co., 1932), p. 213. 23 

Macdonald, op. cit., pp. 269-291. A little more recent treatment of federal centralization is contained in White, Trends, pp. 20–48.

Some see in this situation an entirely new rearrangement of governmental areas with the state diminishing in power and prestige, and the development of a direct contact between the cities, especially metropolitan regions, and the federal authorities.25 They condemn the states for not rising to the aid of the cities in handling unemployment relief before the federal government came in during 1933. Others vision the decline of the county as a unit of local administration. In other words, the federal government and the metropolitan region are to be the dominant entities in future American government, with the states and counties declining in importance.26 

This question of the balance of power as between governmental areas is predominantly one of constitutional law rather than of public management, with which this book is predominantly concerned. No new principles of management springing from the new federal-municipal relationships are now ready for the student, although they undoubtedly are developing quite rapidly. Perhaps the student of public administration a decade hence will have to orient his mind in an entirely new type of federalism.

During the depression years, there has also been a tendency to tighten state administrative control over local administration. in the field of finance. This has taken the form of emergency treatment to correct existing sores, especially to bolster areas faced with imminent default, rather than insistence upon thoroughgoing management reform.27

CHAPTER VI INTERNAL CONTROLS 

The administrative machine must function as a whole with as little friction as possible. To achieve this end there are various possible devices, some of which will work well for some administrators, and others will suit those of still different habits. and temperament. The problem is to counteract an excessive spirit of departmentalism without unduly interfering in purely departmental matters-control and co-ordination without petty domination. As between alternatives, however, the latter is much to be preferred over uncontrolled interdepartmental warfare, sometimes referred to as interdepartmental sabotage, a disease not peculiar to governmental organizations alone.¹ 

Such a condition is characterized by continual struggle on the part of each unit to secure favored consideration without any appreciation of the needs of others: additions to personnel beyond studied needs, development of subdivisions whose activities duplicate those existing elsewhere, and reluctance to submit gracefully to economies containing some threat to departmental autonomy. It is the problem of the new public administration to reconcile this departmental feudalism with the need of the modern age for co-ordination, but to do it without deadening initiative in those matters of peculiarly departmental concern. 

It is believed that this purpose can best be accomplished through the principles of integration laid down in the preceding chapters. Through the integrated organization the spirit of departmental individualism will come under control, and cooperation will automatically take place. Operating economies resulting from improved methods can be made without scaling that cliff of obstructive inertia sometimes erected by officers who

sense a threat to their own security in every proposed change. 

On the other hand, one must acknowledge that integration threatens the department with the possibility of excessive domination by the chief administrative officer. This hazard to departmental autonomy need not constitute hindrance to good administration, for, quite to the contrary, the machine as a whole may be suffering just as much from the excessive individualism of its component parts.

The question of the delegation and devolution of authority by executives is subject to unending controversy. It seems generally agreed that the chief should delegate as much of the detail of direction as possible, in order to spare his own time and energy for purposes of co-ordination and settlement of major issues. Hence, we have the characteristic picture of a successful executive with a desk clear of papers, and duties so happily delegated to trusted subordinates that he may devote the greater share of his time to conferences, interviews, and planning. Practice indicates, however, that this ideal is not so easy to achieve in practice. The natural tendency for the energetic executive is to want to do a great many things himself in order to insure that they be well done. This may be one reason why city managers are about the hardest worked individuals in their respective cities. In addition to the ordinary problems of management, they must keep the holes plugged against the possibility of political attack. The natural result is that they have their hands in departmental activities more than would be necessary under private management. 

As organizations become larger, "one man" operation must give way to "one man" control. The manager of a city of 

20,000 may be pretty well in touch with the daily routine of each department. This will be more difficult in a city of 50,000, well nigh impossible in cities of 100,000, and utterly out of the question in cities such as Cincinnati, Oakland, and Dallas. As the city or department grows from a few to scores, hundreds, and thousands of employees, questions of management supersede those of operation as far as the chief administrative officer is concerned. The big problem is for this functionary to be in touch with the work of his subordinates in order to assure effec-

[Pt. I 

ORGANIZATION 

tive operation all the way down the line without burying himself in detail and routine or deadening departmental initiative.

In cities up to a certain size, the city manager might himself actually perform the functions of city engineer, city clerk, and water works superintendent. He might with his own hands draft plans for a sewer or put a new gasket on a pump. In doing so he would use technical skill and knowledge and would be engaged in operation as distinct from management. In cities of over 100,000, however, the city manager would be required to confine himself to direction and management, for which his qualifications would be general rather than technical.

Elasticity and Flexibility 

One of the prime requisites of public management is that the chief administrative officer be free from that detailed legal control of administration which is so characteristic of our constitutions, statutes, and charters. Nothing can be quite so deadening to effective administrative action as that legal paralysis which results from trying to divine every possible action in advance and form a rule for its guidance in the law. Instead of the control which it aims to achieve, there results delay while 'L. D. White, The City Manager (University of Chicago Press, 1927), p. 233.

[Pt. I 

ORGANIZATION 

waiting for legal opinions, superfluous litigation, and undue caution owing to fear of possible litigation. Then there is the petty political bickering due to controversies over the interpretation of inconsequential charter and statutory clauses. If the subject matter which they try to regulate were left as it should be, to administrative discretion, better control would result. 

Moreover, much administration would be kept out of politics, and public interest would be more adequately protected than under a regime wherein administrators are strait-jacketed in great masses of legal provisions designed to direct their every action.

It logically follows that the chief administrative officer should be given a large degree of discretion in moulding both the form and personnel of his organization. Hence, a statute creating a state police department would define its duties and set the limitations of its powers definitely, but in general terms; define its relation to county sheriffs and municipal police; and provide for its support. It would be going entirely beyond the field of statutory competence in specifying how many captains, sergeants, and patrolmen there should be, where the main offices. should be located, the type of uniform, and the technique of criminal identification to be used. The director should be permitted to determine how to distribute his man power, subject to budget limitations adequately supervised by the department of finance. The same principle applies to field services, the location of which inevitably becomes "pork" when left to legislative determination. This is adequately demonstrated by the maintenance of unneeded army and navy posts and stations, due entirely to the influence of congressmen. 

In 1930 Congress gave the President the authority to transfer certain veterans' activities from other departments and erect a new Veterans' Administration under a director responsible to the President. The statute, but little over a page in length, gave the President practically carte blanche power to accomplish this task as he might see fit, resulting in almost immediate operation economies, and more effective administration. In 1932 the * See letter from Frank T. Hines to House Committee on Expenditures in the Executive Departments, March 5, 1932 (committee print).

Ch. 6] 107 

INTERNAL CONTROLS 

President requested of Congress the further authority to reorganize the administration by executive orders to become effective after "laying before Congress" for sixty days, if that body does not request their suspension. Congress eventually voted the President a large amount of this power just before adjournment in the summer of 1932, and again on March 3, 1933. 

There is little reason why the President should not have the authority requested, especially in view of the safeguard offered." 

The necessary flexibility, together with authoritative legal sanction, can be obtained through the adoption of an administrative code containing the legislative provisions essential to the maintenance of the organization. This has the advantage of certainty and unity so often absent where administrative provisions pertaining to the same subject are scattered among scores of separately enacted statutes and ordinances. Such a code, by the permanent enactment of standard flexible procedure, would tend to discourage the insertion of detailed administrative procedure in every statute lobbied through under pressure by interest groups. By providing for the skeleton of organization, the administrative framework would tend to acquire stability sufficient to resist legislative tendencies toward independent agencies for each new governmental activity. The code should not go too far in adding flesh and blood to the skeleton, however. Ordinarily, an enumeration of the principal departments with their powers and duties will be sufficient, leaving the chief administrative officer sufficient power to make current adjustments, possibly subject to subsequent legislative approval.

Excellent examples are evident in Los Angeles county and city where the number of separate units run in the upper forties and thirties, respectively. It had been said that there should be only from six to nine departments in a good administrative set-up, and the highest limit set by any wellknown authority is twelve or fifteen. Some would say that only exceptional executives could supervise the latter number. 

Let us attempt to generalize in a field where such a venture is hazardous by saying that the six to nine figure is desirable in municipal administration, but that it may be necessary to extend the number to twelve or fifteen in state and national organizations in order to achieve the proper functionalization. 

In Cincinnati there are now nine major units directly responsible to the manager, and these could be reduced by two through the erection of a department of finance. Several of the state reorganizations have reduced the number of departments under the governor to fifteen or less.

Having set up the departments deemed proper, the next question is to determine what machinery, if any, the chief administrative officer is to use in contacting the departments. Is there to be an under-secretary to deal directly with all subunits, or shall there be assistant managers, or executive assistants? Under-secretaries are usually found standing between the department heads and bureaus in national ministries, such as in Great Britain, or the Departments of State and Treasury in our national government.
