After the appropriation acts are passed, the department of finance holds the several departments to the terms thereof, thus preventing them from incurring obligations in excess of resources. It maintains constant current audits to see that every division is handling funds with fidelity and according to the strictest accountability. It sees that all fees, fines, costs, and invoices collected by any agency of the government are promptly turned into the general treasury for accounting and safe-keeping. It purchases all supplies and equipment according to standard specifications, transfers unneeded equipment to where it can be used, and salvages much that would otherwise be waste. Through its personnel divisions it classifies duties and positions so that wages and salaries can be set according to a well-devised plan. It keeps the service rating and personnel records of all employees, and recruits the needed personnel. Some departments of finance may, in emergencies, avoid a deficit by reducing expenditures to less than the appropriations. Such is co-ordination with a vengeance. 

Other Means of Co-ordination 

Staff agencies are among the most important means of coordination. Their purpose is to bring trained and specialized intelligence to bear from an independent viewpoint, free from that bureaucratic self-interest which leads particular departments to view their own as the only problems. Staff agencies study departments with a view toward developing given activities to the utmost efficiency, consistent with the progress of others, and, limited by that consideration, they must resist the ambition of functional chiefs to expand indefinitely at whatever cost. Departments frequently insist that they must have certain things or, so they say, their work will be seriously impaired. If every departmental request were met, the cost of government would become confiscatory. Staff officers and agencies charged with examining line operation critically constitute one of the major answers to this problem.15 15 

1 J. M. Pfiffner, "The Los Angeles Bureau of Budget and Efficiency,"

National Municipal Review (February, 1932), Vol. XXI, No. 2, pp. 107-109.

[Pt. I 

ORGANIZATION 

This really brings into government the element of efficiency engineering, a term which is most descriptive in spite of a certain distasteful connotation which it bears in some quarters. It involves the application of training, experience, and judgment to an administrative problem, with a view toward ascertaining the best way to perform a task with the least possible expenditure of personal effort and materials. The Bureau of Budget and Efficiency of the City of Los Angeles presents an admirable example of a governmental staff agency doing this very thing. For instance, preliminary estimates on steel filing equipment for the new city hall indicated an outlay far in excess of available funds, but a survey by the Bureau resulted in satisfying all needs for five years through the expenditure of $89,100 instead of the original estimate of $196,000. The Bureau is constantly performing work of this nature, some of the recent actual savings to taxpayers being the transfer of the police department to the city hall after a survey of available space, saving hundreds of dollars rent per month, and the establishment of the office of the superintendent of equipment, who keeps a record of all city equipment, often preventing unnecessary purchases through transfers. As a result of the Bureau's recommendation, an orderly method of handling the city's real estate holdings has resulted in increased rental incomes as well as the conservation of jeopardized property holdings. The Bureau of 

Efficiency of Los Angeles County, with recently expanded authority, is carrying out essentially similar functions. 

This type of activity encounters resistance from three principal sources. The first is the politician who does not want the real facts disclosed because they would reflect adversely on his own pet projects or selfish interests. Public employee groups and organizations frequently oppose consolidations and economies which would tend to abolish jobs. In the third place, the term “efficiency" bears a stigma in the eyes of two classes of persons, labor interests and certain types of humanitarians. Labor has learned to be distrustful of efficiency investigators, because their appearance at a plant has often meant fewer jobs and more work at less pay. On the other hand, certain humanitarians associate efficiency methods with stand-

Ch. 6] 

113 

INTERNAL CONTROLS 

ardized procedures which suppress initiative, discourage selfexpression, and breed a race of automatons. As a result, the governmental staff agencies will not be permitted to become ruthless and "hard-boiled" in dealing with the human element, and probably this is as it should be. 

The contribution of bureaus of municipal research to the cause of good government is beyond estimate. Today they constitute one of the major co-ordinating factors in administration in those cities where they exist. Always on the alert to discover friction in the administrative machine, they are frequently able to aid the directing personnel, through advice and dignified publicity, in accomplishing desirable changes in administrative procedure. When originally launched in a community they must appeal for financial support from large taxpayers who may be led to expect corresponding tax reductions for their contributions. This handicaps the relations of the bureau's technical staff with the officials of local government who suspect a design to reduce taxes by wrecking services. As time goes on, however, the staff is able to allay these fears and build up official relations based on mutual confidence. In some cases they are actually solicited for advice, surveys, and installations, for they can bring to bear a detached point of view not possible to obtain through any unit which is a part of the government itself.¹º 

The importance of standards and measurements pervades every administrative problem, but they are of especial significance to executive control and co-ordination. It is said that the chief administrative officer should be able to hold his subordinates responsible for performance. But performance of what? Performance of their duties, of course. But what are their duties and what is a reasonable gauge of achievement? If the chief administrative officer knows what constitutes such standards in every principal activity, and if he receives constant reports on administrative results so measured, the problems of executive control would be materially lessened. The record would easily reflect the cause and degree of maladministration 18 C. Skinner, "The Relation of the Research Bureau to the City Hall in

City Managers' Association. The final chapter of this book is devoted to a more complete statement of current achievements in standardizing and measuring public administration. The staff conference, or meeting of the administrative cabinet, occurs when the directing head meets to deliberate with his chief subordinates. Once each month, the Governor of 

California meets his department heads who read mimeographed reports, which are distributed to members of the public present. 

These contain information on the work and problems of the department, together with a progress report on current projects. 

When first inaugurated under Governor Young, it was said that certain department heads were given an opportunity to see each other for the first time in months. The common arguments in favor of the staff conference are that it will tend to break down departmental individualism by bringing the heads together where they will grow to appreciate each other's viewpoints, exchange ideas, pool resources, and eliminate duplicate effort. The general conclusion is that such meetings are valuable, but their value is dependent upon the spirit in which they are conducted. If properly planned and controlled, they become significant instruments of public management, but if held half-heartedly, just because the scheduled day has rolled around again, the time of important individuals needed elsewhere may be needlessly squandered.

In other words, the staff conference is dependent for results upon the leadership and interest of the chief. A well-known director of regional planning lays great store by his staff meetings, and the general high quality of his organization lends "H. P. Once each week, the staff of the Los Angeles County Counsel holds a conference where questions of law are discussed before they are written into official opinions for the guidance of administrators. On the other hand, one is forced to lend an ear to a city manager of twenty years' experience in six cities, who publicly stated that he abandoned the conference of department heads many years ago because they became irked at the time lost from their own tasks, through listening to, what they considered to be, the irrelevant problems of others. The only conclusion possible is, then, that the staff conference, if properly handled, is a valuable but not essential aid to management. 

Committees composed of selected persons are used as tools of management throughout the industrial field, and they should have their place in public administration. A committee should ordinarily have only advisory or deliberative functions, although occasionally it may be charged with reaching decisions, but it should practically never be charged with performance. The members should be chosen on the basis of particular aptitude, qualifications, and interest rather than because they represent this or that department or group, although some committees will have to be representative in nature. The success of committees will depend almost entirely upon the ability of the chairman to steer discussion to the point, tactfully circumventing heated but pointless argument, and leveling down egos without stifling them.18

After the enactment of the Budget and Accounting Act of 1921,19 a new co-ordination service was set up and attached to the Federal Bureau of the Budget. Normally headed and manned by army and navy officers assigned for this duty, its work was carried on largely through interdepartmental committees. Their field of activity was confined almost entirely to co-ordinating the procurement, use, and disposal of supplies, materials, and equipment. Decisions reached by interdepartmental committees would be binding on all services after promulgation by the chief co-ordinator. The field service was 18 19

placed under nine area co-ordinators who worked through several hundred "Federal Business Associations." These latter would exist wherever there is a centralization of federal agencies. 

They were composed of representatives of each service having a local branch, who would meet periodically for lunch or dinner. 

The organization of these groups was extremely loose. They would elect a chairman who would carry on the co-ordination functions locally. Proposals to purchase would go to the representative of the Federal Business Association for the purpose of ascertaining whether the demand could not be met by transfer without purchase. There is no doubt that this co-ordination service was a splendid first step in the direction of integrating federal housekeeping activities. It was too loosely organized, however, to meet the management problems of a budget out of balance by billions of dollars. Hence, Executive Order 6166 of June 10, 1933, abolished the co-ordination service in the Bureau of the Budget and transferred most of its duties to a new Procurement Division in the Treasury Department. This agency was placed under the supervision of a director of procurement, and was endowed with authority to prescribe rules and regulations, and to carry them into operation with respect to procurement, warehousing and distribution for all divisions of the government. 

While several of the interdepartmental committees of the old co-ordination service were abolished, the committee mode of operation was retained. Thus, the procurement division will have a general advisory committee headed by the assistant director with four other members appointed from the executive departments most interested in procurement and supply. Executive control and co-ordination are practically impossible without information as to what is happening throughout the organization. The best way to secure this information is through a series of written reports based on the original records handed in daily by the man on the job. These are consolidated by the foremen, whose reports are in turn consolidated by the division chiefs, and sent on up until the operations of the department are shown in the master report.2 22 Such records will aid in rating employees, furnish the basis

One successful executive requires each person under his supervision, from himself down to the 'phone girls and messengers, to prepare a brief summary of the day's work. These are filed on cards and eventually consolidated into monthly summaries. At first some of his most important assistants failed to see the value of this procedure and prepared the reports under protest. The work of the office involves considerable contact with real estate interests on a give-and-take basis, the result being that as time went on controversy arose over agreements alleged to have been reached in interviews several months old. 

As it became evident that resort to the file of daily summaries could frequently protect the office in such matters, the original recalcitrants became boosters of the system. It is not here recommended that such a system of reports should be installed in every organization, for it would be workable only where the chief is sufficiently convinced of its efficacy to give it the earnest supervision necessary to make it function. 

It must nevertheless be realized that one of the most effective means of securing co-operation from the top down, as well as of protecting each officer against unfair charges, is to force a record of each and every transaction. This can be done without causing the obstruction alleged to be due to "government red-tape," for most well-run corporate enterprises demand the record of transactions referred to herein. Red tape is caused, not by an excessive amount of paper work, but by an utter lack of pointing a record system to a central purpose. In other words, it comes from an absence of co-ordination. When the research staff of the International City Managers' Association installs its public works records system in the field, it invariably finds that little additional clerical help is needed; that the co-ordination of existing reports with their own new forms produces control and co-ordination without excessive addition to paper work.

Ch. 6] 

119 

INTERNAL CONTROLS 

Records of this nature have two principal purposes from the standpoint of management. In the first place, they produce, as indicated above, information to guide the course of managerial action. A leading example of such a report is the monthly budget summary which indicates whether revenues are coming up to expectations; whether expenditure is staying within predetermined limits; and, if not, what remedial action is possible. 

However, reports have a still more subtle purpose to the manager. They force the potential wrongdoer and slothful worker to make a record of accomplishments, and in doing so they have the moral effect of forcing honesty through fear of the consequences of falsifying a writing. More effective accomplishments also result from the shame and fear of the loss of a job, and in seeing one's name attached to a substandard report of performance. Indeed, there are those who feel that the prime purpose of governmental records of cost and performance is to force public writings on which to base actions against the corruptionist.

CHAPTER VII EXTERNAL CONTROLS 

In the previous chapter we were concerned with administrative control, or with those means used by the chief administrative officer to make the entire organization respond to his direction. Under democratic forms of government it becomes necessary to secure popular control of both the chief administrative officer and his subordinates, a problem of prime importance because it strikes at the very roots of democratic institutions. 

American democracy must create a more congenial environment for the technologist than it has provided in the past. The only other alternative would seem to be dictatorship, or other forms of absolutism. The advocates of the new public administration are democratic at heart and in principle, for they feel that technology can be made to function within the fold of popular government without becoming suffocated and without jeopardizing liberty. The following paragraphs indicate how popular control of the professional administrator is being achieved, and they set forth suggestions for further development in this direction. 

Legislative and Judicial Control 

Under the disintegrated administrative set-ups and negative attitude toward government of the nineteenth century, control was sought by parcelling out authority to a number of agencies independent of each other and of any central officer or body. 

The legislature would attempt to specify in advance through statutory enactment the powers and duties as well as considerable material of a purely administrative and directory nature. 

In case the law were violated, the remedy would be through an action brought before a court of law, either by some other officer, such as the governor, mayor, or attorney-general, or by an 121

[Pt. I 

ORGANIZATION 

interested taxpayer. This type of popular control is valuable and should be retained, with certain modifications; but it should be regarded as a last resort and not as the normal means of holding administration in line and correcting abuses. This is so because litigation is slow, and hence not sufficiently summary for attaining day-by-day accountability. Administrative incompetence, moreover, is not susceptible of judicial proof. 

Constant resort to the courts tends to raise unnecessarily the question of legality in routine matters, which in turn encourages that worship of legal niceties which the new public administration seeks to avoid.

The principal reason why legislative and judicial control should not be regarded as normal remedies against administrative action is, however, that legislators and judges are not qualified to make decisions in the technical fields of administration. 

The legislature is composed of amateurs, and this is as it should be; but these amateurs are not qualified to give detailed instructions, in advance, to administrators. They should decide what should be done, but should leave it to the professional administrators to determine how it should be done. After that it is the function of the legislature to establish checks and audits to ascertain how well administration is acquitting itself of its duties. These checks and audits should be performed by technically qualified persons who report to and advise the legislature. 

In other words, the legislature should have its own staff of persons competent in the technique and technology of administration. They should continuously appraise the performance of the entire administrative branch for the purpose of informing the legislature whether its general directions are being properly carried out. Briefly, then, the proper way for the legislature to control administration is by means of general instructions followed by a thorough check of performance, rather than by detailed specification in advance.2 

¹Chicago Tribune's suit against Mayor Thompson requiring him to refund over $1,000,000 paid to his followers as fees for acting as alleged "expert" real estate appraisers. See New York Times, July 13, 1928, 4:4; ibid., September

EXTERNAL CONTROLS 

The delusion that ours is "a government of laws and not of men" has led to the practice of trying to control administration by the enactment into statutes of detailed instructions to administrators. It has been thought that the only way to hold administrative officers responsible was to specify in detail all their functions and activities, so that their duties would be clearly defined. The result has been the development of a legal formalism which has tended toward rigid crystallization of administrative practice. It is inevitable that where legal formalism. prevails there will be resistance to change. This is due to the tendency of the law to be guided by the norms of the past, and to the predilections of lawyers to regard that which is as inherently good. It is here again that American public administration has suffered from its legal tutelage. Too great confidence is placed in the efficacy of securing the desired action by stating in a law that it shall be done. 

Good men desire to know that they have the confidence of their fellows. They rise to the full stature of their potentialities when given that freedom of action necessary to accomplish results in any undertaking. If they find themselves fenced in by prescribed routine in every attempted move, they will cease to exercise initiative and ingenuity, and either leave for more promising fields or resign themselves to the rôles of mere automatons. The best way to get results is to combine responsibility and power in an official and set up means of holding him to account for his stewardship. Capable men will take their responsibility seriously and welcome the accounting for their acts. Our distrust of executive and administrative power in 

America has failed to take this into account. It must be remembered that the arbitrary acts of colonial administrators were largely due to the fact that they were not accountable to those over whom they ruled. How, then, shall we secure the accountability of the twentieth century administrator?

Control Through the Audit 

The British offer an example in the legislative audit which is a post check by an officer entirely independent of administra-

[Pt. I 

ORGANIZATION 

tion and answerable only to the legislature. The Comptroller and Auditor-General is appointed by the Crown for life, is removable only by a vote of both houses of Parliament, and his salary is considered to be a permanent charge upon the Treasury. 

He is now regarded as a servant of the House of Commons alone, and he audits expenditures and revenues for the purpose of informing that body as to how the administrative services. have carried into effect its previously expressed wishes. These audits seek not only to ascertain fiscal fidelity; they are increasingly concerned with the nature of operations, or in other words, "efficiency.' "3 In the United States many cities and counties have a fidelity audit, but the principle of legislative audit has not attained the same significance here as in Great Britain. For instance, the 

City of Los Angeles has no audit other than by the elective controller who keeps the books for the city and, hence, audits his own accounts. The idea of the more complete operation or efficiency audit by an agency independent of administration, preferably responsible to the legislature, should take deeper root. 

Two obstacles stand in the way at present: commercial accountants, who do much governmental auditing on a fee basis, are not adequately trained in public administration; and standards and measurements are as yet not sufficiently well developed to offer criteria on which the auditor may base his judgment as to the effectiveness of operation. However, these are not insuperable hurdles. In fact, indications point toward their imminent conquest.

One significant, and undoubtedly indispensable, feature of the British legislative audit is the provisions made by the House of Commons for receiving and considering the report of the Comptroller and Auditor-General. At the beginning of each session a Public Accounts Committee is appointed. In order to assure that the party in power will not gloss over adverse aspects of the audit report, the chairman is usually a distinguished 3 On this aspect of the British audit see John Waller Hills, The Finance of Government (Philip Allan & Co., London, 1925), pp. 101-102. member of the opposition, often a former Financial Secretary of the Treasury, whereas the actual Financial Secretary of the Treasury is only a private member of the committee. An authoritative English commentator refers to the committee and its work in the following terms:

Its service is onerous, but sought after. Many distinguished men have sat on it. Party differences affect it little. Meeting year after year, sitting in private, withdrawn from clamour and publicity, its members acquire a sense of corporate responsibility and corporate self-respect. . . . Its work is perhaps the most valuable part of parliamentary control of finance. True, it does not sit till long after the money has been spent, but it renders future misfeasance more difficult. Its business is to see that all parliamentary grants, including supplementary grants, have been applied to the objects which Parliament prescribed. But in reality it does more. It looks into causes as well as consequences. It censures improper expenditure as well as improper accounting. It exposes waste and inefficiency. It has before it the reports of the Comptroller and Auditor-General, and with these in view it carefully examines the accounts, administering advice, reproof and even punishment should it be necessary. 

The Comptroller and Auditor-General sits with it so does a high Treasury official. . . . Nearly all its inquiries, indeed, are on points raised by the Comptroller, one more proof of the usefulness of this high officer of the House of Commons. 

When it has finished its scrutiny, the Public Accounts Committee reports to Parliament. These reports are exceedingly frank and plain spoken. On their receipt, there are two ways in which the sinner may be brought to book. The report can, and should, be discussed in the House of Commons. Very seldom is it discussed. Want of time, lateness in the session, the fact that the misdeeds disclosed are ancient history, and the natural wish of governments to escape blame, all tend to prevent it, and this way is little used. But there is another, very effective and always used, Treasury censure. The Treasury do not spare the rod. The committee's reports are driven home with force and energy. A Treasury Minute, reporting what action has been taken, is presented to Parliament. The Treasury have probably been preaching the same sermon before, but their hearers have not listened. Now it is not they who thunder, but the mighty House of Commons.¹

There is no American counterpart of the British Public Accounts Committee, but it goes without saying that we could adopt the principle for which it stands with profit. American governments of all varieties quite generally lack a systematic method of thoroughly scrutinizing the audit as it comes from the hands of the professionals. Too often the audit is filed as a mere formality, and too frequently there is no audit made to file at all. It was hoped that the Budget and Accounting Act of 

1921 would create in the Comptroller-General a legislative auditor similar to the British Comptroller and Auditor-General, but our Comptroller-General has developed into an instrument of control rather than an auditor." There is little evidence that he is becoming the counterpart of the British functionary. 

Each house of Congress has recently consolidated several committees into the Committee on Expenditures in the Executive Departments. The House committee bearing that name has been fairly active since its organization by the 70th Congress, having handled such recent bills as those transferring prohibition enforcement from the Treasury to Justice, and creating the new Veterans' Administration. The hearings of this committee bring out a useful store of data relative to the operation of administration. One is inclined to wish that it would sit annually to consider the audit report of an "Auditor General" who would be freed from administrative duties and divested of control authority.

In Germany the auditing function has been placed in a judicial body, the Court of Audit or Rechnungshof. This is a collegial group appointed with judicial tenure from those who have qualifications to enter the judiciary, the higher administrative, or higher technical service of the Reich or state. It is independent of both the administration and the legislature. It conducts the annual fiscal audit to see that the budget expenditures were in line with the appropriations. Since the war it has entered more and more into the "efficiency" angle of auditing. The report on the annual audit is sent to the national

Even such an authoritative state as the Soviet Union has found it necessary to devise some means of checking and controlling the bureaucracy. This is carried on through the 

Rabkrin, or the People's Commissariat of Workman-Peasant 

Inspection, which is officially co-ordinated with the control commission of the Communist party. The result is that checks on the bureaucracy are largely in the hands of party leaders. Reports and complaints are invited from individuals. The Rabkrin acts on its own initiative, however, investigating institutions according to a definite plan. 

On the basis of their investigations the party Control Commission and the Rabkrin make general studies of the problems of Soviet structure, and, as a department of government on equal standing with other commissariats, recommend legislative measures to “rationalize” the state administrative and economic apparatus. It is believed that the constant contact with the broader masses of workmen and peasants, guaranteed by the methods used in their work, will prevent these two associated bodies of party and government from themselves becoming bureaucratic. By wide publicity of its work and particularly of its findings, the Rabkrin has undoubtedly done much to reduce arbitrariness in administration." 

Legislative Investigating Committees 

Another means of securing both information and publicity relative to the course of administration is the special committee composed of members of the legislature. This does not refer to the junkets which make flying trips to state institutions, but rather to the group which is charged with investigating a particular problem, department or institution, and directed to bring

It is an effective check upon those bureaucratic tendencies which are bound to appear in every government. It keeps the experts responsive to a body of laymen. The question hour in the House of Commons is probably worth all that it costs the British taxpayer. As a palladium of his rights and liberties it is worthy to be ranked with trial by jury and the writ of habeas corpus.10

Our belief in the desirability of a formal separation between the legislature and executive has prevented a direct day-by-day contact between these branches. It has not been the custom for administrative officers to participate in legislative debate or address the chambers. In fact, a certain coolness has frequently greeted presidents and governors who have sought to deliver personally formal messages to joint sessions. Hence executive communications have usually been transmitted by means other than word of mouth. Many students have felt that this "stand-offishness" is unnatural, stilted, and detrimental to the best governmental interests. This has resulted in various proposals to have executive and administrative officers participate in debate and defend themselves on the floor of the legislature.11

The early advocates of integration were not blind to the dangers of placing administrative power in the hands of one man. To retain its advantages without its shortcomings they visioned the legislature as closely in touch with administration. 

This attitude is most aptly stated in the reports prepared by the

British have developed responsibility of the executive to the legislature since our independence. They made the executive responsible for the same reason that we made the legislature independent of him: to secure government responsible to popular control rather than an arbitrary and irresponsible royal power. 

The British followed the natural way while we embalmed a philosophical error in our constitutions. Many students feel that the resulting artificiality is responsible for much of our governmental difficulty.13 The British apply the theory of the separation of powers to their governmental organization more logically than we do. While executive, legislative, and judicial powers are placed in the same hands, they act in different capacities when exercising the several distinct powers.¹ Thus, the 

House of Lords sits alone as a court when hearing judicial appeals. The House of Commons refrains from invading the 

Minister's administrative domain even though this officer be a member of that body. This is what Mr. Willoughby refers to as a separation of powers organically, and union of powers personally.15

Popular Control of Executive 

The council-manager form of municipal government is overcoming the defects of earlier city charters in this respect. The manager is chosen by the elective council and is summarily responsible to it. That body can usually terminate his services. without delay or formality. At the same time, the theory behind

the code of ethics of the International City Managers' Association prohibits council interference in the manager's administrative problems. While this is an ideal not always achieved in practice, there is concrete evidence of progress toward a tradition of managerial autonomy in his own sphere. On the other hand, the manager is in constant contact with the council and entirely subservient to its wishes on policy matters. He attends its meetings and participates in its discussions. If he is adept at human relationships he can control the deliberations of the council so as to transact the utmost business with despatch and minus friction. He does this not through any legal authority, but by organizing the calendar and knowing his job so well that the council quite naturally defers to him. 

Here we have a preservation of the theory of the separation of governmental powers. The council is the policy-determining body, whereas the manager is in charge of administration. 

Yet the two are so linked in practice as to compel co-operation and automatically secure popular control of administration. 

Mr. Cottrell has admirably expressed the situation in referring to the manager as a controlled executive.16 Probably this development may point toward a more natural relationship between legislatures and administration in America. 

One method of maintaining popular control over administration is to have the principal departments headed by appointees of the political executive, that is, the mayor, governor, or president. This arrangement seeks to make the department heads responsive to those forces of popular opinion which affect the political executive. They are openly acknowledged as political officers whose terms expire simultaneously with that of the political executive. This is the system which quite generally prevails in the United States. It has much to commend it if applied only to the heads of a few well-ordered departments, but when hundreds and even thousands must retire at each change in political fortune, the system becomes vicious.

ernment.

One may well question, on the other hand, whether political department heads are useful or desirable in state and local gov- In Los Angeles County, where administration is directly responsible to an elected board of supervisors, all department heads except three elective officers are under civil service. 

The remarkably high calibre of these men, coupled with their apparent security of tenure, indicates that the political selection of county department heads is not essential. The same may be said of city department heads under a council-manager charter. 

It should be remembered, however, that in both these instances administration is directly under the control of a popularly elected board. Hence, the more intimate the connection of the legislature with administration from the standpoint of control, the less necessary it becomes to have political department heads. 

On the other hand, there is little question that some departments are more in need of political chiefs than others. Because of the fact that police departments are called upon to enforce sumptuary laws not popular with large minority groups, it seems inevitable that police departments be largely under political influence. The tremendously high turnover of chiefs of police seems to lend favor to the idea of a civilian commissioner, appointed by the mayor for a period co-terminous with his period of office. A fire department, however, is dealing with wellaccepted methods based on highly-developed technology. Passion, community strife, and the control of vicious human instincts come but slightly within its sphere. In the federal administration, the department of state, dealing as it does with high questions of foreign policy, will probably always require a political head. But why could not the post office be set up as a government corporation under a professional general manager? Hence, it is not easy to determine whether political department heads should be retained or abolished. Each governmental unit will have to dispose of the question in the light of its own needs and desires.

EXTERNAL CONTROLS Miscellaneous Control Devices 

By extra-governmental investigations is meant an examination of the processes of government by individuals or commissions not regularly engaged in the government being investigated. One of the most famous recent examples was the 

National Commission on Law Enforcement and Observance.18 

Many states set up citizen commissions to investigate a wide variety of administrative questions and report to the next session of the legislature. Sometimes these bodies engage a technical staff of considerable size and make thorough and exhaustive researches. Again, a technical agency with remote headquarters may be charged with the entire investigation. 

Such was the case with the survey of higher education recently made for the state of California by the Carnegie Foundation for the Advancement of Teaching. 10 In the 1931 legislature various local or regional interests were clamoring for sectional, state-supported, senior colleges, opposition coming from the University of California. The matter was temporarily disposed of by referring it for investigation to the Carnegie people who have but recently made their report. Such a report made by an outside technical agency may be more trustworthy than when a citizen commission has had a hand in it. The Royal Commission comes into existence when sufficient opinion is aroused to warrant an impartial investigation. If guided with imagination and courage, such commissions are admirable means for taking the nation to school.

Therefore ample time for thorough study is essential. There must be a total lack of the urgencies of the immediate, indifference to the compromises that may become pertinent after the problems are duly analyzed and alternative proposals for action suggested. Reference has been made elsewhere in this work to advisory councils or commissions. While they are not supposed to have any administrative authority, one of their major purposes would nevertheless be to serve as a control of administration. They would accomplish this purpose not by issuing orders, but by furnishing administration with outside technical advice. In addition, they would apprise administrators of the temper of public opinion on specific matters and projects. It is assumed that such procedure would have a healthy moral influence on the course of administration. Officials would naturally be hesitant to undertake projects which the advisory council had cautioned against. Wholesome publicity might also be expected to result from the council's deliberations. If no regular press releases resulted, or even though the council were to hold executive sessions, it would be impossible, nevertheless, to restrain recalcitrant members from voicing their indignation.

While the common law afforded certain extraordinary means of judicial procedure against officials, England and the United States have lagged behind the continent in providing redress to the injured citizen. Neither the federal government nor the states have been suable in tort without their own consent. 

An action against officials, while possible, generally proves unsatisfactory because of lack of property upon which to execute a judgment. There is indication, however, that American statute law is beginning to make provision for recovery by an injured citizen who has been damaged by a governmental act or operation. If such proves to be the case, the result cannot help but to make administration more sensitive at those points where citizen contacts might result in actions for damages. 

High civil officers can generally be removed by impeachment, which usually means a decree handed down by the upper house of the legislature after a lengthy hearing of a judicial nature. 

In England, impeachment has become obsolete because ministerial responsibility has furnished an easier and more summary F. Frankfurter, The Public and Its Government (Yale University Press, 1930), pp. 162–163. Quoted by permission of the publishers.

control. In the United States, impeachment can hardly be counted on as an instrument of current administrative control. 

Its use is slow and cumbersome. Usually only high crimes are subject to the impeachment process. Furthermore, to secure an impeachment requires judicial proof of wrongdoing, and administrative incompetence usually exists without any question of a criminal act. Hence, impeachment can be regarded only as an exceptional measure for externally controlling administrative acts. Nevertheless, one must always reckon with the threat of impeachment as a moral influence toward playing the game within the rules.

It is not easy to generalize on the value of the grand jury as an agency for public control of administration. Every observ ant citizen can doubtless recall, however, instances when a diligent grand jury has probed the affairs of a derelict official, resulting in indictment and conviction. This procedure, also, must be regarded as exceptional and extraordinary, and not as a method of summary control. Grand juries will naturally respond to the diligence of the prosecuting attorney, under whose control they are usually found to be. The writer's observation is that the Los Angeles County grand jury pays greater attention to administrative matters than elsewhere. is charged with conducting the annual independent audit for which purpose there is an appropriation for engaging professional auditors. The moral influence of the threat of grand jury investigation must have no inconsiderable part in holding potential wrongdoers in line. It

The recall, initiative, and referendum, unquestionably constitute effective forces for controlling administration. One might venture the statement, however, that their abuse is more detrimental than otherwise to administration. One of the best examples of such an abuse is the California city whose charter permits popular recall of the city manager. 23 This is an unwarranted confusion of politics and administration. importance. One often wonders, however, whether the California voter is not called upon to bear too great a burden in this respect. The student of administration, at any rate, frequently sees the electorate deciding at the polls on matters which are eventually going to cause considerable embarrassment to both administration and taxpayers. One example is the 1931 amendment to the Los Angeles city charter taking the pensions for policemen and firemen off the actuarial basis. Another is the recent amendment to the state constitution giving plenary power over fish and game to a commission independent of the administration. These are but chance examples where strong minority groups use direct legislation to serve their special interests. The countless multiplication of these instances results in popular obstruction to the processes of administration by and large. Hence, direct popular participation in government should be regarded as an emergency remedy, and not as a current and ordinary means of controlling administration. 

Effective public administration cannot endure long without watchful, intelligent, and militant citizen backing. So often. high-class reform groups have taken hold of a city only to find that the lay leaders elected to the council would become tired of the civic burden after a term or two. This would enable the machine politicians to return unheralded, but nevertheless firmly entrenched. One of the best examples of a citizen campaign to assure good administration is furnished by Cincinnati. 

There a citizen charter committee secured the adoption of charter changes by the sheer force of community organization. 

However, when the charter changes were placed in operation they were not left to run themselves. That is the secret of its success. The original charter group kept its organization intact for the purpose of electing council members favorably disposed toward the council-manager charter. This they have been able to do in four successive elections, with the result that Cincinnati is achieving an administrative record which is the envy of the entire nation. This is being accomplished, furthermore, in a city which in 1923 was ruled by a local party machine of the type so familiar to American cities. Such are the possi-

bilities where the new public administration receives intelligent and organized citizen support." 24 In closing this chapter on external controls of administration, too much emphasis cannot be laid upon the merit system. of personnel management (popularly known as civil service) as a control. The bogey of bureaucracy is not to be dreaded half so much as the paralyzing spoils of political machines. 

Experience in Germany and England demonstrate beyond a shadow of a doubt the inherent honesty of the professional civil service. To be sure, there is that tendency to protect class interests which enlarges staffs and allowances, perhaps beyond the dictates of needs at times. On the whole, however, the taxpayer and the citizen have much more to expect from the professional civil servant than from the spoils politician. This has been demonstrated many times by the advent of a city manager into cities which have been politics ridden for decades. At first the same services would be rendered at much lower cost. 

Then the public would gain confidence in its city government and demand this and that, even at acknowledged higher taxes. 

In other words, the citizen saw he was getting a fair return for his money and was willing to pay for it. The citizen will always get his greatest dollar's worth in honesty, effort, and service from a controlled professional civil service. PART II PERSONNEL

CHAPTER VIII  

99 Past public personnel practice in the United States has been largely unco-ordinated and decentralized. Haphazard employment and personnel policy has been widely accompanied by the so-called "spoils system.' Probably beginning in 1883, with the enactment of the Pendleton law establishing the federal civil service commission, the last fifty years have seen the development of the civil service movement. The pioneers of this cause deserve the undying gratitude of every living advocate of a skilled and professional public service. Especially is this true of the National Civil Service Reform League, which is still rendering excellent service in the cause of better government. Concrete results are evidenced by the existence of civil service commissions in some two hundred states, cities, and counties. If additional testimony is required, one need but point to the more than 400,000 federal officers and employees whose employment is the result of competitive examination.2 

In spite of this imposing achievement, however, the "civil service" movement has largely failed to give the governmental units of the United States unified and co-ordinated personnel administration. The duties of civil service commissions, in the past, have been concerned primarily with administering entrance tests. To the state and local units has been added the task of hearing appeals of removed or suspended employees, frequently with power of reinstatement. Emphasis has been placed on the so-called negative aspects of "civil service," the

thwarting of the spoilsman. There was a corresponding lack of attention to those technical phases of personnel administration by which contemporary practice is beginning to lay so much store. These include the maintenance of classification and compensation plans; control of time off, vacations, and sick leave; efficiency ratings, and the improvement of working conditions in general. Under the "civil service" régimes the chief object of the commission was to remain aloof from the politicians, whether the "ins" or the "outs." The principal weapons in achieving this end were competitive examinations and the quasi-judicial hearings of discharged workers. 

Without desiring to belittle the positive accomplishments of the civil service movement, one is compelled to say that it has failed to answer the personnel needs of today. The professional personnel administrator is impatient of the limitations placed on technical progress by his masters on the amateur commission. A great many intelligent laymen look upon "civil service" as a scheme to protect government employees from the normal consequences of indolence and incompetence. In no small number of cases these suspicions have been confirmed in practice by the experience of vigorous administrators, such as certain city managers, who have found difficult removal provisions disastrous to morale.

These criticisms are not aimed at the merit system. The term "merit system" must be distinguished from "civil service." A civil service commission may be in effect a centralized agency for dispensing patronage or for ratifying such patronage. The merit system goes much farther than the mere form of a personnel agency, however. It demands a certain spirit in conformity with the dictates of merit, an intelligently directed and well-supported effort to make appointments and promotions and fix compensation on the merit basis. A merit system may exist minus the usual trappings of "civil service." It is entirely conceivable that a rather thoroughgoing merit system could exist without a commission to give examinations. It has been actually demonstrated that a merit system can exist where a 3 In Cincinnati and the state of Wisconsin the commissions do not control examinations.

145 

In other discharged employee is given no legal recourse.* words, good personnel administration is not dependent on any magic formula known as "civil service." It results, rather, from an application of the merit spirit through a personnel program based on a desire to utilize the most reliable technical progress in the field.

Essentials of a Personnel Program 

What are the essential functions of a personnel program? 

Many would say that the first and most important is the formulation and maintenance of a classification plan. Adequate compensation schedules to fit into this plan would have to be developed, perhaps through co-operation with the budget agency. 

Then would come the adoption of approved methods of selection and promotion. This would naturally necessitate the maintenance of employment and re-employment lists, the making of certifications, and the requiring that appointment and the proper returns thereof shall be promptly made and duly recorded. The personnel agency should be in a position to regulate effectively all such matters as transfers, vacations and sick leaves, uniform hours of service, efficiency ratings, and the training of employees in the service. Furthermore, it should regulate procedure respecting the separation of employees from the service through removal, suspension, resignation, or retirement. Other miscellaneous activities of a personnel agency would include the establishment and maintenance of rules and regulations and the checking of payrolls. It should, however, possess rather extensive investigative authority, including power to make surveys of those aspects of departmental operations which are most directly concerned with the personnel program. From this should result the development of policies for the improvement of the working conditions of the service." Federal civil service, and County of Los Angeles, and many councilmanager cities.

Data based on the year 1926 have led to the estimate that 3,500,000 people worked full-time and part-time on governmental payrolls in the United States. They received $3,898,- 

649,000 in compensation, which amounted to 63% of the total operating budgets of the governmental units which employed them. These figures, which are thought to err on the side of conservatism, if at all, must surely emphasize the importance of the personnel program. They indicate the necessity of a wellordered régime for handling the housekeeping problems arising from the employment of thousands of persons. It is to meet this need that the new public personnel administration is coming into existence.

Not long ago a joint committee of the Civil Service Assembly and the International City Managers' Association sought a standard solution to the personnel problem in council-manager cities. Questionnaires were sent to all city managers. The representative of the Assembly on this committee was dismayed when a large percentage of the managers replied that they had no personnel problem. It was evident that the managers did have a personnel problem, but that it need not always be solved by orthodox methods, the solution for the smaller units often differing from that for the larger jurisdictions. What these managers meant was that in the smaller cities they had no need for civil service commissions, elaborate examinations, and the technical devices that ordinarily go with handling personnel on a large scale. These managers wanted to hold the personnel situation in their own hands. They felt that they were in close touch with the situation and doing an acceptable job. The adding of personnel machinery would be superfluous and might tie the managers' hands. Indeed, informed observers have more than once agreed that the managers have in many places inaugu- "W. E. rated a merit system without the disadvantages of civil service. 

The joint committee eventually came to substantially the same conclusion. In the smaller cities personnel activities were to be directly under the jurisdiction of the manager's office. As the number of persons employed approached one thousand it might be desirable for the manager to engage a skilled personnel director. The managers did have a personnel problem. It need not always be solved by orthodox methods, and the solution for small units may differ from that for larger jurisdictions. 

Is Personnel Administration an Extra Expense? 

A personnel program involves the expenditure of money. 

With it come technical specialists: examiners, classifiers and job analysts, psychologists and statisticians. Appropriations must be made for the support of personnel agencies. In criticism of such expenditures, one sometimes hears that they constitute a needless demand upon the taxpayers. If the various departments were allowed to handle their own personnel problems this expense would be avoided, so it is said. This charge can be readily answered, however. A good personnel agency should more than save its cost. The money which it spends is more than made up through economies coming from the proper application of approved personnel technique. An adequate classification of positions alone will form the basis for savings which should pay for the upkeep of a personnel agency, for here the central agency can act as a check upon departmental desire to hang on to unnecessary positions. It will help pay its own keep in countless other ways: checking payrolls; requiring proper records of employment; improving personnel through improved recruiting; not to speak of superior morale resulting from the operation of the merit principle. In the light of these considerations, the maintenance of a personnel program is not an extra expense. 

It is a positive necessity in the interest of economy. 

Denials of the Merit System The actual administration of the so-called "civil service" has not always been such as to excite the admiration of its

[Pt. II 

PERSONNEL 

friends. Because of indifference, public apathy, and the purely negative tactics of reformers, spoilsmen have been able frequently to mould the system to their own purposes. In other cases an uncreative and self-satisfied type of administration. has all but nullified the merit spirit. Some of the means of denying the merit system are set forth below. 

Provisional Appointments 

Regulations usually permit filling positions temporarily without examination. This is a wholly justifiable arrangement which, if properly handled, need not violate merit principles. 

When such appointments include from one-fifth to one-half of the service, and when they are continued indefinitely for months and years, they result in serious abuses. It is said that at one time forty per cent of the Chicago service consisted of such appointments. Recently in a particular state, 4,200 persons were found to be working in permanent civil service positions under temporary authorization and without civil service status. This amounted to one-third of the state service. An effort of the 

Director of Finance to correct this situation by requiring these incumbents to qualify in open competitive examinations aroused a hornet's nest of opposition. Tried testing procedure based on years of experimentation had to be abandoned for the time being. This all seems to have come about as the result of provisional appointees who had failed to pass the tests, bringing political pressure to bear upon the governor and members of the legislature. The Director of Finance was criticized for enforcing the law which had been evaded by previous administrators. 

Exemption of Specific Positions 

Civil service laws sometimes exempt specifically named positions, thereby removing them from "civil service" status. 

Chief among these are certain private secretaries, secret investigators, and lawyers. A chief political officer may need from time to time a person or two in whom he has implicit faith. 

There is no objection to permitting him to choose these associates without contacting the personnel agency. Any large num-

Ch. 8] 149 

ber of such positions, however, immediately raises the suspicion that they are created merely for spoils purposes. Positions requiring the qualifications of an attorney, for instance, are frequently exempted. Friends of the merit system have maintained that there is no good reason why legal personnel cannot be selected by the accepted competitive methods. It is also the usual practice to exempt "common" labor and certain other positions, usually highly technical or specialized ones. The reason for this is the difficulty of defining just what constitutes a “common laborer," which often leads to widespread abuses of the merit system. The exemption of such workers leaves open the door to "spoils" appointments in the lower ranking classified positions, such as clerical, trades-skilled and semi-skilledlaboratory, engineering, and others. The merit system is evaded by appointing persons as common laborers when the work is actually of such a nature that it should be ranked in the classified service. Obviously, frequent exemptions of positions from examination on the grounds of impracticability of competitive tests is an admission of one of two things-either the incompetency or the political-mindedness of the personnel agency. 

A third type of exemption is becoming increasingly popular. 

This is the practice of securing personal services on a contract basis, handled through the central purchasing agency or the legislative body. Such procedure originated in the securing of consulting service through contracts. It has recently been extended in many jurisdictions to cover a wide variety of positions. 

The exemption of common labor, non-competitive, and contract positions may so reduce the jurisdiction of a central personnel agency as to nullify its effectiveness. This condition may exist even where such an agency has a high professional reputation. 

Indeed, this very fact may serve to screen from ordinary notice its lack of jurisdiction.

Control of Promotions and Compensation 

The merit principle may be vitiated by lack of central control over promotions and compensation. In any jurisdiction there are a number of relatively low-grade positions. Political favorites can secure appointments to these posts by passing the

[Pt. II 

PERSONNEL 

required tests in a thoroughly above-board fashion. It is a common practice, however, to transfer or promote these favorites to more lucrative positions after they have once been regularly appointed to original minor posts. While the outward appearance of merit in appointment is maintained, for all practical purposes it is completely nullified. 

Withdrawal of Financial Support 

Personnel administration is generally handicapped by the lack of adequate financial support, but occasionally the spoilsman resorts to the drastic means of starving the merit system by withdrawing all support. This is the case in Kansas where the law still remains on the statute book, but the commission has not functioned for several years because no funds have been voted for its maintenance. A more recent occasion of this kind. was furnished in 1930 by the city of St. Louis where the appropriation of the personnel agency was cut from $29,739 to $3,739. It would seem that the reduction was due to the fact that various political factions, failing to secure the appointments desired, recriminated by accusing the agency of political manipulation and voting to stop its funds. The Bureau of Public 

Personnel Administration claims that five dollars per year per employee in the service is none too much for the support of a central personnel agency. Others would insist on ten dollars. per employee as an absolute minimum. No city should attempt a merit system without at least $5,000 per year as a minimum support, and preferably $10,000. The recent tendency to place personnel agencies under the administration in departments of finance has been due, partially at least, to the feeling that better financial support would be secured if the governor, mayor, or budget authorities were given more intimate control over personnel matters. 

Political Control 

Outright political control of commissioners, in the sense that the personnel agency is run as a spoils vehicle, may be relatively 

Mind Your Business (St. Louis Bureau of Municipal Research, May 

29, 1930).

Ch. 8] 

151 

rare.

Political influence is usually more subtle. It takes the form of financial starvation, perfunctory testing, and exemptions. It is quite possible, moreover, to have good personnel administration under a more or less partisan board. It often happens that commissioners with an avowedly partisan flavor will have a sincere belief in the fundamental purposes of the merit system. On certain matters of vital partisan concern they will bow under the pressure of their political chieftains. At the same time, the great mass of personnel work will go on with reasonable attention to accepted standards. Even civil service. commissions desiring to enforce the merit spirit will find themselves thwarted by the contamination of a patronage environment. One of the irritating aspects of federal personnel administration is the tendency of discharged or disaffected employees to seek the intervention of Congressmen. A disgruntled individual can frequently create sufficient stir to get a Congressman to take a personal interest in his case. This often leads the department to overlook delinquencies in individual efficiency in order to avoid unpleasantries. Such a situation is a direct product of the widely prevalent "patronage mind" known in France, where it probably reaches its supreme fruition, as deputantism. The elected representative is an intermediary between his constituents and the administration. He is supposed to get them jobs, see that they retain them afterwards, obtain special pensions, and see that his district is not the object of unfavorable discrimination in the distribution of official favors and governmental largesse. In private conversation with politicians one frequently learns that activity of this nature is distasteful to them and of doubtful political value. Yet it must possess tremendous power to build up machines and personal followings. Deputantism is a universal symptom of what is probably the chief weakness of democracy. 

The British and the French have, however, succeeded in retaining democracy while at the same time developing professional standards for the civil service. Prior to the middle of the nine- 

See William E. Mosher's reference to the "patronage committee" in

L. D. Upson, (Ed.), The Government of Cincinnati and Hamilton County (City Survey Committee, Cincinnati, 1924), p. 153.

teenth century the British civil service was an object of patronage for the British politicians. The government service became a haven of refuge for young men who had no chance of success in the open competition of the legal, medical, and mercantile professions. A series of developments in the third quarter of that century have led to the virtual elimination of the more objectionable forms of patronage and the substitution of a rigorous merit system. It has been said that the development of democracy itself brought this change. The British upper classes, alarmed at the broadening of suffrage, desired to preserve the higher administrative posts for their own kind. This they did by enacting and promulgating the several civil service measures which sought to reserve the direction of administration to upper class competence. Deputantism has been of negligible importance in British democracy largely because of the lack of influence in the individual member of the House of Commons. The cabinet system renders the member impotent except as a cog in the party machine. The entire British system and tradition is built to resist patronage. Witness the lack of an organized veterans' movement even remotely comparing with that in the United States. In France, on the other hand, a large portion of the deputy's time is devoted to intervening with departments in the interests of his constituents. It is his duty to call on ministers and write many letters soliciting employment, especially in the state supported schools. The French mind, however, imagines the deputy's influence in appointments to be much greater than it is in fact. Deputantism in personnel matters now results in a great deal of lost motion. A merit system of appointment has developed, but the old practice of writing letters persists. Both the appointing officer and the deputy carry it on as a window dressing to satisfy the great French public which expects its deputies to produce jobs. If the applicant fails in his examination the deputy produces a splendidly worded letter from the minister expressing regret. 

If an appointment results, the deputy also produces a letter in which the minister seems to say that success has been due to the deputy's intervention. The result is a smoke screen which cloaks merit appointments in a setting which also satisfies the

Ch. 8] 

153 

average Frenchman's demand that his deputy intervene for him.

Educational Requirements 

It frequently happens that members of city councils and civil service commissions are persons who have attained their positions in the world without much formal education. They feel that mere school attendance is no criterion for assuring performance in any particular post. There is constant political pressure on them to lower educational requirements for entrance to examinations. Along with this goes a resistance to the introduction of the newer type psychological tests. It is demanded that tests be "practical." This cry is frequently a political subterfuge for lowering recruiting standards.

Opposition of Professional Groups 

Certain professional groups have voiced opposition to civil service regulations. Among them have been the city managers, librarians, and educators. They have felt that their own system of selection has been superior to that of the local civil service commission, and they have too frequently been correct in this assertion. This constitutes a permanent indictment of central personnel management. The personnel group realizes that many of the indictments of past practice are valid. One spokesman, referring to the disaffection of the library group, has explained it as follows: 

All too frequently they find themselves irked by what seem to them foolish requirements as to local residence for professional librarians who cannot be trained locally; by regulations as to annual leaves which deprive them of the thirty days of vacation with pay on which they set great store; by selective tests which do not command their respect; and by rules and regulations intended to thwart the spoilsman, but which also hamper the able administrator with the best intentions." 

Capitulations to the demands of other interest groups not professional in nature may have the effect of denying the merit principle. It is felt by many that veterans' preference is inimi- 

Editorial, "The Status of the Merit System," Public Personnel Studies (November, 1928), Vol. VI, No. 11, p. 221.

cal to the best interests of good personnel administration. This matter will be treated at greater length later. 

In an editorial entitled "Denials of the Merit Principle," the Bureau of Public Personnel Administration has summarized the hazards of good personnel administration. Among these are the large number of "exempt" positions, exceeding in some counties, states, and cities the number in the classified service. 

Veterans' preference and the large number of temporary and emergency appointments operate against the merit principle.

Artificial handicaps are too often placed upon women. Finally, the merit principle is all too frequently disregarded in such matters as granting leaves of absence, determining the order of layoff when forces must be reduced because of lack of work or funds, or making removals.

Organization 

The form of organization that should be adopted for the personnel agency is a matter on which general agreement has not yet been reached, either among students or among administrators themselves. The forms taken by civil service commission structure in practice are too numerous for fruitful enumeration here. Suffice it to say that the typical central personnel agency has been headed by a commission appointed for overlapping terms by the chief executive with the affirmation of the council or senate. This body takes general charge of the personnel matters placed within its jurisdiction. Of late years there has been a reaction away from the commission in favor of a single-headed personnel agency placed directly in the administration. The fact remains, however, that good personnel administration is found to exist under various types of organization. Without belittling the importance of organization, the quality of personnel administration is probably more dependent upon the sincerity, vigor, and competence of the staff than upon any other factor. 10

Dissatisfaction with the civil service commission, on the 

10 Editorial, "Improving Public Personnel Administration," Public Per sonnel Studies (May, 1930), Vol. VIII, No. 5, pp. 65-66.

other hand, has become too widespread to deny the importance of organization problems. Probably the chief indictment against the commissioners has been their tendency to control minutely the technical details of administration. Some ap- pointments of commission members have been purely political in nature and intent. In such cases the commission would come under the control of persons lukewarm, if not hostile, to the merit principle. All too seldom have people of experience in the management field found their way into these bodies. Indeed, distinction in the community is rarely a basis for selection; mediocrity is more often the rule. In those cases where persons friendly to merit principles do receive appointment they frequently take an attitude which militates against merit in. practice. They regard themselves as the protectors of the employees in all removal and discipline cases. This factor, more than any other, has served to alienate the city managers, many of whom have been thwarted by civil service commissions in attempting to remove employees whom they deemed insubordinate and incompetent. This protectionist complex of "civil service" has tended to cause many sincere friends of the merit system to become critics of it. For this situation the commission cannot escape the chief blame whether it be just or unjust. 

There has been a reaction against commission control of personnel administration. There is a gradual departure from the old conception that civil service is an inviolable domain to be shielded from the encroachments of governors, mayors, and city managers. The new personnel administration is to be an integral part of the central administrative machine. In many cases it is to be intimately tied in with the budget agency, if not an actual part of it. This is dictated by the fact that so many phases of personnel work are of a budgetary control nature. Classification of duties and formulation of the compensation plan are of just as much concern to the budget people as to personnel administrators. Yet they are coming to be recognized as the most effective means of personnel control. 

Other personnel activities possessing a marked budgetary angle include such items as sick leave, vacations, retirement pensions, and checking payrolls. Hence, the alliance of the personnel

[Pt. II 

PERSONNEL 

agency with the financial offices is no stilted or artificial move. 

It is the result of a perfectly natural grouping. 

Most people are accustomed to the old type "civil service" wherein an independent commission was supposed to protect the classified service from the spoilsmen. Many will, therefore, object to placing all personnel matters directly under the mayor, governor, or city manager. In reply, the proponents of the new movement would say that political influences have on countless occasions nullified the merit system under the old civil service institutions, in spite of all legal safeguards. They furthermore declare that personnel officers will be no more at the mercy of politics than under the old arrangements. On the contrary, they may be able to gain the confidence of governors or mayors by working with them instead of—in the eyes of the mayor or governor-at cross purposes. One of the favorite ways of nullifying civil service laws in the past was by starving the personnel agency financially. It is thought that more adequate support will result from connection with the chief executive's budget agency. Experience has tended to show that alliance with the executive has given the personnel agency far more authority and real power than it ever had before. There is also a growing opinion that in those communities where civil service is an accepted institution, the danger from spoils constitutes one of the lesser hazards of public personnel administration. 

Instead of standing aloof from the departments as an ever-suspicious watch dog, the new personnel agency is to be a friendly guide and technical adviser to them. In this capacity it will attempt to correct faulty classification and compensation plans, smug satisfaction with the adequacy of shop-worn means of testing, and general complacency relative to loose methods of administration. These conditions may exist without spoils influence, and they are thought by many to constitute the real enemies to civil service.

The actual organization of public personnel agencies takes great diversity of form. The Report of the Conference Committee on the Merit System, published by the National Municipal League in 1926, recognized no less than six types. The common form is the bipartisan appointed commission or board hav-

Ch. 8] 157 

ing an odd number of members with overlapping terms. The second type calls for an appointed part-time commission or board consisting of an odd number of members with a full-time technical administrative expert who is by statute the executive officer of the board or commission. The third is an appointed bipartisan commission or board with one active full-time member and two associate part-time members. The fourth is an appointive commission consisting of one person; the fifth, a commission or board consisting of one person chosen through competitive tests; and the sixth, a commission or board with an active full-time executive member selected by competitive tests and two appointed and elected associate members." This by no means exhausts the possible ways of organizing a personnel agency. 

It is believed possible, however, to reduce the general classification to three. These are: the commission type; the personnel director under the chief administrative officer with a quasilegislative and (or) quasi-judicial commission; and the single headed type with no commission. The following pages will set forth the general characteristics of these types of organization. 

Commission Type 

By far the most common organization of a personnel agency is, of course, that wherein an appointive commission exercises control. This commission will consist of three (or five) members appointed by the President, governor, or mayor with the affirmation of the senate or the city council. Terms will overlap, only one member retiring in any one year. Usually there is a requirement that two political parties must be represented on the commission. In the county of Los Angeles, three political parties must be represented, while in the City of Los Angeles the commission is, at least nominally, non-partisan. In the larger services the commission is aided by a full-time technical administrator frequently known as the secretary and (or) chief examiner. The members of the commission themselves "O. C. Short, The Merit System in Government (Civil Service Assn. of

rarely devote full time to the service. They do, nevertheless, frequently meddle with administrative matters. They usually have the authority to direct the details of administration if they so desire. It is this interference with administration by laymen which produces most dissatisfaction with a personnel agency headed by a commission.
