The second general type of personnel agency embodies a director of personnel directly under the control of the chief executive, chief administrative officer, director of finance, or manager.

This official is in charge of the technical and purely administrative aspects of personnel work. With respect to these phases he is effectively insulated from interference by the commission. The commission, on the other hand, is given certain quasi-legislative and quasi-judicial duties. 

An example of this type of arrangement is offered in the Wisconsin personnel law of 1929. That statute sets up a per-

The Single-Headed Type 

A third general type of public personnel agency has no board. 

It is headed by a single officer, frequently known as the director of personnel, who is charged with the administration of those activities commonly appertaining to a central personnel agency.

City managers have frequently expressed impatience and dissatisfaction with certain aspects of "civil service" as they have seen it practiced. At some of the earlier annual conferences of the International City Managers' Association discussion of the subject bordered on antagonism. Investigation usually revealed that the managers who thus expressed their hostility had encountered difficulty in seeking to remove employees whom they deemed incompetent, and in some cases absolutely disloyal. Hearings before the civil service commission had frequently created tense situations as the result of the reinstatement of men removed by the manager. 

More often than not this situation would arise in the police department, which is always the manager's most prolific source of worry. 

It was seen that this situation stood in the way of a happy understanding between professional personnel administrators and city managers. In 1929-1930 a joint committee of the two groups sought to study the problem. Composed of John N. Edy, now manager of Dallas, Texas, and Clifford N. Amsden, now secretary and chief examiner of the Los Angeles County Civil Service Commission, it reported in 1930. The recommendation drew largely on a tentative report of a committee working on the personnel provisions of a then forthcoming edition of the National Municipal League's Model City Charter.¹¹ 

In general, it was suggested that all aspects of personnel administration should be left largely to the direction of the manager in the smaller cities. He was to prepare rules governing personnel procedure and present them to the council for adoption. He might appoint some one "familiar with the science and skilled in the art of personnel administration" to assist him.

Today, the better type of city manager is keenly appreciative of the good that may result from professional personnel administration. One will still find him quite sensitive, however, to the embarrassment that may accrue from difficult removal provisions under "civil service."

Another organization problem presents itself when individual departments become so large that they present personnel problems in themselves. Each considerable sub-unit should have its own personnel officer. He should be an able executive with a service-wide point of view, whose duties are to see that individual grievances and needs are sympathetically dealt with. 

While such a person should be under departmental administrative control, he should nevertheless be in intimate contact with the central personnel agency at all times. Indeed, much of the latter unit's normal relationship to the departments would be through the channels of their several personnel officers. These officials should not be mere clerks or secretaries detailed to handle personnel routine in addition to their regular duties. 

They should be professionals "skilled in the art and trained in the science" of personnel methods. Mr. Feldman observes that the federal service is singularly lacking in personnel executives of this type, there being not more than six in Washington.' A similar observation could undoubtedly be made for most state, county, and municipal units.

The British Treasury 

An example of how a central personnel agency might work is furnished by the British Treasury which exercises effective supervision over all personnel matters. While there is a civil service commission, it is concerned almost entirely with giving examinations. The commission is not even its own master in this sphere. The Treasury must approve all examinations as to subject, content, preliminary standards for qualifications of applicants, questions, methods of conduct, and time and place of examination. It must also approve eligible lists prepared by the commission as well as appointments made by the departments from such lists. It can readily be seen, therefore, that the civil service commission is hedged in on all sides by Treasury control. 

The Treasury also has direct supervision over problems of classification, salary, and terms and conditions of service.21 While the British Treasury system in its entirety may not be adaptable to American environment, there is no denying that it has certain merits which could be adapted to the federal situation as far as the integration of personnel administration is concerned.

Professional Organizations

The official organization for those interested in public personnel work is the Civil Service Assembly of the United States and Canada. This is a very loosely organized group consisting of lay commissioners and professional administrators from some two or three hundred jurisdictions over the United States and Canada.22 The Assembly's existence is usually manifested by an annual meeting held in various large cities, and by holding not more than four regional meetings each year. Membership is on the basis of personnel agencies, with dues graduated according to the population of the area each member agency serves. Membership of individuals not attached to a member agency is voted by a majority of the Assembly. 

Very closely associated with this group was the Bureau of 

Public Personnel Administration. Originally located in Wash ington, D. C., the Bureau moved later to a location adjacent to the University of Chicago campus. For several years the 

Bureau was financed through grants by Mr. John D. Rockefeller, Jr. For about eight years ending in 1931 it published a technical monthly journal named Public Personnel Studies. 

The Bureau also made studies of specific personnel problems which were sometimes published in technical pamphlets and volumes. Considerable standardized and unstandardized test material was developed and sold by the Bureau. Personnel agencies could write to the Bureau for advice on a wide variety of matters, and members of the staff were available for consultation on such subjects as classification and compensation plans. 

There was a very intimate relationship between the Bureau and the Civil Service Assembly, the latter contributing toward the support of the former. 

After a period of inactivity, beginning about 1931, the Bureau of Public Personnel Administration ceased to exist officially in June, 1934, turning its assets and equipment over to the Civil Service Assembly of the United States and Canada. 

A headquarters office of the Assembly is located with the other organizations adjacent to the University of Chicago. It will 

The constitution of the Assembly is published in Public Personnel 

Studies (October, 1928), Vol. VI, No. 10, pp. 209-211.

[Pt. II

carry on the research, experimentation, publication, and consultation work of the Bureau. 

The development of these professional organizations augurs well for the future of scientific public personnel administration in the United States. The growth of professional consciousness undoubtedly leads to higher standards of honesty and efficiency. The professional who sees an assured and honorable career before him is much less likely to risk his reputation in questionable undertakings than a politician who knows his days to be numbered. Furthermore, a part, and frequently a large part, of the professional's compensation is the intangible income derived from mere enjoyment of one's work. The more administrative processes come into the hands of men who are not mere jobholders, the sooner will public service be manned by individuals with a high sense of personal honor and honesty. That a professional civil service is conducive to honesty is attested by the traditions of both the British and German bureaucracies. 

Not so long ago some British Treasury officials were discharged for speculating in foreign exchange on the basis of knowledge secured in the course of official duties. The incident caused much scandal and received widespread comment, because such dereliction on the part of a British civil servant was rare. One wonders whether American public opinion would have condemned these officials. Our utter individualism in such matters would undoubtedly have led many to justify their action as a "smart" move. They were on the "inside" and did what any astute person would have done under similar circumstances. 

Perhaps such a conclusion is unfair to our growing sense of social responsibility in such matters. Yet it cannot be denied that such a philosophy pervaded a large section of the American population during that wild scramble for wealth at any cost, from 1919 to 1929.

Although there may have been weaknesses in the old German civil service, they did not arise from dishonesty and corruption. 

Most observers agree, moreover, that the German civil service was universally efficient. One of the chief counts of the "Nazis" against the Republic was that the spoils system had crept in and was corrupting the old standards of honor and hon-

Ch. 8] 167 

esty. Whether this accusation is false or correct cannot be definitely ascertained at this writing. The fact that Hitler could make political capital of it indicates, however, that a professional bureaucracy may secure a place in the confidence of the masses. 

In Germany the bureaucracy possessed social attitudes which motivated towards reaction. It was of the old régime, never whole-heartedly embracing the Republic. The problem of the 

United States is to nurture a bureaucracy which will possess social vision, efficiency, honesty, and professional outlook.23 

The last three characteristics are inseparable. For that reason, the development of technical and professional associations is to be desired and encouraged.

CHAPTER IX  

There are in general two philosophies of public personnel recruiting, one followed for the most part in Europe, the other prevalent in the United States. The European practice emphasizes entry of the most talented youth of the land into an honored governmental career at an early age, selection being based on academic examinations of a cultural and broad fundamental nature rather than upon specific administrative tasks. Sufficient salary, perquisites, and social position have attached to the civil service to insure a stream of high grade recruits. In the 

United States, on the other hand, a combination of circumstances has conspired to emphasize the so-called practical aspects of recruiting. The Jacksonian, equalitarian political doctrine has been sufficiently strong to retard efforts to establish high entry standards. Political forces have worked in the direction of keeping the job-holding qualifications low enough to satisfy the greatest possible number. The higher directing positions are predominantly subject to political appointment. Because every entry examination requires a certain minimum of experience, willing and qualified youths are discouraged from choosing a governmental career. The resulting mediocrity has created a remarkably low prestige value for all branches of governmental service, whether federal, state, or local. Even those who would like to believe otherwise must admit the truth of the situation. Up until the 1929 depression the public service in general had little attraction for the really accomplished section of American humanity, by whatever standards measured. 

Civil service laws usually contain a clause requiring tests to be practical. There are few, if any, countries where formal education has had such low prestige for entry into the public service. The men making the civil service laws have frequently 170

Ch. 9] 171 

been of the "self-made" variety, distrusting attempts to establish scholarship standards. Much of this is sincere emulation of equalitarian political doctrine. On the other occasions the attempt to make tests "practical" has been a smoke screen to keep them from being too effective. For instance, few public personnel agencies today dare utilize even a major portion of known advances in testing technique. If they did so, the political repercussions would shake them out of office. This does not necessarily mean that these personnel agencies are politically managed. It simply means that the man in the street is not willing to permit his public personnel agency to experiment with "new-fangled" ideas of testing which do not place him or his friends on employment lists. It is extremely easy to call on one's councilman and complain about a so-called intelligence test which was thought to have no possible relation to driving a fire truck. And certain councilmen will be very happy to institute an inquiry into testing methods-especially if the personnel agency has been rather strait-laced in resisting overtures for preferment of councilmanic nominees for positions. The result is that the average public personnel agency prefers to let well enough alone and avoid the embarrassment frequently resulting from the introduction of innovations. The public expects these civil service agencies to know how to select the best men for the jobs. Too much experimentation would be interpreted as indecision and weakness. The best way to live and let live is to do the best one can with testing methods traditionally used in the jurisdiction, with a cautious advance here and there from time to time when sure of one's ground. 

The European practice, British as well as continental, has been to recruit for the higher branches of the civil service from the aristocracy and upper middle class. University graduates have come from these groups to a greater extent than in the United States. Entry to the higher civil service posts is based largely upon examinations of a purely academic nature. In 

England the tests for positions in the administrative class have been based on the largely classical Oxford and Cambridge "honors" courses. The result has been that graduates of these institutions have dominated the upper branches of the

[Pt. II 

PERSONNEL 

permanent service. A similar practice prevails in France and 

Germany. Even for the sub-executive and clerical services, English recruitment is through a purely academic examination based on the achievement presumed for the British school system at the age of appointment. Entry occurs during the late 'teens or early twenties. American writers are accustomed to admire the British recruiting system based on early entry after academic tests. They compare it favorably with what they interpret to be the American practice of testing for job performance on the basis of knowledge of how to perform a specific task. American public personnel administrators rather resent this comparison as being only a half-truth. They claim that the writers are segregating a small part of the British administration and generalizing as to recruiting methods for the entire service. This gives a distorted impression. The fact is, so they say, the great mass of British examinations are of a specialized nature, designed to test the applicant's ability to perform specific technical tasks. This applies to such positions as engineer, stenographer, draftsman, plumber, mechanic, and the mine-run of skilled or semi-skilled callings which make up the backbone of any public service.

There is no fundamental conflict between the writers and personnel technicians on this point. A certain element of truth prevails in the statement that American tests have been too closely aimed at job technology when they could more profitably have measured general fitness. Why should a police recruit be expected to know the criminal code, for instance? 

The American personnel group is quite justified, however, in objecting to the making of this single point the basis for a comparison unfavorable to them. A fairer measure for comparison of British and American services is an entirely different consideration, which, however, lies at the basis of the controversy. 

The British have created administrative and executive classes with recruitment confined to young men who have achieved certain academic standards. In America there is no such thing as an administrative or executive class as such, although the work of the Personnel Classification Board aimed at such a goal for the federal service. The higher administrative and executive

Ch. 173 

offices in America are usually political, whether elective or appointive. Where they are under civil service, progress toward them is by way of an uncertain route, with academic attainment often playing an inconsiderable, and sometimes negative part. There is no clearly marked avenue in the United 

States whereby young people graduating from a university may look forward to a well-defined career in the civil service. This does not mean that many of them do not eventually find their way there; they do, but usually after a circuitous route involving experience elsewhere. Hence, there is good reason to suspect that the most talented of American university youth does not enter the public service.

The American recruiting system is stacked heavily against the promising youngster and in favor of the mediocre mature person. This is due to the fact that entry to tests requires specific periods of experience in work similar to the position for which the test is given. There is no objection to this requirement of experience if some classification were provided which would permit the inexperienced graduate to enter the service in an apprentice capacity. This is just what the British, French, and Germans have done; and it is what American political scientists have admired in those services. What is needed in America is the creation of an administrative and executive class, progress toward which might be anticipated by a class of college graduate apprentices each year. The Rogers Act creating the 

Foreign Service is a step in the right direction. An American administrative class could not, of course, exclude those noncollege men who have demonstrated fitness by performance. 'In the fall of 1934 the United States Civil Service Commission announced an examination open to recent graduates or those about to graduate from colleges of liberal arts. The test was general in nature and based upon a liberal education rather than on job technology. A section of the test also sought to take cognizance of personal characteristics. About 3,500 out of 8,500 who took the test were placed on an eligible list. Originally announced as a test for the Commission's own position of junior personnel examiner at $1,620 per year, the eligible register was offered to other departments for a wide variety of positions in the salary range from $1,400 to $1,600. Appointments from it are being made throughout the federal service. 

It is contemplated that a similar examination will be repeated periodically. 

This innovation promises to open career opportunities in the federal service for the graduate of the liberal arts college.

[Pt. II 

The American fear of scholastic attainment in positions of trust and responsibility is unfounded in fact. The person who has achieved academic success is not the diffident and eccentric fool of caricature. The net result of several studies made in recent years indicates quite emphatically that the higher the achievement in college studies the greater the probability of success in after life.2 

W. S. Gifford of the American Telephone and Telegraph

Company surveyed the achievement of hundreds of college men in his organization. Those in the top third of their classes were receiving higher salaries than those in the second third, and those in the second third of their classes were receiving higher salaries than those in the lowest third. Most readers will be aware of the fact that entry to the Phi Beta Kappa Society is based almost entirely upon scholastic attainment during the undergraduate years of college. In 1927 there appeared some statistics revealing this organization's contribution to public life. 

When the first 29 persons were selected for the Hall of Fame in 1900, no less than 13 were members of Phi Beta Kappa. The contribution to national eminence included II presidents (now 

12 with Franklin Roosevelt), 5 of the 10 Chief Justices, 26 of the 63 Supreme Court Justices; and 18 of 40 Secretaries of

State. In the then current issue of Who's Who roughly one out of four and one-half were members of Phi Beta Kappa. 

Surely the nation is losing by not providing a means of convenient entry to its permanent civil service for such a prolific reservoir of capable manhood and womanhood.

Composed of department heads, and headed by the president of the Civil Service Commission, it is designed to deal more effectively with the entire federal personnel problem. 

These events indicate that the federal authorities are perhaps more keenly aware than ever before of the advantages of coordinating the work of the universities and the federal service.

One should not infer from the foregoing paragraphs that the European plan of academic tests is the ultimate answer to American recruiting problems. As a matter of fact, it is sometimes questioned whether the members of the British administrative class are not somewhat handicapped by their upper class experience and outlook. It is likely that their knowledge of society has come from books, offices, and artificial glimpses of life from sheltered and protected vantage points. Those who have this criticism to offer feel that the highest group of civil servants should have the life experiences, environment, and background common to a larger section of the nation. The intricacies of the civil service in a technical age demand, moreover, some emphasis on management in the pre-entry phase of training, although many British would deny this. The new American university education in public administration is laying considerable emphasis on management, probably at the expense of desirable broad fundamentals. In the United States the tests of the future will undoubtedly be a compromise between the British concept of "testing for the service" and the American practice of "testing for the job." Our equalitarian political doctrine is so strong that it will always be difficult to maintain high educational qualifications as flat prerequisites for entry. The average American is far from being convinced that competence is limited to educated classes. The new psychological approach to the discovery of mental and personality traits may prove to be far superior to all academic and educational standards of the past. The new experimental psychology is attempting to discover what goes to make up individual competence and how to detect it in specific persons. In this field, American personnel agencies are said to have gone much further than have British civil service tests.*

Types of Tests 

The traditional type of written test is known to the college student as an essay examination and to the personnel examiner as a free answer test. Each testee is given a typed or mimeographed paper containing a number of questions. He is expected to read and analyze each question and then write his answer on a separate piece of paper. Until recently this variety of test was used by all civil service commissions for the intermediate classes of positions. The free answer test is thought by many to place a premium on ease of written expression and facility with pen or pencil, whereas these qualifications may have no relation whatsoever to ability to perform on many jobs. Certain persons may have superior aptitudes and yet be unable to express themselves satisfactorily. Difficulties in spelling, punctuation, and paragraphing are common in people with high degrees of competence. Others fail to record well-known information due to a form of stage fright or to mechanical difficulties in using the pen. Administrative considerations raise further objections to free answer tests. They must be graded by high-salaried examiners, whereas the newer tests are easily and accurately scored by low-salaried clerks. Probably the major count against free answer tests, however, is their lack of objectivity. It has been found that no two readers will score a given test with equal results, and frequently the scores vary so widely as to cause skepticism relative to the test's value. It should not be concluded from this discussion that the free answer test has been entirely abandoned. Some agencies use it a great deal more than others; but practically all utilize it for certain types of positions, particularly where the subject matter is professional and technical in its nature and the number of For the opinion on these matters of the Commission of Inquiry on 

Public Service Personnel see its report entitled Better Government Person nel (Whittlesey House, McGraw-Hill Book Co., Inc., 1935), pp. 25-36, 79 ff.

Ch. 179 

testees relatively few. Examination for executive and supervisory positions make frequent use of this type of test. A few free answer questions are often included in conjunction with other means of testing.

There is no question, however, that since 1920 (if an arbitrary date must be set) the free answer test has been widely displaced by the newer short answer varieties. The usual types are: the true-false, where the testee is required to indicate whether a statement is correct or incorrect; the multiple choice, where he is asked to select the correct answer or answers from a series; and the completion, requiring him to supply a missing word or phrase. The tests are usually mimeographed, a copy going to each testee. Each short answer test should contain from one hundred to two hundred questions if a proper distribution of abilities is to be secured. In other words, a longer list of questions will tend to eliminate elements of chance and secure a better distribution of scores for the group tested. It is definitely known that in any average group of human beings, abilities will be distributed according to what has come to be known as the normal distribution curve.

A certain small percentage will be superior; a still larger percentage above average; and the great middle group will demonstrate average capacities. Others will be slightly below average, and the small remainder will exhibit a decided inferiority. It is known that where the sampling is large enough, both as to the extent of the test and the number of testees, a normal distribution curve will result. The grades of those taking the test will fall into the categories described. When plotted on a graph they will tend to form a curve as shown on page 235. From this comes the term "biological curve." If a given test presents a curve varying markedly from the normal with an abnormal proportion of high or low grades, there is immediate reason for suspecting its validity.

The short answer test has become popular for several reasons. 

In the first place, it is much more objective than the older forms of examination. The testees are graded in accordance with a standard of measurement which can be applied to all with equal fairness. There is but one way of answering a question cor-

[Pt. II 

PERSONNEL 

rectly. The varying judgment of readers and scorers cannot enter to confuse comparative grades. An answer is either entirely correct or all wrong. There is no variant in between, left to the scorer's discretion. This tends to establish the confidence of both examiner and testee. The second chief advantage is that short answer tests will cover a much more extensive field in a shorter time. Instead of spending several hours on six to twelve topics, in a hit and miss essay, the testee's grasp of a larger number of problems can be explored. The examiner is thus enabled to secure a more accurate cross-section of the applicant's fitness for the job. In the third place, for large groups and assembled tests are now given to thousands at a time-short answer tests are cheaper to administer. If given the proper keys and stencils, unskilled junior clerks can score them with facility. Fourthly, and most important, short answer tests are thought to be more reliable. However, it is not yet possible to present unanswerable proof of validity." 

This is largely due to the fact that no extensive study has been made of the correlation between test scores and job performance. It is known in a general way, however, that the introduction of short answer tests has tended to produce a higher type recruit.

The last decade has also seen a more widespread use of intelligence tests. During the World War, the army of the 

United States sought to devise some means of classification for the hordes of inexperienced material with which it had to deal. 

This resulted in the popularization of the Alpha test, which is probably more widely used than any other intelligence test for public personnel purposes today. Psychologists do not seem to have fully agreed on a definition of intelligence. It has been said to consist of brightness, smartness, brains, keenness, and A test is reliable if it measures accurately whatever it happens to measure; it is valid if it measures those traits, abilities, aptitudes, and skills which it is designed to measure. Public personnel technicians sometimes speak of "scoring reliability," a term which has a different meaning. A test has scoring reliability when several examiners achieve substantially the same results in scoring it. alertness. Its opposites are stupidity, dullness, inability to catch on and understand, inability to learn rapidly, and inability to face novel situations with resourcefulness.8 

Intelligence testers would like to believe that they are examining for innate and hereditary qualities. In this sense intelligence is supposed to be something distinct from acquired knowledge. There is some evidence to show, however, that school children can materially improve successive scores by being drilled on the subject matter of a given test." Nevertheless, experience with the Army Alpha in public personnel work indicates that testees do not generally improve their grades in successive attempts. The score achieved on the intelligence test is expressed in terms of the Intelligence Quotient, commonly referred to as the "I.Q." It is indicative of mental age, but this term should be used with caution. Consternation once resulted from reports that the average mental age of Americans was fourteen years. The mental testers regard mental maturity as being achieved at fourteen to sixteen years. There is not exact agreement as to what the I.Q. means in terms of mental development. Probably a fairly general consensus of opinion is that 69 and below represented feeble-mindedness; 

90 to 110 normal; and anything above 130, quite superior. 

The intelligence quotient is not used in scoring intelligence tests for public personnel administration, the reason given being that the I.Q. method is not adapted to testing adults. The I.Q. is figured on the basis of mental age as compared to chronological age. Thus if a child has a chronological age of 8 and a mental age of 10 the I.Q. is 125, for 10 is 125 per cent of 8.

The public personnel people have not capitulated to the conclusion that mental growth ends at 16 or thereabouts. The 

Army Alpha, which is the intelligence test most widely used by public personnel agencies, has a numerical scoring of zero to 212. The scores achieved can be converted into figures which

In public personnel work the intelligence test is used to advantage in a number of positions where the qualities desired are general rather than specific. There are a number of positions where mental alertness is a leading requisite. The Army 

Alpha has fully demonstrated its adequacy for selecting policemen and firemen. In one large city a recent test for firemen was confined to the physical and Alpha tests. The chief afterwards stated that it was the best appointment list he ever secured. However, there is a political hazard in the use of intelligence tests. They constitute convenient targets for that numerous element which seeks to block higher standards for entry to the public service. This is probably the principal reason for the wider use of the Alpha as against other intelligence tests. It became known to thousands in the army, and because of that fact it bears a certain degree of authority and prestige denied to perhaps superior tests more recently developed by educators. It is usually given in conjunction with other written tests.

Aptitude tests are commonly referred to as synonymous with intelligence tests. Both were developed by psychologists and employ a similar technique and approach. However, the aptitude test aims at an entirely different goal. Instead of innate general mental qualities, it seeks to discover the ability to learn some special thing. Mechanical aptitude tests, for instance, are widely used in the public service. Perhaps confusion would be avoided by referring to both intelligence and aptitude tests as psychological tests.

Public personnel tests strive to discover three different characteristics, depending on the goal. These are traits, aptitudes, and skills. A skill is presumed to consist of those habits of efficiency or performance which are acquired after birth through education, training, or experience. A trait is inherited and cannot be changed to any appreciable extent by education, 10 For a complete discussion of intelligence tests from the public personnel standpoint, see "Measuring Abstract Intelligence in Public Personnel Work,"

Validity of Tests 

How is the personnel examiner to know that his tests have the proper selective value? An unimpeachable answer to this question would be welcomed enthusiastically by most administrators. No infallible objective means of determining the validity of tests has been developed to date. This does not mean that no attempt has been made to experiment in this field; rather, it means that the experiments which have been made show no definite correlation between placement in the entrance examination and subsequent job performance. Such data are lacking primarily for a single reason-the failure thus far to develop generally acceptable criteria for judging job perform- In other words, the test validity problem inevitably becomes tied up with the vexing question of service ratings. 

Until the latter problem is more satisfactorily solved than at present, test validity must remain largely speculative. Today several progressive personnel agencies are running statistical analyses of test results." They attempt to discover the answer to such queries as how many times specific questions are missed, how many average or median results are obtained, and how large a percentage received poor or excellent results. If a specific question were missed by half the group it might be eliminated from consideration or eliminated from the file for future tests. Sometimes these statistical studies are made after the employment list is established, merely for purposes of constructing future tests. In other cases, as in Detroit, the statistical validation is an integral part of test scoring. Scores are figured for each division of a test battery, and the results are then weighted in the combined score. This in turn forms the basis for a more successful oral interview. 

Objective modes of examination have resulted in the development of the standardized test. This is a short answer 

"The Construction of Tests in the Short Answer Form," Public Per sonnel Studies (July, 1927), Vol. 5, No. 7, pp. 130-137.

test of several hundred questions, which has been evolved through a series of experiments. Statistical analyses have been made on several groups of tests, the results correlated, adjustments and corrections made. Because of the information thus accumulated, it is possible to predict in advance the results to be achieved by any group taking the test. In this sense, such a test has high predictive power and is said to be standardized. Standardized tests of general intelligence have been available for some time. It remained for the Bureau of Public 

Personnel Administration to develop standardized and uniform, and also unstandardized, tests for the public personnel field. 

Between 1925 and 1930 this agency worked out 66 separate tests for nearly as many types of positions. They are available for personnel agencies at nominal sums. Some degree of informal standardization is also achieved through the practice of exchanging test materials. 

The Examining Staff 

The objective and psychological approach to public personnel testing has necessitated a new type of examiner. Persons with academic training in experimental psychology and mental measurements must be supplemented by others with experience in industrial psychology and psychiatry. The more progressive directors and commissions have made efforts to recruit young persons with academic background in psychology. Had it not been for the retrenchment due to the depression of 1929, and the consequent reduction of personnel agency staffs, a few years hence might have seen a veritable revolution in this respect. 

In the past, examining staffs have been recruited from specific fields of knowledge, such as engineering or accounting, the mechanics of testing being learned subsequently on the job. 

Frequently teachers were selected because of their presumed acquaintance with examination procedure. On other occasions those employed as clerks, stenographers, or assistants by the personnel agency have been promoted to examining positions because of familiarity with the methods used. Only rarely were selections made from persons with an academic background

Ch. 9] 185 

in the principles and mechanics of test construction and familiar with the statistical analysis and interpretation of test results. 

Realizing the desirability of recruiting such individuals, the Bureau of Public Personnel Administration has developed a test for junior personnel examiner with such an end in view.12 

The minimum qualifications were listed as follows: 

Education equivalent to that represented by graduation. from a four year course in a university of recognized standing with major work in mental measurements or statistics; knowledge of the psychology and principles of test construction, or the mechanics of preparing short answer material, and of the statistical analysis and interpretation of test results; knowledge of modern employment practice; familiarity with test investigations and the literature relating to personnel work; ability to size up situations and people and to get along well with others; ability to meet deadlines; possession to a high degree of scientific spirit; statistical integrity; good judgment as to testing procedure and the content of tests; resourcefulness. 

The Bureau frankly stated that only a small percentage of examiners employed at the time would be able to pass the suggested test. Emphasis is placed upon statistical terms and conceptions, requirements which will be accepted as commonplace in examiners of the future.

This emphasis on psychologically trained examiners tends to make the examining staff more self-contained. In the past some agencies have gone outside to hire persons with specialized skill and experience to participate in particular examinations. 

This practice was based on the assumption that no regular member of the staff could possibly become sufficiently well versed in the subject matter to make a proper selection. However, those skilled in the new examining technique take issue with such an assumption. They maintain that with a knowledge of testing methods any good examiner can conduct a test for any position.13 This is similar to the claim said to have been made by a professor of education that one well versed in teaching

Selection of Directing Personnel 

A supervisor, executive, or manager in the public service requires personal traits which are in some respects contradictory. 

He must be politic without being a "politician"; he must be firm enough to get work done without antagonizing employee interests; he must be well-versed in the theoretical aspects of various techniques, yet he must be "practical" in their application. In the past there existed in private management a certain premium upon shrewdness approaching cunning, combined with driving force. The quota had to be met or the output increased regardless of the cost in human anguish and physical wear and tear. 

The "hardboiled" type of executive has little place in governmental units. There management is so hemmed in by political consideration that compromise becomes inevitable. The best public manager is one who can get things done as they should be without antagonizing vested community interests. Such a person must be vastly more than a good operating executive; he must know the vagaries of human nature and deal with it without compromising his personal integrity. When a member of the board of supervisors sends the son of his neighborhood banker to an executive for a job, the executive finds himself in a dilemma. The supervisor's enmity can reduce his appropriations and even dismiss him from the service. The local civil service reform league will create unfavorable publicity if a nonmerit appointment is made. The banker's demands cannot be ignored entirely, as his support is vital to the supervisor's political progress. The moralist will say, of course, that there is no

Ch. 9] 

187 

ethical compromise for this situation. Whether compromise or not, the public executive, while trying to produce a reasonably well-run organization, must meet situations of this kind continually. A large part of his job consists of pacifying community cantankerousness. The most successful city managers are those who quietly and unobtrusively can harmonize community factions and still produce effective and efficient administration.

In addition to being politic without being a politician, the public executive must have an extremely wide range of experience and technical background. The general manager of the ordinary manufacturing concern needs no more, if as much, knowledge of the essentials of various techniques than does the city manager of Cincinnati, for instance. The latter must form judgments on the operation of such diverse services as public health, sanitation, police administration, fire prevention, traffic regulation, welfare administration, receiving hospitals, public recreation, and works construction. He must do this and at the same time keep his 450,000 employers satisfied. The problem of selecting persons to fill executive positions is not an easy one.

The qualities essential in directing personnel are generally lumped under the heading of "executive ability." It is usually conceded that these qualities are largely intangible and not measurable from an examination standpoint. Numerous experiments in testing personality are under way, but they have not yet resulted in the elimination of the judgment interview as the principal step in the examination of executives. One psychologist has recently made a study of the characteristics or traits going to make up executive ability. He has come to the conclusion that they can be segregated under four main headings: (1) mental alertness or general intelligence, (2) social intelligence or tact, (3) energy or drive, and (4) loyalty to the organization. Objective tests are available for the first two, and metabolism tests for the third are being experimented with. 14

It is possible that executive ability as such may at some future date be blocked out in large outline so as to be at least partly perceptible from the examination standpoint. At present it must be reiterated, however, that no substitute for judgment based on the oral interview is widely used for selecting directing personnel. This does not mean that no written tests are used for such positions. Probably progressive practice approaches a combination of a written general test, an intelligence test, and an oral interview.15

The oral interview is used in testing for a wide variety of positions not necessarily of a directing or supervising nature. 

In the great mass of tests a certain weight is given to the written portion, probably six or seven points out of ten, while the remaining weight goes to experience and general fitness as determined in the oral interview. If preponderant weight is given to the oral interview in tests for positions of a routine nature, suspicion of political manipulation may be justified. The interview is administratively difficult and expensive, and is decidedly inferior to the written test in measuring factual information. 

It is still the only means available for measuring purely personal traits such as speech, dress, bearing, ability to comprehend oral statements and questions, quickness of oral response, adaptability for the specific activity, tact, and total effect of personality. 

Also it is almost the only hope for eliminating in advance the neurotic and temperamentally peculiar. Many personnel people express dissatisfaction with the oral interview, saying that it indicates only that some individuals and groups are obviously unfit, and that a few outstanding individuals possess certain desirable traits to an unusual degree.16 Hope is constantly being expressed that some more objective measure of personal qualities will be developed. The Induction Process 

The common mode of administering tests to large groups is to assemble all testees and give them the written portion in one room simultaneously. This is what is known as the assembled test. During the depression of 1929, and following, the demand for positions on the public payrolls has been so great that thousands have taken a single test. This has sometimes necessitated engaging an assembly hall for the purpose. 

Another problem arising out of the depression has aroused criticism of personnel methods among groups clamoring for tax reduction. Sometimes a test which in normal times would attract 15 or 20 applicants, attracts several hundred during periods. of industrial unemployment. The cost of administering the test to such a large number may run out of all proportions to the number of vacancies expected. The public personnel agency is between two fires. A cheap means of elimination, which would reduce the number of testees to reasonable proportions without necessitating the formal examination of all applicants, would raise the cry of favoritism and invasion of constitutional rights. 

On the other hand, the expenditure entailed in the examination of all applicants makes the entire personnel program vulnerable to economy critics.18 This is another one of those depression problems which will have to be solved by new technique if industrial unemployment proves to be perennial. 

The opposite of the assembled test is the non-assembled, used in selecting the directing personnel in the federal service. Applicants are evaluated on the basis of experience, professional

attainment, and professional and scientific writings. The more likely candidates will then be summoned to Washington for separate and individual interviews by departmental officials. 

The problem of administering examinations for the more popular federal positions is a troublesome one. The testees are assembled in various cities all over the country, sometimes at hundreds and even thousands of points. The Civil Service 

Commission has field secretaries at key points, and these officials are aided by local examining boards composed of local departmental officials detailed temporarily to examining duty. 

When the testees have completed the examination and the various scores have been determined, an appointment list-sometimes referred to as the eligible list—is prepared from the names of those who were successful. This appointment list becomes a roster from which appointments can be made during its life, most lists lapsing at the end of a stated period, usually two years. 

Appointment lists should be maintained at all times for those classifications to which frequent appointments are made. For classes with only one or two positions wherein vacancies seldom occur, it would be obviously unnecessary to maintain lists constantly. On the other hand, failure to maintain appointment lists necessitates temporary appointments. These may grow to unwieldy proportions where the personnel agency, owing to scanty support and inadequate staff, is unable to keep up with its examining program. 

After the appointment list is completed names are ready for certification. The most common practice is to certify to the appointing officer the highest three, any one of whom may be and one of whom usually must be appointed. In other words, when the department head desires to secure a person to fill a certain position he asks the personnel agency to certify names on the eligible list of the appropriate class. He is furnished with the names of the three standing highest on the existing appointment list and may choose any of the three. It has been urged that the appointing officer should be required to select the person standing highest on the list or explain in writing his reasons for not doing so. Proponents of this idea urge that failure to appoint the highest is in large degree a negation

Ch. 191 

19 of the merit principle. They argue that tests used by public personnel agencies are so valid and reliable that personal interviews by the appointing officer can add little or nothing to the selective process.

Most appointing officers would fail to agree with this doctrine. Selection of names from eligible lists can be abused. A familiar means of evasion is to make successive appointments and discharges, continuously demanding new eligibles until a favored testee far down the list is reached. 

Another means of circumventing the list principle in promotional examinations is to bring pressure to bear on the higher testees to waive their rights so that a favored person lower in the list may receive appointment.

It is advisable to do all in the personnel agency's power to assure public confidence in test administration. Some unsuccessful candidates are bound to be disgruntled. Certain common precautions will reduce to a minimum opportunities to question the motives of those who conduct tests. A very general device is to have test papers identified by numbers rather than by names, thus hiding the identity of the testee until the paper is corrected. This is not always possible in the case of higher positions, where the examiners cannot help identifying those with whom they have had long association in the service. 

While the concealment of identity may not be an essential part of sound testing, it is nevertheless advisable as a means of inspiring the confidence of the public. It is also good policy to allow the testee access to his corrected paper for purposes of inspection and explanation of the position he achieved on the appointment list. Most state and local agencies permit such inspection under prescribed conditions as to time and convenience. 

The federal Civil Service Commission, on the other hand, has successfully resisted various attempts to gain access to its test records.20 19

This period, usually limited to six months, should properly be regarded as a part of the testing procedure. During this time the appointing officer is free to discharge the probationer without recourse. There is almost universal criticism that probation is not generally used as a part of the selective process. In the federal service rejection during probation is so rare that the conscientious executive hesitates to discharge a probationer, because such action would make him conspicuous." 

It is urged that some affirmative action on the part of the supervising personnel should replace the automatic completion of the probation period. In other words, instead of allowing the end of probation to slip by unnoticed, probationary status would continue until the appointing officer had furnished written notice that the appointee had given satisfactory evidence of his ability to fill the job. To counteract the occasional abuse of appointing and immediately discharging probationers to get to a favorite further down the employment list, various safeguards are proposed. 

One is that the probation period must last a minimum number of days or weeks, thus rendering the manipulation process unduly long. It is also thought that the personnel agency should have the authority to return to the employment list persons who have failed on probation—a practice prevailing in many jurisdictions. Such individuals represent quite an investment on the part of the government. Failure to satisfy probation requirements in a single department may have been due to a clash of personalities, unfavorable environment, uncongenial associations, or any number of causes not directly traceable to the probationer's own faults. A proper study of placement would undoubtedly prove many who failed on probation to be valuable workers if properly situated.

Ch. 193 

 Common Labor 

One of the most perplexing problems in public personnel administration has been the recruiting of common labor. If too much attention is given to the examination aspects of the recruiting process, costs are raised out of proportion to the results achieved. On the other hand, if recruiting of this class of personnel is not subjected to the control of the central personnel agency, the door is left wide open to political preferment in this section of the service. As one personnel man put it: “The agency which does not succeed in solving the recruiting problem in this class is likely to build a good superstructure on a leaking hull." As a matter of fact, the technicians consulted on this point will agree almost unanimously that it is not safe to leave the recruiting of common labor entirely in the hands of foremen, for they will be pressed to appoint men suggested by aldermen and other persons having either political or personal influence. 

A considerable amount of nepotism will also creep in. Employment on the basis of priority of application also has certain drawbacks. The men who are ahead on a list prepared in this manner are likely to include a heavy percentage of the less competent, because they will have been among those first laid off by industrial plants which lay off the least competent first. The arguments are largely in favor of a cheap and quick procedure which will sift out the incompetent. Probably a majority of jurisdictions have not developed means entirely satisfactory to themselves. In many cases this is due to the fact that local opinion is not ready to apply the merit principle to common labor. There is a technical problem in administering labor lists where employment occurs over wide geographical areas, but personnel technicians believe they could solve this difficulty if given complete freedom to do so. In many instances the de facto exemption of this class has given a much desired opportunity for spoils appointments. Various skilled and semiskilled positions are filled by favored individuals who are employed as common laborers to avoid the examination process. 

Public personnel administrators are accustomed to pay considerable respect to the methods of recruiting common labor

[Pt. II 

PERSONNEL 

normally used in the City of Milwaukee. About 1925 the city service commission employed an examiner of labor, and a clerk was detailed to take care of applications and do other necessary clerical work. Medical examination, started in 1919, was continued. It was found that the nature of the duties required of those under the category of common labor varied considerably even under the strictest control. Some required a predominance of brute strength while others needed some agility and athletic ability. In yet other cases a rough familiarity with rudimentary mechanical processes was desirable. To meet this situation common labor was divided into six general groups. A simple examination process begins by writing in an application blank certain facts regarding the applicant's past history and employment. A space is set aside for the report of the medical examiner and the examiner of labor. The rating given by the latter is determined largely in a short oral interview designed briefly to check mental reactions. The relaying of flashed numbers, the repetition of oral instructions, and the reading of street signs constitute samples of the tests used. After being rated on the basis of 100, the names are filed according to groups in such a manner that those having the highest rating will be the first appointed regardless of the time of application. A provision that names are removed after a year eliminates the least fit from the list. The appointment lists are, therefore, continually revolving, for testing is continuous. It is said that under this system a far better class of laborers has been secured and that aldermen and other persons in political positions do not attempt to interfere with it.

Owing to abnormal economic conditions, the recruiting of labor for permanent city positions practically ceased in Milwaukee in 1932 and 1933. In common with most other cities, it was attempted to combat the unemployment evil through a program of "made work." In other words, welfare funds were allocated on the basis of allotting so many days labor on public works to unemployed persons. Milwaukee was an exceptional city in that the recruiting of the "made work" contingent was placed under the control of the central personnel agency. All applicants were required to have a medical examination, so as to

Ch. 9] 195 

mum. hold workman's compensation and medical expense to a mini- Time and absence reports were checked by the city service commission (personnel agency), which acted as co-ordinator for the work relief program. 

Probably a summary of good practice in common labor recruiting can be made without incurring the dangers inherent in excessive generalization. In the first place, all labor positions should be controlled by the central personnel agency. Each applicant should be subjected to a medical examination. Otherwise the city will incur unnecessary medical and workman's compensation expense arising from such common ailments as heart disease and hernia. The applicants should then be graded, the usual practice being a brief oral interview combined with the testee's statement of personal history and past employment. 

Sometimes there is a test of strength, such as the lifting of weights and the tossing of heavy sacks. This may immediately precede the medical examination in order to detect abnormal heart action. Some progressive agencies find it desirable to test for literacy, mental agility, and the ability to relay and follow instructions. These take the form of very brief and practical tests, such as the repetition of a series of numbers or the reading of a street name sign. Still other agencies separate laborers into several general groups, as in Milwaukee. The appointment list should be maintained on the basis of competence rather than on priority of application. These general criteria constitute a basis upon which any agency may proceed to experiment with the recruiting of common labor. 

Veterans' Preference 

In most civil service jurisdictions the law requires that a certain number of points, usually five or ten, be added to the earned ratings of veterans of the nation's wars. If a veteran should earn a grade of 83, for instance, five points would be added, thus giving him a rating of 88. One of the most liberal provisions in this respect is that of the federal government, wherein the able veteran is given an advantage of five points, and a disabled veteran and his wife or widow, ten points. When the disabled veteran, his wife or widow, receive passing grades

[Pt. II 

PERSONNEL 

on any test, their names are immediately placed at the head of the appointment list. If they fail the test, but if the ten bonus points, added to their earned scores, lift their scores to the passing point, they automatically go to the head of the list. This means that a disabled veteran, his wife or widow, who fails to achieve a passing grade can be appointed ahead of testees with earned ratings of 95 or 100. While employed in government positions secured as a result of this preference, many veterans may also be receiving disability or other veterans' compensation in addition to salary. This whole question of public emoluments to veterans is so confounded with emotional patriotism, military appeal, and genuine compassion for maimed bodies and lives that unbiased judgment is all but impossible. The following is merely the opinion of one person. Many personnel technicians and students agree with it, however. 

There would not be a great deal of objection from any one to adding five points to the earned score achieved by a veteran who has passed a test. Disabled veterans, their wives and widows, should be taken care of through disability pensions fully adequate to keep them in modest comfort. Receiving such compensation in excess of a certain amount should constitute an absolute bar to government employment. Obviously, if a person is disabled he should not be able to earn a salary. If he is able to earn a salary he should not be receiving disability compensation. Disabled veterans who take civil service examinations should do so with the understanding that they must compete on a basis of equality with other testees, and that if appointed they must give up their compensation. The acceptance of employment should be prima facie evidence of the end of disabled status. The practice of certifying disabled veterans, their wives and widows, ahead of those with higher earned ratings, should be discontinued; it means that inferior persons from a test standpoint are entering the service. Such preference cannot help but have a deteriorating effect on morale, discipline, and general efficiency. Preference, if granted at all, should be limited to adding five points to the scores of those who have passed the examination.22 

22 For the opinion of the Commission of Inquiry, see op. cit., pp. 70-72.

 Summary 

The dominant note in public personnel recruiting today is the psychological approach. This is evidenced by the community of interest between the public personnel technician and both the academic and industrial psychologist. Testing procedure lays increasing emphasis on objective short answer tests standardized through statistical analysis. Intelligence and aptitude tests, in combination with other examining procedure, are looming larger in the induction process. While intangible personality traits must still be evaluated on a judgment basis through the oral interview, experienced examiners trained in psychological methods exercise judgment somewhat better than the chance of yesterday. A major defect in recruiting methods is failure to appeal to the talented youth of the nation. Entrance requirements as to experience, age, and a too practical examination content, have barred the recent college graduate because he has not marked time at a routine task. It is to be hoped that the immediate future will see established a widespread system of apprenticeships in administrative positions. Thereby inexperienced youths would be given opportunity to develop as public executives of the future under the tutelage of the administrators of today. The recruiting of common labor should be under the control of the central personnel agency. The exaggerated veterans' preference orders of the federal government are inimical to the best interest of the public service. 

Public personnel testing has made a decided technical advance in recent years. Practical political considerations in many jurisdictions, however, prevent the utilization of more than a fraction of known technical procedure.

CHAPTER X  

Probably over half of the budgeted expenditures of governments go for personal services in the form of wages, salaries, and fees. If debt service were excluded from the computation, salaries and wages would constitute, in some jurisdictions, as high as 80 per cent of the total of current expense. These facts should serve to emphasize the very intimate relation of personnel administration to the budgeting process. An increasing realization of this fact is tending to bring the personnel and budgeting agencies into close contact with one another. In some cases this is beginning to take the form of physical union. 

Budget officers are extremely interested in duties classifications, compensation plans, the number of persons needed to perform any particular job, and every other personnel matter affecting expenditure-and what personnel matter does not affect expenditure? The accounting officers are just as concerned about making correct payments for personal services as they are in drawing warrants for supplies; indeed, they should be more so, for personal services constitute greater totals. Are sick leaves, vacations, disability, and retirement payments predominantly budgeting or personnel problems? Obviously there is no categorical answer to this query. The only reasonable conclusion is that the housekeeping phase of the administrative process is not divisible into independent compartments; it is a single, unified process into which the various technical services should merge to achieve the most effective results. That is why the British have found that the Treasury can best exercise budgetary control over personnel. There are several indications that we are evolving in a similar direction. The following pages discuss, under the caption "Budgeting Personal Services," those procedures and activities which combine personnel and budgetary characteristics. 200

Ch. 10] 201 

 The Classification Plan 

Many personnel workers regard the classification plan as the keystone of a sound personnel program. The term "classification" is sometimes used in more than one sense. It is frequently said that certain positions are not in the classified service, and that others are in the classified service. What is meant is that some positions are not under the merit system while others are. Referring to the classified service in this sense, while quite common usage, is not technically accurate and may lead to much confusion. The term will not be used with this interpretation in these pages. Reference to the classification plan hereafter will mean the "duties" classification. Positions not under civil service or not subject to the merit system may be governed by the duties classification plan. Hence, it is not accurate to say that they are not classified. The duties classification refers to the allocation of positions to classes on the basis of duties performed, the responsibilities involved, and the authority and supervisory functions concerned. In other words, positions with like functions and like responsibilities are grouped into a single class, without regard to the department or service in which they are located. In determining the classifications, no consideration whatsoever should be given to the qualifications or personal characteristics of individuals who happen to occupy particular posts, as the process of classification is impersonal. 

It also disregards departmental boundaries. It works on the principle that a stenographer in the health department should have the same qualifications as a stenographer for a tax commissioner. Positions are grouped into classes on the basis of ability to subject them to common treatment with respect to compensation, recruitment, and other personnel activities. Members of the same class will ordinarily have the same pay, their duties will be almost identical, and they will have been chosen by the same selection process. In other words, it should be possible to fill all positions in the same class from a particular employment list.

The classification plan is prepared by the personnel agency. 

Most of the necessary information is secured from question-

[Pt. II 

PERSONNEL 

naires filled out by the employee himself, with the addition of supplementary comments furnished by his official superiors who are not permitted to alter employee comments. Thus, if an individual tends to think too well of his responsibilities there will be a balancing check provided by comments from his chief. 

Special circumstances may occasionally require the classification officer to observe performance on the job. However, the expense of such personal attention to each position is prohibitive. 

An experienced classification worker will be sufficiently wellversed in the vagaries of human nature to detect most of the inaccurate statements. Those who deal with questionnaires 

I will also be familiar with the classes common to the various services as the result of years of contact. It is also possible to obtain fairly accurate results through having a representative of the personnel agency "spot check" various positions by observation of the performance of specific positions. When the questionnaires have been turned in to the personnel agency they are sorted into classes. To each of these is allocated a descriptive class title by which the class will be subsequently known in the various accounting, personnel, and budgeting processes. 

Then follows the writing of the class specifications, which should be so worded as to distinguish clearly each class from every other class. In doing so the class title should be defined by including statements of duties and responsibilities, typical tasks, and qualifications required. The following class description is taken from a proposed reclassification for the State of Ohio, prepared under the direction of Harvey Walker with the consulting assistance of the Bureau of Public Personnel Administration: 

COLLEGE DEAN DUTIES: Subject to the administrative approval of the

A. from a college or university of recognized standing and five years of successful experience in teaching or educational administrative work; or (2) any other equivalent combination of education and experience; ability to size up situations and people and to get along well with others; administrative ability; ability to give counsel to students; firmness; initiative; tact; discretion; good judgment; good address.

What are the uses of class description? Why does the 

American personnel technician regard them as the keystone of his work? Convincing answers to these queries are not lacking. In the first place, classification produces a comparative measure of duties which permits equal pay for equal work. 

Thus, a proper control of the classification plan will tend to reduce and eliminate favoritism in pay matters. In the second place, an objective standard of duties forms the measure for setting salaries and rates of pay in terms of what the performance of similar duties would command elsewhere. Thirdly, a proper delineation of duties aids in setting standards of job perform- A fourth advantage accrues from the ease with which organization charts can be built from properly prepared duties questionnaires. In the fifth place, an adequate classification plan will clearly indicate the path of promotion: whether a given class will lead up a blind alley or to a progressive career. A sixth merit lies in the aid to recruiting provided by class definitions which clearly set forth the desired personal qualifications of workers. Tests can be constructed with definitely stated ance. 1 

Proposed Classification and Compensation Plan for the Public Service of the State of Ohio (Columbus, 1930), p. 129. * For a view not favorable to classification see R. M. Dawson, The Civil 

Service of Canada (Oxford University Press, London: Humphrey Mil ford, 1929), pp. 154-177.

[Pt. II 

PERSONNEL 

objectives in view. Under a seventh heading can be grouped a host of considerations accruing from the impetus given to effective budget control by the classification plan. Each class may be given a code number for the purpose of identifying the position, thus facilitating accounting operations. There is an increasing tendency, however, to abandon the code and use the title of the position to identify it. The creation of positions by codes leads to abuse by creating special jobs. An unnecessary duplication of positions can be detected by the descriptions and standards of job performance resulting from the classification study. Merit, rather than inertia, haphazard chance, and political favoritism, forms the basis for job holding. Classification permits the elimination of gross inequalities and the adjustment of rates of pay in accordance with duties performed. Indeed, the theoretical arguments in favor of the classification plan are endless and almost unanswerable. 

The Compensation Plan 

Classification is essential to an adequate compensation plan, but the converse is not true. A compensation plan is based on the classes previously designated in the classification plan. 

Rates of pay are specified for each one of these classes and formal rules are prescribed regulating the installation, administration, amendment, and adjustment of the compensation plan. 

One of the first steps is the determination of the compensation policy. What factors, principles, or general policies are to govern in determining rates of pay? Are they to be no greater than those similarly employed in local private enterprise, or is a decent minimum standard of living, irrespective of competitive rates, to be the guiding factor? What consideration is to be given to the scale of union labor? Shall compensation levels be made flexible so as to meet fluctuations in the cost of living as indicated by price indexes? What salaries and wages can the government afford to pay? The general compensation policy having been decided upon, it is possible to proceed to the allocation of pay rates to classes. This is usually done by fixing a minimum paid to new appointees and a maximum which is the

Ch. 10] 205 

highest paid to any one in that class. There will also be, between this minimum and maximum, one or more intermediate rates which will be attained only by demonstrated proficiency. 

Progression from lower to higher pay rates within a class should not follow automatically after length of service. Care should be taken to avoid making the minimum rate of any class any lower than the maximum rate of the next lower class. In preparing a compensation plan, data relative to wages paid for comparable work by other employers in the same locality are almost indispensable.

The fundamental aim of a compensation plan based on classification is equal pay for equal work. A junior accountant in a budget bureau should be no more valuable from a pay angle than a junior accountant in a controller's office. If he is doing the work of a budget investigator his class and salary should be changed to conform to his actual duties. If a person has capabilities in excess of the maximum requirements of his class he should be rewarded by promotion, not by special exception in his existing class pay rates. In a classification study recently made of the New York State service, it was found that for persons performing the duties of what should be senior clerks there were fifty rates of compensation ranging from $696 to $4,000. Those functioning as assistant typists received fiftytwo different rates of compensation varying from $744 to $3,000. These examples are not such absurd exceptions as might be imagined; they can be duplicated in a great many services. The demoralizing effect of such discrepancies is apparent. 

Aggressive department heads are able to secure salary increases for favored employees without reference to the competitive or comparative value of services rendered. Under such conditions, compensation tends to depend on political influence, favoritism, and nepotism, instead of proficiency in job performance as should be the case. A compensation plan based on class definitions will furnish a technical structure of great value in administering fair pay policies. However, this technical structure alone cannot produce equitable compensation methods; it must 3 

H. Eliot Kaplan, "Reclassification of the New York State Service," National Municipal Review (June, 1932), Vol. XXI, No. 6, p. 404.

[Pt. II 

PERSONNEL 

have the support of a sincere community desire to maintain the merit spirit in such matters. 

Compensation levels in the various public services may or may not be the result of deliberately determined policies or principles. The chances are that in any given jurisdiction the interaction of group interests has a tremendous bearing on the situation. The Personnel Classification Board found that federal pay exceeded that for private employment in positions where the compensation was less than $2,000 per year. Where salaries exceeded that figure the opposite was true. 

The salaries paid by private concerns to their major executives exceeded federal pay for positions of similar responsibility anywhere from 100 to 500 per cent. A similar conclusion undoubtedly can be drawn for state and local jurisdictions. The average voter is a person of very modest income who cannot possibly see how anyone can earn a salary in excess of $5,000. On the other hand, the representatives of union labor constantly bring pressure to bear to maintain union wage scales in all of the labor classes. 

Employee organizations often wield sufficient political power to see that their wage interests are not ignored. The President of the National Federation of Federal Employees claims that his organization is responsible for such improvement as resulted in federal pay from 1923 to 1928.5 There are numerous cities where policemen and firemen have militantly campaigned for charter amendments setting favorable salary scales. These conditions exist so generally that it is difficult to state any prevailing principles of pay level determination. There are places where sheer inertia creates an underpaid service, and there are other jurisdictions where many of those who are in the public service are paid more than they would receive for similar duties in the competitive market.

In times of industrial depression, taxpayers' groups exert tremendous pressure to reduce governmental expenditures. It is inevitable that the principal burden of the resulting retrench-
