ment should fall upon salaries and wages. Employee groups usually resist the inevitable as long as possible. Eventually, however, they must accept a percentage cut in salary, take furloughs or vacations without pay, or even be forced to join the unemployed. From the standpoint of technical personnel administration, retrenchments should be effected with a minimum loss of personnel morale. If left to the free interplay of political pressure groups, the result will depend on the comparative strength of employees and the large taxpayers. Where the employees are highly organized, as in New York City and San 

Francisco, needed retrenchments may be too long delayed.

Where they are loosely organized or poorly led, the demand for reduced taxes may create severe injustices. 

Fred Telford, formerly Director of the Bureau of Public

Personnel Administration, estimates that it may be possible to reduce the payroll 10, 15, or 20 per cent without materially affecting existing pay rates. When it becomes necessary to retrench, the governing body should ascertain the amount which should be borne by the personnel and ask the personnel agency to furnish a plan for accomplishing the desired reduction. The first step should be the creation of an adequate classification plan, followed by the allocation of rates of pay to the classes thus set up. The number of jurisdictions having workable classification plans is so small that this step would be very generally necessary in acquiring the facts essential to orderly retrenchment. It will then be possible to eliminate those doing inferior work and to refrain from filling their posts. In many instances this can be done on the basis of service ratings. Superannuated employees can be retired, vacancies left unfilled, and non-essential projects curtailed or abandoned. If, after all of these and other devices have been tried, the reduction of salaries is compulsory, a straight horizontal cut should be avoided. The various classes and pay scales should be studied in the light of changed economic conditions. Reductions should be graduated, no cut being made in certain lower classes. There should be a comparison with the compensation rates prevailing among other employers. Caution 

"How Can the Public Payroll Be Reduced," Public Management 

(March, 1932), Vol. XIV, No. 3, pp. 85-88.

PERSONNEL 

should be used, however, in interpreting depression salary data. 

Desperation may lead a considerable portion of workers to accept wages below a subsistence standard. The government, as an employer, should never stoop to profit from such human misfortune. It should, in so far as possible, seek to follow a plan of action suitable for a model employer. When retrenchment is desirable, makeshifts should be avoided. The budget and personnel agencies should be charged with studying the situation and furnishing plans of action based on well considered data and approved technical procedure. 

The City of St. Paul apparently has attempted to solve the salary retrenchment problem by means of a fluctuating scale based upon the cost of living. Salaries are adjusted each year on the basis of price indexes reflecting changes in the cost of living. Inaugurated in 1922, the plan worked smoothly with two or three point variations until 1931, when certain employee groups foresaw sharp declines in the indexes and secured its suspension for that year. It was restored by the city council in 

1932, however, to meet further needs for retrenchment, Reductions have been made without friction, the employee and taxpayer each feeling that he is being treated fairly and in accordance with principles of justice. It is an idea which merits the investigation and consideration of all salary-fixing bodies. 

Administration of Classification and Compensation 

Momentous questions of power and authority are involved in the actual carrying out of the classification and compensation plans. Should the classification plan be passed upon in detail by the legislative body? Should every subsequent change in class require legislative enactment? And should the allocation of positions to classes be an administrative or a legislative procedure? The better view favors a maximum of administrative discretion in these matters. The legislation should be basic rather than detailed in character. It is ordinarily sufficient to enact a statute or ordinance naming or creating the administrative agencies to be in charge of the work. These agencies should be authorized to make the classification and compensation plans,

Ch. 10] 209 

to make rules and regulations governing the administration of the plans, and to see that the various administrative subdivisions observe the rules.

In a large number of jurisdictions, practice and habit demand a rather detailed legislative control through segregated appropriations. Where this is the case an attempt should be made to provide a legislative procedure in such matters that will not be too cumbersome. The classification plan should be formulated and administered by the central personnel agency. The compensation plan, on the other hand, should be administered by the central budget bureau. In the allocation of positions to classes the various departments should have adequate opportunity to make their desires known. Every possible effort should be made to avoid friction, yet complete success will not be achieved unless the central personnel agency has the ultimate determination.

In the installation of classification and compensation plans various questions arise relative to the treatment to be accorded to previously existing positions. After they have been allocated to the new classes, there should be a formal announcement of the change so that the new class title will appear on payrolls, accounts, and personnel records of various types. The allocation of positions under a new classification plan should not affect the tenure of those occupying the positions, even though they may not meet the minimum qualifications specified in the new class descriptions. The acknowledgment of such a principle will avoid a great deal of embarrassment to the plan as a whole, and will tend to allay the fears of those who frown on any innovation touching their jobs. The same is true of the compensation plan. An existing rate below the minimum for a class to which a position is allocated should be raised to that minimum. 

Where the existing rate is at one of the rates of the class, it should not be changed at installation. If an existing rate falls between two of the rates for a class, it should be raised to the higher of the two. If the existing rate is higher than the maximum for the class, the incumbent should be permitted to retain his former rate as a special consideration to him. These exceptions should last only while the existing incumbents hold

[Pt. II 

PERSONNEL 

office. The exceptions are made only to forestall excessive legislative lobbying and opposition to the plan. 

No duties classification can be so wisely devised that it will function automatically. A well-run personnel agency will be constantly alert to see that its classification is in harmony with changing conditions of administration. It will question requests for the establishment of new positions, to see that they are not mere political subterfuges to secure greater rates of pay for individuals whose duties would fit into existing classes. 

Unless such supervision is provided, the classification plan may be stretched and warped to suit the political convenience of those who are opposed to the merit principle. Gradually several codes, with widely varying salaries for the same duties, will appear, quite often for no other purpose than to "take care of" specific individuals; men performing the tasks of common labor will be carried as mechanics; mechanics will be carried as skilled artisans; and those doing merely clerical work will carry the title of accountants. Such a situation can only be avoided by giving a personnel agency the power and authority to exercise constant vigil and act in the interests of good administration. 

Some changes in the classification plan are desirable. New positions must be created, and the nature of the duties of existing classes will be altered by uncontrollable circumstances. The introduction of functions not hitherto undertaken often means the creation of new classes or the adjustment of old ones. The 

Bureau of Public Personnel Administration estimated that there is a normal expectancy of fifty to one hundred amendments per year in a service of 5,000 positions. In spite of utmost vigilance, moreover, it will be impossible for a personnel agency to be aware of all the changes in duties constantly taking place. 

Hence, it is desirable to overhaul entirely a classification plan every two to five years. The continued administration of the compensation plan involves the mechanical factor of being sure that the persons on the payroll are actually at work. Although not yet solved, there is also the problem of securing an adequate 

"Proposed Rules for a Public Personnel Agency, with Explanatory Comments," Public Personnel Studies (June, 1928), Vol. VI, No. 6, pp. 

117, 123.

Ch. 10] 211 

quantity and quality of work. Adjustments will have to be made from time to time in existing pay scales for specific classes. 

As changing duties alter old class limits, accompanying salary variations must take place. From time to time the entire compensation plan must be re-examined in the light of altered economic and social conditions. 

Personnel Reports and Payrolls 

Payroll padding has been one of the most prevalent forms of petty graft. Mr. Merriam refers to the amusing case of "L. C. 

Smith" who was carried on the payroll as a typist, but who ultimately turned out to be a typewriter. There are a number of other personnel abuses which could be reduced to a minimum by the proper system. These include chronic tardiness, uncontrolled time-off, absence due to sickness, and general attendance. 

The customary payroll procedure provides that the payrolls be made out by the employing departments, preferably upon uniform blanks centrally prescribed. However, progressive opinion favors central preparation of the payrolls." The data upon which the payrolls are based should be built up from attendance records which should be maintained by persons specifically designated in each department for the task. The department head and finance officer of the department should make frequent checks to see that these attendance records are being accurately kept. These same officers should be required to certify to the correctness of such reports before they are forwarded to the payroll authorities. It is customary to require that the persons whose names appear on the payroll have been legally employed. 

The accounting office should check also to see that the positions on the roll have been authorized and the funds provided. A certification of the auditing agency acting as representative of the legislature may also be required. It is not necessary to have each of these three agencies conduct a separate check. The personnel agency and controller's office may unite in supporting a

Co., 1929), p. 29.

clerk who prepares and checks the payroll for both. The use of addressograph equipment constitutes a considerable saving in the preparation of both payrolls and checks. There really is little reason for paying other than by a check signed by a single responsible financial officer. The distribution of these checks goes preferably through department channels, followed from time to time by an auditing officer's post-audit of the payment. 

The titles used in the class descriptions should be required in preparation of payrolls. Deviation from standard official titles, while rather common practice, presents certain dangers. It may be conducive to an adjustment of salary rates according to payroll titles which have no fixed meaning, rather than to titles the meaning of which are defined. Such laxity may, deliberately or through inertia, result in thwarting the purposes of the classification and compensation plans. For accounting and control purposes it is thought well to designate the various classes by codes composed of letters and numbers. Such combinations furnish convenient designations for ledger and report columns without writing out the entire title.10 Each payroll should carry the name of the employee as carried on the records, the surname first, with the names of each organization unit in alphabetical order. In addition to the class title and (or) code, the payroll period, the rate of pay, and the total pay for the period should be set forth. The amount of time-off because of vacation, sick leave, special leave, or for other reasons should also be indicated. 

After the payroll is certified by the personnel officer charged with that duty, it should be forwarded to the controller. After satisfying himself that the positions have been authorized and that appropriations are available, this official should proceed to prepare the warrants which authorize the treasurer to pay. 

It is now coming to be recognized that one of the essential administrative reports is that which tells the story of employment. This is usually known as the monthly personnel report and is an accumulation of totals from statements made by departments to the central personnel agency. It should show

213 

such information as the number of employees added during the month, the net change in payroll totals, the monthly labor turnover, and such other facts as extent of absence, tardiness, and overtime. Such a report should be of value for showing trends, both for management purposes and for public information. It would undoubtedly aid in the determination of employment policy by the legislative body. While periodical information of this kind has been relatively rare in many units, it surely is essential to that new type of public management which bases its decisions on analyses of the facts. 

Vacation and Leave 

Regular vacations should be aided and encouraged by good personnel administration. Their advantages consist in the relief from nervous strain, the refreshing effect of a change in environment, not to speak of the rest involved. In many instances, vacations offer the opportunity for broadening contacts and self-improvement. Personnel management should encourage workers to take vacations regularly. To those critics of the public service who regard governmental workers as shirkers and drones it will doubtless come as a surprise to learn that federal employees do not take vacations up to the full extent authorized by law; in some departments they do not utilize more than onehalf of the possible time off." The Bureau of Public Personnel 

Administration, in its proposed rules for civil service commissions, has worked out a scheme of vacation time-off based on a scale of work hours per week. This approximates two weeks per year for most services. Scientific, professional, and educational workers are sometimes given longer vacations, possibly to compensate them for similar privileges accorded to their brethren in academic pursuits.

There would seem to be very little uniformity in handling sick leave. In the smaller governmental units it is frequently taken care of without any specific legal provisions, other than in those cases where workmen's compensation applies by law. In those larger units where charter or ordinance makes specific pro- "H. Feldman, A Personnel Program for the Federal Service, 71st Cong., 3d Sess., House Doc. 773 (Government Printing Office, 1931), pp. 210-212.

[Pt. II 

PERSONNEL 

vision, a definite number of days off each year for sick leave often is allowed. The difficulty in administering such an arrangement lies in the propensity of a certain percentage of employees to regard it as a matter of right whether needed or not. They look upon sick leave as so much additional vacation and devise subterfuges to get it. Where only a certificate of the employee's physician is required, cases have been known where doctors were willing to "stretch a point." A means of meeting just such a contingency, frequently used in private personnel management, is to have a company nurse call at the home of one who absents himself from work because of sickness. If the nurse finds him away fishing, or occupying his time in such a manner as to indicate a reasonable degree of health, disciplinary measures may be taken. The means of controlling sick leave suggested for the public service is to make it cumulative. If a worker closes a year without illness his sick leave for that period is carried on over into the next. The Bureau of Public Personnel Administration recommends that each employee who has been in the service for six months should be allowed sick leave on pay not to exceed 90 working hours in the calendar year, provided that the unused sick leave in any year can be accumulated from year to year to a total of 500 hours for employees who have been under civil service continuously not to exceed ten years, and up to a total of 1,000 hours for those who have been under civil service continuously for more than ten years. This would mean several months on pay for older workers who incur the misfortune of critical and prolonged illness. 

Retirement Systems 

Workers and students in the personnel field usually agree that an old age retirement system is desirable. Unless automatic retirement on adequate pensions is provided, the various services become overloaded with aged employees whose efficiency has ebbed considerably. One large city recently had fifty laborers over seventy years of age in its street cleaning depart- Of this number one had attained the age of ninety-six and another ninety-four; and several had entered the city service ment.

Ch. 10] 215 

for the first time after reaching the age of seventy. Thus, the city suffers not only from the burden of carrying along its own superannuated workers, but it makes up for the lack of social insurance for the aged cast-offs of private enterprise. Prior to the enactment of the federal retirement legislation of 1920, the departments were burdened with older workers, some of whom had to be brought to the office in wheel chairs.12 If the retirement payments are too small, many will waive the pension and stay on the job as long as possible. Frequently this is permitted by special action of the legislative body or of a high administrative agency. During the depression year of 1933 there was a strong reaction against this practice, resulting in forced retirement of those who were eligible for retirement. Prevalent opinion felt that those who had pension rights should be required to exercise them and thus create employment for younger people with neither work nor income. A universal social problem of tremendous magnitude is involved in the care of the aged. If governments will take care of their own aged, they will have accomplished two worth-while objectives. The efficiency of administrative operations will have been incalculably benefited, and the social problem of dependency will have been solved on a sizeable sector. But some one has to pay for pensions! That is the omnipresent difficulty. 

There are two general ways of financing a retirement plan. 

One is to budget pension payments with no special attention given to the final obligations incurred. This procedure is sometimes known as the cash disbursement plan. The other method is the actuarial plan, wherein the future retirement obligations are known and provided for in the case of each new recruit to the service. The cash disbursement plan is subject to the same weaknesses as assessment life insurance. The charges are relatively light at the beginning when the workers are young and few are retiring. As the average age of the group increases more will reach the retirement age, frequently causing the burden of payments to exceed the taxpayer's ability or willingness to pay. A little foresight in the beginning would avoid this 

12 Feldman, op. cit., pp. 195-196.

[Pt. II 

PERSONNEL 

calamity by requiring at the start greater payments with which to build up a reserve to meet future contingencies. This reserve drawing compound interest through the years would lighten appreciably the immediate burden on the taxpayer. 

Pension plans are not conceived, however, in the scientific spirit. They are usually the result of agitation on the part of employee groups who have to overcome the disinclination of the legislature to raise taxes and the unwillingness of the taxpayer to pay. The employee organizations are under pressure to make initial showing of low cost. Anxious to secure a promise to pay retirement annuities, they accept what they can get. In cities, this frequently takes the form of a charter amendment authorizing a specific tax levy for the payment of pensions to firemen and policemen. An effective campaign to influence the voter is organized. Emotional appeals are based upon the chivalry and bravery of the firemen and policemen who constantly risk their lives to protect helpless women and children. In states not having home rule the general incorporation law will be amended by the legislature in such a manner as to require cities, or certain cities, to levy a tax to pay pensions. Let us suppose that a five-mill general property tax is levied under such a law. 

Immediately several old-timers retire and become a charge on current funds. Over a period of four or five years, so many policemen and firemen are killed in action that the charge for current payments to pensioners and descendants exceeds the receipts from the special tax. Nothing is being laid up for future contingencies. Such an impasse existed in the Firemen's Pension Fund of Kansas City, Missouri, in 1930.18 During 1929, income of the fund totaled $9,524.70 less than expense. A reserve amounting to $142,500 in 1923 had been reduced at the end of 1929 to $82,000. At that time a number of persons were eligible to retire but could not do so because the funds on hand were not even sufficient to continue payments to existing pensioners. A proper reserve for those already receiving pensions would have amounted to $1,238,111, as against the actual fund of $82,000. Such are the pitfalls of unsound retirement sys- 

13 Kansas City Public Service Institute, Kansas City's Public Affairs, 

August 14, 1930.

Ch. 10] 217 

tems; they can be avoided by starting at the very beginning on an actuarial basis. 

An actuary is a person who forecasts future obligations on a scientific basis and figures out mathematically how much money will be needed at specified times to meet them. If a particular group of public employees is to retire at the age of sixty-five, the actuary's task is to figure how much must be on hand to continue payments so long as each is likely to live. In setting the average amount needed to carry an annuity from age sixty-five to death, he must find the average life span after sixty-five for people in that branch of the public service. While he cannot foretell this with absolute accuracy, statistics are available which give a reasonable index to mortality rates. Having calculated how long the average employee is likely to live past sixty-five, his next task is to ascertain how large a sum will be needed, exhausting principal and interest, to pay the annuity during the average lifespan. He must leave plenty of leeway for an adverse mortality experience, because a small group may accidentally contain a large number of persons who live longer than the expected average. Neither can be given too much credence to the longevity statistics of the population in general, for it is well known that annuitants live longer, due to the contentment engendered by financial security. Having determined the amount necessary to purchase an annuity at age sixty-five, the actuary can then foretell with accuracy the amount of equal annual payments which must be set aside. These funds are invested so that with compound interest the annuity purchase price will be available when needed. A well-conceived system of this nature will liquidate itself. By this is meant that if it were discontinued the reserve on hand would be sufficient to pay existing pension rights without further contributions either from taxation or employees. 

Obviously this explanation has been over-simplified. A great many complications arise in the ordinary pension plan, from the necessity of arranging for disability payments and annuities to widows and minor dependents of deceased employees. In other cases withdrawal rights create problems for the actuary. For these and other reasons, it is recommended that an actuary re-examine and revalue the plan periodically,

[Pt. II 

PERSONNEL 

probably every three or five years. This will facilitate adjustments to take care of those intangible expectancy factors which actuarial science cannot control. 

Retirement schemes may be classified upon the basis of whether the employee contributes all from current salary, whether the employee and the government both contribute part, or whether the government contributes all. A consensus of current opinion probably would favor the joint contributory plan wherein the employee and the government both share a portion of the burden. It is frequently argued, however, that this is a matter of indifference, because if the employees do not contribute, their salaries will tend to be reduced by the amount of the government's contribution. This may be true as a general principle, but it might be rather difficult to prove in specific cases. 

As a rule, it is better to permit those leaving the service to withdraw the sums they have contributed plus interest. Such a privilege will promote freedom of movement. It will also tend to counteract the overburdening of the service with mediocre persons in search of pension security. That is why so many favor the savings bank idea of retirement accumulation. In such a plan each individual employee's account is kept separately as in a savings bank. His contributions plus interest are added and he is periodically furnished with a statement. While no set retirement allowance is guaranteed, he is told that if he continues to contribute at the existing rate, his own accumulations, together with the government's contributions, will purchase an annuity of such and such an amount. He is further informed that his own contributions plus interest may be withdrawn on leaving the service, but that the funds set aside by the government are retained. This procedure is said to have a very salutary educational effect. The pension is no longer something for nothing; it is a service to be obtained only by purchase at a price. 

The employees soon learn why it is desirable to base a retirement plan on actuarial science. They display great interest in the rate of accumulation in their own individual accounts. Such a plan would avoid an unhappy situation which arose in one police department. There the contributions of the men alone exceeded the amount currently paid out in benefits. The amount added

Ch. 10] 219 

to reserve equalled the tax contribution. When real estate interests attacked the pension scheme in a tax reduction campaign, the members of the force were led by their own spokesmen to disavow the warnings of two separate actuarial studies. Each of these said that to maintain the current payment rate taxes would have to be raised instead of lowered. Many of the men could not understand how this could be when their own contributions were more than sufficient to pay current claims. If the pension account of each policeman had been segregated, and he had been acquainted with the purchase price of annuities at various ages, such a contingency might have been avoided. 

When existing pension systems fail to heed the warnings of actuaries, as in the case just mentioned, there will be a day of reckoning in the future. Any one, or a combination, of three or four things can happen. The government can realize the error of its ways and clear up the actuarial deficit in the reserve by payments in addition to the normal over a period of years. The actuarial deficit is the difference between the amount now in the reserve and the amount that the reserve should now have from an actuarial standpoint. The federal government is now liquidating an actuarial deficit amounting to hundreds of millions of dollars, the result of failure to make appropriations to the reserve during the first few years of operating the civilian employees retirement system. The reader must bear in mind that there can be an actuarial deficit even when millions of dollars exist in the reserve. What happens if this deficit is not taken care of? A time comes when the members of the service have a higher average age than when the plan was inaugurated. A steadily larger number become eligible for retirement. Eventually it becomes apparent that existing reserves will soon be exhausted. Some are ready to retire but cannot do so because the pension reserve is dry. In this event the government can maintain the existing retirement rates by appropriating from current revenues. In an old service this will create a burden full of political dynamite. A great many influential taxpayers will not understand why public employees should be given free pensions when the taxpayers are assured no such guaranty. The other alternative will be the adjustment of retirement benefits so

[Pt. II 

PERSONNEL 

that existing reserves and appropriations can maintain them. 

The chances are that the whole system will then be revamped, with serious respect given to an actuary's advice. 

One of the most difficult problems met in starting a retirement plan is the manner of caring for the older employees who are almost ready to retire. No reserve has been built up for them, and it is not equitable to pay them pensions out of reserves now being contributed by the younger men. If these older workers are to enjoy the benefits of the plan, large payments to make up the accrued liability existing in their cases are inevitable. 

There are several ways of handling this situation. The government can start liquidating the deficit by a series of payments covering several years. Each year the entire reserve for the older employees retiring at that time can be set aside. The governing body may elect to budget the benefits as a part of current expense; or, as will rarely be the case, the deficit in the accounts of the old employees may be liquidated by paying one lump sum into the reserve. The older employees will also be required to contribute a higher percentage of their salaries than those who may look forward to longer service. Normally, the government's accrued liability will be taken care of by a series of approximately equal payments extending over a term of years.

The question arises as to whether a governmental unit should manage its own pension funds or purchase annuities outright from insurance companies. The answer resolves itself into a determination of how large a number of annuitants is required to obtain a normal mortality experience. The larger the group the further the risk is spread. If, for instance, pensioners were supposed to live fifteen years after retirement, a small city would be running a greater chance of having them live eighteen years than a large city. This is not because small city pensioners live longer, but because mortality expectancy tables are valid only for large groups. The small city runs a greater chance of experiencing an adverse selection. Chance, good or bad luck will be more likely to make itself felt. Thus, the purchase of annuities from insurance companies is advisable for rather small units. 

In other cases it is decidedly advantageous for the government

Ch. 10] 221 

to manage its own pension fund. There will be a savings in selling and management, and a higher interest return can be earned.

CHAPTER XI  

Promotion Promotion means something more than an increase in compensation. To be sure, a salary increase usually accompanies promotion, but one can receive higher pay without being promoted. This is the case where a worker is advanced from a lower to higher pay level within the same class. His duties have not been changed but his salary has been raised. If, on the other hand, he had been moved to another class, presumably more difficult to fill, and with increased responsibilities, he would have been promoted. The change in duties is the essential characteristic of the promotion process. It is assumed, of course, that progress to a more difficult class will involve an increase in compensation, but this feature is more incidental than distinctive. 

The essential factor being the change of duties, it quite naturally follows that a good promotion procedure must be based on an adequate classification plan. It will be practically impossible to build the public service on a career basis without an arrangement of the duties classifications in such a manner that the possibility for progress from a subordinate to a higher position is indicated. Promotion, then, is progress from a lower class to a higher class involving a corresponding change of duties. It is highly desirable that the promotion policy be well understood by those who man the service. Fairness in this respect will generate and maintain morale; superior personnel will be encɔuraged to remain in the service rather than to hasten to greener private pastures. This can be facilitated by having the paths of progress well marked from class to class, and by publicizing the standards and attainments expected for admission to successive posts. 223

[Pt. II 

PERSONNEL 

There are two basic standards of promotion. All others are variants of one or the other, or of both. The seniority standard would base promotion almost entirely on length of service. 

The other, which for lack of a better name might be termed the ability standard, seeks to find the most capable individual irrespective of length of service. Most students and administrators would not base promotion entirely on seniority, although they would give it some consideration. The amount of weight given seniority would vary with the type of work. For some jobs the experience acquired by successive performance adds to expertness. In others the skill produced by length of service has no relation to higher duties. Seniority promotion is more justifiable in the routine tasks of the lower classes. One who is successful at routine tasks may utterly lack the qualities needed for advanced work. A system of promotion by seniority will frequently result in raising to supervisory and directing positions persons who have "crank" complexes. Frequently advancing years, unmellowed by the give and take of competitive life, acquire an intolerance in non-essentials which dampens the initiative of subordinates. Seniority alone will tend to fill the higher places with incompetents. It will discourage the ambitious and remove those incentives which develop personality, courage, self-reliance, and progressive outlook. It will foster self-satisfaction, a dead level of mediocre performance, and that general let-down which goes with security. Employee organizations are frequently found working for the recognition of seniority. This probably is owing to the feeling that the great preponderance of routine workers would benefit. For choosing the higher officers, however, selection based on length of service is ordinarily unjustifiable. It should be given preponderant weight only in those branches providing rigorous selection at an early age, coupled with effective elimination of incompetents and forced retirement before senility sets in. These conditions prevail in the United States army, where considerable weight has attached to seniority at different times, but not in the civil services. 

If it is finally concluded that promotion should be on the basis of ability, the question is far from being solved. The next

Ch. 11] 225 

step is to determine what abilities are desired and how best to secure them. This leads into an uncharted realm of opinion, speculation, and controversy. Is promotion to be founded on competitive tests? If so, who shall be allowed to take these tests? Cannot selections for promotions be left entirely to department heads? Why not judge progress through efficiency or service ratings? These queries and many others, do not admit of categorical answers, for there is perhaps no single promotion procedure suitable for all occasions and environments. 

Probably promotional tests are sufficiently important to merit prior attention.

The authorities are not agreed that written competitive examinations are desirable in all cases. The leading commentators on the federal personnel system favor a large degree of administrative discretion. As the rules now stand, the promoting officer may devise his own test of fitness, if the Civil Service Commission does not disagree. The exception to this rule prevails when promotion will lead to a position which has entrance tests different from those now occupied by the candidates. In that case a promotional test is given by the Commission, but it is non-competitive and given only at the instance of the department involved. It is felt that criticism of the federal promotion procedure does not arise from powers contained in existing federal executive orders, for they are adequate in that they permit the necessary discretion. Reform needs to take place in the practice rather than in the rules. Promotion by competitive tests is more justifiable for the elimination of political influence than as a means of selection. For this reason such tests may be justifred as inspirers of morale. They will serve to assure the employees that promotion is based upon equality of opportunity rather than upon favoritism or nepotism. 

Another controversy centers around the question whether entry to higher positions should be closed or open to outsiders. 

The logical procedure involves leaving this determination in

each particular instance to administrative discretion, ultimately the personnel director. He should be motivated in reaching his decision by the availability of suitable material within the service itself. Some departments, because of the nature of their work, do not develop the qualities needed for executive positions. 

Furthermore, the American system of recruiting places much emphasis on immediate technical proficiency as opposed to broad fundamental background. This tends to deprive the service of persons having those intangible qualities which make for success. When recruiting does aim to secure individuals with broad general preparation coupled with positive personality traits it will be entirely safe to fill the higher positions from within. Such persons cannot be attracted to the service in the beginning, however, unless lured by attractive career opportunities. Mr. Feldman rightly questions whether the United 

States ever will be able to compete on an equal basis with private business for the most competent administrative ability.2 In 

England and other European countries, at least in the past, adventurous and ambitious youth has found economic opportunities with the state quite comparable to competitive private enterprise. It may be that if industrial unemployment becomes semi-permanent, a more competent section of American manhood may be attracted to the public service. Until that condition prevails, administrators should be free to fill the higher positions either by promotion from within or recruitment from without, as conditions may justify.

The Bureau of Public Personnel Administration, in its model rules for civil service commissions, stands committed to competitive promotional tests for the higher positions. Ample discretion is given the personnel director and commission, however, to make exceptions in any particular instance. In some cases it may be desirable to permit competition from both within and without, because the number of present employees qualified to fill higher posts is not large enough. In such instances morale will be fostered by creating two appointment lists, one for those now in the service who have passed the test and one for outside appli- 

2 Op. cit., p. 100.

Ch. 11] 

227 

cants. None of the latter will be certified and appointed until the employee list is exhausted. A difficult problem is presented in the determination of the area of competition within the service.

Who shall be permitted to take the promotional tests if these tests are to be limited to those now in service? The model rules would leave this determination to the personnel director who would designate certain classes as providing the correct training and experience. Those who had filled positions in those classes for a period of one year or more could compete. 

Opportunity would be given others to submit proofs that their experience in the classified service had fitted them to perform the duties of the higher class. 

It should not be overlooked that there is a strong sentiment in some quarters in favor of leaving promotion largely in the hands of the operating department. Many administrators feel that unfettered discretion should be placed in the hands of the appointing officer. Others would trust the department head with ultimate choice for promotions, subject to the approval of the central personnel agency. Where the latter is a part of an integrated department of finance, the administrative officer in charge of housekeeping functions would also have a check. 

Advisory promotional boards, now undergoing trial in the British service, may have a great deal to contribute. Mr. 

Mayers, who regards promotion by civil service tests with disfavor, suggests promotion by the appointing officer upon recommendations made by departmental boards composed of high administrative officials with representatives of the civil service commission. For the federal service, Mr. Feldman suggests organized planning for promotion by a central agency, presumably the personnel establishment, which would maintain a chart of paths to advancement; put pressure on the appointing officers to advance the more capable and search for those with talents for higher posts; assist in bringing about transfers which would facilitate advancement; and render the educational facilities and advice desired by ambitious employees. This agency would 

Op. cit., pp. 342-343. 

Op. cit., p. 104.

[Pt. II 

PERSONNEL 

possess latent power to require competitive promotional examinations, but would exercise such a prerogative only in case the promotional policy of particular departments resulted in holding back the most talented. Then, in order to generate morale, it could step in and exercise its right to hold promotional tests. 

Normally, however, promotions would remain in the hands of the operating departments. 

The opportunity to achieve promotion should be national or regional and not local, especially in the higher technical and administrative positions. If an individual has made an outstanding record as a health officer in a city of 50,000 at $4,000 per year, it should be possible for him to look forward to service in a municipality of 100,000 at $6,000 per annum. Residence requirements for the higher posts are largely traceable to narrow provincialism. It is frequently argued that an officer must have had long residence in the community in order to become familiar with "local conditions." As a matter of fact, unfamiliarity with "local conditions" may constitute a positive advantage to an administrator. It may free him from entangling alliances which many a local man would like to avoid but cannot because of long association. Differences in local conditions are due, furthermore, to political situations and not to fundamental variations in administrative problems and procedure. The personal qualities and training that would produce administrative leadership in Seattle would do the same in Baltimore, politics permitting. The manner of administering a fire department should not differ essentially between St. Louis and Kansas City. If professional careers in local government are to be fostered, promotion from city to city must be facilitated. This will require abolition of local residence rules coupled with abandonment of the provincial spirit. A similar change must be produced in the federal field. There the local offices of the field units are regarded almost as airtight cells, especially in such extensive branches as the Postal Service, the Customs Service, and the 

Internal Revenue Service. A proper promotion procedure would throw open the path of advancement by permitting progression from a smaller local unit to a larger-from postmaster in Buffalo to postmaster in New York.

Ch. 11] 229 

 Transfers 

Placement will be greatly facilitated by a more flexible transfer procedure than has prevailed in most public personnel jurisdictions. During normal times a transfer in the federal service has been all but impossible. The necessity of finding work for those whose positions were abolished through retrenchment has liberalized transfer practice during 1932-1933. A proper transfer system should be based upon a sound duties classification. 

Otherwise, there are no very definite criteria for ascertaining whether the position to be left compares favorably with the proposed new post. There are a number of accepted meanings for the term "transfer." For present purposes it will be understood to include no change in class but a change in organization unit. 

In this case the employee is moved from one supervisor to another either with or without material change in duties. Why should it be desirable to make such a change? From the standpoint of the employee there may be several advantages. In the present position there may exist adverse situations vitally influencing performance and efficiency. A given worker may need to be placed largely on his own to attain his utmost effectiveness, and yet find himself under the supervision of a tyrant who directs in great detail the efforts of his subordinates. One may find that workers in his class in his present unit are in a blind alley, but that those in similar work elsewhere have ample opportunity for promotion. Another may desire to work closer to his home or to move to another city nearer to friends and relatives. It is generally agreed that within reasonable limits transfers to meet justifiable ends should be permitted. It is presumed that a proper system of entrance examinations would minimize the necessity for transfers. An excessively large number of such changes may indicate a defective recruiting system. The Bureau of Public Personnel Administration has estimated a normal number of transfers involving change in organization unit but not of class at from 75 to 125 in a service of 5,000 workers.

The question arises as to the motivation of transfers. 

Should an employee be permitted to transfer at will whenever

[Pt. II 

PERSONNEL 

he can engineer a deal for a job in another department? Should he be permitted to leave his present unit against the will of his superior officer? Frequently the "breaking in" of an employee represents a considerable expenditure of time and effort and quite naturally his chief is loath to lose him and thus be required to repeat the irritations and labor connected with "breaking in" another. Questions such as these cannot be answered dogmatically and categorically. Their solution in particular cases should be entrusted to the discretion of the personnel agency. 

The latter's power to effect transfers, almost non-existent in the past, should be greatly expanded in the future. It should be charged with aggressively fostering desirable transfers, in addition to acting as intermediary for those initiated by appointing officers or employees. The personnel unit also can thwart abuses that may arise from a flexible transfer procedure. For instance, appointing officers quite frequently dislike to discharge unsatisfactory workers. Instead, they arrange to transfer such employees out of their jurisdiction. It is thought that the head of the organization unit to which it is proposed to make the transfer should be informed of the reason for such a change. Problem nuisances should not be permitted to drift indefinitely from unit to unit. A central personnel agency, with the proper system of records, would be familiar with all such instances and consequently in a position to deal with them effectively. 

The well-organized personnel agency of the future undoubtedly will possess a division of vocational guidance. Such a unit will be charged with directing the vocational interests and careers of, not only apparent misfits, but also those giving satisfaction to both themselves and their superiors. It will be manned by persons trained in industrial psychology and psychiatry, and will have access to the counsel of those experienced in employment processes. It will aim to discover and develop the special aptitudes of all members of the service to the end that the jurisdiction concerned may reap the benefit of a complete utilization of personal capabilities. If, as Mr. Probst's experiments on service ratings lead one to suspect, entrance tests are highly unreliable in predicting adaptability for particular tasks, transfers under the direction of vocational guidance may become the

Ch. 11] 231 

accepted practice. Such an eventuality, however, must be based upon the superior reliability of vocational guidance-a conclusion hardly justified at the present time. Placement after entry is certain to loom ever larger in personnel programs both public and private. Indeed, if government control of private enterprise becomes general during the next generation, labor problems will have to be settled by scientific placement through industrial psychology. As the Great War brought industrial psychology into army placement, so may the depression emergency necessitate its utilization in solving the personnel problems involved in the new Rooseveltian schemes of social planning. 

Lay-Offs 

The depression years immediately following 1929 saw what was for all practical purposes a new phenomenon in the American public service. During the two previous decades there had been a steady, and sometimes rapid, increase in personnel for most establishments. Now came a time when governmental revenues began to shrink. The years 1930 and early months of 1931 were bridged without acute discomfort, but 1932 and 1933 brought such a shrinkage of income that drastic economies had to be undertaken. Private industries could contract their forces with comparative ease, but the discharge or lay-off of public employees is a disagreeable task full of political potentialities. Pressure is brought to bear from all imaginable sources to block lay-offs in this bureau or that service. Eventually, after a depression has worn on for some months, drastic retrenchment becomes inevitable. With lay-offs staring some as yet undesignated individuals in the face, the employees find themselves in a state of nervous apprehension. Those who are to be separated from the service may be chosen by means of various criteria, used either singly or in combination. Some of the more common to be given weight are seniority, efficiency, war-veteran status, pension eligibility, marital or family status, place on original eligible list, and discretion of appointing officer. 

"L. D. White, Trends in Public Administration (McGraw-Hill Book 

Co., 1933), pp. 242-245.

The most important factor is unquestionably seniority. 

While a number of jurisdictions render lip service to efficiency as one consideration to govern separations, few use it in practice. The reason for this lies in the lack of a device for scoring efficiency which possesses the widespread confidence of managers, employees, and personnel workers. The difficulties encountered in administering service ratings are discussed elsewhere in this chapter. Seniority has the merit of being concrete and objective. Employee organizations seem to regard it with much favor. The reverse side of the picture, however, depicts the younger workers, often with higher efficiency ratings, being forced to retire in favor of older workers. Nevertheless, there are many worthy arguments for giving efficiency some considerable weight, perhaps in combination with seniority. 

Mere length of service as a criterion for awarding benefits tends to foster all of the alleged evils of bureaucracy. These include that self-satisfaction bred by a knowledge of security. A person satisfied with himself and his lot may cease to be overly concerned about the sensibilities of others. This lack of responsiveness frequently causes lay citizens to criticize public employees. Ultimately the latter would be much better off collectively if they would foster means of counteracting selfsatisfaction among their individual members. Surely efficiency, as against seniority alone in awarding service benefits, would be a considerable incentive in that direction."

The heartache arising from contraction of the service in 1932 and 1933 was eased to some extent by the use of certain humane and sensible devices. In a great many jurisdictions, normal recruiting and testing came to a standstill. Instead of inducting new workers, the personnel staff-often itself depleted by forced separations-directed its attention to the problems of a contracting service. This took the form, in various places, of finding employment elsewhere in the service for those whose positions were abolished. For this purpose re-employment lists or registers were maintained for those already laid off, while many still Factual material for this section taken largely from Raymond M. at work were assured continued employment by means of transfers. In most cases the existing rules permitted reinstatement only in their own class or in classes with very similar duties. 

There has been a tendency, however, to liberalize such restrictions and permit greater flexibility in placing laid-off workers. 

If properly administered, such arrangements are highly desirable. 

Service Ratings 

Service ratings, sometimes referred to as efficiency ratings, are attempts to evaluate capability and performance on the job. by a worker's superiors and supervisors. In the past they have constituted estimates based upon the subjective judgment of the person making the rating. For this reason they should not be confused with personnel records. The latter are only bookkeeping entries, usually filed in card index form, setting forth the employment history of each worker. These latter contain such data as age, employment record, education, physical examination, sick leave, vacation absences, salary, transfers, and promotions. While this information may be of value to the rating officer for purposes of reference, they constitute mere routine records of facts not involving judgment. Every administrative agency will have to keep personnel records of some kind, but very few have had more than perfunctory experience with service ratings. The latter involve the exercise of judgment; they constitute a recorded statement of an administrator's estimate of a subordinate's worth. 

There is probably no field offering a greater clash between theory and practice than grading the efficiency of workers. 

Theory says it would be splendid to rate employees according to performance and worth. Management so avows, and workers agree in principle. No sooner is an attempt made than it is blocked, or its effectiveness is impaired by almost insuperable obstacles. Theory says that employees should see themselves as management sees them. Permitting them to view their own service ratings will furnish them with the basis for self correc- For a rather complete bibliography on service ratings see F. F. Bradshaw, "Revising Rating Techniques," The Personnel Journal (December, 1932), Vol. X, No. 4, pp. 232, 242-245.

[Pt. II 

PERSONNEL 

tion. When actual flesh and blood workers see their own ratings making individual defects a matter of record, however, the reaction is too often one of resentment rather than an inspiration to self improvement. It would seem that probably work-a-day humanity may not be so anxious to see itself as others see it. 

After all, is not a major section of any population not content with security and a meal ticket? Perhaps an automobile and radio should be added in the United States. At any rate experience has demonstrated that difficulties of major proportion must be surmounted by those who would rate workers on the basis of comparative efficiency. In private management, where the workers, at least in the past, have had little option other than to accept orders from their superiors, perhaps the environment is more favorable for service ratings. In the public service, as 

Mr. Munro has so ably pointed out, the employees are to a considerable extent their own employers. If they are disgruntled over ratings they can, in many jurisdictions, create such protest as seriously to embarrass the personnel agency. If the law still requires such ratings the spirit of the law can be nullified without violating its letter. An innocuous form can be filled out and filed perfunctorily. Sometimes all workers are given identically the same rating, so lightly do certain executives regard the task. As a matter of fact, superior officers, even though they may believe in the rating principle, are frequently glad to shirk the responsibility. Ratings which speak the truth may provoke the wrath and recrimination of substandard but influential workers. In other cases they may raise the cry of favoritism. As in the case of removal, discussed in the following chapter, an honest attempt at service ratings may "put the rater on the spot." All of which makes this a legitimate question: "Do employees want to be rated effectively?"

Not all of the difficulties encountered by service ratings, however, have their source in this query. Service ratings of the past have possessed genuine defects. It has not been an easy matter to select traits that are conducive to performance. A person with a paper rating far above average might be seriously impaired by a trait not taken into account by the rating. It has also been difficult to eliminate personal bias in evaluating a trait

Ch. 11] 235 

that has been selected as suitable for rating purposes.

These are some of the reasons vhy certain administrators have lacked confidence in service ratings and have used them only in a perfunctory manner where required to do so by law. The rating score has usually been achieved by securing a composite of weighted points allocated to various traits, such as quality and quantity of work, accuracy, neatness, promptness, co-operativeness, and a variety of others. This is usually expressed as a numerical percentage with 100 as perfect. Some departments mark relatively high, others relatively low. This alone is sufficient to impeach the rating system for comparative uses. In the federal service it is known that ratings have been manipulated- 20 15 10 E-ED-D C- C C+ B B+ A A+

In spite of known shortcomings, the promise of service ratings is so alluring that experimentation goes on. Why this perennial search for such an elusive goal? The answer is contained in the decidedly beneficial uses which could be made of reliable ratings. In the first place, the examiner would know that a high correlation between tests and ratings would indicate the validity of his tests, whereas a poor correlation would show the tests to be unsatisfactory. Mr. Probst has already run experiments which indicate that certain entrance tests possess doubtful validity when correlated with the Probst rating.10 Any just conclusion on comparisons of this nature would depend upon whether Mr. Probst and the tests were measuring the same things. If service ratings were highly reliable they would most assuredly constitute an important guide in developing test material. The fruition of such an ideal would remove testing from its present status of uncertain reliability to a position of high predictability. In the second place, accurate service ratings would greatly simplify the problem of promotion. While efficiency in some jobs might not indicate success in a higher position, if the service were properly classified service ratings could be much weightier factors in promotions than they are now. 

As a matter of fact, the British annual report form contains an item pertaining to the individual's fitness for promotion. In the third place, the difficult problems of discipline and removal would be aided greatly by the record of service value contained in successive ratings. It has been suggested, for instance, that any one who twice received the grade E under the Probst system would be dismissed automatically from the service. On the other hand, a series of satisfactory ratings might constitute valuable protection for a worker charged with a disciplinary offense for the first time. So manifold are the possible beneficial uses of service ratings that the continued experimentation of personnel workers should be no source of wonder.

a device consisting of a slide rule and stencil. As the slide rule would pass back and forth the stencil would reveal certain combinations of checks upon the rating form. These would unfold slide-rule readings which in turn would be translated by formula into the ultimate scores. Any moderately intelligent clerk could readily learn to operate the device. The scores were devised on a biological curve basis, letter ratings running from high to low as follows: A+, A, B+, B, C+, c, c—, D, D—, E, E—. 

The three C categories constitute the average, a perfect distribution allocating a larger number to them than to the others, in accordance with the biological curve principle. Experiments have amply proven that the biological curve applies to the Probst ratings. Successive runs have shown the A score allotted to 5 to 7 per cent, B 14 to 17 per cent, C 49 to 57 per cent, D 17 to 24 per cent, and E 4 to 5 per cent.

Mr. Probst has utilized several statistical devices to test the reliability and validity of his ratings. He was of the opinion that a reliable rating plan should show substantially identical results for the same group of employees in successive ratings. 

He has shown conclusively that where the Probst reports are applied successively to identical groups, a plotted graph tends to produce a symmetrical grouping, whereas a great scattering results when certain other rating forms are used. The conclusion is that successive ratings under the Probst plan produce little change in individual scores, whereas other forms create so many changes in individual ratings as to render their usefulness of highly doubtful value. To test the validity of the Probst rating system, a number of experiments were directed toward correlation with judgment ratings. Supervisors and other persons familiar with those to be rated were asked to express their judgments upon them. In some instances they were asked to assign the same letter scores as used by the Probst reports; in other cases they ranked the subjects in numerical order. Then the Probst rating was taken on each. The resulting correlations were relatively high in a number of instances. The difficulties encountered issued largely from inability to get the supervisors to agree upon their judgment ratings. Where the officers did reach substantial agreement, correlation with the Probst reports

Ch. 11] 241 

was high. It was also found that the Probst system appraises the service value of professional and technical workers more accurately than routine or non-technical personnel. Some of the data and circumstances brought to light tended to prove the highly unreliable nature of judgment ratings as compared to the Probst reports.¹¹

The Probst Service Report, General Form, is the edition being supplied in January, 1935. It is reproduced here with the permission of Mr. Probst. Special forms are available for the police, fire, labor, and educational services. 

Probably some statement as to the future of the service rating idea is expected at this point. One finds it exceedingly difficult to be very certain. Mr. Probst is carrying on his experiments with apparent confidence; no sooner have his reports met reverses in one jurisdiction than they are tried in another. It is reasonable to expect that they will continue to be used indefinitely in at least some of the places where they have been inaugurated. 

Experience will undoubtedly develop a diplomatic means of handling the human nature elements encountered in administration. Service ratings will never be successful if they antagonize employee groups. It may be that there is fallacy in the idea. that ratings should be open to employee inspection. In the future it may be found to be desirable to make them secret tools of management alone. On the other hand, as one personnel technician recently said, service ratings may never be suited to the public service where political considerations throw obstacles in the way of management. It may also be true that those employees who have made it difficult for rating schemes to operate are entirely correct in condemning the attempts made thus far. Prudence dictates reticence on this subject. CHAPTER XII  

The right of employees of the state to organize presents the same class conflicts as are traditionally involved in the antagonism between labor unions and management. Management demands unfettered freedom to set wages, hours of work, conditions of labor, and size of force. The unions seek to place restrictions on management's freedom by means of collective bargaining. Experience has demonstrated that public servants will be neglected in matters of pay unless they are militantly vocal through their own organizations. On the other hand, if employee organizations become too strong they may exert an influence which interferes with a sound public management. 

There is the example of the automotive repair shop working on a revolving fund replenished by invoicing the repair charges to the operating departments. The latter began to complain that the charges were excessive-far higher than private garages would charge for similar jobs. Investigation showed that no provision existed for a flexible labor force. When ten mechanics were available and there was only one vehicle on the floor, the time of all ten was charged to the single piece of equipment. Employee interests had successfully fought the flexible force arrangement, and they had been able to maintain the union wage rate, which was 50 per cent higher than that paid in private garages which were almost one hundred per cent open shop. 

Many liberal thinkers balk at acceptance of state socialism because they cannot cross this philosophic hurdle. The Soviet industrial system is reported to have encountered it as one of the foremost obstacles to the operation of the great new factories built under the Five-Year Plan. Management was made subservient to the wishes of workers' committees. Factory executives permitted gross inefficiency to prevail, knowing very well that any attempt to curtail workmen interference would result in 244

Ch. 12] 245 

reprisals against the management. This was one of the large causes of factory breakdowns under the Five-Year Plan. 

Hence, the crucial problem in public employment lies in compromising and harmonizing the divergent interests of management and politics. The government must be efficient, yet it cannot pursue the ruthless employment policy which private enterprises of vaunted efficiency have practiced. Management is severely limited by the political weapons which public employees can wield both singly and collectively. This is one of the principal reasons why the efficiency of governmental personnel and enterprises has been held in such low public esteem in the United States. The Washington department head is narrowly limited in the disciplinary measures available against a subordinate who is a protégé of a United States Senator.¹ A mayor or manager of a city must think not only twice, but three times, before he sponsors any administrative arrangements frowned upon by policemen's and firemen's organizations. Especially is this so where these forces have available the initiative and referendum with which to secure desired pension and salary arrangements. Hence, management in the public service is working under a greatly different environment than is management in most private enterprises in the United States. Public management is not always free to discipline employees, nor is it free to lay off employees when work is slack, or to employ whom it will. 

What is more, public management is likely to find itself in an occasional position where employees are able to dictate policies opposed to management's desires. For these reasons it has been said that the problems of morale and efficiency in the public service are not capable of being solved by the dictates of management alone. Management must temper its employment policies by reckoning with the political weapons of the personnel itself. 

The Right to Organize

Professional and scientific personnel does not, however, tend to become what may be designated as "union-minded." Even though unfairly paid, such workers tend to refrain from participation in general employee movements to force higher pay and better working conditions. The scientific and professional services of the federal government were vastly benefited by the classification work of the last decade, yet the federal employees' organizations complain of the aloofness of the men in these followings. When referring to employee organizations, therefore, attention is directed primarily to the mass of workers amenable to unionization. This will include the great bulk of workers exclusive of managerial, professional, and scientific positions. 

Formerly legislatures and executives maintained a hostile attitude toward the unionization of the public services. Especially marked was this antagonism in the federal administration where for many years employees were legally barred from jointly dealing with Congress or the executive. Finally, in 

1912 legal barriers were removed and since that time employee organizations have conducted powerful lobbies. There can be little doubt that the substantial improvement in such matters as pensions and pay is directly traceable to the efforts of employee organizations in the last twenty years. Indeed, experience leads to the conclusion that governmental employees need expect little unless they organize. Executives and legislatures are constantly under pressure from large tax-paying interests to keep down expenditure. These same interests organized as chambers of commerce, local improvement associations, or taxpayers' associations demand appropriations for various types of ventures. A large proportion of federal employees belong to units directly affiliated with the American Federation of Labor, and the same can be said of several of the larger cities.* If public employees are permitted to unionize, the next question to arise has to do with the right to strike. Most thoughtful individuals will immediately call to mind the hazard to public safety if policemen and firemen were to strike. Yet the most celebrated police force of the Anglo-Saxon world has experienced at least four strikes in its century of existence. The 

Boston police strike of 1919 is of recent memory. There the minions of the law had been receiving $1,100 per year and furnishing their own uniforms, when craftsmen were earning $14 per day. The strikers were denied the privilege of returning to work, but their newly recruited successors received $1,400 per year, plus uniforms. Undoubtedly, the general right to strike should be denied those who man those services which are indispensable to public safety. Yet it is hard to censure them for using the strike weapon when all other means of securing tolerable working conditions and a living wage have been exhausted. 

The public can avoid the strike by providing adequate salaries and favorable conditions of public employment. The employees have learned from experience that desirable results can be achieved by use of their own organizations without striking. 

Political pressure applied through the lobby and the mobilization of public opinion through the use of the initiative and referendum, have proved to be effective weapons. The policemen's and firemen's organizations have used them to improve their condition. They have secured minimum salaries by vote of the people by means of initiative ordinances and charter amendments. The dominant concern of each individual is security in his job. This desire for security becomes at least the latent motivation for all of the acts of the organization. Each individual tends to sympathize with a fellow employee who has been disciplined or removed, seeing a menace to his own security therein. The community of interests thus generated leads efficient workers to overlook the deficiencies of their less competent comrades. Police protective associations have been known to fight prolonged legal battles to secure the reinstatement of officers who were not worthy of their profession. An organization composed of average humanity probably must be geared to the aspirations, desires, and mentality of the greatest common denominator. This is at once the weakness and strength of human organizations in general. Mr. 

Average Worker who may be said to constitute this greatest common denominator is more interested in job security than anything else.

Post-war developments in Great Britain offer a significant experiment in what may be termed the joint council ideacommonly referred to as Whitleyism. The various Whitley councils are composed of an equal number of two types of representatives: one speaking for the official or government interests, the other for the "staff" or workers. These meet periodically and discuss agenda pertaining to various personnel problems. 

There is one National Whitley Council acting for the entire civil service. Each department may have its own Whitley Council, besides which various industrial units or plants have Whitley organizations of their own. The British civil service had always been characterized by strict and unchallenged Treasury control of all personnel matters. A literal interpretation of the powers of the Whitley Councils might have led some to expect their decisions to stand against Treasury disapproval. 

As a matter of fact, however, the government and the Treasury still hold the whip hand. The experience of the last fifteen years seems to have been developing a working formula whereby the Whitley Councils could deliberate and reach workable de-

Ch. 12] 249 

cisions without embarrassing the government. For this reason, probably more than any other, Whitleyism may not have lived up to the full expectations of all its critics and well-wishers. 

Observers seem agreed, however, that its positive accomplishments have more than justified its existence. Whitleyism is still an experiment, but one well worthy of observation by the United States. The system of group representation recently developed in the federal postal service offers some analogies worthy of note."

Morale Morale has to do with the employee's mental attitude toward his job and working environment. Low morale is linked with shirking, a sense of frustration, lack of forward outlook, and general dissatisfaction. High morale is associated with pride in work, desire to perform correctly, and all-around satisfaction with employment. Lack of morale is attributed to adverse conditions variously referred to as depressives or "de-centives." 

Dull and tedious routine seems unavoidable in any bureaucratic organization, yet industrial psychology can do much to avoid its harmful effects upon morale. Proper guidance and placement procedure will see to it that individuals with initiative and ambition are not tortured in a prison of deadly routine. Large-scale organization, whether public or private, tends to develop a “mind your own business" complex. A not insignificant number of supervising chiefs are jealous of their subordinates. The latter may assume the initiative by making suggestions for improvement, but are repulsed. Not many repulses of this nature are needed to seal the lips of the ambitious and produce a sense of universal frustration. The adverse effect of such a situation on morale is apparent. To avoid and counteract the evils involved, various types of incentive have been suggested and used. 

The pay level, of course, is probably the most vital factor related to the general satisfaction of employees. If income opportunities are decidedly unfavorable as compared to compara- 

H. Feldman, A Personnel Program for the Federal Civil Service, 71st
