ble pursuits in private endeavor, a low grade personnel will drift into the public service and bring with it the mental outlook of those at the lower end of the biological curve. A satisfactory morale can hardly be maintained under such conditions. The problems of morale cannot be wholly solved, however, by improvement in rates of pay. Under our existing economic order there is a limit of expenditures beyond which governments cannot step. Consequently, it is not within the realm of physical possibilities to pay each employee in accordance with what he thinks he deserves. For purposes of this discussion it must be assumed that a fair compensation plan (whatever its basis may be) has been adopted. Beyond that, morale is dependent upon a wide variety of non-financial incentives. One of the most important of these may be termed the service motive-a combination of high prestige and pride in one's job. Where these incentives prevail, individuals will be so satisfied with their working environment that they will refuse to accept more lucrative work elsewhere. Proper and certain means of recognizing merit are essential factors in developing such a spirit. This necessitates promotion procedure commanding the complete confidence of the force. Recognition in the form of praise must be unstintedly yet judiciously offered. Police officers are known to covet citations for bravery in the daily bulletin, yet incentives of this nature may become impotent because they are used in excess. There is no royal formula which will insure the maintenance of morale. Whether it exists in a given unit will depend to a great extent upon the personal qualities of the directing chief. If he is a suspicious person, aware and fearful of superior qualities in certain key subordinates, a sense of frustration may pervade the entire personnel. Such directing heads find their way too often into the public service through advancement under the seniority rule or through political pressure. There are, on the other hand, numerous public agencies where inspired and talented leadership has created marvelous esprit de corps in spite of severe economic handicaps. 

There has always been some skepticism as to whether the public service can ever offer the same incentives as private enterprise. Those who argue in the negative lay great store by eco-

Ch. 12] 251 

nomic laissez-faire, individualism, and survival of the fittest. 

They say that people will work only if spurred on by the incentive to greater wealth and profit. If industry is operated by the state for the common good, and the profit motive thereby removed, workers will fail to put forth their best efforts because of the new sense of security. Management will atrophy and become ineffective because managers no longer have anything to work for; clever and adroit management will not yield them personal gain. Public bureaucracies can never offer a substitute incentive for the individual profit urge, so it is said. As a consequence, the socialization of industry is likely to fail. These declarations, however, do not go unanswered. A large and increasing school of thinkers, students, and humanitarians see increasing socialization as inevitable. They believe that there are incentives to superior work and endeavor available within a bureaucracy. Indeed, they regard the insinuation that men are actuated by the profit motive alone as an unwarranted slur upon the character of mankind in general. The patriotic motive incites soldiers to risk their lives without hope of financial return. Throughout the ages great causes have inspired strong souls to court martyrdom without thought of a gold reward. 

What are some of the incentives that may be generated within a bureaucracy? First come social incentives: spurs which give bureaucractic action prestige, make it fashionable, the thing which the best people do. There is considerable evidence that this type of incentive is being used with success in Soviet Russia. Mr. White has conclusively demonstrated that membership in the bureaucracy has had a remarkably low prestige value in the United States. On the other hand, it has frequently carried considerable social position in Europe. Bureaucracy need not be entirely devoid of financial incentives. Attractive salaries in the upper classifications, with fairly administered paths of promotion, should furnish all of the financial incentives which private enterprise has to offer to the competent but impecunious youth of the nation. Then there is the contentment that

comes from the love of one's work: a reward which the bureaucracy can surely furnish. Indeed, there is evidence that it can do so on a more extensive scale than private endeavor has done in the past. The service motive has been effective in creating a certain romantic halo around some public enterprises, notably the military branches. This appeal need not be lacking in civilian units; witness the hundreds of capable young people who each year take college work in preparation for the diplomatic service when the Foreign Service takes on only a handful of recruits annually. The clerical and monastic callings in the middle ages certainly held out no pecuniary lures for the great mass of novitiates, yet the church beckoned the best manhood to a distinguished career. Probably it is this desire for distinction in fields approved by the existing social mores which forms the basis for all incentives, distinction and power. Surely a bureaucracy could furnish ample opportunities for both. 

Security 

The entire question of morale is tied up with the problem of security. Without a reasonable degree of security, morale will be lacking; yet an excess of security may serve to deaden the incentives to morale discussed in the foregoing paragraphs. 

Contrary to what may be the general impression, governmental employment offers greater security than private enterprise in the United States. Every study that has come to our attention indicates that the turnover is greater in private enterprise than in public employment. Observers agree, however, that this condition may not be entirely healthy; the turnover in governmental departments may be lower than that which is essential to the maintenance of operating efficiency. Special significance at taches to this consideration in those services where, in normal times, turnover can be attributed largely to the departure of the most competent to accept more lucrative work outside. Removals, as will be pointed out below, are distasteful and difficult, with the result that the average department head will do everything possible to avoid the embarrassment attendant upon a removal. 

The result is that the security attached to the public service frequently serves to retain incompetent, inefficient, and unnecessary

Ch. 12] 253 

employees. If the presence of an undesirable worker becomes unbearable at a particular post, the easiest solution is to send him "to the sticks"-transfer him to a remote and unimportant place.

In spite of these drawbacks, a reasonable amount of security is essential. The principal obstacles to security are offered by the spoils system and political despoilers. The result is that civil service workers are required to refrain from active participation in politics in return for immunity from the vicissitudes of politics. All modern bureaucracies have attempted to obtain freedom from political despoliation by one means or another. 

As the culmination of a century and a half of development, pre- Hitler Germany had accepted the professional public servant as the obvious. His absence was much more to be questioned than his presence. His security was assured by a well-established jurisprudence which invoked effective remedies for trespasses on his vested rights. By law the civil servant was guaranteed tenure, salary, pensions, and other perquisites. He had a property right in his office, respect for which could be enforced by suit in both administrative and ordinary courts. Cases requiring discipline had to pass through prescribed procedure, calculated carefully to protect the interest of both the state and the official. In 

England, the civil servant has none of these legal guarantees enforceable at law, although Whitleyism may evolve in that direction; yet the British civil servant enjoys a high degree of security. This can lead to no conclusion other than that legal safeguards, while perhaps desirable to an undetermined degree, are not essential to security. Rather, an effective bureaucracy should be rooted in traditions of official integrity and honor, fortified by widespread public confidence in its functioning and motives.

Removal The effort to obtain security has created one of the most perplexing public personnel problems in the United States. The establishment of tenure was dependent upon the abolition of political removals. The natural course was to create legal safeguards which would make unjustified removals difficult.

[Pt. II 

PERSONNEL 

Experience has shown, however, that legal obstacles to removal constitute a two-edged sword which cuts both ways. Difficult removal provisions undoubtedly protect efficient workers, but they also prevent dealing properly with cases where removal is desirable. A few years ago the friends of civil service were surprised by the opposition and condemnation directed at civil service by the city managers. Here was a new body of professional public officials, brought into existence largely by the very elements responsible for civil service reform, and it was quite reasonable, therefore, to expect them to be friendly, yet in their annual conferences antagonism cropped out in every managerial Their stories setting forth their experiences with difficult removals under civil service offered the explanation. sector. 

A typical grievance story of a city manager who has had unhappy experience with civil service would probably run as follows: In most small and medium-sized cities, the civil service provisions apply only to policemen and firemen. The police department in most instances causes the manager more worry and anxiety than all other departments taken together. It is a constant source of anxiety because of its inevitable association with liquor, bootleggers, vice, suppression of radicalism, strikes and labor disputes. Furthermore, law enforcement positions have a peculiar attraction for persons of questionable past, character, and morals. When large civil service jurisdictions began to fingerprint applicants for law enforcement positions, as high as 8 to 10 per cent were found to have had criminal records. 

To go back to our typical managerial experience, let us suppose that an influential newspaper starts to print stories intimating that members of the police department are in league with bootleggers and dive-keepers. At first the administration passes it over as the normal baiting of the press, which is to be expected and must be endured. Soon, however, there is produced strong evidence incriminating a certain police captain and several of his subordinates. These are suspended, but they appeal their case to the civil service commission. On the day of the hearing, a key witness against the men has mysteriously disappeared, and all efforts to locate him are of no avail. Without his testimony all damaging evidence is merely circumstantial. The clever

Ch. 12] 255 

attorney for the policeman is a master of popular psychology. 

By insisting on the observation of jury trial rules of evidence he is able to add to the hearing a touch of melodrama in which the manager is the villain and the deposed officers the defenseless victims. Here and there subtle references are made to official family skeletons, aired with the conscious purpose of casting reproach on the manager and questioning his being in a position. to be accusing others. The men are restored to duty. The manager's only recourse is to place them where they will do the least harm. With a sense of frustration he throws up his hands in despair and denounces civil service. Can he be blamed?

Probably the most common mode of effecting removals is to allow the appointing officer to suspend an employee, permitting the latter to demand a hearing before the civil service commission within a given number of days. The commission is given authority to confirm the removal or reinstate the discharged person. This procedure is general, although there are certain notable exceptions. In both the federal service and in Los Angeles County the decision of the removing officer is final. The degree of success achieved by this type of quasijudicial hearing has varied with the personnel of the commissions. Where the commissioners have been imbued with a thorough appreciation of and sympathy with the objectives of the merit system, justifiable removals have not been difficult. 

On the other hand, weak or politically-minded commissioners have been known to permit these hearings to degenerate into the medium for protecting the incompetent. Just as much political pressure can be brought to bear to preserve a job as to turn out a political enemy. Civil service commissions are not infrequently manipulated directly for political purposes. 

On other occasions sincere friends of the merit system are actuated by a "protection complex." They suspect personal and political motives behind every removal, and in their effort to give the employee the benefit of any far-fetched doubt they vote for reinstatement. Too often the removing officer has found the hearing manipulated in such a manner as, in effect, to place him on trial rather than the employees whom he seeks to remove.

[Pt. II 

PERSONNEL 

A great deal of the dissatisfaction with commission removals is attributable to the presence of attorneys who demand formal legal procedure. Issues are clouded before lay commissioners by insistence on jury trial procedure, with its frequent haggling over the admission of evidence. The scene takes on the aspects of a criminal trial, in which the removed are pictured as innocent victims of unjust persecution. The fallacy of this whole procedure springs from the fact that incompetence or inefficiency is difficult to prove judicially. A worker may be highly incompetent and inefficient, and yet he may not have committed an overt act. This is especially true of those positions where objective performance standards are not yet available. If a good and well-meaning executive is effectively barred from ridding his service of those whom he knows should not be there, the result can be only an impaired morale. Many observers, fully aware of its drawbacks, feel that the commission hearing is an effective bar to spoils removals. Various suggestions for counteracting existing evils are proposed, among which is the subordination of the attorney's rôle. They would not deny the right of counsel, but they would prevent them from controlling the conduct of the hearing. Commission hearings, instead of assuming the proportions of a criminal trial manipulated by attorneys, would become occasions for hearing and acting on independent administrative investigations. The reports of the personnel agency's own investigators would have considerable weight in the evidence.

It cannot be denied that civil service employees often have a feeling akin to a proprietary right in their jobs-even though the theory of Anglo-Saxon law now fails to recognize such a property right. It is admitted that a government should be a model employer, but that does not necessitate the carrying of incompetents upon the payroll. Even an industrial Utopia probably would have to deal with a certain number of misfits. 

The proper organization of society will place every individual in the position best fitted to his various capabilities, in so far as they can be ascertained. We happen to be living, however, in a society that is far from perfect. Every effort should be

Ch. 12] 257 

made to replace misfits through the medium of transfers intelligently guided, but incompetents should not be retained in the bureaucracy. Sometimes the argument is raised that persons removed from the service will become social charges. 

Actual government administration should never be confused with welfare relief or charity. If the government engages in relief work, it should clearly differentiate between relief jobs and the normal administrative positions. Administrative posts should never be regarded as charitable in nature. 

Leading technical men have been inclined to favor placing greater responsibility for removals in the hands of the public personnel agency itself, as distinguished from the commission. 

The procedure would involve informal, quiet, and dignified investigations by professional personnel workers. The Bureau of Public Personnel Administration has stated that best results have been obtained when the central agency has been given final power regarding removal. Especially has this been true when investigations and hearings have been held with a minimum of formality and with the idea of giving prompt and substantial justice. Maryland offers an example where this type of procedure has been followed. There the personnel director, who is also a one man commission, prescribes by rule what may be cause for removal. After hearing or investigation, or both, the commissioner has authority to restore, demote, or order the removal of the employee. In practice the removals under this provision have occurred after thorough, efficient, and fair hearings and investigations. Instead of being conducted in accordance with the formal procedure of a court of law, however, they have been carried on in much the same manner that a budget agency would look into a request for appropriations. 

The federal regulations provide no legal safeguards against unjust removal. The provisions applying to those under the merit system require that the person removed shall be given notice in writing of the reasons for such action, and a reasonable time in which to make a written reply. The whole proceeding must be made a matter of record by both the depart-

ment and the civil service commission. The latter has no authority, however, to overrule the department and reinstate the discharged individual. Some authorities look with favor on this system, claiming that political removals are frustrated by reason of the fact that successors must be chosen from civil service lists. The Bureau of Public Personnel Administration, on the other hand, feels that no such procedure has proved efficacious unless the central personnel agency has been given authority to restore employees to their positions or take such other action as it considers proper. Still others have pointed out that there are practically no dismissals in the federal service on the grounds of inefficiency; that there is a natural reluctance of department heads to incur the unpleasantness resulting from dismissals. Indeed, there is genuine doubt as to whether sufficient removals to maintain service efficiency are being made. 

The statutes of most states authorize the removal of public officials by means of a legal action charging them with misfeasance, malfeasance, or nonfeasance in office. It is quite proper that this provision should exist as an extraordinary remedy to be used in extreme emergencies, but a judicial remedy of this nature should never be regarded as a substitute for administrative removal power. It is a holdover from the days when most state and local officers were elective, and hence immune from administrative removal. Integration is correcting this situation. As has been pointed out above, under modern technical administration incompetence can exist without criminal culpability or the committing of an overt act. This renders judicial proof of incompetence exceedingly difficult, and frequently subjects it to the emotional exigencies of jury trial. Normally the remedy for official incompetence should be, therefore, administrative.

The legal digests are full of cases involving discharged employees who failed of reinstatement before the civil service commissions and appealed to the courts. Almost without exception the courts have allowed the administrative ruling to stand. Frequently there arises in practice, however, a peculiar situation which actually reverses the written legal precedents. 

Lewis Mayers, The Federal Service (D. Appleton & Co., 1922), p. 93.

Ch. 12] 259 

A politically strong employee group contests certain dismissals through its own attorney. This individual may know his law, but he is also adept in the arts of psychology. An elective local judge, who cannot help but be mindful that hundreds or thousands of employees will vote when he is up for re-election, may find a way of reinstating the discharged individuals. An elective city attorney, probably also aware of approaching elections, may advise against appealing the case on the ground that it would incur expense which the city can ill afford. At the same time employee representatives may bring pressure to abandon appeal to the higher courts. This type of judicial interference with administration becomes especially harmful when employees are reinstated with the provision that they must be paid thousands of dollars of back salary. Let it be emphasized again that these occurences take place when the written judicial precedents of the jurisdiction would seem to discountenance them. This is just one more proof that the practice of administrative law may vary sharply from the reported cases. Training Systematized training for the public service has been lacking in the United States. Spoils appointments, the elective political nature of desirable local offices, and the general lack of prestige for public employments have all contributed to this end. That frontier spirit which made each man a self-sufficient jack-ofall-trades, the frontier's disdain of theory and exaltation of the practical: these operated well into the opening decades of the twentieth century to keep public service open to persons of minimum technical qualifications. Anglo-Saxons have always been skeptical of book-learning as a basis for practical procedure. Post-war events have demonstrated, however, that vanishing frontier conditions are giving way before the industrial revolution. A technological society needs technically trained administrators and it is slowly but surely beginning to get them. The old-time police administrator disdained formal training. His formula was to give a raw recruit a gun and tell him to go out and arrest persons caught breaking

[Pt. II 

PERSONNEL 

any one of the ten commandments. Happily, opinion is reversing itself on these points the country over, and police training schools are increasing in number. A familiar sight to travelers is the drill tower beside fire stations. On these firemen in hundreds of localities daily practice jumping, climbing, and rescuing. As a matter of fact training programs, although spasmodic, intermittent, and geographically spotted, have been sufficiently widespread and sustained to warrant the conclusion that there is a genuine training movement gradually gaining momentum. 

One of the significant evidences of the demand for training is the response of the universities during the last decade. An ever-increasing number of institutions of collegiate grade now claim to offer some professional courses in public administration, and a number of these confer special degrees in that subject. There is some speculation as to just how far the universities can profitably venture in teaching the practical technique of public management. At a round table of the American 

Political Science Association held at Cleveland in 1930, the preponderant opinion among teachers of public administration seemed to frown on technical instruction very early in the college career. It was felt that the university's rôle should be confined very largely to furnishing preparation along the lines of basic background and broad fundamentals. In this connection it is well to recall that the administrative class of the British Civil Service is chosen through tests on purely classical academic subjects. As a matter of fact, when the British talk about teaching public administration, even at the London School of Economics, they do not refer to courses in management. They are skeptical about whether that can ever be taught except through the hard school of experience. They are beginning, however, to place value on historical, legal, and philosophical approaches to government problems. 

In the United States we are attempting to teach management in the universities. Most of the institutions confine the courses in management to the graduate year, after the student has had a general political science major somewhat weighted with courses dealing with administration from the legal and

Ch. 12] 261 

organization standpoints. One of the chief obstacles to intensive development of these courses has been inability to place graduates in governmental employment. The apprentice system has been tried out with some success by the Syracuse School and the National Institute of Public Administration. The city managers, in spite of their earnest desire to take in apprentices, have had to proceed slowly because of local political exigencies. 

In most places, neither the council nor local sentiment will countenance making a place for an outsider whose only claim to preferment is academic preparation. The personality factor offers some hazard to the apprentice idea in operation. A prominent city manager complained that the apprentices sent him were well prepared academically, but they lacked that tact, charm, diplomacy, and personableness which is so essential to leadership. This is a problem which probably never will be solved satisfactorily. The universities should not be unduly blamed if a crop of introverts should graduate from professional courses in public administration. However, teachers should exercise judgment in making their recommendations. Only harm can result ultimately from sending one who is obviously diffident and socially retiring to be the apprentice of a city manager. The apprentice system has much to offer. It has furnished a number of men now employed in key positions, both in actual administration and in governmental research. There is every reason to believe that it will be more widely developed to bridge the gap between the academic training at the university and that part of the technique of management obtainable only through experience.

At the same time that the universities have become interested in offering pre-service preparation, much progress has been made in training those who are already on the job. Such training is more and more regarded as desirable and necessary, and worthy of expenditure from public funds. A catalog of all of the short courses, institutes, and departmental training programs would fill a volume. Of peculiar significance are the so-called fire colleges operated by metropolitan departments in New York and Los Angeles. State leagues of municipalities have increasingly offered short courses at convenient locations,

[Pt. II 

PERSONNEL 

attended by officers and employees of several cities. Noteworthy in this respect are the efforts of the New York Conference of Mayors and Other Officials. The program of educating policemen at Berkeley has attracted attention for some years, and now its graduates are finding their way into law-enforcement positions in other parts of the nation.10 Several of the federal departments have made progress in the field of training during recent years. There is little doubt that all branches of public administration in the United States have become more conscious of the need of training. Such training will tend to become more systematized and standardized with experience. 

It will gradually create for itself respect and prestige, which will in turn benefit the professional and technical aspects of the public service. There is some evidence that just this thing has already occurred in several instances. 

The Commission of Inquiry on Public Service Personnel, sponsored by the Social Science Research Council and financed by the Spelman Fund, conducted extensive hearings and investigations in 1934. Its report, which was released in 1935, advocated with considerable emphasis the need for a career public service based on pre-entry education." The clerical service would be recruited after not less than two years of high school study and would be trained for the special techniques of their jobs after entry. Members of the professional and technical services would secure their special training prior to entry. This group would seek entry into the public service between the ages of twenty-three and twenty-eight. 

Those who make up the administrative service would secure a general education, presumably of college grade, and begin their careers immediately after its completion. Training after entry will be directly conditioned upon the age of the applicant at the time of recruitment. If recruitment takes place before the appropriate education has been secured, opportunity to complete it will have to be offered. PART III FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION

CHAPTER XIII FINANCIAL ORGANIZATION 

The organization of financial agencies in the governmental units of the United States has been weak and disintegrated. It was not until well into the nineteenth century that the movement to consolidate the financial agencies into a single department under the chief administrative officer received any great momentum, and even at this writing (1935) the number of such integrated departments in existence is exceedingly few. Accordingly, in our state, county, and city governments it is the general practice to have the chief financial operations, such as budgeting, accounting, treasury, assessment, and purchasing, in several different departments, each of which is independent of each other, and some of which are not subject to the administrative control of the mayor, manager, or governor. In other words, the prevailing plan of financial organization is decentralized and unco-ordinated. 

A treatment of financial functions should, undoubtedly, be prefaced by a statement of the powers, duties, and functions of the principal financial officers and agencies. Every governmental unit should possess a chief or central accounting agency. 

This is usually headed by an individual known as the comptroller, controller, or auditor, the latter title being misleading and not technically correct for reasons stated below. "Comptroller" and "controller" are terms used interchangeably. The office of the comptroller keeps the general accounts, supervises accounts kept by individual departments, and installs accounting systems. This agency also keeps the budget control accounts, pre-auditing all proposed obligations before they are incurred. If the comptroller finds that funds are not available, or that a particular proposed expenditure is not legal, he should refuse approval, thus making it impossible to obligate the gov- 267

FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION 

ernment in that particular case. It is also the duty of the comptroller to make current checks of the financial operations of the government, sometimes referred to as the administrative audit, which includes a pre-audit of expenditures and current control of revenues. His approval must be secured for making payments out of the treasury, an act usually performed through the medium of a warrant signed by the comptroller. Such a warrant tells the treasurer, in effect, that the comptroller has found the obligation regularly incurred, the goods delivered or the services performed, and that the bearer has a legal claim on the treasury in the amount named.¹ It is also the duty of the comptroller to prepare for the other officials and for the public, reports on the results of current financial operations. 

It is the duty of the treasurer to collect taxes, special assessments, and miscellaneous revenues. Such revenues as the individual operating services themselves collect, should be turned over to the treasurer at once. The treasurer should maintain a current auditing control of departmental revenues in order that he may know the amounts due, and see that they are collected and turned into the treasury. The treasurer has physical custody of governmental funds, which in former days meant that he kept large sums in cash in his vaults, but today practically all of these funds are deposited in bank accounts or invested in securities specified by law. The treasurer has an important part in the administration of the public debt, including the issuance of bonds, the payment of principal and interest. the management of sinking funds, and the conduct of refunding operations. Sometimes he is charged with the management of specific trust funds, such as pension or endowment funds. In connection with the preparation of the annual budget, the treasurer estimates the revenue expected for the ensuing fiscal year. He also pays out of the treasury all sums authorized by warrants issued by the comptroller, if funds are available for that purpose. The laws of many states provide that the treasurer shall register the warrants, if funds are not

Wherever the executive budget system is in operation, there will always be found some officer or agency in actual charge of the preparation of the annual budget. Sometimes this task is performed perfunctorily by clerks or junior accountants attached to the office of the mayor, manager, or comptroller, without very much actual discretionary authority. There is a growing tendency, however, to set up a budget bureau, such as the federal Bureau of the Budget, in complete charge of budget planning, subject, of course, to the wishes of the executive. It prepares the annual budget and investigates and reports to the executive and legislature on current matters involving expenditure and revenue. It may conduct exhaustive surveys of departmental operations and render advice to the various governmental services as to how they might affect economies. There is a growing tendency among consultants and observers to suggest that the budget bureau should administer personnel functions.³

The purchasing agent buys materials and supplies, supervises departmental purchasing, and approves and promulgates specifications for articles to be purchased. He manages the general stores and supervises stores and warehouses operated by the departments themselves. A fitting activity of the purchasing office is the salvage and resale of surplus, obsolete, and damaged equipment.

Every governmental unit should have its accounts audited periodically by someone independent of those who are in charge of keeping the accounts. This is known as the independent or post-audit, which can be performed either by private accountants retained for the specific job, or by a regular full-time officer. Existing Financial Organization 

The completely centralized British Treasury type of budgetary control has not been adopted by our federal government, although moves in that direction were taken by the executive orders of 1933. The formulation of the budget plan is lodged in the Federal Bureau of the Budget under a Director of the Budget who is appointed by the President and who holds office at the pleasure of the latter. This arrangement places the responsibility for the preparation of the budget directly under the President. The Bureau of the Budget had only nominal powers of budgetary control of expenditure up until June, 1933, when by executive order it was given certain authority to approve executive allotments. Most matters relative to taxation, debt administration, and revenue in general are under the Treasury Department, one of the principal executive departments under a Secretary of cabinet rank responsible to the President. By executive order, under blanket authority given the President by Congress in 1933, the Treasury Department has set up a system of budgetary control accounts. By the same authority there has been set up in the Treasury Department a Procurement Division which has ample power to co-ordinate all federal purchases, stores, and warehousing.

Under the Budget and Accounting Act of 1921 many of the more important phases of budgetary control were placed under the Comptroller General, head of the General Accounting

He must affirm all issues into and all withdrawals from the Treasury; prescribes uniform systems of accounts for all administrative agencies; makes an independent audit of the accounts of all federal departments; and settles claims, whether the government is claimant or defendant. It seemed that the Act of 1921 contemplated making this office a gigantic instrument for expenditure control, but the Roosevelt Executive Orders of 1933-1934 seemed to move in the direction of assigning this task to the Treasury Department and the Bureau of the Budget.

Prior to 1933 it was common for technical observers to refer to the utter lack of correlation in federal financial administration. Budget planning was lodged in one agency; another administered revenue and the public debt; still another supervised accounting and settled claims; while budgetary control, in its modern sense, was largely absent. The spending departments enjoyed a very considerable degree of autonomy in matters affecting budgetary control. The executive orders of 

1933, placing the power to govern executive allotments in the hands of the Secretary of the Treasury and the Director of the Budget, will be regarded by most technical observers as steps in advance. They go a long way toward setting up that central federal housekeeping agency which has so frequently been suggested in the past. Such proposals have included in the new housekeeping unit such functions as budget planning, purchasing, accounting control, personnel, and efficiency investigation.

For all practical purposes the first three, in addition to treasury and tax administration, are now in the Treasury Department, which bids fair to become the vital controlling force in expenditure matters, a rôle which in the past it played in name only.

Furthermore, why should the fiscal activities of the Treasury Department be excluded from an administrative unit supposedly in charge of federal housekeeping functions? No proposal to unify the fiscal activities of the federal government will be complete unless it takes into consideration the proper realignment of the administrative functions now entrusted to the general accounting office. The settlement of claims and the keeping of accounts are administrative activities and as such should be placed in this new service."

The financial organization of practically all of the states up until the recent movement for reorganization-and even yet in most of them-was highly decentralized. The principal operations were put into the hands of constitutional officers elected by the people and consequently free from the administrative control of the governor. Effective reorganization was blocked by the necessity of amending the constitution in order to get rid of these officers, and, in some places, to modify their functions. The officers usually elected are the auditor and comptroller and state treasurer. Recent trends in financial organization have been toward setting up a budget agency under the control of the governor, or toward the setting up of a department of finance with power to formulate the budget, superintend accounting operations, and control the execution of the budget. However, the difficulty of amending state constitutions has slowed down this movement. Thus, in some

In some cases the department of finance has virtually found it necessary to set up a duplicate system of control accounts under its own supervision, in order to meet its needs; such action being due to the fact that the elective controller was a politician with neither aptitude nor inclination to adapt his office to changing needs. 

It was not until the beginning of the present century that a great deal of concern was given to the organization of municipal financial agencies. The traditional financial officers were treasurer, auditor or comptroller, and assessor. They usually were selected by popular election, which made them independent of each other and of the mayor. The mayor, therefore, had no powers of general supervision over the officers and agencies administering the finances of the city. The idea was, undoubtedly, that such disintegration would promote a system of checks and balances whereby an honorable officer would thwart dishonesty and corruption. This would come about as the result of a system of checks and counterchecks by means of which transactions would not be complete unless authenticated by others. The political philosophy of the United 

States has always emphasized fear of the concentration of power in the hands of a single officer or agency, resulting in a general lack of businesslike organization for the purpose of administering municipal finance.Ⓡ 

Progressive thought in the field of local government has come to regard this situation as a serious obstacle to effective administration, for today monetary losses are more likely to result from incompetence than from dishonesty. Tremendous expenditures for specialized services, through widespread impersonal bureaucracies, necessitate the use of the best management methods. Management implies co-ordination, which in turn cannot be achieved without the integration of control over expenditures. An increasing realization of this fact has, in recent years, produced a movement toward executive control

over financial operations which takes the form of placing the principal financial agencies under the direct supervision of the mayor or manager. The consultants who make surveys usually go so far as to advocate that all financial activities, with the exception of the post-audit, be situated in a single department of finance under the governor, mayor or manager, although very few governments have gone that far. As a matter of fact, a survey of existing municipal organization would reveal a large degree of disintegration still remaining, most cities still electing two or more of the principal finance officers. Nevertheless, there has been a decided movement toward integration in the past two decades-a trend probably accelerated by the fiscal difficulties encountered during the depression of the early nineteen thirties.

American students of government finance should become acquainted with the status and functions of the British Treasury. This venerable institution is one of the principal executive departments. Its actual head is the Chancellor of the Exchequer who is invariably one of the principal officers of the cabinet. 

The Treasury has a far-reaching control over the housekeeping activities of all of the administrative establishments. In budget making, it formulates the estimates and the Chancellor of the Exchequer defends them on the floor of the House. A feature of Treasury supervision which up until very recently has been foreign to American experience, is the strict control of expenditure exercised by this central fiscal agency. A British appropriation is not authority for a department to spend; it is permission to spend, if necessary, with the permission of the Treasury. 

Thus, departmental expenditures are always made with the consent of the Treasury. In the great number of ordinary transactions this consent is presumed to be implied, but if there is any departure from customary policy or expenditure for new projects, the Treasury must be consulted."

The Treasury appoints a high official of each department to act as accounting officer. This official prepares the estimates, "W. F. Willoughby, W. W. Willoughby, and S. M. Lindsay, The System of Financial Administration of Great Britain (D. Appleton & Co., 1922), pp. 165-197.

supervises the execution of the budget, and acts as the contact officer. The Treasury prescribes accounting methods and systems, investigates administrative practices, and in general has its hands on the pulse of governmental business in all establishments. It is an integrated department of finance in which is centralized budget formulation, budget control, accounting control, treasury operations, and revenue administration. No department can spend a penny without its consent. Its control even extends to approval of the examinations of the civil service commission, and such personnel functions as classification. and determination of salary plans are directly under the Treasury. This brief description of the British Treasury is offered here because it has features worthy of emulation in the United States. Indeed, that type of fiscal control which emanates from an integrated department of finance in the better type of councilmanager city is a rather close approach to the British example. 

Some students would establish a bureau of administration with a similar rôle in our federal government. 

Probably in a majority of states the city clerk, treasurer, and auditor in cities under the general incorporation act are popularly elected. The same may be said of state comptrollers, auditors, and treasurers. These officials are all purely administrative. They perform duties for which there is presumably a settled technique; that is, there is a more or less definite way of carrying on these activities in accord with sound practice. It should be assumed that they would be best handled by persons who possessed a certain minimum of technical knowledge and skill obtained through training, study, and experience. The manner in which they should function is not capable of being determined by a decision of the voters at the polls. As a matter of fact, electing these officers at general elections leads to their selection on grounds entirely foreign to the manner in which the office should function. Choice may hinge on a wide variety of irrelevant considerations such as religion, war record, organization membership, and various personal antagonisms, instead of individual capacity.

It has been thought in the past that financial officers should be elected in order to maintain their honesty and fidelity. This

[Pt. III

is a fallacy. Experience indicates that elective officers, being independent of administrative control from any other quarter, will often set up their offices as inviolate fortresses where no one else is allowed to enter. Thus they are able to cover up irregularities long after they would have been discovered if the office had been under administrative control. They frequently refuse to co-operate with the rest of the administration, backed up in such action by confidence in their own political strength.

American legal philosophy is so influenced by eighteenth century dogmas relative to checks and balances and the separation of powers that lawyers are frequently unable to take a rational view of the needs of modern administrative organization; and accountants are frequently so intent upon maintaining the niceties of internal and external checks that they fail to grasp the main administrative problems. Thus, a firm of commercial accountants, auditing one of the principal manager cities of the west, recommended the splitting up of its well-integrated department of finance in order that the accountant's mania for checks be satisfied. At any rate, it is the opinion of the more progressive students of public administration that there is no real reason for electing financial officers.

Model Financial Organization 

The private consulting agencies which make surveys and formulate recommendations for the reorganization of governmental units favor, almost unanimously, the integrated department of finance. This view is largely concurred in by teachers of government,¹¹ professionals in the field of government research, and certain national agencies and institutions devoted to civic betterment. The unified department of finance would contain bureaus or divisions charged with carrying on the principal financial activities of the government. It would be headed by a single officer, either a director of finance or the comptroller, 10 The Efficiency Commission of Kentucky, The Government of Kentucky

Coupled with this unification of fiscal operations should go the entrusting of their management to qualified experts. While the public is fairly well accustomed to placing the affairs of the health, school, and engineering units in the hands of professional technicians, such has not been the case with financial administration. Prior to the depression years, certified public accountants were rare in public offices. The fiscal affairs of 

12 Buck and others, Municipal Finance, pp. 17-27.

Ch. 13] 279 

FINANCIAL ORGANIZATION 

governmental agencies were in the hands of persons with no special training or experience qualifying them for the task. 

Frequently they were downright amateurs chosen for purely political reasons, while in other cases incumbents were presumed to be qualified because they had been shopkeepers, real estate agents, bankers, or were experienced in some other commercial activity. Now it is coming to be realized that more than mere mediocre success in modest business callings is essential to administer the financial affairs of a large city, county, or state. 

The administration of government finance is coming to be a science with a technique all its own, consisting of a body of procedures, systems, principles, and operations not familiar to all types of successful business ventures. The result is that only trained and experienced persons should be selected as auditors, treasurers, purchasing agents, and comptrollers. 

The question always arises as to whether integration of the financial operations into a single department under the chief executive will tend to secure this type of personnel. The counter proposition is always advanced that such personnel would produce efficient administration irrespective of integration. 

The answer to this assertion is that disintegration produces a certain inertia which is conducive to mediocrity; and popular election leads to political selection, and each financial officer, being interested in maintaining his political fences, acts with that end in mind. The integration of financial operations is not in itself a cure-all for this situation. While political selection may still exist after integration, there is, nevertheless, an inevitable tendency to recognize competence, largely due to the fact that organization obstacles to co-ordination have been removed. 

A large portion of the reasons for the stalemate or inertia, referred to above, is removed. In practically all governmental units, irrespective of the existence or non-existence of political motivations, individuals are present who are technically- and professionally-minded. They have seen, probably for years past, the necessity for greater co-ordination. With the structural obstacles removed, they are able gradually and cautiously to suggest and secure authority for taking the steps which they have known to be desirable.

[Pt. III 

FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION 

There is also the further consideration that the government sometimes comes into the hands of groups which actually desire to make administrative improvements. Integration of financial operation enables them to adopt improved methods. During the last decade there has been a decided advance in such fields as purchasing and accounting control. The advantages accruing are so apparent that no incoming administration would dare to abandon them. Frequently these improvements are identified with specific personalities around whom the progress is popularly supposed to have been built. In a number of these cases, removal by an incoming administration would cause too much undesirable publicity, while in other instances the increasingly technical nature of financial administration is making those familiar with operations indispensable to any newly elected political executive. The result is that the advance of science is slowly but surely forcing the recognition of technical competence in financial officers. To what extent is financial integration responsible for this? It has furnished an environment which permits the installation of advanced procedures. Technical progress and integregation are congenial mates; for technical progress insists upon—and eventually obtains competent personnel, in spite of any opposition which politicians may muster.

The authorities are fairly well agreed as to the main outlines of a municipal department of finance. 13 At the head should be the director of finance. In some cases the comptroller could be both the head of the bureau of accounts and director of finance. 

The four or five bureaus in the department could be designated as: bureau of accounts; bureau of purchase and supply, or bureau of procurement; bureau of taxation; bureau of the treasury; and bureau of the budget, or bureau of personnel, or even bureau of budget and personnel. The director of finance should be regarded as the chief financial officer of the city, to whom the council and executive should look for advice and guidance on all municipal fiscal matters. The comptroller would be head of the bureau of accounts. 

This agency would be charged with keeping the general accounts of the city, supervising departmental accounting systems, and, especially, budgetary control operations. It would, necessarily, have a large share in the preparation of all financial reports. It would also maintain a current audit of all municipal agencies and activities, furnish the administration and council with current information as to financial status, and compile data for the budget. The current check of expenditures maintained by the bureau of accounts should not be confused with the independent or post-audit. This should be arranged for by the city council. itself. It should be conducted by some agency absolutely independent of the administrative branches. In some states, such as New York, Indiana, and Iowa, an audit of cities is made by the state, while in many others the council engages a firm of private auditors to make a periodic check.¹4

The bureau of the treasury, headed by the treasurer, would collect, keep, and pay out the municipal funds only upon the authority of the comptroller. The bureau of taxation, under the assessor, would be charged with the assessment of property, the taxing of businesses, and the determination of benefits and privileges. The bureau of purchasing, headed by the purchasing agent, would have control of the procurement of materials, supplies, equipment, and certain contractual services for all branches of the city government. This bureau should also have supervision over all printing. The purchasing agent should not enter into contracts or place orders until the comptroller has certified that unencumbered appropriation balances are available for their payment.

Public sentiment usually is not prepared for the complete integration suggested in the foregoing paragraphs. Long after the evils of loose financial organization are apparent, people fear that change might bring worse evils. Finally, however, it becomes evident that something has to be done; so, generally, the first step is the establishment of an independent budget and (or) efficiency bureau. Nominally under the control of the executive but independent of the other units administering finance, the budget bureau at first has only advisory powers. It prepares the annual budget for the chief executive, makes surveys of the operation of the various departments, and reports on current matters affecting expenditure which have been referred to it for investigation. It has no coercive power, however; it can only recommend. These budget agencies come very near to exercising only pure staff functions. Examples are the federal 

Bureau of the Budget, the Bureau of Budget and Efficiency of the City of Los Angeles, and the Bureau of Efficiency of Los Angeles County. At first regarded with suspicion, these bureaus have to prove their right to trust and esteem. 15 Report of the Waterbury Charter Commission, opposite p. 512.

There was published in 1930 the results of a survey, with recommendations, of the state government of New Jersey by the

The American county has violated all of the principles of good administrative organization. The amateur, political, and elective treasurer, assessor, and auditor have been in immediate charge of the details of financial administration. Where counties have had budgets at all they usually have been both formulated and executed by an elective board which has delved into the details of expenditure solely with an eye to the exigencies of practical politics. It is, therefore, of interest to note the organization proposed in the new Model County Manager Law of the National Municipal League." There is a strong department of finance under a director appointed by and responsible to the county manager. The director of finance is to be in charge of both formulating and executing the budget, treasury operations, assessment, tax collection, accounting, and purchasing. An annual audit by "an accountant who is not a regular officer or employee" must be secured by the county board, but a state audit may answer as a substitute therefor. Thus, the strong department of finance idea that has previously been recommended and has found some justification in practice in states and cities is now advocated for counties by a group of men versed both in the theory and practice of county administration. 20

There is an unmistakable and inevitable movement away from a number of the most dearly cherished American political credos of the past. There is gradually dawning on the harassed owner of real property the realization that if taxes are to be greatly reduced he must consult some other authority than the Jacksonian common man who has been elected to public office. 

Economy in expenditure is a matter of consolidating overlapping bureaus, relieving payrolls of superfluous personnel, the classification of positions and standardization of salaries, and studied adoption of short-cuts. All this demands a technically trained personnel with authority to accomplish results more or less immune from political pressure. The only way to accomplish this is to consolidate the financial activities in one department under the control of the chief administrative officer. 

Instead of independent elective financial officers under no administrative control, technically qualified administrators are to carry on under integrated supervision. Such is the trend as evidenced in surveys, charters, statutes, and the writings of consultants, experts, and students. The number of adoptions of the integrated department of finance is relatively small as compared to the whole number of political subdivisions. Nevertheless, its advocates are gaining greater confidence and more converts.

CHAPTER XIV  

Public budgeting is a comparatively recent development in the United States. If an arbitrary date had to be set one could probably say that every major development in the budgeting field had taken place since the initial work of the New York Bureau of Municipal Research in the first decade of the twentieth century. The principal advances in American public budgeting have taken place in the last thirty years, yet these three decades have not resulted in the adoption of sound budget methods in all governmental units. Many of the smaller cities and counties have been practically untouched by the movement, and probably most of the states and cities purporting to possess budget procedures fail to measure up to those standards set forth in the following paragraphs. The depression years of the early 1930's have placed such a strain on public finance, however, that one senses a profound revolution in process. The federal government has a system of positive expenditure control for the first time in its history; state after state has overhauled its financial procedure; and local government in all parts of the country has been forced to adopt modern budgetary control. The existing practice represents such great variety, however, that a descriptive treatment would only be confusing. 

Consequently, it is advisable to select those principles which experience has dictated to be sound and from them expound the fundamentals of good budget practice.

The initial step in budgetmaking is usually an announcement by the chief administrative or executive officer of the financial 1

The next step is a preliminary estimate of revenue and expenditure. In the federal government the revenue estimate is made by the Secretary of the Treasury and revised by the Director of the Budget. 

In the City of Los Angeles this is a joint task of the Director of the Bureau of Budget and Efficiency and of the Controller. 

Mr. Buck feels that while it is probably better to underestimate revenues than to overestimate them, "it seems both possible and desirable to make estimates which will be at least within 5 per cent of the actual receipts.' After these preliminary announcements and forecasts, it is time to call for departmental estimates. 99 2 The budget agency sends to the departments the estimate forms on which there will be columns for (1) code numbers, (2) expenditure classifications, (3) amount spent for the same item in one or two immediately completed fiscal years, (4) the amount estimated to be spent in the current fiscal year, and (5) the amount requested for the year to which the proposed budget applies. If the accounting is decentralized, the data, on past experience, will be filled in by the departments; if centralized, by the comptroller, before being forwarded to the departments. The head of the department or the budget officer immediately under him should give close attention to the proper framing of the estimates. After ample time has been given for departmental consideration, the estimates as requested by the spending units are sent back to the budget agency for review and revision. In the federal practice the departments submit estimates twice. Preliminary estimates are reviewed by the Bureau of the Budget and returned to the spending agencies with instructions to reframe them so as to stay within the designated maximum amounts.

The budget agency subjects the departmental estimates to a most thorough scrutiny and examination. A properly organ- 

Buck, Public Budgeting, p. 317.

[Pt. III 

FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION 

ized budget bureau will have a permanent staff of investigators who will have been making prolonged and thorough studies of the operation and needs of the various departments throughout the year. As the estimates start to come in from the spending agencies they will be specifically assigned to the various investigators for review and report. Padded estimates can usually be detected at once by these men. After analyzing the estimates assigned to them they will confer with the department heads. 

Finally, the estimates will come up for review before the higher officials of the budget agency. In the federal practice there is a board composed of ten of the higher officers before which the department may appear and defend its requests. In the City of Los 

Angeles, the assistant director, or a ranking efficiency engineer, holds an informal hearing at which the department head defends his requests, and the budget investigator assigned to that department presents his views. Here an agreement is reached which usually corresponds to what eventually appears in the appropriations. There is, of course, a subsequent hearing before the political executive. In the City of Los Angeles the mayor sets aside specified hours for budget hearings. There are present the department representatives, the chief officers of the budget agency, the controller's representative, and certain interested citizen representatives. In the federal government the President holds no budget hearings, but he is kept informed of the progress in the budget process through conferences at the White 

House with the Director of the Budget. 

British budgeteers have habitually given more attention to the revenue side of the budget than has been the case in the United States. They have regarded certain revenues as elastic and have readjusted them annually to balance the budget. In the United States, the balancing of revenues and expenditures usually has been a hit and miss matter at best. Our revenue legislation has been considered permanent; it has not been reenacted each year. During the fiscal years from 1931 to 1934 the federal government experienced a huge deficit arising from the lower income tax revenue caused by the economic depression. This same business crisis brought tax delinquency and

Ch. 14] 293 

other loss of revenue to cities and states. In practically every case the budget agencies have been required to estimate the revenue available under existing regulations, but further than this estimate they have had practically no concern with revenue. 

The question of taxation and the creation of revenues is such a controversial issue that administrative officers tend to avoid it. 

The customary procedure in a municipality is to estimate the revenue anticipated from sources other than taxes. This will include such items as licenses, fees, fines, interest, rents, and the sale of surplus property. This can be estimated fairly accurately by experienced persons who know what past experience has been and who are aware of any special circumstances that may qualify past experience during the coming fiscal year. After this has been arrived at, the result will be subtracted from the proposed expenditures and a general property tax levied to meet the balance. In other words, the general property tax is the elastic source of municipal revenue. In those cities which have charter tax limits, the tendency will be to levy the limit at all times. In this case the city must keep its expenditures within a fixed revenue or increase revenue from sources other than taxation which then become the flexible revenue element. Since 

1930, many governments have had a shrinking tax base owing to the assessor's reduction in valuations. Under these conditions, all the budget-maker can do is try to make as accurate an estimate as possible and hold expenditures within such estimate. 

The estimate of revenue should be within 5 per cent of actual subsequent receipts. The federal authorities have been notoriously inaccurate in their estimates, whereas the budget authorities of the City of Los Angeles have frequently come within I or 2 per cent. The British pre-war estimates were extremely accurate.³

The impression should not prevail that budget agencies never should be permitted to attack the revenue problem from its larger angles. It is merely pointed out that their hands are tied in that respect at the present time. As it becomes increasingly evident that something will have to be done to relieve real estate of its Buck, The Budget in Governments of Today, pp. 175-179.

FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION 

tax burden, why would it not be sensible to assign the revenue problem to the budget agency for study? The question of taxation and revenue is so inextricably tied up with the question of balanced budgets that such an eventuality surely cannot be long delayed. 

It is, of course, common knowledge that no expenditures can be made under the budget until the legislative body has made the appropriations. It is quite the usual practice in the United 

States, whether it be county, city, state or nation, that the budget document is merely advisory; it does not bind the legislature except in a relatively small number of states and cities including Maryland, the City of New York, and Boston. The legislative body is usually free to do as it pleases in the matter of appropriations.* It can ignore the budget plan prepared by the President, governor, mayor, or manager; it can modify it; or it can enact the provisions of the budget document without change. 

When the budget document is introduced in the legislature, it is usually accompanied by a budget message from the President, governor, or mayor. It is then referred to a committee, or committees. The practice of having a single committee in each house of the state legislature in charge of appropriations is steadily growing and is to be commended. After the appropriations or finance committee has gone thoroughly into the proposals, the appropriation bill or bills are reported to the house with recommendations for enactment.

There is a tendency frequently to confuse the budget with the appropriations. The budget document is the printed plan prepared by the chief executive and transmitted to the legislature together with his budget message. It is increasingly becoming the practice for the chief executive to draft and submit bills to the legislature, the enactment of which will transform the budget plan into lawful appropriations. It is well for the student to note the distinction in terminology between the budget and appropriations. The one is simply a proposed plan, while the other is a legally binding enactment known either as an appropriation 

4 Ibid., pp. 100-106.

Ch. 14] 295 

ordinance or an appropriation act. Sometimes the appropriations are referred to officially as the enacted budget. 

The inherent nature of budgeting in its broader sense will be simplified by analyzing its various phases. Part of the budget process is legislative and part is administrative. The failure of legislatures to recognize this is largely responsible for the financial ills afflicting our states and cities. The preparation of the budget plan is administrative, while the enactment of this plan into law, with such modifications as may be desired, is purely legislative. The supervision of the spending process, after enactment, constitutes an administrative task. Finally, the legislature should check up on administrative performance to see that its will has been properly carried into effect. The chronological steps in budgeting are as follows:5

Performance The reader should be cautioned that this classification of the stages of the budget process into administrative and legislative is far from being accepted in practice, especially in local government. The ordinary city council and county board is in varying degrees the planner, determiner, and executive combined. In a considerable majority of cities with the weakmayor form of government the council is quite predominant in budget matters. Indeed, in many of the smaller cities the only budget is the tax levy, as is the case with California cities of the sixth class. The departments incur obligations and the city clerk receives the bills and invoices and presents them to the council at periodic meetings. Resolutions authorizing payments are passed, and the mayor and chairman of the finance committee proceed to sign warrants for payment. This procedure is archaic and inefficient; it places a burden upon the council for which it is ill-adapted. A recognition of the proper boun-

daries of administrative and legislative budget activity would result in the enactment of a well-planned annual appropriation ordinance a document too often lacking in our cities. 

Budget documents differ very widely in makeup and size. 

Probably the best guiding standards that we possess are those proposed by Mr. Buck. Two sizes seem to possess equal merits. 

The letter size (about 9″ x 12″) can be filed in the upright cabinet in general use; the book size (6″ x 9″) fits very well in a bookshelf. The larger and unwieldy sizes in use in some states seem to be unnecessary.

Mr. Buck recommends that the budget document be composed of three principal parts. The first section should contain the budget message, a brief one-page budget summary where the reader can get a bird's-eye view at a glance; and some general supporting schedules from the totals of which the budget summary is compiled. The second part should contain the detailed estimates, and it comprises the bulkiest portion of the document. The third and last division is comprised of the budget bills for enacting the proposals into law." 

Expenditures may be classified by function, by organization unit, by character, and by object. A classification by function is one which places under one heading all of the expenditures for a single purpose. Examples would be protection to life and property, public works, and education. In a well organized administration the departments would be, in general, unifunctionally organized; that is, all of the expenditures for a single function would be in one department. Under such conditions the classification by functions would be synonymous with classification by organization units. 

Classification by character refers to the time element in expenditures. It segregates the various items in accordance with whether they relate to obligations incurred in previous years, such as debt service, expenditures for current consumption from current resources, or capital outlay for things to be used in future fiscal years. Classification by object consists of an enumeration of the things to be bought: personel services, Buck, Public Budgeting, pp. 56-57.

Ch. 14] 297 

supplies, and contractual services. Each major object classification is subdivided and each subdivision has a code number which tells the budget-maker or accountant at a glance that one item is food, another item is clothing, and so on." 

These several means of classification are not separable or optional in practical use. The budget estimates should make use of all of them. Let us take the 1931-32 estimates of the 

Custodian Bureau of the City of Los Angeles: 

Custodian Bureau (Organization Unit or Function) Current Expense (Character) Salaries and Wages (Object) Expense (Object) Acquisition of Property (Character) Equipment (Object) Lands, Buildings, and Improvements (Object) 

One of the weaknesses of public budgeting to date has been the practice of exempting certain branches of the government from the jurisdiction of the central budget. In cities these usually have been the humanitarian and social service agencies which frequently had been neglected in the past. Libraries, schools, parks, and public recreation fall in this category. The friends of these activities have eventually become impatient with their failure to secure proper support from the general city government. They have gone either to the legislature or to the electorate and secured charter changes setting up independent boards with separate taxing power. Thus, in many cities the library, park, and playgrounds departments have their own boards, each with taxing power, and in no way subject to the supervision of the central budget agency. 

Each governmental activity should share in the total amount of money available on the basis of equitable division with other departments. To say that certain departments are to have maximum levies of five or seven mills means that they will levy this maximum each year, whether needed or not. Budgeting by means of such special levies will not result in a well co-ordinated budget plan for the entire government. It is believed

FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION 

that as professional budget agencies are developed in the years to come, the justification for these special mill levies will disappear. Administrative budget planning will protect the departments against the politically motivated deprivations which originally caused the special levies. 

These remarks refer as well to other special sources of revenue which have been earmarked for specific purposes. In general it is considered bad practice to allow departments to expend their own revenues. Proper budgeting should be based on needs; and the fact that a department is creating a great deal of revenue does not ipso facto mean that it should have the unrestrained right to spend it. Such revenues should be turned daily into the central treasury, assigned for the most part to the general fund, and be centrally budgeted and controlled. If the allowing of additional requests in the budget will be an incentive for increasing revenues in a certain department, a good budget agency will take this factor into account. A department of the general government, however, should never be permitted to spend its own revenues independent of central budget control. 

In practically all jurisdictions today there are certain appropriation items which do not require reenactment each year or biennium. The authority for expenditure is contained in some permanent provision of law which continues to operate until repealed. Almost one-third of the expenditures under both the 

American federal and the British budgets are of this continuing nature. In the state of California over 70 per cent of the budget "is made up of fixed charges, comprising items which have been appropriated in recurrent amounts by the legislature, and for expenditures definitely fixed by vote of the people.' 

This practice is considered to be adverse to the interests of good budgeting. It prevents the budget agency from reconsidering the entire expenditures of the government each year, from the standpoint of needs under new conditions. The defense of permanent appropriations is weakened by the fact that there is "8

Both administrators and students agree that the general public should be given a hearing on the budget some time before In cities and counties this can take place at a specified time before the council or board of supervisors. In practice the budget hearing does not as a rule attract a large attendance or widespread interest. Instead of being attended by hard-pressed taxpayers striving for reduction in expenditure, those desiring increased appropriations for specific purposes are more likely to be present and vocal." Occasionally an extraordinary personality in the mayor's office, or an unusual circumstance will attract a large citizen attendance, but the great number of budget hearings sees only a handful present. This result has produced among certain observers and administrators a skepticism relative to the value of budget hearings. It is nevertheless thought that democracy will be best served by affording the citizen this opportunity to express himself whether he avails himself of it or not.

Public budget hearings seem to secure more interest in times of financial depression. There was a marked increase in attendance at local budget hearings after 1930, when real estate interests all over the country were active in exerting pressure for tax relief. The situation would seem to be as follows. 

In an era of normal business activity the citizen is more or less indifferent to government expenditure. The natural desire of the community for improved public works as a civic progress venture, tolerates a considerable amount of expenditure in the nonessential class. The ordinary citizen becomes non-vocal at such times, and the governing body is subject to more strenuous
