demands for expansion than retrenchment. When the days of depression come, the tax burden, especially on real estate, becomes a positive menace to the small home owner, the landlord, the subdivider, the land speculator, and the farmer. At such times public interest in budget matters seems to be accelerated by the force of self-interest. 

There are, in general, three types of budget authority: (1) where power to formulate the budget plan is placed in the hands of the chief executive or chief administrative officer such as 

President, mayor, governor, or manager; (2) where budgetmaking is delegated to a board of administrative officers; and (3) where such authority rests with an agency responsible to the legislature. Of these, the executive budget is much to be preferred and is growing in popularity. It is in effect in a considerable majority of the states, in the federal government, in the four-hundred and more council-manager cities, and in the growing number of strong-mayor municipalities. 

The difficulty with most of the executive budgets today is that the chief administrative officer does not have a trained staff agency to assist him in the budget work. Governors and mayors too frequently have to rely upon hit-and-miss or ruleof-thumb methods in making their budget decisions. There should be a more widespread adoption of the permanent budget bureau, as in the City of Los Angeles. The latter is a purely advisory corps of technicians, under civil service protection, which practically takes over bodily all of the administrative work in connection with the preparation of the mayor's budget. 

This bureau is largely responsible for the fact that Los Angeles has gone through the depression without great financial difficulty.

Of recent years there has been considerable interest in budgeting public improvements for longer than one year. There are several advantages in this. Need rather than political strength of councilmen would then govern the location of new projects; some worthy improvements, such as jails, would not be passed over for more showy memorial halls. Bond issues would be more readily voted where a definite plan forecast the

Ch. 14] 

301 obligations incurred. Furthermore, the future needs of the community would be subject to the analysis of trained minds, thus avoiding haphazard development, inadequate facilities for expansion,¹º and premature obsolescence of structures.

The principal difficulty lies in the fact that public improvements in any particular metropolitan area are under the jurisdiction of several independent governing bodies: city, school district, county, and others. Any well-ordered plan for public improvements would require the co-operation or consolidation of these agencies.11 The idea of the long-term budget is that it will plan the public improvements that are to be constructed for five or ten years in advance, adding a new year as each immediate year is completed. Even though such a plan may not be binding on officials coming into power subsequent to its formulation, it is deemed quite worth while to formulate it for purely advisory purposes. Occasionally a considerable part of a plan can be made legally effective through a bond election as in St. Louis, Cincinnati, and Kansas City.12

It is obviously impossible to foresee from one year to two and one-half years in advance every possible expenditure need. 

Consequently, it becomes necessary to enact additional appropriations. These are authorizations to spend in addition to the main appropriation act or ordinance. They constitute an evil because their abuse is one of the most frequent causes of deficits, but a certain minimum amount of such appropriations seems inevitable. Deficiency appropriations are really contrary in theory to the Anglo-American principle that governments should spend no money not previously authorized by the representatives of the people. They, in fact, are nothing else than a legalization of expenditure already incurred. Under certain conditions this can be done in both Great Britain and in the United States. 

Each year Congress is asked to pass deficiency bills amounting to many millions of dollars. Frequently states find it necessary to incur unauthorized expenditures subject to subsequent legislative legalization. This is not necessary in cities and counties because their legislative bodies are in continuous session and can pass additional appropriations when needed. Deficiency appropriations constitute an evil which cannot be effectively dealt with until the people and legislators are willing to recognize the administrative nature of budget control. 

On the first of every month, and even at some intermediate periods, some governmental agency in the United States is beginning its fiscal year, which, briefly, is merely the annual period used for budgeting, accounting, and fiscal purposes. 

The federal, state of California, and California municipal fiscal years all begin July 1 and end June 30. The British fiscal year begins April 1, and ends March 31. No great problem is offered except that of uniformity. For the sake of comparative statistics and reporting it is desirable to have a uniform fiscal year.

Problems are obviously presented by situations wherein the taxes become due some considerable time after the beginning of the fiscal year. Thus, in California the fiscal year begins on July 1 and real estate taxes are not paid until November.

CHAPTER XV  

With the adoption of the appropriation act or ordinance, the budget battle is less than half won. The best of plans are of no avail if the spending departments are permitted to incur obligations without regard to the expenditure program. The third phase of budgeting, namely, administrative control of expenditure, is therefore the crucial turn in the budget cycle. Spending agencies will inevitably present seemingly unanswerable reasons for being allowed to spend in excess of original appropriations. 

Unless the control agency is endowed with strong powers to require the departments to stay within their allotments, the balance between income and outgo will be thrown sharply out of line. The control which is necessary becomes largely an accounting problem, the chief accounting officer being charged with holding the spending branches to the letter of the appropriations.

Most governmental areas in the United States have accounting systems which take cognizance merely of cash receipts and cash disbursements. These are known as cash accounting systems, and are defective in several respects. Where every department does its own buying, there is no satisfactory way of finding out how many orders for goods are outstanding. If departments are free to buy without regard to appropriations, overexpenditure of appropriations will result. There is no central administrative control of expenditure; and there is never a time when a consolidated statement of current assets and liabilities is obtainable. The same is true of revenues. Under a cash accounting system no attention is paid to how much revenue should be received; only that actually coming in is shown. 

It is such laxness in the past that has largely been the cause of wholesale tax delinquencies in many cities. Without an ac- 306

Ch. 15] 307 

counting system which accrued revenues, it was no one's business aggressively to pursue collection. 

Writers generally refer to the correct type of appropriation accounting as the accrual system. This is probably too broad a term, however, because the question of just how far the accrual method should be followed in governmental accounting is still a matter of controversy. Practically all are agreed that there should be accrual appropriation accounting, so we shall refer to it by that name. Such a system should provide as follows: 

I. A pre-audit of all purchase orders and authority for employment. 

2. The encumbéring of the appropriation accounts with all incurred expenditure obligations. 

3. An accurate estimate of all income and revenue. 

4. The accrual of this revenue on appropriate ledgers. 

5. The entry of revenue collections on these ledgers as encumbrances just as in appropriations. 

6. The furnishing automatically of a periodic budget statement, at least monthly showing: (a) Expenditures to date as compared to appropriations. (b) Rate of expenditure as compared to expectations. (c) Revenues to date as compared to expectations. (d) Overruns and deficiencies in specific sources of revenue. (e) Expenditure as compared to revenue. 

Pre-audit is an examination of a requisition for goods or services by the accounting officer before the obligation is incurred. Usually the accountant will have the authority to question only the legality of the proposed obligation and whether or not there is a lawful appropriation authorizing it. If he so finds he will enter an encumbrance upon the appropriation ledgers covering the amount of the requisition, and then validate the requisition or purchase order before it is sent to the vendor or the purchasing agent. If the purchasing agent completes purchase negotiations before sending the purchase order to the accounting officer the sum entered as an encumbrance will be

FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION 

correct and require no further change. If, however, the accountant receives the requisition before it goes to the purchasing agent, the amount of his encumbrance may have to be changed to agree with a slightly different price on the subsequent invoice. 

This, however, occasions no great difficulty. 

It can be readily seen that such a system should prevent overexpenditure of budget resources if properly administered. No administrative service will be permitted to spend one cent without the certification of the accounting office that there is an appropriation for that specified purpose, with an unencumbered balance sufficient to pay for it. 

In the United States, budget planning takes place as long as eighteen months ahead of the time when some of the expenditures are to be made. Thus, a given city will start planning its 

1937-1938 budget in January, 1937; but expenditure will not be completed under it until June, 1938. Obviously it would be impossible to foresee all contingencies under such conditions. 

The elasticity necessary to adapt the budget plan to changing conditions can be secured under an integrated administration, however, by the system of executive allotments and work programs. Allotments and work programs constitute separate phases of the same procedure. For their proper utilization the appropriation act or ordinance should be adopted in lump sums for each department or subdivision. The utmost elasticity should be permissible. The operating departments should understand definitely that they are not to incur any expenditure until their work programs have been approved. After appropriations have been passed, the chief administrative officer calls upon the head of each spending agency to furnish detailed plans of expenditure. These plans cover definite periods of the fiscal year-months or quarters and are known as the work programs for those periods, the series for the entire year being presented at the same time.

When the chief administrative officer receives these work programs he will subject them to a thorough scrutiny. If changes are desirable, department heads are called in for individual conferences, usually resulting in amicable agreements.

Ch. 15] 309 

When the chief administrative officer is satisfied with a work program, he signs it and sends it to the chief accounting officer, and it is then that the work program becomes an executive allotment. The items contained therein are set up on the appropriation ledgers for purposes of accounting control, no department being permitted to incur an obligation unless it is contained in the allotment. The result is broad elastic spending authority by lump sum appropriations, coupled with detailed, but elastic, administrative control of expenditure. At the end of each allotment period, the work programs for the remainder of the year are revised in the light of experience thus far. A health department, for example, may have been confronted with an unusual epidemic during the first quarter. To meet the situation it secured the permission of the chief administrative officer to exceed its allotment, but at the beginning of the second quarter the health department will be asked to revise its work program for the remaining periods. In this way it can still remain within the annual appropriation by practicing the studied economy necessary to make up the deficit incurred during the first quarter.¹

The allotment system has several merits. In the first place, it is the most reliable administrative device to prevent departments from spending in excess of available funds. It is considered good practice to require each work program to set up a certain percentage of the appropriation as saving, which becomes equivalent to saying: "We are trying to run our department on 5 per cent less than the appropriation." If there are no abnormal emergencies, each department will have a surplus to turn back to the general fund at the end of the year. On the other hand, the savings allotment can be used as a cushion to meet unexpected expense in subsequent quarters. Often it will permit taking care of emergencies without tipping the budget out of balance. In the second place, the allotment system will enable the chief administrative officer to take measures neces- ¹H. M. Rocca, Council-Manager Government in Berkeley (City of Berkeley and Chamber of Commerce, 1929), pp. 29-30; J. H. Jamison, "Methods of Budgetary Control," City Manager Yearbook (International City Man agers' Assn., Chicago, 1931), p. 65.

FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION 

sary to meet unexpected shrinkage in revenue. He can call in the department heads, explain the situation, and ask them to revise their work programs so as to keep the budget in balance. 

The chief of police may be requested to use some patrol cars another year, in lieu of purchasing new ones for which provision has been made in existing allotments; the departments may be requested to refrain from filling vacancies for the remainder of the year; and a vast variety of similar economies can be made in time to avoid a deficit. Too often, in disintegrated financial set-ups, decreasing revenues will result in pyramided deficits because individual departments are permitted to spend to the maximum with no automatic check. Governing bodies and financial officers are disinclined to incur the resentment inevitably connected with the curtailment of spending. 

The resulting stalemate or inertia permits preventable deficits to take place simply because no single person or agency has the authority to take the necessary preventive steps. Under the allotment system the responsibility for a balanced budget is placed directly on the chief administrative officer who, if alive to his trust, will be able to balance budgets under the most trying conditions.2

Large administrative units, such as states or the nation, are not well adapted to central budgetary accounting control. Time and distance become such an important factor that sending proposed obligations to the central accounting office for the purpose of pre-audit would entail a great deal of bureaucratic delay. It is here that the work program and allotment idea come in. The spending units can keep budgetary accounts of their own, on which are accrued their various obligations as they occur. But their ledgers must remain within the limits set by allotments determined by the central financial agency. 

These allotments have been arrived at by work programs furnished by the spending units themselves. The latter forward periodical reports of expenditure to the central financial agency which maintains certain ledger records in large outline. This

system achieves central co-ordination of expenditure while permitting a certain desirable degree of decentralized budget accounting."

It is precisely such a system of control that is contemplated in President Roosevelt's Executive Order No. 6226 of July 27, 

1933, which in effect makes the Director of the Budget responsible for the administration of a system of executive allotments or apportionments. Enactments dating back to 1905 had attempted to prevent overexpenditure of appropriations through allotments. These provisions established no presidential or treasury control of departmental expenditure, however; the departments were merely warned not to spend in excess of their appropriations for a given fiscal year. To accomplish this purpose they were to set up monthly or other allotments of items of regular expenditure which were to be exceeded only in case of sudden emergency involving loss of human life or the destruction of property. Allotments were subject to no executive control outside the department, and if exceeded, the department head was merely required to justify the deficit in writing to Congress when asking for deficiency appropriations. For a brief period following the enactment of the Budget and Accounting Act of 1921, the Bureau of the Budget attempted to strengthen the administration of the allotment provision.5 

Departmental opposition, plus the fact that it had doubtful legal authority, doomed the move to only partial success. Not until the Roosevelt executive orders of 1933 has there been a legal and administrative basis for effective executive control of expenditure.

Treasury Department Circular No. 494 of August 5, 1933, contains the detailed instructions necessary to put the new allotment procedure into operation. The departments are required therein to set forth the funds available for expenditure, together with equal monthly apportionments, on Form A. The department heads were required to furnish the Treasury Department with such reports as the Department might require, the information thus acquired to be made available to the Bureau of the Budget for purposes of allotment control. These provisions, by subsequent executive orders, were made to apply to emergency units as well as regular establishments. 

In Great Britain, appropriations are considered as grants to the Treasury whose consent must be secured before any expenditure obligation is incurred. In the United States, appropriations have been made direct to the spending services who have not been subject to the administrative control of any other agency in matters concerning expenditure policy. Such American developments as the state reorganization and the councilmanager movements have tended toward the British type of Treasury control. Of course, this practice is so new to our experience that it has spread slowly. Nevertheless, it is an almost indispensable phase of administrative budget control.

action is necessary to balance the budget? Such power in the hands of the chief administrative officer is the keystone of budget strategy.

Let us suppose that revenues have failed to come up to expectations. The chief of police is asked to use his old car until next year, even if there is an appropriation for a new one; the superintendent of parks is asked to refrain from spending that $5,000 item for improving Prospect Park; all departments are requested not to fill vacancies until the next fiscal year; and so on down the line-expenditure is pruned to the limit to stay within reduced revenues. Of course, it is presumed that sound judgment will be exercised; otherwise the economy program may become a boomerang. There is, nevertheless, a considerable leeway within which a strong administrative officer, unhampered by too many political considerations, can curtail expenditures to meet the failure of revenues. It is believed that a chief administrative officer should have this power where administration is well integrated. 

Lump Sum or Segregated Appropriations? 

The controversy as to whether appropriations should be made in great detail or under a few major headings is perennial. It would seem that a good deal of the purely argumentative aspect of the problem could be avoided if the difference between a budget and an appropriation act or ordinance were recognized. Practically every one agrees that the budget, being merely an informational advisory document, can be in as great detail as is desired. The controversy, therefore, is in regard to the form of appropriations, not the budget. 

A great deal of misunderstanding could also be avoided by realizing that charter organization and lines of administrative authority are quite different from place to place. This has an important bearing upon the detail of appropriations. For instance, in a council-manager city where administration is well integrated, the council can control expenditure through its manager.

It is consequently unnecessary to appropriate in great detail. When, on the other hand, there is no central depart-

[Pt. III 

FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION 

ment of finance, the chief accounting officer is elective, and a generally weak administrative budgetary control exists, it may be that segregated appropriations are the only possible means of control. In other words, the question is not: “Are lump sum appropriations better than segregated?" It is rather: "Which are better suited to our conditions, lump sum or segregated appropriations?" This can be illustrated by referring to two specific cities. It is believed that in Cincinnati lump sum appropriation fits the situation well, whereas Los Angeles has need for greater segregation.

Cincinnati has a modern council-manager charter with a well-integrated administration under a manager with ample powers. The annual appropriation ordinance contains only sixty-two allocations for the general fund. These are single items making lump sum grants to specific departments, divisions or activities, these items not being broken down in any manner whatsoever. The effectiveness of administrative control of lump sum expenditure is demonstrated by fiscal results, for while many other cities were experiencing defaults and the registration of warrants, Cincinnati went through the difficulties of the early nineteen thirties without embarrassment. Indeed, she entered 1934 with a comfortable surplus, reducing taxes 12 per cent for that year."

The charter organization of the City of Los Angeles differs greatly from that of Cincinnati. In the California metropolis the city controller, who keeps the general control accounts, is elective and consequently is not subject to the administrative control of either the mayor or council. The spending departments are for the most part headed by boards, the members of which are appointed by the mayor with council affirmation for overlapping terms. The mayor can remove members of these sixteen or more boards only with the concurrence of the council. The chief executive, therefore, has no supervision over the controller and only indirect control of the departments headed by boards. The mayor's budget is in practice prepared by the bureau of budget and efficiency, a unit guaranteed financial sup- 

City Manager's Annual Budget, 1934; An Ordinance No. 1, 1934.

Ch. 15] 315 

port by the charter, and the head of which is appointed under civil service rules by the mayor. 

A system of accrual appropriation accounting is maintained in the controller's office. No expenditure can be incurred by any of the departments under the general budget until the controller has pre-audited the purchase order, made the proper encumbrance on the appropriation ledger, and sent it forward with his approval. Thus, no obligation can be incurred for which there is not an appropriation. Control is maintained through appropriations made in considerable detail. There is no distinction in form between the appropriation ordinance and the budget document. In this way the control is largely legislative rather than administrative. It is maintained that this is the only type of control possible under the loose organization of the Los Angeles charter. For purposes of judgment let us again look at results. During a decade when Los Angeles was doubling her population (1920-1930), she lived within her income and built up a cash surplus exceeding $6,000,000 on June 30, 1930. On January 1, 1931, she had the smallest debt, both absolute and per capita, of any city in the million class in the United States. With such results one could hardly say that budget control had been ineffective. Much consideration has been given to budgetary control in Cincinnati and Los Angeles because, up to 1935 at least, each was achieving excellent fiscal results under diametrically opposite types of organization. Accordingly it would seem that lump sum appropriations are good for Cincinnati and segregated control is good for Los Angeles. The prevailing opinion among administrators, consultants and students, however, is in favor of integrated administrative control with lump sum appropriations. It is thought that this system gives necessary elasticity to budget control. Under a council-manager charter the executive is controlled by the council, which body should be willing to delegate authority to its own servant without binding him in a 

C. E. Rightor, "Bonded Debt of 257 Cities," National Municipal Review 

(June, 1931), Vol. XX, No. 7, p. 352. "Buck, op. cit., pp. 127-135; W. F. Willoughby, Principles of Public Administration (Johns Hopkins Press, 1927), p. 468.

strait-jacket of detailed directions relative to the minutiae of expenditure. Good administrators thrive on responsibility. If our charters and constitutions establish well-defined lines of administrative responsibility there is no danger, but a positive merit, in granting corresponding power through lump-sum appropriations. If, on the other hand, charters and constitutions do not combine power and responsibility, if they place fiscal control in the hands of independent and elective agencies, then it may be wise to control by segregation. The whole matter simmers down to the question: "How far can you trust your administrative officers and hold them to a summary accountability?" 

One way of avoiding additional or deficiency appropriations is to leave a portion of the year's resources unallocated so that they may be used to meet emergencies. The proper way to do this under administrative budget control is to set up an appropriation item from which the chief administrative officer can make transfers to other departments at his discretion. 

This is done at Berkeley by means of the manager's emergency fund.10 In the City of Los Angeles, where there is considerable legislative budgetary control, there is set up in each annual appropriation ordinance a so-called unappropriated balance. 

This can be allocated later, to meet emergencies, only upon authority of the city council. For 1931-1932 this unappropriated balance constituted slightly in excess of one per cent of all appropriations, while in Berkeley, transfers from the manager's emergency fund usually stay within one per cent of total expenditures. Under an integrated administration, the Berkeley system is to be preferred; while under a weak-executive organization, such as the Los Angeles charter, the unappropriated balance, subject to council control, seems to meet the needs. 

It is considered good administrative practice to permit transfers of unneeded money in one appropriation item to other activities. Practice varies in this respect. In Great Britain, transfers are permitted within votes (appropriation subheads) 10 Helen M. Rocca, Council-Manager Government in Berkeley (City of

The chief administrative officer should have a very wide transfer power, where the administration is well integrated as under council-manager charters. This will permit that elasticity and strategy in budgetary control which is so necessary in effectively balancing income against outgo.

What Is a Fund? 

One of the least understood and most loosely used terms in governmental finance is "fund," for in common practice any allocation of public money is referred to as a fund. Thus, the segregation of expenditure for stationery is spoken of as the "stationery fund." Such usage is not technically correct.

Funds, strictly speaking, are aggregations of resources and liabilities set aside to be dealt with as a unit. A fund has its own accounting. It may exist at any given time without cash or expendable liquid resources. It is, however, capable of producing its own balance sheet of resources and obligations, or assets and liabilities; and its own operating statement of revenues and expenditures, and receipts and disbursements. It also has its own surplus or deficit.

There will be a general fund and several special funds for any given governmental unit. The general fund may be expended for any purpose to which the legislature wishes to apply it. It is the unrestricted fund applicable to general purposes, as the name implies. Usually the major part of governmental income is allocated to the general fund. The special funds, on the other hand, restrict certain revenues or resources for specific expenditure purposes." Thus, many states will earmark gasoline tax money for highway building and maintenance. 

"Griffenhagen and Associates (Technical Staff), Report of the Waterbury 

Charter Commission, 1930, pp. 46-47.

FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION 

The federal government has a reserve fund for civil retirement purposes, part being derived from employee contributions. A given county will have a law library fund maintained by a charge of one dollar for every legal action filed. It is generally thought that there should be as few funds as possible, for a large number of funds complicates financial planning and budget procedure. The government's cash resources will be scattered in many places where they cannot be mustered to meet periods when income is low, thus compelling the government to borrow for some funds when a consolidated balance sheet of all funds would show a very good cash position. Special funds devoted to specific purposes, such as millage levies for libraries or parks, substantially amount to permanent appropriations. 

These services are, for all practical purposes, removed from effective budgeting. It has been thought in the past that it was necessary to segregate accounts into independent funds in order to see that appropriations were not diverted to some purpose other than that intended. It has been demonstrated conclusively, however, that legal restrictions will not bar a governing body from borrowing between funds, forgetting to pay back. 

The special fund system is a failure as an agency of expenditure control.12 An individual does not need separate checking accounts for his grocer, his landlord, his milkman, his tailor, and his insurance; yet the special fund system operates on just such an assumption. The best way to secure control of expenditure is to give the chief accounting officer ample authority to see that moneys are devoted to the purposes intended. He can do this best if he is not hampered by special fund restrictions.¹ª

319 dependent upon the development of adequate standards of cost and performance. The California Taxpayers Association has effectively used inmate costs per year in reviewing the estimates of state institutions. The most promising current effort in this direction is probably that of the research staff of the International City Managers' Association which has recently completed the installation in Brunswick, Georgia, of a system of budgetary control based on the report of the Committee on Uniform Street Sanitation Records. Work programs based on standard costs for recognized work units form the bases of such control. These work programs are tied in with monthly budget allotments by the city manager. Thus, we find the yearly estimate for refuse removal was 55,000 cubic yards at 30 cents each, or a total of $16,500. This was spread through the twelve months with a July peak of 5,500 cubic yards due to the vegetable and melon season, and a minimum of 4,000 cubic yards in certain winter months. Catch-basin cleaning, with an estimate of one dollar per catch basin, was confined to three months, April, July, and October.¹¹

Here again the distinction should be made between the budget and appropriations. Unit costs never should be stated in the appropriations. The Brunswick appropriations are divided merely into two categories, personal services and all other expenditures. Several years ago, a unit cost budget was attempted in New York City. This early experiment failed largely because the amount that could be spent per unit was stated in the appropriation ordinance. The resulting lack of administrative flexibility doomed the experiment to failure.15 Appropriations under a unit cost budget should be lump sum in nature, thus permitting adjustment of work program to varying cost situations. 

Cost accounting is merely the process of finding what it costs in dollars and cents to perform a certain unit of work, service, or operation. The results may take several forms; thus, one

administrator may wish to know the total costs of main functions, such as protection to life and property, education, and so on. Another may want to know the costs of sub-functions and activities. The universal tendency today, however, seems to be toward getting sub-functional costs based on units of performance, such as the street-mile swept, the ton of garbage removed, kilowatt hour of electricity, and the mile-yard of gravel hauled. Not all governmental areas are getting a wide range of such costs. In fact, it probably could be said that most cities have no idea what their various activities and services are costing them. Widespread interest is being evidenced in this direction, however, especially in the sanitation and engineering fields. 

The Bureau of Engineering of the City of Los Angeles is now getting accurate costs on over a hundred items. The system was recently elaborated at the instance of the Bureau of Budget and Efficiency which wanted extensive cost data in order more effectively to scrutinize the budget estimates of this spending unit. Cost accounting also serves the additional purpose of requiring many operations to be made a matter of public record which would otherwise be covered in obscurity. This tends to discourage the misapplication of government money.

If cost accounting is to be accurate the general accounting system must charge all costs to the proper department. Thus, in the City of Los Angeles there is a central shop for the repair of automotive equipment. If a truck is repaired for the engineering bureau the repair shop will keep a record of labor and material costs, add a percentage for overhead shop costs, and send the bill to the engineering bureau. In the meantime the shop will have financed its costs from a revolving fund which is always being expended and replenished. Charges are figured so as to keep the resources of this fund constant. The fund's outgo is reimbursed by charges against the appropriations of the various departments. Thus, the motor vehicle costs can be accurately charged to the work units to which they apply. 

This does not in any way interfere with securing accurate costs for the shop itself, because they can be obtained from revolving fund operations and interdepartmental invoices.

Ch. 15] 321 

Accurate functional or unit costs will require that some attention be given to indirect as well as direct costs. For instance, the expenditures necessary to maintain the city council and the mayor's office should be borne to some extent by the entire government. The director of public works gets a salary which comprises a part of the costs in garbage collection, sewer repair, and paving construction on force account. On the other hand, a motor truck which is paid for out of the appropriations of a single year is used for three or four years. Would not an accurate cost record spread its original cost over subsequent years in which it is used? This is attempted in good cost accounting systems. The difficulty lies in the lack of agreement and uniformity as to just how to go about it. Suppose a number of trucks are given a uniform four-year span of life for accounting purposes and half of them are still in the service at the end of seven years. How much of the general government expenditure is to be charged to each department. These are questions which have to be decided more or less arbitrarily in each instance. Comparative costs between cities will begin to mean something only when there is uniformity in these matters.

The Auditing Function 

One elementary principle which has failed of recognition in national, state, and local governments is that the ordinary administrative features of accounting and fiscal supervision should be separated from the post-audit. The auditor should be entirely independent of the administration and responsible to the legislature. 

Properly the duties of the Auditor should be three. First, he should examine past transactions. The accounts and reports of all persons or agencies having the receipt, custody, or disbursement of public moneys should be examined to insure proper accountability, or fidelity. Second, the transactions of public funds that have been expended, have been received, or that should have been received, should be examined in respect to the question of legality. Third, the auditor should report the result of such examinations to the general assembly

which is the branch of the government acting as a check upon the executive and administrative branches. The functions of a Comptroller, on the other hand, are the settlement of claims, either of or against the state, and, as an incident of this, the keeping of the central accounts of the state and the prescribing of the subsidiary accounting systems in field offices and institutions. These involve purely administrative duties. 

The Comptroller will make an administrative pre-examination of all claims for the purpose of determining their expediency, propriety, and classification, as measures of administrative control and record.16

This elementary principle of fiscal control is violated by combining the functions of comptroller and auditor in a single office, as in the governments of the United States, California, and the City of Los Angeles. This results in the auditing agency checking its own accounts. Not until such confusion is eliminated will public financial administration be on a sound basis.

There is quite general agreement that an annual audit should be made by someone independent of the administrative offices who have spent the money. The British national practice offers an example in this respect worthy of emulation. The auditing officer, referred to as the Comptroller and Auditor General, is appointed by the Crown for life and can be removed only by a vote of both houses of Parliament. This gives him a high degree of independence of the administration. He conducts annual test audits in each department and eventually reports to the Standing Committee on Public Accounts of the House of Commons. Presided over by a chairman chosen from the parliamentary opposition, this committee proceeds to review the results of the audit in the presence of both the Comptroller and Auditor General and representatives of the Treasury. As defective administrative practices are brought to light, the Treasury will issue rules and regulations designed to correct them. These rules are called Treasury Minutes. Eventually the Standing Committee on Public Accounts will report to the 10 Report on a Survey of the Organization and Administration of the State Government of North Carolina, Institute for Government Research of the Brookings Institution, 1930, p. 320; on this general theme see G. C. S. 

Benson, op. cit., pp. 15-35.

Ch. 15] 323 

house. There is a defect in this procedure, however, in that the House seldom, if ever, has time to consider and debate the report.

It is the preponderant opinion of students of public finance that the independent post-audit should be performed by an agency responsible to the legislature. The traditional confusion resulting from placing the accounting and auditing functions in an elective officer has nullified the effect of the audit in American state and local government. Many cities, however, are getting good audits, either by a state agency as a requirement of law, or by private firms of accountants. The difficulty with the latter method is that city councils are not willing to pay the prevailing fees for time sufficient to make the work effective. 

This has resulted in some sections of the country in a practice of asking auditors to bid on the local job. Frequently, the more professionally competent persons will refuse to enter this competition and cities will get a second-rate audit by a secondrate auditor. More often a fairly competent worker will go into only the surface aspects of things, failing to be thorough because he cannot afford to be for the fee at which the contract was awarded. This encourages poor workmanship performed by the "scabs" of the profession. There is also the consideration that auditors of private accounts frequently do not understand governmental accounting.

The Operation Audit 

Mr. Upson has said that if "the public is to keep its hands off of the technical processes of government, such compulsion can only come by measuring the results that these technical processes produce, and condemning or rewarding public servants accordingly." 17

In order to inform the public on official competence, the results obtained by administrators should be checked periodically by an auditing agency independent of the administration. Presumably there would be a permanent recurrence of such administrative surveys as are now being undertaken for states and cities by such organizations as the National Institute

of Public Administration,18 Griffenhagen and Associates,19 and the Institute for Government Research of the Brookings Institution.20 Such operation audits will be based upon standards and units of measurement accepted widely enough to secure popular confidence. The organizations mentioned above develop standards of their own in matters of organization which students in general believe to be valid and which increasingly are finding their way into administrative practice. In only a few fields of activity, however, have definite standards of work appraisal been developed. It is believed that the independent auditing agency should increasingly assume the task of measuring the effectiveness of work performed. This was pointed out by the Brookings Institution report on North Carolina:

Relieved of all ministerial duties, the auditor will be free to devote his time not only to fidelity auditing but also to that important collateral duty of scrutinizing and analyzing expenditures which may have been improperly made, or which may have represented to him an unwise or wasteful use of appropriated funds. Through the periodic or occasional audit of all government offices, institutions, and agencies, the Auditor will become possessed of an intimate knowledge of their financial transactions. He cannot fail to see evidences of extravagance, waste, questionable practices, or inefficient methods, and, being independent of the administrative branch, he can carry his criticism annually to the governor and biennially to the General Assembly with a view to effecting executive and legislative action correcting such practices.21 

It is significant to note in this connection that in recent years the British Comptroller and Auditor General has become a critic of the nature of expenditure as well as an auditor of fidelity.22

CHAPTER XVI PURCHASING 

By centralized purchasing is meant the maintenance of a central office which procures for all or most of the agencies of the government the needed things other than personnel. It is agreed by practically every one, except politicians, that centralized purchasing is desirable. It lowers both overhead and unit costs, the volume of paper work is reduced, and it permits the adoption of standard specifications. Through this form of procurement, there is secured centralized supervision over inspection of deliveries, storage and distribution of stock, and interdepartmental transfers and sales of surplus stock. Centralized purchasing facilitates closer accounting control over expenditures, and it permits saving of discounts through prompt payment of invoices. The employment of a full-time purchasing staff improves buying technique and tends to eliminate graft and favoritism. The central purchasing idea is said also to aid the vendor because he can save money and time by soliciting business at one buying office instead of at many; he saves by reducing orders and deliveries for the same sales total; and he is thus enabled to reduce his paper work on government accounts.¹ 

The person in charge of the purchasing office, bureau, or division is usually called the purchasing agent. It goes without saying that he should be chosen on the basis of his qualification for the work. He should be appointed by the chief administrative officer, under civil service rules, and his tenure should be secure during good behavior. Purchasing is a staff function which should be intimately tied up with the other financial functions, preferably occupying a bureau in a central department of finance. Much of the complaint relative to "red-tape" connected with centralized purchasing is due to the fact that the 

Russell Forbes, Governmental Purchasing (Harper & Bros., 1929), p. 10. 1 328

Ch. 16] 329 

PURCHASING 

purchasing office is separated from the accounting authorities in the administrative structure. Various personal considerations, as well as faulty charter organization, keep the purchasing agent from bringing about the type of co-operation which would eliminate unnecessary paper work and delay. If the accounting authorities and the purchasing bureau were in the same department under a director of finance with co-ordinating power, the accounting routine could be simplified so as to: (1) prevent delay through the cluttering of requisitions on desks of departmental officers; (2) departments could be compelled to group their orders and raise the gross purchase per order; and (3) the number of orders could be reduced. In other words, departmental routine which, if excessive, tends to nullify the good effects of centralized purchasing, could be brought under control. 

Bills signed by the Governor on September 1, 1933, and on 

May 23, 1934, brought central purchasing to New York City.

The legislative acts also provided for central control of stores and standard specifications under a commissioner of purchase to be appointed by the mayor. The jurisdiction of the central purchasing agency includes all city departments except the board of education. It was estimated that a saving of $5,000,000 would be effected the first year on a turnover in the neighborhood of $30,000,000. Mayor La Guardia appointed Professor 

Russell Forbes of New York University as Commissioner of 

Purchase. In January, 1935, the mayor expressed extreme satisfaction with progress for the first year, saying that a saving of $500,000 had been effected on fuel oil and printing alone. 

The department had cost no more to operate than during the previous year.2

The federal government has but recently seen fit to create a central purchasing office with wide powers. An Executive 

Order, No. 6166, of June 10, 1933, set up a Procurement Division in the Treasury Department with a Director of Procurement as its head. To this new division was transferred the office of the Supervising Architect. The Procurement Division also takes care of warehousing, distribution and the disposition "New York Times, August 24, 1933, 2:4; September 2, 1933, 5:4; September 3, 1933, 4:4; May 24, 1934, 6:2; January 11, 1935.

of surplus materials. The Federal Co-ordination Service was abolished, and certain of its activities were transferred to the

Subsequent regulations provided for an advisory committee of five members, the permanent chairman to be the Assistant Director, Branch of Supply. The other four members were to be selected from executive departments having a predominant interest in procurement matters. This committee was authorized to study procurement policy and form regulations for carrying into effect the general objective of the Division. Such regulations were to be approved by the director before becoming effective. Supplies for those requirements which can be anticipated and consolidated are to be purchased through the Branch of Supply, either directly or by one or more designated executive departments. The same is true of those supplies for which requirements cannot be consolidated for definite quantity purchase but for which common contracts can be made with advantage. 

In certain cases departments are permitted to handle their own procurement services. In other instances arrangement is made for joint warehousing of two or more adjacent units. The principal objective is to achieve the benefits of centralized control and co-ordination while retaining the desired degree of flexibility and departmental autonomy. Purchase procedure provides that the requisition must be accompanied by a certificate showing that the proposed obligation has been encumbered on the appropriate ledger of the departmental budget accounts. 

Under the Budget and Accounting Act of 1921, a Federal 

Co-ordinating Service was attached to the Bureau of the Budget. A chief co-ordinator, usually a high officer of the army or navy, was assisted in this work by a score or so of army and navy officers detailed to that duty. The country was divided into nine co-ordination areas, each headed by an area co-ordinator. At each geographical point where several departments were represented there existed a federal business association consisting of a representative from each department. The coordination activities of this rather loose organization consisted chiefly of efforts to conserve matériel. Personnel and the per-

331

sonal element in management concerned them only secondarily, if at all. In Washington, the Co-ordinating Service worked through a number of interdepartmental committees charged with determining policies concerned chiefly with the procurement of supplies and materials. It was only natural that Executive 

Order 6166 of June 10, 1933, setting up the new Procurement

Division, should also abolish the Co-ordinating Service. The retention of both would have resulted in sheer duplication. 

The Procurement Division was given much wider powers than the old Co-ordinating Service. However, the same scheme of interdepartmental co-ordinating committees was retained. 

There is, for instance, the Federal Standard Stock Catalog 

Board, headed by the Director of Procurement and composed of representatives from each department. The decisions of this board, after approval by the Director of Procurement, are binding on all executive departments. The Federal Specifications 

Board, headed by the Director of the Bureau of Standards, prepares standard specifications for federal purchases. The Federal Contract Board prepares standard contract forms, studies, and recommends changes in contract procedure. The Procure ment Division is granted authority to co-ordinate the government's freight, express, and other traffic activities. It has also been authorized to control all real estate activities, a movement in line with recent progressive municipal practice. All leases and transfers of real estate must clear through the Director of Procurement. This latter official also has control over the disposition of surplus and seized property. The Procurement 

Division is given ample authority to control the purchasing and warehousing of supplies for all governmental subdivisions.³ 

Standardization 

Standardization in purchasing is based on the idea that there are a great many commodities or items which can be used in more than one branch of governmental service. Certain 3 

³ Executive Order No. 6166, June 10, 1933; Order of the Secretary of the Treasury, October 9, 1933; regulations of the Director of Procurement 

(mimeographed and not dated).

FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION 

highly specialized commodities are not capable of being advantageously standardized, but there are a number of items available in almost identical quality from many competitive bidders. These include coal, automobile tires and tubes, lubricating oil, textiles, office equipment, and furniture. Established standards of quality and performance in these and many other such staples will enable the government to consolidate the requirements of the various using agencies into large orders. 

Then it can go into the market as a large buyer and reduce unit costs both by quantity orders and increased competition. Effective standardization avoids the use of trade names or brands, thus encouraging competitive bidding. It aids quantity purchasing, reduces stocks, necessitates the carrying of fewer items, and lessens the possibility of becoming overburdened with obsolete items. It enables buyers and sellers to speak the same language.

The preparation of standard specifications is a co-operative process. Success cannot be achieved by forcing on the using departments technical specifications in the preparation of which they have had no voice. Experience has demonstrated that the services which use supplies and materials should share in framing specifications. A convenient means of bringing this about is through interdepartmental advisory committees. Thus, the Federal Specifications Board consists of representatives designated by heads of the executive departments, with the Director of the Bureau of Standards as chairman ex officio. 

It is attached to the procurement division of the Treasury Department, and its decisions are effective when approved by the Director of Procurement. There is a growing tendency toward the establishment in the larger governmental units of scientific agencies whose duty it is to test materials and formulate specifications. Such a bureau of standards, as is its typical designation, could just as well be a part of the purchasing agency, although sometimes it is found in the department of public works. The Bureau of Standards of the federal Department of Commerce is a scientific research agency of high reputation which aids in formulating specifications for the federal govern-

Ch. 16] 333 

PURCHASING 

ment. Federal specifications are published and thus become available to states and cities, many of which use them extensively. 

A recent survey made by the Municipal Reference Bureau of Cincinnati indicates that of eighteen large cities, nine generally buy on specification and nine do not.*

Purchase Procedure 

Forbes divides requisitions into two categories. The first, called the estimate, is based on a forecast of future needs during a definite period. After being checked with the budget appropriation it is turned over to the purchasing agency to be used as a guide in planning future purchases. Owing to the fact that governmental needs can be estimated more definitely, the estimate is more useful in public than in private purchasing. It is recommended that the purchasing agency be given authority to call for estimates at such times and for such a period in advance as it may deem necessary. The agency's use of these estimates must always be confined, of course, to the restrictions imposed by the expenditure control system in effect at the time. Where such controls permit sufficient elasticity, the buyer will be able to enter the market at the most favorable time and under the most favorable conditions. He is in a position to call for estimates from several spending agencies on standardized items and buy in bulk lots at great savings as compared with what the cost would have been if procured through the ordering of many small lots. This procedure should result in reduction of the number of requisitions. The estimate system need not entail additional storage facilities if the purchases are made under contracts specifying delivery at any time at a stated discount from market quotations.

The other kind of requisition is a statement of a present need, requiring procurement at once or in the very near future. 

It is much more common, being found in every purchasing system. It should contain: (1) the number of the requisition; 

Municipal Reference Bureau, Municipal Purchasing Methods and Pro cedure (mimeographed, Cincinnati, November, 1933).

FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION 

(2) the date of the requisition; (3) the name of the requisitioning agency; (4) a statement of what is wanted, with a clear-cut description or reference to specifications; (5) the quantity required; (6) the delivery date required or preferred; (7) the delivery address; (8) the account or appropriation to be charged; and (9) the signature of the requisitioner and of the approving officer. It is a common practice to issue the requisition in triplicate, one copy to remain with the requisitioning department, one to remain with the purchasing agency, and one to be sent to the accounting office. The most popular size of paper is 

8½ x 11 inches, since it can be kept in standard filing equipment. 

The requisition form is frequently made to do double duty as both a requisition and a purchase order. This is said by some to eliminate the task of copying the description, but Forbes points out that this "advantage is lost when requisitions from several using agencies are consolidated into a bulk order, for the quantity data and description would necessarily have to be copied anyway." " 

Purchasing agents should study market trends. They should have data constantly available relative to the course of prices for the principal commodities. Forbes states that few public buyers have such information, either from lack of incentive or lack of initiative. Instead of relying on past sources of supply, there should be a constant search for new vendors. Sentiment, friendship, and partisanship should not be motives prompting the selection of a buyer's market. To this end a supply list indicating the sellers of each commodity should be maintained and currently revised. 

The cheapest way of notifying vendors of prospective purchases is by posting a list of items to be purchased on a bulletin board a given length of time in advance. Constitutions, charters, and statutes frequently try to prevent favoritism and graft by requiring that sellers be notified through newspaper advertisements of all purchases above a certain minimum value. 

Forbes says, however, that this procedure fails of its intended purpose. Newspaper advertisements are not read by sellers; 

Forbes, op. cit., pp. 122-143, 143. • Ibid., p. 150.

PURCHASING 

the purchasing process is slowed up to the government's disadvantage; and the cost is excessive. It has also been shown that the newspaper advertising requirement can be evaded by "tipping-off" favored suppliers, and by "splitting" the orders into small enough amounts to come under the minimum. Postal card notices of intention to buy may be effective where it is not necessary to rush the purchase. 

Forbes feels that direct requests for quotations are most effective in securing publicity. This may take the form of telephone calls, but in most cases a special form will be sent to prospective bidders whose names appear on the supply list. 

This will contain a description of the goods desired and a space where the price can be filled in. The form will then be returned to the purchasing agency. The form requesting quotations should provide for: (1) the inquiry and requisition numbers; (2) the name and address of the supplier; (3) the time limit for submitting quotations; (4) delivery terms; (5) description of the commodities to be purchased; (6) the price quotation; (7) the discount terms; (8) the signature or affidavit of the supplier; and (9) it should indicate the number of copies of the quotations required.

A more formal procedure is usually required by law for purchases above specified amounts. It is common to require an affidavit in which the bidder swears to facts relative to his financial responsibility. The requirement for the posting of surety is quite general. It may be in the form of cash, certified check or bond, and is returned to the unsuccessful bidder after the purchase is awarded. Forbes is of the opinion that this surety requirement has been carried too far. The amount of surety together with the determination of the cases in which it should be required should be left to the discretion of the purchasing agent. A formal bid form should contain adequate and specific instructions to bidders. Samples are frequently required, but they are costly to bidders, and Forbes believes that they are not necessary wherever an exact specification is available and can be used as a substitute. 8 Ibid., p. 169.

FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION 

The sealed bid is distinctive of governmental purchasing, being seldom used in private enterprise. Those desiring to sell goods to the government are required to submit their prices in sealed envelopes. These envelopes are opened publicly under certain prescribed conditions and at a stated time, when the contracts are read and awarded to the lowest responsible bidder. 

There is usually provision for rejecting bids from illegal bidders, such as relatives of the purchasing agent or those who have defaulted on past contracts. It was formerly thought that this procedure insured automatically that the government would be able to purchase the best materials at the most favorable terms. 

It was even argued that the system itself obviated the need for professional buyers. The error of these assumptions is now apparent, for under the sealed-competitive-bid system it is possible that only favored bidders are aware of pending purchases. 

Frequently vendors bid higher than they would sell at through informal purchase, because they do not want to disclose, and trade association discipline restrains them from exhibiting, their bottom prices to competitors in an official bid. Purchasing agents know that a much more advantageous agreement could have been negotiated informally. The sealed bid sometimes leads to collusive bidding, that is, to a price agreement reached in advance by all bidders. sense.

The practice of requiring competitive sealed bids may be necessary as normal procedure in public purchasing. It should, however, always be subject to exception and applied with common The right to reject all bids is usually reserved, but this necessitates readvertising and repeating the same formalities. 

Forbes favors the San Francisco practice which permits purchase in the open market when all bids are the same."

It is quite a prevalent practice to require bids to be awarded local bidders, all other factors being equal. There would appear to be nothing inherently wrong with this practice as long as local bidders are not given the preference of a price differential, and as long as the purchasing agent is not restrained from securing a wide variety of bids from non-local sources of supply. 

Forbes, op. cit., p. 178.

PURCHASING 

Formerly, governments required their purchases to be awarded to the lowest bidder irrespective of such tempering factors as quality and responsibility. The tendency is now in the direction of permitting the purchasing authority to exercise judgment. The lowest-priced bid should not be accepted if the bidder is not responsible and if the goods are of inferior quality. 

Bids are usually available for public inspection after they are opened. There is some disadvantage in this because the government is deprived of the benefit of "confidential" bids and price-cutting which firms do not like to have known.10 11 A bidder is usually required to submit with his bid surety in cash, certified check, or bond equal to a small percentage of the amount of the bid. If he is awarded the contract he must leave this amount on deposit, and frequently add to it, as a guaranty for the performance of the contract. Forbes points out that interest on cash and checks and premiums on bonds must be paid. by some one, and that the contractor tends to include it in the price of the bid.¹¹ Furthermore, irresponsible contractors seem to be as successful as others in securing surety bonds, resulting in a higher premium for all. While surety is necessary, its excessive cost, which is eventually paid by the government, could be reduced by permitting the terms to be varied to suit each individual contract, instead of stating in the law or charter a flat percentage for all contracts. However, present conditions are such that it seems as if the practice of requiring surety bonds must be continued until both authority is given and responsibility is placed upon the purchasing agent. 

The form of contract most generally used is that calling for a definite quantity and amount. This has the advantage of definiteness, but has the disadvantage that the government cannot take advantage of a declining market. There are also forms of contract which are indefinite as to the precise quality, the quantity, the price, the length of the contract, and the place and frequency of deliveries. Forbes seems to favor wider trial of the indefinite price and quantity contract, with a constant discount

from the current market price.12 Bidders would agree to deliver specific supplies or materials at any time during the contract period at a given discount from the market price. The responsible bidder offering the largest discount would be successful. 

A good example of such a contract is one by which the city buys gasoline at a fixed discount from tank wagon price. Market price could be determined from sources stated in the agreement. 

These might include the quotations published in a specified daily newspaper, in a trade journal, the official quotation of a duly constituted exchange or market, or the bulletin of an established broker. The alleged advantage of such a contract is that the government would be assured of a constant supply at lowest current prices, while still maintaining the spirit of competitive bidding. "Cost plus" contracts agree to deliver at cost plus a certain percentage or plus a certain sum. They were widely used by the federal government during the World War. They are conducive to extravagance and waste, "since the contractor's profit is in direct ratio to the cost, he is encouraged to spare no expense. 99 13 

Emergency Orders by Using Agency 

It is necessary to permit the administrative units to purchase. items for emergency purposes without going through the central purchasing agency. The difficulty arises in interpreting just what constitutes an emergency. Without some form of central control the tendency will be for normal needs to become emergency purchases as a subterfuge to retain the purchasing authority in the department. There seems to be no fool-proof solution. for this problem. Some governments require post-examination of emergency purchases by the central buying agency. Forbes mentions four means of inspection without seeming to insist on any preference.15 Inspection by the receiving agency may tend to emphasize quality at the expense of price, while the reverse may be true for inspection by the purchasing office. Inspection by an independent office, such as the finance department, will constitute a check on the purchasing agency. In some cases, outside organizations are used. All of these forms are used in practice by various governments. In the United States government, the receiving agencies do their own inspecting. Where this plan is in effect in cities, it seems to be good practice to furnish the purchasing agency and the auditing agency with any inspection report. An unusually large number of cities would seem to give the inspecting to the purchasing agent. The expense of central inspection would seem to be too great in large organizations and in states where receiving stations are geographically scattered.

If inspection is to be thoroughgoing some means of testing should be provided. Laboratories for physical and chemical testing have been set up in many places. Probably the most effective testing organization in existence is the Bureau of Standards of the United States Department of Commerce. Where possible, requests for this service are referred to commercial and college laboratories. A directory of these latter agencies has been published by the Bureau. "To the selling price plus transportation must be added the cost of handling the goods at least twice-when put in storage and when issued; clerical and labor cost of stores accounting; rent or interest on storeroom building and equipment; interest on stock investment for storage period; and depreciation of goods through obsolescence." From this computation there can be reached a decision as to which items can be most economically stored and which procured through current delivery. The question of whether the articles will be currently available must, of course, enter into the determination. 

The point is that the storage of all things used by the government is not an end in itself. Some items should be stored and others should not. Price trends, availability for current delivery, and the cost of storage are the chief considerations in determining what should and should not be stored.

Even though the individual departments store their own goods, it is desirable to have some sort of control over these activities. The central control agency should be supplied periodically with inventories of stock on hand, as well as with statements of items received and issued. This tends to prevent loss and gives the purchasing office data necessary in making future purchases. Such reports also constitute a means of budget control by informing the budget agency how the departments are keeping within their allotments for supplies. Some storekeepers find perpetual inventory systems convenient, both for furnishing data for these reports and for maintaining their own control. 

The purchasing division should have at least advisory authority over methods of keeping records and methods and times of taking inventory. While central warehouses might be very expensive in certain given instances, the arguments seem to be largely in favor of keeping a central storehouse. It is claimed that costs are thereby reduced; easier and cheaper deliveries are secured;

the total investment in stock is less; storage space is provided for bulk purchases; and the delay inherent in special purchases is reduced. The territorial layout must inevitably have some relation to the number of storehouses. Central storage is found in only a small percentage of governments. The central stores should be very closely associated with the purchasing agent, preferably under his control. Physical inventories of stock on hand should be taken at least once a year.18

Storerooms supplying more than one organization unit should be operated on a revolving fund basis. The agency in charge of financial functions should have control of revolving funds. A revolving fund is established by making available to the storage agency a certain sum which represents a capital operating fund, from which supplies are purchased and paid for. 

When a department requisitions goods from stores, it must reimburse the revolving fund by a debit to its appropriations. 

Hence, each administrative unit is charged, for budget purposes, with every item it receives from storage. The cost of storage should be added to the purchase price in making the charge to the requisitioning department. Sometimes this is obtained by adding a flat 5 or 10 per cent. This method of adding the cost of storage to the purchase price is preferred to a direct budget appropriation for the support of the stores unit, because then the cost of storage is reflected where it belongs for accounting purposes.

Central control over both supplies and equipment prevents the spending of money for things which may be on hand unused in another department. Thus, the City of Los Angeles has recently provided for centralized control of equipment with this end in view. Interdepartmental transfers should be permissible at the discretion of the central control agency, and this control should be very closely associated with the purchasing department in order to prevent unnecessary purchases. Accounting control over purchases is greatly facilitated if the purchasing office is a part of the department of finance. One cardinal principle of financial administration, unattainable by those governments where only cash accounts are kept, is that no purchase should be made unless it is definitely known that funds are on hand for its payment. The purchase order should therefore be "pre-audited" by the finance office to find whether there is money for its payment in the appropriation accounts, whether the purchase has been legally authorized, and whether it fits into current plans of budget control. If the pre-audit covers only the requisition, the encumbrance on the appropriation ledgers will be only an estimate, thus necessitating an adjustment when the invoice comes in with the correct price. The preferred practice is to pre-audit the purchase order after it comes from the purchase office, but before it goes to the vendor, for it will usually contain the correct price. Forbes believes that invoices should be submitted directly to the purchasing office for examination and verification.20 They can then be forwarded to the accounting office with the knowledge that purchase and contract terms have been fulfilled. The department of finance should be permited to make immediate payment of invoices in order to take advantage of discounts. The practice, prevalent in many small cities, of having city councils approve all invoices before payment, answers no useful purpose and is conducive to delay and consequent loss of discounts.
