CHAPTER XVII TREASURY, BORROWING, AND ASSESSMENT The Treasurer 

The treasurer is the officer whose duty it is to collect, to have custody of and to disburse, the money of the government. His duties being largely routine and technical in nature, he should be appointive and subject to the administrative control of the governor, mayor, or manager. He might very well head a “bureau of the treasury" in the department of finance. State and city treasurers, however, are very largely elective. This should not be, because the duties of a treasurer are not of a policy-determining nature. While there are no statistics to prove such a contention, observation suggests that there are more cases of defalcation by elective than by appointive treasurers. This is largely because the elective treasurer is not under the administrative control of the chief administrative officer. As a result periodical checks are not made; administration becomes lax because the elective treasurer resists encroachment on his domain by the council or manager; and consequently those niceties of accounting practice which would soon reveal defalcation are not observed.

Oakey lists six methods by which a treasurer may default. 

The concealment of the theft of cash receipts may be attempted by omitting the record. Cash receipts may be taken with the intention to return them and make the record at that time. 

Bond interest coupons may be presented a second time for payment by the treasurer himself before being cancelled. Another way to steal is through the "theft of unissued bonds, the forging thereon of the signature required to complete, and the hypothecation of the sale thereof." Coupons may be stolen from bonds held in the treasury for safe-keeping and there may be collusion 344

Ch. 345 

with brokers in order to effect overpayment in settlements for bonds purchased.¹ There are many other ways of defalcation.

Custody of Funds 

Funds may be retained in cash in the government treasury, they may be deposited in banks, or certain special funds may be invested in specified securities retained in the custody of the treasurer. As an aftermath of the "wildcat" banking era, several states maintained the "independent treasury system" far into the twentieth century. Because of the fear of banks, the liquid resources of the government were kept in the form of cash in the treasury vaults.2 Practically all governmental areas today deposit their surplus monies, applicable to current liabilities, in banks. These are placed in two types of accounts, one active for checking purposes and the other inactive. The inactive accounts far outnumber the active accounts because they earn a higher rate of interest just as do savings accounts for individuals. 

Governments usually demand a favored position as bank depositors. They require some sort of assurance that their money will be paid whether the bank fails or not. This is one of the reasons why governments receive lower interest on bank deposits than individuals. There are, in general, three ways of trying to insure absolute safety for government deposits: personal surety; the deposit of collateral security bonds; and the furnishing of corporate surety bonds. By the first plan, supposedly responsible individuals are asked to sign instruments purporting to make them responsible for loss of government funds in a specified bank. Experience has demonstrated this to be the least satisfactory means of obtaining security, usually because such bonds are signed by officers of the depository. In case of failure, their assets are usually lost as well as those of the public. 

The second mode is used by the city as well as the county of Los Angeles. Banks are required to keep on deposit with the city 1 

¹ Francis Oakey, "Standards of Financial Administration," American 

City (May, 1928), Vol. XXXVIII, No. 5, pp. 161, 163. 

M. L. Faust, The Custody of State Funds (National Institute of Public 

Administration, New York, 1925), p. 6.

treasurer bonds in which they have their funds invested. The banks still own the bonds and receive the interest on them, the difference being that they are in the vaults of the government instead of the bank. If the bank should fail, this part of its resources would be segregated to pay the government deposits in full while the other depositors would have to take what was left. 

This type of security is satisfactory but difficult to administer. 

The most satisfactory is the corporate surety bond. The bank pays a premium to a surety corporation which guarantees to pay the government in case of loss. Supervision should be maintained so that irresponsible corporations are not permitted to assume surety liabilities in excess of their resources. 

It is quite uniformly agreed that all government funds should be promptly turned into the treasury. This should be done each day, where distance permits. Departments which collect revenues in connection with their normal operations should not retain and spend them even if such receipts have been appropriated for expenditure. They should be promptly turned into the treasury and disbursed only under the regular rules applying to budgetary control. It is not necessary to advance cash to departments to pay their obligations. These can be liquidated by pre-audited vouchers presented to the treasurer for payment. 

In some instances, it may be advisable to permit departments to have petty cash funds under treasury accounting control.

Governments should seek to place their surplus funds where they will earn adequate interest. If these monies will be needed for expenditure soon, banks are the most convenient depositories. If government deposits in banks are not protected by surety or collateral, as described above, the comparative safety of banks becomes a matter of concern. Under such conditions there was an element of danger in placing public funds through competitive bids. The post-war epidemic of bank failures has led, however, to the enactment of certain guarantees. State laws have required surety or collateral, while national legislation of 1933 has placed guarantees on deposits in general. Such being the case, there is no reason why governments should not select their depositories on the basis of competitive bids, the com-

Ch. 17] 347 

petition being based on the amount of interest the bidder is willing to pay. Court decisions formerly tended to support the doctrine that the treasurer was responsible for only the principal and was, therefore, free to pocket the interest himself. Today most governmental areas require interest to be paid on deposits and this interest is the property of the state, not the treasurer. 

It would seem desirable that funds should be distributed among depositories on the basis of their financial strength. After the depositories have been designated on this basis and supervision has been established to insure continued strength, it would seem that the best way to set the rate of interest is by competitive bidding among the banks themselves. Wherever this system of competitive bidding has been unsatisfactory, it has been so largely because the depositories have not been well chosen in the beginning, and because continued supervision has been lacking.* 

The proposed Waterbury charter provided that city deposits "shall be placed with the banks offering the highest rate of interest." 5 Regulation of banking under national laws of 1933 and 

1934 tends to require uniform interest rates on various classes of accounts, thus operating against competitive bidding. 

Treasurers are required by law to do many things which prevent the best husbanding of treasury resources. Frequently, a? statutory interest rate is much less than that which banks could afford to pay.

More often, they are required to maintain separate funds and cash balances for many purposes and borrow at high interest rates for certain funds when money is actually on hand in others. Reference has been made elsewhere to the evils of this special fund system.

It is frequently the practice to maintain the office of tax collector independent of the treasury. There is nothing to be gained by this, and positive harm may come from the resulting decentralization of authority and lack of administrative control. 

The treasurer should collect all monies due the government.

There may be considerations dictating that the persons who actually receive the money should be physically present in other departments for the convenience of taxpayers. In these cases, however, those who take the money should be under the jurisdiction of the treasurer. 

The treasurer must obviously have something tangible on which to issue payment. This is usually the "warrant" of the chief accounting officer. It indicates that the latter has thoroughly examined into the legality of the claim, that the obligation was lawfully and in fact incurred, that the goods or services were received, and that payment is now due. The treasurer will then honor the warrant either by paying it or by issuing an order on a bank for payment. Sometimes he will merely sign a form which will act as both warrant and check. 

It is sometimes necessary for the chief accounting officer to "cover" money into the treasury. Thus, in the federal government money which may be already collected and physically in the hands of the treasurer is not legally available for expenditure until the comptroller general has issued a "covering warrant" which has the effect of saying that "this amount of money has been legally collected and is now charged to the treasurer of the United States." In Great Britain, two Lords of the Treasury sign a requisition on the Exchequer which is addressed to the Comptroller and Auditor General. The latter issues the necessary credit, there being no actual transfer of funds. It should be noted here, however, that the Comptroller and Auditor General is an auditing and not an accounting officer. 

One of the advantages of having the treasury located in a department of finance is that current administrative auditing control can be maintained. In the past we have paid lip service to checks and balances and have failed to observe them in fact. 

This has largely been due to the fact that we have assumed that making financial officers elective and independent of each other would automatically provide checks and balances. While priding ourselves on our practicality as a people, we have here become highly impractical. It has been shown repeatedly that 

A. E. Buck and others, Municipal Finance (The Macmillan Co., 1926), p. 288.

Ch. 17] 349 

under an elective system a state or city treasurer can successfully resist that type of auditing control which either prevents defalcation or quickly uncovers it, and which accurately assesses the amounts due the government and sees that the treasurer is energetic in pursuing collection. 

The chief accounting officer should have constant and immediate auditing control over the treasury. He should maintain control accounts of monies accrued as due the city. These control accounts should tell him at a glance whether the treasurer's office is diligently carrying out its collection duties. Through current audits and controlled stationery, the accounting office should have a constant check on treasury transactions. By controlled stationery is meant serially numbered forms so arranged that the comptroller's office is furnished a copy of the original record of each transaction. For instance, some cases are known in southern California where elective city treasurers have defaulted by issuing receipts out of serial order. Suppose a taxpayer calls to pay a tax bill. The printer has recently delivered a number of receipt books numbered from 1 to 10,000, one hundred receipts in each book. The treasurer starts by using the books numbered from 1 to 100. One day he needs money for a payment on the family automobile, so he reaches down and gets the book numbered 9901 to 10,000. The taxpayer is issued a receipt numbered 9901. No record is made of it, and no copy is sent to the comptroller. The treasurer hopes to be able to enter it in its regular order when the time comes and reimburse the amount taken.

In the meantime the elective accounting officer, for political reasons, or because he is incompetent, fails to maintain any semblance of auditing control over the treasury. The treasurer uses the last receipt book to cover other defalcations. The independent auditor comes in once a year, but he has accepted the work at such a low bid that he can afford only a superficial audit. 

He probably gives the treasurer a clean bill of health. Some day the treasurer is unfortunate enough to use the irregular receipt book for a taxpayer who protests payment. The accounting office sees that the serial number is out of line with those in

FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION 

current use. Suspicions are aroused. Some "dummy” transactions establish the commission of overt acts by the treasurer and he is sent to the penitentiary. The type of auditing control whereby the controlled stationery would be issued by the comptroller to the treasurer, probably a book at a time, would have prevented this.

This illustration covers merely one aspect of auditing control. 

The comptroller should audit the depositories to see that they are furnishing the proper security, and that the legal maximum for each bank is not exceeded. Receipts from bond sales should be carefully checked, and it should be determined whether the treasurer is taking the necessary steps to protect the city's interests in delinquent tax collection. The comptroller should receive daily reports on treasury collections. A later administrative audit of amounts shown on stubs or original records will allow him to reconcile both of these with accruals and bank balances. 

Control of this general nature will accomplish two purposes: it will reduce defalcations to almost zero; and it will assure states and cities of thousands of dollars now rightfully due them, but which are not collected because of lack of that accounting control which knows what monies are due and takes vigorous steps to see that they are collected.

Investment of Permanent Funds 

Governments commonly have certain trust or endowment funds, the interest (and sometimes the principal) of which is to be spent over a long period of time. It has been quite a prevalent practice in states to leave the choosing of securities for such funds with ex-officio boards composed of the auditor, treasurer, and some other official. The practice of ex-officio boards has been quite generally condemned of late. There seems to be no good reason why these duties cannot be vested in the treasurer alone if the law adequately regulates the type of securities that may be bought. It is to be presumed that an appointive treas- "Note the ex-officio duties of the Missouri treasurer, as described by M. L.

A clear-cut law should also be provided which would permit the comptroller to check the adequacy of securities in the course of frequent administrative audits.

Debt Administration 

In the summer of 1933, $1,200,000,000 of principal and interest, of a total municipal indebtedness of $18,500,000,000, was in default. This situation is not especially new in American history. There was an epidemic of state defaults in the 

1840's. A number of southern states have refused to honor and pay obligations incurred just after the civil war, and a committee of foreign bond holders is still trying to collect about $75,- 000,000 in principal owed by eight American states. Inasmuch as a state cannot be sued without its own consent, there is apparently no legal way to collect. Several cities also defaulted on bonds during the period 1840-1850. Real estate booms and railroad-aid borrowing hastened further municipal defaults in the 1870's and 1880's, while the panic of 1893 brought a few The era from 1900 to 1929 marks a period of high municipal solvency with comparatively few municipal defaults. 

The worst period for cities, however, seems to be that in which we are living the era of general deflation after the World War. 

The history of a new era of default on municipal bonds is just being written. Beginning with failure to meet special assessment obligations in Washington from 1921 to 1926, we see whole groups of municipalities in the Winnipeg and Saskatchewan districts failing to meet their general bonded indebtedness obligations in 1923. In each case, the Canadian provincial government had to enter as dictator and administer the financial more.

In 1930, more than forty Florida cities, including Miami, St.

The real estate market collapsed after the boom of 1925. The inflation bubble broke, and taxes levied on excessive values could not be paid. Much damage was caused by hurricanes and the

Subsequent bank failures did not improve the situation.10 At least two American state legislatures, in 1931, passed acts authorizing the state to step in and administer as receiver cities which had defaulted or were about to default on their bonded debt. While general depression conditions are mainly responsible for this situation, many cities could have avoided default by utilizing good budgetary practice. With some notable exceptions which prove the rule, those in the worst debt chaos were those which defied the modern methods of fiscal practice set forth in these pages. 

Those cities taken over by state receiverships, especially, had been plagued with municipal mismanagement. 

What is done when a governmental agency does not pay its debts? The United States and the states cannot be sued without their own consent; hence recovery through the judicial process is not ordinarily possible." Municipalities can ordinarily be sued, so it is possible to obtain a judgment against them; but a judgment is of no avail if there is no money to satisfy it, or if the temper of the people is opposed to paying it. The history of default in the United States shows conclusively that it is useless to

The best way for creditors to secure a settlement is through conciliatory negotiations.12 Sometimes it would be wise to grant concessions involving the scaling down of interest and principal. The difficulty in effecting such an adjustment comes from the fact that a scaling of interest or principal requires the consent of 100 per cent of the bond holders. 

This consent can be obtained frequently from 80 to 90 per cent but seldom from all of the creditors. 

The federal bankruptcy law was amended to meet this situation on May 24, 1934. The measure applies to any municipality or other political subdivision of any state, any county, city, borough, village, parish, town, or township, unincorporated tax or special assessment district, and any school, drainage, irrigation, reclamation, levee, sewer, or paving, sanitary, port, improvement, or other districts. Such a governmental unit may file with a federal court a petition declaring its inability to pay its debts and ask for a readjustment. Such a petition must present a plan of readjustment approved by the holders of at least 30 per cent of the indebtedness in the case of all other districts. The court may confirm the readjustment plan, after examination, if agreed to by creditors holding two-thirds of the claims in each class and 75 per cent in all classes. Confirmation by the court makes the plan binding upon the governmental unit and all creditors.13

FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION Debt and Tax Limitations 

It is quite the general practice to provide in state constitutions, statutes, or charters that no city may incur a total bonded indebtedness in excess of a certain percentage of its assessed valuation. 

The bonds which will be retired from revenues other than taxation, such as public utility rates, are usually excluded from the limit. While limitations of this nature have undoubtedly had some effect in keeping down the debt, they constitute a purely negative means of control. They are arbitrary in nature and entirely unrelated to the economic condition of the community. 

It has been demonstrated that the debt limit can be circumvented in fact by erecting side by side, or one on top of the other, a number of new ad hoc governmental areas each of which has a tax limit of its own, independent of the city but with the same assessed property as the base. In so far as assessed valuation is not a true criterion of taxpaying ability, it cannot be the best basis for limitation. Nor has assessed valuation anything to do with the credit needs of the community.¹4 14 It has been a rather common assumption that expenditure for local government could be reduced automatically by limiting the levy on general property. To accomplish this objective, tax limitations have been placed in charters, statutes, and in state constitutions. In 1933 several states passed constitutional amendments imposing drastic limitations which would cut the revenues of local government by half or more. 

These provisions were usually passed in a frenzied and unreasoning spirit of protest against tax levies on real estate. 

At least half a century of experience with this type of tax limitation in a wide sampling of states shows rather conclusively that it will not bring a corresponding reduction in expenditure. In a large number of cases, it has only served to increase the debt burden. Local governments have continued to spend in excess of limited revenue. 

They have not always done this wilfully, nor have they been motivated by a spirit of irresponsible extravagance. The very 

14 Studenski, op. cit. pp. 50-62. Remarks on constitutional debt limitation in Capital Expenditure, p. 14, a publication of the United States Chamber of Commerce.

Ch. 17] 355 

people who vote for tax limitations demand a minimum standard of governmental services. The result is that local governing bodies find themselves unable to restrain administrative departments from spending in excess of revenues. Annual deficits are carried over from year to year. Carried temporarily in the form of bank borrowings or registered warrants, a friendly suit permits them eventually to be turned into judgment bonds without exciting notice. By failing to levy enough to take care of sinking fund obligations in their entirety, this practice can go on for years without increasing the tax levy for debt service to the protest point. Eventually, however, higher taxes must result. 

There is always a day of reckoning in borrowing for current expense. The authorities are overwhelmingly of the opinion that negative legal restrictions on the tax levy do not bring economy in government.15 They tend rather to increase debt. 

This does not mean that tax limitations constitute an absolute evil. There are undoubtedly many instances where a fair limit has acted as a moral deterrent. There is a certain minimum below which revenues must not fall to furnish desirable standards of service in any given governmental unit. If a tax limit is reasonably near that minimum, it may constitute a wholesome guidepost to expenditure. If it is below that minimum, however, expenditures will tend to exceed income in spite of legal provisions to the contrary. Ordinarily, relief will come through borrowing by means of subterfuges of which the community may or may not be aware. In other instances special ad hoc districts with their own special tax levies will absorb functions formerly belonging to the city. Sometimes assessed valuations will be increased; again, special concessions from the legislature will circumvent restrictions.

FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION 

The best and surest means of controlling both borrowing and the tax rate is the adoption of sound principles of budget administration. Public expenditure can be controlled, but not by negative means alone. Limitations and restrictions, if reasonable, may constitute valuable standards; but positive day-to-day management is needed to balance a fair budget. There are many sound and convincing arguments in favor of enlarging the expenditure of any given governmental department. There is only one way to resist the clamors of those who would spend more. That is through executive budgeting, with day-to-day expenditure in the control of responsible professional administrators. The latter must have the confidence and backing of the executive and governing body. As long as city councils and 'county boards retain day-by-day control of expenditure, so long will deficits continue. Cities operating through the depression with a professional manager have maintained, quite uniformly, a sound financial position. That is because the executive type of budget control, which accompanies council-manager administration, tends automatically to prevent deficits. 

It has been contended that state administrative control would check excessive local debt and expenditure, and the Indiana plan has been offered as a panacea. 

In that commonwealth, a state commission has the power to lower local budgets and lower or reject bond issues on the petition of a small number of taxpayers. It is purely a negative means of control which does not go to the heart of the problem. There may be no particular objection to it as an occasional remedy to prevent abuse, but it is no cure-all for tax difficulties. In some other states, a state agency has the power to prescribe accounting systems and fiscal procedure for local governments. In at least two notable instances, the state department has been so backward and conservative that progressive cities have found it necessary to break the law in order to adopt modern procedures.16 State administrative control may or may not be of value. No general rule will cover every situation. The system of appointment is so "politi- 

16 See remarks of Lent D. Upson and Luther Gulick, in Condensed Report of Proceedings, Conference on Research on the Problems of Metropolitan 

Areas (University of Chicago, November 26, 1933), pp. 34-35.

Ch. 357 

cal" in many states that the prospect of appointing desirable technicians is remote. The number of instances is not small where the administration of specific cities is far superior to that of the states in which they operate. Yet a competent state municipal bureau could be of inestimable value in pointing the way to improved municipal budget procedure.

Studenski opposes the authorization of bond issues by popular vote. "It leads to the decision of the question, whether bonds should be issued, by political manipulation or accident, rather than by consideration of what is sound financial policy." 17 

Bond elections habitually draw out light votes. A New York legislative committee found that in many cases only the "antis" voted, delaying necessary public works which had to be authorized at increased costs later. The better way would be to allow the governing body to decide on bond issues, permitting the voters to petition for a referendum on any particular issue. 

Bonds should be paid off as rapidly as possible. Studenski lists three criteria for fixing their terms. First, there should be taken into consideration the financial resources of the government; its probable future requirements, and the state of its debt. 

The status of the bond market is the second consideration. The third is that the economic conditions of the community and the trend of interest and prices must be heeded. It is wrong to assume that it is always desirable to issue bonds for the estimated life of the improvement; but they should not be for a term longer than that. Terms should be much shorter than at present-ten, fifteen, and twenty years are long enough in most cases.18 It is impossible and unnecessary to try to allocate accurately to each generation its share of the cost of the public works, the use of which it enjoys. 

Borrowing for current expenditure is justified only for two purposes. One is for temporary financing in anticipation of tax revenues later in the fiscal year. The other is for emergencies, unforeseeable at the time of the tax levy, or of such great magnitude as to make it inadvisable to finance them in a single fiscal The latter group includes welfare work made necessary p. 62. year. 

17 Studenski, op. cit., 18 Ibid., p. 96.

FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION 

by such catastrophes as earthquakes, tidal waves, drouths, famines, or excessive unemployment. All other borrowing should be for capital expenditures, that is, permanent improvements. 

It should not be assumed, however, that it is justifiable to borrow for all permanent improvements. 

Financing Public Improvements 

Not all permanent improvements are of an extraordinary nature. Many structures are merely replacing others which have become obsolete or unusable. Still others are of such a nature that new construction will continue at a steady rate over a considerable period of years. Where this is true, at least a considerable portion of the cost should be paid from current taxation. At first it is cheaper for the taxpayer to borrow, but as debt increases the point is rapidly approached where the tax cost of debt service equals, and sometimes exceeds, what would have been the annual cost of an all-tax program. In this case the taxpayer would be losing, because he is paying out in interest money which should have gone into improvements under an alltax program. As long as expenditures for permanent improvements continue to increase at a rapid rate, it is advisable to borrow. Such was the case in southern California during the decade 1920-1930. When these outlays again become normal, however, a tax and borrow policy is preferable. In some cases an all-tax or pay-as-you-go policy may be advisable.19 

One of the greatest evils of the all-borrow system in the past has been the tendency of city councils to evade principal payment because of the political hazard in raising the tax rate. 

Long-term bonds would be issued with no provision for paying the principal. At maturity they would be refunded, that is, paid off out of the proceeds of a new bond issue. In other cases, sinking funds for principal payment would be set up. Only enough taxes would be levied to pay a part of the principal. In still other cases, the sinking fund would be robbed by borrowing from it for other purposes and failing to repay. Practices of 

19 A comparison of pay-as-you-go with an all bond program is worked out mathematically in a publication of the United States Chamber of Commerce entitled Capital Outlays, p. 20.

Ch. 17] 359 

this kind, together with the creation of operating deficits to be paid with deficiency bond issues, have been tremendous factors in bringing about the need for municipal receiverships in many parts of the country. Borrowing has been easy and taxing unpopular. On the other hand, the demand for public improvements has been insatiable. The result has been a great deal of borrowing for projects which should have waited or else been completed from current taxes. The use of serial bonds with a compulsory tax levy for retirement is being widely adopted as a corrective for this situation. 

Under ordinary circumstances, it will probably be advisable to pursue a policy which will build permanent improvements from resources secured from both taxing and borrowing. This is known as the tax and borrow plan.20 It is based upon the premise that the public improvements built in any one year should be paid for by taxing up to an amount which represents the average expenditure for public improvements in past years. 

Expenditures in any one year above this average should be financed from borrowing. The "borrow" point for any one year is to be computed by adding the total and dividing by the number of years. This will give the average expenditure for public improvements in past years. For improvement expenditures in the current year below this average it is proper to tax; above it, to borrow.

The same computation would be repeated every year and a new "borrow" point procured. As public expenditures increase, the taxes would automatically increase and pressure on the government would tend to call a halt to construction. As improvement expenditure decreases, the tax rate would lower. It would be impossible for legislatures to authorize borrowing to take care of the obligations so incurred. The bond limit would be automatic and rational rather than legal, arbitrary, and irrele- The borrowing limits would be automatically regulated by the pressure of the tax rate on the community, because debts would have to be reflected in current taxes. They could not be put off for the next generation to pay. vant. 20 

Studenski, op. cit., pp. 127-128; Buck and others, op. cit., p. 473.

FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION 

Under this scheme, bonds would not be earmarked as belonging to specific improvements. They would be general improvement bonds issued for a term to be determined by the state of the debt. Maturities would be made to fit into the years not yet encumbered by other maturities. All bonds would be issued for short terms-ten to fifteen years. Transitions from present methods to such a plan should be made gradually, rather than by sudden change in a single year.

Term bonds are those where the entire issue is issued to run a definite number of years, the principal payment on all bonds being due on the same date. They are sometimes referred to as sinking fund bonds because provision is made to retire them by establishing a sinking fund. This is a special fund into which regular payments are to be made, so that with compound interest from the investments purchased there will be sufficient money on hand to retire the principal when due. Sinking funds are correct in theory. The difficulty has been that political officers have abused their administration. They have either feared to levy taxes to pay sufficient money into the sinking fund, or they have borrowed from it for pressing, immediate needs without later making reimbursement." In some cases they have even sold their own unprofitable investments to the sinking fund.

Serial bonds require that a definite amount of the principal be paid periodically, usually every six months, on July 1 and January 1. There is a tendency to enact legal provisions, as in 

Iowa, requiring governing bodies to levy a tax sufficient to retire all bonds due during the fiscal year. This has the effect of forcing immediate principal as well as interest payment, thus avoiding the situation wherein weak officials shunt the onus of tax levy off onto their successors. 

It is believed that serial bonds ordinarily are to be preferred over term bonds because of their greater ease of administration. 

Assuming that the sinking fund would earn at a rate equivalent to the interest on the bonds it is designed to redeem, there is little difference in cost in the long run between term and serial "For typical examples see remarks relative to Phoenix in Arizona Taxpayers' Magazine, August, 1930, p. 5; also situation in Kansas City, Mo., in 

Kansas City's Public Affairs, No. 445, March 12, 1931.

bonds. Past experience with sinking funds, however, seems to point toward the superiority of serial bonds purely on administrative grounds.

Assessment for Taxation 

If there is one administrative activity that has been an almost uniform failure, it is the assessment of property under the general property tax. Where county taxes are imposed on bases set separately by city and township assessors without careful equalization, the county rate has been inequitably spread because each assessor has a different conception of true value. Local assessors have vied with each other for lower valuations so as to shunt state and county levies off on to their neighbors. Sometimes the opposite has appeared because of the necessity of raising valuations to expand the bond limits and create needed revenue under a limited tax rate. Politically-minded boards of equalization have even been known to sell revaluations to individual taxpayers. The inequalities resulting from political assessment are really at the bottom of Chicago's financial difficulties which began in 1928. The courts refused to permit a tax levy on the existing inequitable valuations. It took about two years to make the new assessment, during which time the city had to get money wherever it could. The taxes for three years were eventually levied simultaneously at the nadir of an industrial depression. The result was abnormal tax delinquency.22

Assessment in the United States is quite generally in the hands of either elective assessors, or boards quite closely connected with the political life of the community. There is slowly taking place a demand for the removal of the assessor from politics. This is taking the form of setting up the county as the unit of assessment, under the administrative control of a state tax commission or other state agency. There is no reason why the assessor should not be chosen on the merit basis, with indefinite tenure, other than the fact that many politically influential 

H. D. Simpson, Tax Racket and Tax Reform in Chicago (Institute for 

Economic Research, Chicago, 1930), pp. 3-119.

FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION 

people do not want fair assessment. They prefer to perpetuate inequality which redounds to their benefit. 

One can enter practically any state of the Union and find the property of different cities, townships, and counties assessed at different percentages of true value. Within a given city or township, the tendency will be to assess small parcels at greater percentages of true value than large parcels. This practice of assessing at a percentage of true value has its basis largely in a competitive effort to shift the tax burden from one tax-levying unit to another. Thus, if City A assesses at 40% of true value and City B in the same county at 60%, City A will be bearing a smaller share of the county and state property tax than City B. 

An elective assessor will sometimes curry community favor in this manner to secure re-election. Under such conditions, a system of scientific assessment cannot exist. 

The logical remedy is to assess all property, especially real estate, at true cash value. The definition of the taxable value of any piece of property has been stated by Philip H. Cornick as the "probable price at which it would have been sold, had it been sold, on the taxing date at a sale between a willing buyer able but not compelled to buy, and a willing seller able but not compelled to sell, if both buyer and seller had been fully conversant with the property and with current public opinion concerning prices in general." 23 The determination of such a price. is more easily described than arrived at. Assessors could come very close to it, however, if they were permitted by law and politics to do so.

California municipalities have the option of doing their own assessing or contracting with the county to do it for them. The latter procedure obviates a double operation because the county must do its assessing whether the city does or not. Counties are willing to do this work at a cost to the city which is usually an infinitesimal fraction of the cost of separate assessment. The writer was once asked by a board of freeholders whether the charter they were framing should require county assessment. 

On examination it was found that the prevailing county assessment was about one-third lower than that of the city. With a 

23 Buck and others, op. cit., p. 313.

Ch. 17] 363 

limited tax levy which had reached the maximum in practice, this would cut off about a third of the city's revenue. From the taxpayer's immediate standpoint this would have been desirable, but from that of the general welfare of the city it would have been disastrous. 

In another city, the people had voted for expensive public improvements without providing for the revenue to finance bond retirement or increased costs of upkeep. The only alternative was to create new revenue by the city itself, making a reassessment of property. The conclusion would seem to be that it is much cheaper, from the standpoint of administrative expense, to have the county set the municipal tax base. This advantage may be more than offset, however, by requiring a city with a limited tax levy to accept a county base which will not provide revenue sufficient to maintain municipal services at a fair standard of efficiency. It is much better to give the city council the option of determining whether it will provide for its own assessing work or contract with the county for such services. 

Inasmuch as the technique used in the assessment of land differs from that employed in the valuation of buildings, it is an axiom of good assessment procedure that land and buildings should be assessed separately.24

Maps in Assessor's Office 

One of the best assurances of fair assessment is full publicity of assessment operations. The assessor's office should contain two sets of maps available for the inspection of the taxpayer. 

One should show the unit-front-foot value of the land frontages of every block in the city. They need not be drawn exactly to scale, but should allow the citizen to locate at a glance his block and the value placed upon property in it. 

With very little calculation the total of any land assessment of any parcel of property can be determined and checked against the actual assessment as appearing on the assessment rolls, and be compared with any other property desired. The publication of such land value maps is always highly desirable, 24 L. D. Upson and C. E. Rightor, "Standards of Financial Administra tion," National Municipal Review (February, 1928), Vol. XVII, No. 2, pp.

119-132, 123.

FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION 

since it stimulates a widespread interest in the land values determined upon by the assessing authorities.20 

In addition to these tax value maps there should be a set of tax maps giving the exact dimensions of every parcel of property within the city. This will enable the taxpayer to get the dimensions of his property from one detailed map drawn to scale, and then turn to the value maps to find the unit-front-foot value for the block on which it fronts. Knowing the depth rule or scale in effect in his city, and the adjustments made for such items as corner influences, he can figure the valuation of his property and compare it with the valuation of the property of others whom he might suspect as being favored at his expense.26 

Scientific Assessment of Land and Buildings 

Administrators in several of the large cities of the United States have worked out a scientific approach to the assessment of urban real estate which, while it may differ in its details from city to city, is nevertheless based on principles which are uniformly applicable in all cities. The first element is the selection of a unit of value. This is a piece of property one foot wide facing on the street in the middle of the block and running to the depth of the normal lot. Appraisers and assessors set the value on this unit. It is the only time that judgment enters into the value of a parcel of land. After the unit value is once set, the assessment of a parcel of property in that block is figured from it by the use of precise mechanical rules. 

These rules are based primarily upon the assumption that land near the street is more valuable than that in the rear. Thus, each city works out what is known as a depth rule, setting a definite percentage of decrease in value as the rear is approached. 

For the sake of illustration, let us set an arbitrary depth rule known as "4, 3, 2, 1." This would mean that where there is a depth of 100 feet, the first quarter depth or 25 feet has 40 per cent of the value, the second 30 per cent, the third 20 per cent, and the fourth 10 per cent. Let us suppose a unit value of $1,000 and a center lot with 25 foot frontage and 75 feet deep. The 

25 Upson and Rightor, op. cit., pp. 123-124. 

Ibid., p. 124.

Ch. 17] 365 

unit value would be that of a lot 75 per cent of normal depth. 

We add 40, 30, and 20 to find that such a lot would have 90 per cent of the value of one with a normal depth. This would be $900 per unit foot. Twenty-five multiplied by 900 would give us $22,500, the assessed value of the lot.27

The above illustration assumes a square or rectangular lot in the middle of the block. If the lot were near the corner, additional computations are necessary. Mathematical rules are devised to ascertain corner influence, that is, the additional value of property arising from its proximity to the corner. There is less agreement among authorities and greater variation from city to city in the practice of setting corner values. Nevertheless, many cities use a scientific approach to the problem which gives equitable assessment when uniformly applied.28 Workable rules can also take the place of rule of thumb for determining the value of irregularly shaped lots, those not rectangular in shape. 

It seems to be much more difficult to devise a scientific approach to the assessment of buildings than to land. That is one reason why there is greater similarity between cities in the assessment of land than of buildings. However, there is a way to reduce "rule of thumb" to a minimum. That is by dividing buildings into appropriate classes and establishing relatively uniform norms of valuation for each class. Having allocated a building into a particular class, a cubic or square foot factor can be applied to determine its value. 

In the assessment of buildings, some cognizance must be taken of depreciation. Structural depreciation is the loss in value resulting from wearing out. It is relatively easy to determine, and rules and tables can be applied to each class of buildings with a fair degree of accuracy. Economic depreciation is more difficult to ascertain. This includes decreasing usefulness because the structure has been outgrown, because the trade has moved away from it, or because it is not adapted to the installation of new developments in technology. Economic depreciation might exist in a building which is structurally sound. It is probably a greater factor in modern urban valuation than structural depre- "For a table showing different depth rules, see Buck and others, op. cit., P. 348. pp. 356-363.

PART IV ADMINISTRATIVE LAW

CHAPTER XVIII  

The phenomenal growth of industry in the United States since the last quarter of the nineteenth century, the accompanying increase of population with concentration in the metropolitan areas of the nation, and the revolutionary improvements in transportation have brought about many changes in the administrative machinery of government. The change from an individualistic political philosophy to a social consciousness, and the need for social and industrial legislation and public control, have manifested themselves in the recent governmental development and progress. 

The response of government to the needs of our modern society is reflected in the creation of the many administrative tribunals for the regulation of health and morals, the professions, industry, immigration, and other such activities which are peculiar to a populous and wealthy country. These administrative agencies, possessing limited judicial and ordinance-making powers, are promulgating rules, regulations, and orders which have not been enacted by the legislatures, and are rendering adjudications not in their entirety subject to judicial control or review by courts of law. The relation of these administrative tribunals and their powers to our system of law and courts, constitutes what is referred to as Administrative Law.¹

The administrative law of today deals with all legal phases of the administrative aspects of government. It is as broad as

Proposal," Iowa Law Review (January, 1933), Vol. XVIII, No. 2, pp. 233240; F. J. Goodnow, Principles of the Administrative Law of the United 

States (G. P. Putnam's Sons, 1905), Ch. I; Felix Frankfurter's General Introduction to E. H. Patterson, The Insurance Commissioner in the United 

States (Harvard University Press, 1927), pp. xi-xviii.

administration itself, which therefore means that its ambit and outlook are widening each day. The administrative law is concerned with the organization of public offices; the powers, duties, functions, and status of public officers and employees; and the relation of public employees and private citizens to the government. It deals also with the provision for remedies against illegal governmental acts, including judicial review and control; the granting of powers to the administration, and the methods of enforcement of the laws. 

Until very recently, Anglo-American jurisprudence has refused to recognize the existence of administrative law as such. 

It had developed as a separate system of jurisprudence on the Continent, especially in France, but was regarded by the British lawyer and jurist as a development alien to common law traditions. Administration in the common law was, and still is in its statutory counterpart, a branch of private law dealing with the settlement of estates. As a term dealing with a branch of public law, administrative law has found its way into the cases very gradually in recent years. Not that we have lacked any administrative law; it has always existed, but not as a distinct and separate entity. When the dean of a law school was recently asked why he did not offer a course in administrative law, he replied that it was hardly necessary when the student could secure an adequate knowledge of the subject in such existing courses as constitutional law, public utilities, and taxation. 

A misunderstanding of the French droit administratif has led Anglo-American lawyers and jurists to resist efforts and tendencies to establish a separate branch of administrative jurisprudence. Dicey is largely responsible for this antagonism because of a comparison of English jurisprudence and French administrative law in his Law of the Constitution, which went through many editions and had a profound influence upon Anglo-American legal thought. Dicey said that the French droit administratif is repugnant to English ideals which demand that all Englishmen be subject to the same law administered by 3

the ordinary courts. Englishmen who were civil servants were subject to this law as well as those engaged in private enterprise. 

In France, Dicey said, there are separate courts independent of the ordinary courts, administering a separate body of law applying to the state and its servants only. This was said to be repugnant to English ideals because it gave the officer a privileged position. It was also stated that administrative law as such did not exist in England.* As a matter of fact, administrative law does exist both in England and the United States. To be sure, the sharp line of demarcation developed in France has not yet taken place, but in both countries adjudication has been transferred to administrative bodies and officers to such an extent as to cause jurists steeped in the traditions of the common law to cry out in despair." 

The rapid development of administrative law in the United States and England in recent years will form the subject matter of the next few chapters. 

Why the Recent Interest? 

A major contribution of the twentieth century to government is the immense expansion of the discretionary power of administrative authorities over persons and property. This growth of administrative determination has been largely inevitable; in many instances it has come whether we liked it or not. It has been accepted grudgingly and with mental reservations. The 

Interstate Commerce Commission achieved its present status through a period of forty years of gradual accretion of determinative authority. The Federal Trade Commission came into existence as the result of the failure of judicial and legislative control to achieve its purpose under the Sherman Act. The industrial revolution had so changed conditions in this country that our traditional governmental machinery no longer functioned efficiently. In 1824, the City of Detroit engaged in 'See Frankfurter's General Introduction to Patterson, op. cit., pp. xi-xviii.

Astounding as this may seem, it is fair to reason therefrom that a similar expansion of governmental activities has taken place in all governmental areas from the federal on down. The indispensable concomitant of this expansion of governmental functions has been an ever-increasing delegation of administrative discretion and determination.

In both Great Britain and the United States, during the first half of the nineteenth century, individuals and businesses were regulated by what is known as legislative control. The legislature would pass general laws setting forth what was proper conduct. These laws were largely self-operating in the sense that no particular executive agency was set up to administer them. To be sure, the regular peace officers were supposed to take the necessary steps in case of a breach of law, but this was largely a negative procedure. Conduct as outlined in the law was relatively well known by probable offenders; life was agrarian and comparatively simple; individuals were not nearly so interdependent as today. The result was that this type of legislative control largely sufficed under nineteenth century modes of life. Today the machine age and metropolitan mode of living are swinging the pendulum toward administrative regulation." 

Those who were injured in person or property by public officers under the old system of legislative control had the right to apply to the courts for redress. This frequently led to actual control by the courts. For instance, the method of dealing with public utility regulation up until twenty-five years ago combined elements of both legislative and judicial control. The city would issue a franchise under regulations laid down by state law. So far the control was legislative. The company would apply to the courts for interpretations of the law and franchise on disputed points. Thus control became judicial.

An example of the change that has taken place is illustrated by the rise of the industrial accident commissions. In the beginning, the employer's liability for injuries was determined by certain common-law doctrines enforceable in the courts. Today employers in many states are required to carry insurance on employees, and questions giving rise to disagreement relative to the liability of the insurance company are determined before industrial accident commissions. 

Many persons whose opinion should be taken seriously, fear that this growth of administrative determination will impair the Anglo-American doctrine of the "supremacy of the law." 

Lord Hewart, citing Dicey, has described the rule of law as, "first, that in England no man can be punished, or can be lawfully made to suffer either in his body or in his goods, except for a distinct breach of law established in the ordinary manner before the ordinary Courts. It means, secondly, that in this country not only is no man above the law, but every man, whatever his rank or condition may be, is subject to the ordinary law of the land and the jurisdiction of the ordinary Courts. 

And, finally, it means that the general principles of our Constitution are mainly the result of judicial decisions determining the rights of private persons in particular cases brought before the Courts." 10 11 The Anglo-American jurisprudence to a certain extent has regarded law as opposed to government. The courts have been looked upon as relief stations to which the citizen might resort when his rights have been invaded by the acts of the government. The citizen has been taught to regard government as a necessary evil the less of it the better. The growth of bureaucracy was to be viewed with apprehension and alarm. Laissez Faire and the Common Law 

The common law inherited by the United States was intensely individualistic in spirit. It came to us when economic individualism was achieving its greatest vogue. Adam Smith's The 

Wealth of Nations had been published just long enough to have its effect on English law. Mercantilism with its regulative doctrines was superseded by the dogma that the utmost good to all must result from allowing individuals unrestrained freedom in their efforts to make a living. This resulted in the placing of too much legal emphasis on the rights of property as opposed to the general welfare. This extreme individualism may have caused no particular difficulties in the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries. The increased interdependence of people in the machine age, however, has necessitated a retreat from extreme individualism to one of increasing governmental regulation. 

This regulation has permeated into almost every human activity.

From a contemporary American teacher of law we learn that the change came because competition "did not achieve the results expected of it. Governmental interference through the agency of the legislature, court and executive was often little more than an aggravation. . . . Necessity called for a more vigorous exertion of power; this led to a reconsideration of the lodgment of power. . . . Leaving the old organization intact, we have withdrawn from the operation of the traditional machinery certain subject matters and have committed those subjects to the regulation of new agencies." A British student and lawyer explains it by the fact that "there has arisen a need for a technique of adjudication better fitted to respond to the social requirements of the time than the elaborate and costly system of enforcement provided by litigation in the courts of law." 

12 Ibid., pp. 32-33. 

13 Howard L. Bevis, “Administrative Commissions and the Administration of Justice," University of Cincinnati Law Review (January, 1928), Vol. II, No. 1, pp. 17-18.

Ch. 18] 377 

There is no doubt, furthermore, "that the revival of administrative law in England is very largely due to the creation of new types of offenses against the community, the growth of a new conception of social rights, an enhanced solicitude for the common good, and a lessening of that belief in the divinity of extreme individualistic rights which was evinced in the early nineteenth century.' 9914 The legal process involved in this increase of governmental regulation has usually taken the form of the expansion of the police power. Courts and jurists have insisted that it is not possible to define precisely the police power. In general, it is the power of the states to legislate in the interests of the public safety, public morals, public health, and public welfare. The federal government has no police power as such, but it accomplishes the same purpose by enacting regulative legislation under the commerce, postal, and taxing powers. The exercise of the police power has meant the restriction of the authority of individuals and the subjection of their property and persons to restrictions which are deemed to be in the interests of society as a whole. The use of this power is constantly expanding, generally in proportion to the degree to which the public is willing to allow it to grow. For instance, the courts have been willing for some years to permit restrictions on the use of property through zoning. They have supported restrictions on billboards because they impeded public safety and morals, not because they lacked beauty. It is entirely possible, however, that in a few years the concept of the police power will have expanded to permit restrictions on private property purely in the interests of aesthetic considerations. The law of an agrarian society steeped in the philosophy of economic individualism is being adjusted to the needs of the machine age by expansion of the police power.

Mere legislation has not been sufficient to meet the needs of modern society, however. Legislators have neither the time nor the technical training to foresee and provide the details of carrying into effect the day-by-day operation of government. 

Even though they were highly proficient in the technical fields, 14 Robson, op. cit., pp. 32-33.

the processes of application do not lend themselves to regimentation into well-defined paths and grooves. In other words, administration is a human process which requires judgment and flexibility for application in its details to concrete situations. Hence, the inevitable result of the expansion of the police power has been the necessity of delegating discretionary authority to administrative officers, boards, and commissions. 

We have passed from a period of regulation of individual discretion by law to positive prevention by administrative officers. Instead of the law saying that things shall be so-and-so, there is set up administrative machinery to make them so-and-so. More and more are we drifting under an evergrowing police power toward a government which finds it advisable and necessary to place determinative authority in the hands of trained technicians located in the administrative branch." 15 Two examples of this expansion of administrative power should suffice to illustrate the prevailing tendency. While the old common law recognized the liability of an employer for injuries traceable to his own negligence, the worker was without relief in about seven-eighths of the work-injury cases.16 Under one rule the employer's liability was dissolved because the worker voluntarily assumed known risks; under another there was no liability if the employee had contributed to the injury. through his own negligence; and again, the master escaped liability if it could be proved that a fellow servant had by his carelessness contributed to the injury. Furthermore, to secure redress the worker would have to bring suit in the courts. 

This may have worked without serious injustice in a handicraft, industrial age. In the day of electrical cranes, huge flywheels, belts, conveyors, speed elevators, and thousands of other mechanical devices, it is not easy to locate responsibility for accidents. Society has, therefore, decided that industry shall bear the costs of industrial accidents. Legislation has been

Instead of a recession of the movement, the public is demanding more and more administrative regulation. Abuses develop; the interdependence of mankind in the machine age makes them more acute than ever. The widow whose insurance was dissipated by bad company loans cannot so easily go to live with brother John today, because under urban living conditions an additional person in the home is a burden on income. The Question of Delegation 

With the expansion of administration came the necessity of delegating discretionary powers to administrative officers. Here constitutional barriers were encountered. It became necessary for officials to exercise certain powers which were legislative and judicial in nature. Under a strict interpretation of the separation of powers theory embodied in American constitutions, it was not possible for an executive officer to exercise either legislative or judicial power. We had inherited this concept from the French philosopher, Montesquieu, who derived it from an erroneous understanding of the principles underlying the British government. Desiring to discover the reason for the comparative freedom of the English people, he went to the governmental structure, where he found both courts and parliament acting with a considerable degree of independence from the monarch. It was practically the only country of the world with an independent judiciary at that time. Montesquieu exaggerated the independence of the departments, however. A more intimate understanding will show that the "See comments of Justice Rosenberry of the Supreme Court of Wisconsin as to the inevitability of the growth of administrative tribunals, in “Administrative Law and the Constitution," American Political Science Review (Febru ary, 1929), Vol. XXIII, No. 1, pp. 32, 35; also his opinion in State v. Whitman, 196 Wis. 472, 220 N. W. 935 ff. (1928).

Ch. 18] 381 

executive runs parliament through ministerial responsibility, that parliament can change the common law built up by judicial interpretation at will, and that judicial and administrative authority have been confused in practice at least as far back as the beginning of equity.21

The difficulty in the United States has largely arisen from the fact that the separation of powers was embodied in our constitutions, whereas elsewhere it was merely a political philosophy. 

Thus, the constitution of California provides as follows: 

The powers of the government of the State of California shall be divided into three separate departments-the legislative, executive and judicial; and no person charged with the exercise of powers properly belonging to one of these departments shall exercise any functions appertaining to either of the others, except as in this constitution expressly directed or permitted.22

The injunction that no one of the three departments of government should perform any of the functions belonging to another necessitated a definition of legislative, executive, and judicial powers. The constitutions fail to throw light on this matter, so it was necessary to look to the decisions of the courts in any particular state for guidance. There are, however, a few generally recognized principles. In the first place, each department must be completely free from the control and influence of the other. Secondly, the separation of powers principle does not apply to local government. Thirdly, each department may exercise the powers necessary to its independence; for instance, judges may appoint inferior employees of the court. 

Lastly, the legislature may delegate legislative and judicial powers to local authorities. 23

It was recognized at a very early date that no scientific classification of legislative, executive, and judicial functions or duties could be made in practice. "For a criticism of Montesquieu, see Goodnow, Principles, p. 25; Robson, op. cit., Ch. I.

They are overlapping, and of necessity must be so. An executive officer must, in the performance of his statutory duties, construe and apply the law. When courts reach out and by means of a receiver operate a great system of railways, they are performing administrative and executive duties which have historically found their way into the judicial department.24 

At the end of the nineteenth century and the beginning of the twentieth, there developed a rapid acceleration of delegating legislative and judicial powers to executive commissions and officers-now coming to be known as administrative tribunals and officers. How did the courts justify this delegation in view of its apparent prohibition under the separation of powers theory? The law simply developed a subterfuge or legal fiction. 

When a public utility commission is exercising judicial power it is not exercising judicial power; it is acting in a “quasijudicial" capacity. When the Interstate Commerce Commission issues a rate schedule compulsory on a group of carriers, its action is "quasi-legislative," not legislative. 

The situation demonstrates how a more or less firmly imbedded and rigid rule of law can be modified to meet changing social needs. Administrative agencies could not exercise judicial and legislative powers, but changing social conditions made it seem imperative that they do so. Hence, it was decided that the judicial activities connected with the executive branch of government were not truly judicial, but merely "judicial in nature." By calling them quasi-judicial, juridical erudition could be appeased; the revered dogma of the separation of powers could be rendered lip service; and the needs of adapting the law to social progress could be met. Thus, quasi-judicial and quasi-legislative powers are merely the administrative exercise of judicial and legislative functions under a modified name in order to evade legal prohibitions. 

Thus, the tremendous growth of administrative discretion. in the last few years has come as a practical necessity in spite of the fact that the law seemed to forbid it. Courts gradually saw the need for it and developed subterfuges to circumvent the

letter of the law. "Courts have recognized the situation and under one pretext or another have upheld laws in recent years that undeniably would have been held unconstitutional under conditions which existed prior to the Civil War." 25 Administrative law has been to American jurisprudence an unwanted stepchild, resisted at first but gradually tolerated as an unavoidable nuisance. To many students and jurists this is regarded as regrettable because a "refusal to recognize the facts as they exist and to give administrative law its rightful place in our legal theory has prevented a logical and symmetrical development of that law." 26

It is encouraging to note that both the bar and legal profession are taking a wholesome interest in administrative law. 

There is even an inclination to justify the delegation of legislative and judicial power on grounds other than subterfuge. A most auspicious turn of the judicial barometer recently came from the pen of Justice Rosenberry of the Supreme Court of Wisconsin in State v. Whitman. The state insurance commissioner had been given wide discretionary authority to approve or reject provisions in standard insurance policies. The constitutionality of this delegation was at issue. The court was of the opinion that the time had arrived for the frank recognition of the fact that certain types of legislative power had been legally delegated for many years. If the power which was delegated was exercised by the legislature itself it would be called legislative power. Why call it otherwise when exercised by an administrative agency? law, to fix the limits within which the law shall operate—is a power which is vested by our Constitution in the Legislature and may not be delegated. When, however, the Legislature has laid down these fundamentals of a law, it may delegate to administrative agencies the authority to exercise such legislative power as is necessary to carry into effect the general legislative purpose.27

What Powers May be Delegated 

Any delegation of power would be unconstitutional if the separation of powers doctrine were strictly construed. However, an absolute separation of powers was not intended. The power to make a law, and the conferring of an authority and discretion as to its execution, which authority is to be exercised under and in pursuance of the law, mark the distinction between powers which the legislature can delegate and those which it cannot delegate.28 The delegation of quasi-legislative powers will be sustained where the legislature has laid down so far as is practicable the limits within which such powers are to be exercised in accordance with a primary standard as prescribed by statute. 

Congress cannot delegate "the power to make the law, which necessarily involves discretion as to what it shall be," but "the authority or discretion as to its execution to be exercised under and in pursuance of the law" can be delegated.29 A state law creating a registration board of physicians which empowered the board to say what physicians were duly and legally registered, and to forbid the practice of the profession to those not duly registered, was a legal and reasonable delegation of power." 30 The requirements of the state legislature that no milk shall be received for sale or delivery to a city without a permit from an administrative tribunal and subject to the conditions of such

The turning point of British jurisprudence relative to the delegation of judicial and legislative powers to the ministries, centers around the Arlidge case (1915). There it was decided that judicial power could be delegated to an administrative officer or agency, and that such an agency could exercise this power in accordance with rules of its own making which need not be in accord with common-law principles." As a matter of fact, administrative determination is probably far more intrenched in Great Britain than in America because Parliament has the power to insulate administrative decisions against judicial interference, as has been done in some cases. CHAPTER XIX ADMINISTRATIVE ADJUDICATION 

In recent years, a host of administrative tribunals have been created and endowed with the power to settle disputes and make determinations on matters arising between individuals, or between individuals and corporations, or between either and the government. These tribunals have been given a jurisdiction in the first instance sufficiently extensive to create a vast field of adjudication outside the realm of the ordinary courts of first instance. Thus, the work accident indemnity commissions hear disputes arising under workmen's compensation; the Interstate 

Commerce Commission holds hearings on a representation from Los Angeles shippers that the San Francisco rate to Chicago on citrus fruit is discriminatory; the public utility commission holds a judicial hearing on a complaint from a city that a company has violated its franchise. The citizen who claims over-assessment on his income tax presents his case to the board of tax appeals; and the radio station owner whose license is in peril must justify his leave to continue broadcasting by presenting evidence before the Federal Communications Commission. 

This constitutes but a partial glimpse of the rapidly expanding field of administrative adjudication.

It is frequently difficult to say that an officer or tribunal is acting either judicially, legislatively, or administratively. In rate cases the deliberation takes the form of a controversy between two parties. A complaint is filed and an answer returned. 

Then there is the taking of evidence with counsel and witnesses in attendance. So far the proceedings have been strongly judicial in nature; yet the promulgation of the resulting rate is legislative if it has a continuing effect on all shippers. An insurance commissioner may seem to be issuing a mere administrative order when he requires an examination of an insurance 388

Ch. 19] 389 

ADMINISTRATIVE ADJUDICATION 

company, or when he suspends its license; yet he may be taking preventive measures essentially similar to the rôle of a court of equity in injunction and receivership matters. Practically all boards or officers having judicial power also have the authority to issue rules and regulations which are legislative in nature. 

The point is that these powers seem to complement each other. 

Occasionally they blend so that distinction is difficult. This occasions no particular hardship in actual administrative practice, but it does give opportunity for obstructive litigation to those who are averse to expanding administrative powers in particular fields.

Jurisdiction and Parties 

The jurisdiction of an administrative officer or tribunal is usually specified in the statute or constitutional provision which gives it life. It is common for jurisdiction to be acquired by the filing of complaints, which in a way take the place of pleadings in the ordinary courts. Such complaints may be generally filed by interested members of the public, or by associations and organizations. It is sometimes provided that complaints before public utility commissions be filed either by a public authority, such as a city council, or by a certain minimum number of consumers. In California the number is twenty-five.¹ Frequently, distinction is made between formal and informal complaints. 

Examples of informal complaints are furnished by those instances where a public utility commission acts as a friendly and impartial intermediary between a utility and its patrons. 

They may be based upon disputed bills, service extensions, or claims of faulty meters. A mere letter or oral complaint can start the proceedings.2

For some classes of cases more formal complaints are required. For instance, before the California Railroad Commission complaints involving the reasonableness of rates must be 1

Probably one of the chief distinctions between a court of law and an administrative tribunal is that the latter can take jurisdiction of its own volition. Judges cannot go out and seize jurisdiction. A judicial action must be a lis inter partes, that is, there must be a plaintiff who comes before the court and makes a complaint; and the party to whom the order of the judge may prove detrimental must have the right to oppose. A state railroad commission, on the other hand, may initiate as much as 80 per cent of its own cases. In the Federal Trade Commission practice, the complaint itself is the first step in the legal proceeding. All complaints are orders of the commission, making certain charges and setting a date for a hearing thereon. 

Prior to issuing the complaint, however, the Commission has made an investigation sufficiently thorough to give it reason to believe that a violation of the law has been committed. In other words, it issues both the indictment and judgment, and it takes jurisdiction on its own initiative. In these respects, adminis-

Public a Party 

999 The development of administrative adjudication is, to a large extent, a recognition of the public interest in cases which were formerly considered to concern only two parties litigant. The new theories of social justice have demanded that they be taken from the realm of individual litigation and handled in a manner in which the interests of the community can be asserted. The informal complaint, referred to above, affords the opportunity for individuals residing in remote regions to bring alleged abuses and irregularities to the notice of the public utility commissions. 

It has been stated that at least one such body "will pay just as much attention to a complaint written on a postal card as to one drafted in the most formal and painstaking manner.' It is the importance of the complaint which counts, not its form. 

This recognition of the public's interest is further evidenced by the frequent existence of a privilege whereby any interested person may appear at an administrative hearing and bring forth such testimony as he may desire.10 Furthermore, administrative tribunals can take jurisdiction of their own volition. This is done to enable them to protect the public's interest where abuses are occurring, but where no complaint has been filed. "It was, indeed, the failure of the judicature to endow the general public with an enforceable interest in matters where a regard for the social good is of the first moment that led to the devel opment" of administrative tribunals." The Federal Trade 

Commission can issue a complaint only when a public interest exists.12

At any rate the rules do actually vary from function to function and commission to commission.
