A special effort is made to avoid the dilatory tactics of attorneys by eliminating demurrers and motions to strike. At the inception of the California Railroad Commission, its proposed rules were presented to the attorneys of the state for comment. The absence of the customary dilatory processes raised a storm of protest from certain members of the bar.¹4 The rules were adopted, nevertheless; and it is said that these same protesting lawyers are now their most ardent champions.15

Where the administrative exercise of power is clearly judicial in nature, the requirements of due process of law would seem to demand notice and hearing. While due process as applied to administrative tribunals does not require the formality of courts of law, it does demand that there be opportunity "to be present during the taking of testimony, to know the nature and contents of all testimony, and to present all relevant evidence and contentions." 16 In other words, the party against whom an administrative order or complaint is directed must have his day in court, even though that court be purely administrative in nature." In some cases, commissions have to handle thousands of cases a year. It would be obviously impossible for the whole commission to sit en banc at individual hearings for each case. 

This situation is commonly taken care of by the appointment of examiners or referees who are delegated to hold hearings and take evidence for the commission. The common method of hearing before the Interstate Commerce Commission is to assign an examiner to go to the place most convenient for the parties. There he swears the witnesses, takes the evidence, and reduces it to written form. He then transmits it to the Commission together with his own findings.19 An examiner of the Wisconsin Industrial Commission takes the testimony as the lawyers offer it. "He listens to these hypothetical questions, he takes the answers as they make them, he takes the objections as they are made, and accepts the testimony, as any other referee does, subject to the objection." He has no discretion; he reports back his testimony as taken to the Commission which sits in judgment upon the record. 20

Evidence 

The rules of evidence as applied in administrative hearings are determined by the statutes creating the commissions, the rules adopted by them, and the judicial decisions in appellate The nature of the functions of administrative tribunals and the reasons for their creation, are such that their methods of procedure and operation should be different from those of the courts of law. The application of the rules of evidence would seriously interfere with the work of the commissions, and their effectiveness is greatly increased by a disregard or violation of the rules of evidence. The conduct of the hearings before the commissions and boards, as well as the carrying on of their

Administrative hearings differ from those in courts of law in one other vital respect. The commissions can send out their own examiners, accountants, engineers, and investigators to secure evidence. Before a court only the parties litigant can introduce evidence. This is one more indication of the interest of the public in general in administrative adjudication. Instead of being a purely private controversy the effects of which have no concern to society at large, the government itself has an interest in administrative cases. The commission, representing the public interest, makes sure that no stone will be left unturned in unearthing the facts. To this end it sends its own experts out to find the truth where they can and listens to their sworn testimony on the witness stand.26 28 Many of the federal administrative agencies maintain their own bar. Among them are the Department of the Interior, the 

Post Office Department, the Department of the Treasury, and the United States Patent Office. Certain formalities are prescribed for entry, and disbarment can take place under specified conditions. The member of a departmental bar need not always be an attorney.27 Certified public accountants may be admitted to practice before the United States Board of Tax Appeals. 

One object of administrative adjudication has been to make justice cheaper as well as speedier. Thus, the Wisconsin Industrial Commission sends a woman who has been made a widow by an accident a form letter telling her that she need not incur the expense of an attorney. Lawyers objecting to this are shown that the legal compensation is just as great as the maximum possible recovery in a suit at law. Lawyers who work on a contingent fee basis, that is, paid only if they win, are limited to a maximum of $100 or 10 per cent of the amount recovered, unless the commission permits other arrangements. 

This rule does not affect lawyers who are retained on a straight per diem basis.29 There is some indication of a tendency for

Argument 

Briefs constitute the customary mode of argument before the Interstate Commerce Commission. Oral arguments will be heard only when specially ordered by the Commission.30 In those tribunals where the evidence is taken largely by examiners and a decision reached without a formal hearing before the full bench of commissioners, oral arguments are out of place. In the case of the Federal Trade Commission, however, the full commission, or a quorum thereof, eventually sits to hear oral argument. 31 Eventually an authoritative judgment will issue from an administrative tribunal. This is usually known as an order. 

Generally, administrative agencies cannot enforce their orders or decisions without resort to courts of law. There are some exceptions to this, such as the Railroad Commission of the 

State of California.32 The Interstate Commerce Commission cannot enforce its own orders, but must seek enforcement through a circuit court.33 In America there is always the opportunity of staying the effect of an order while applying to the courts for judicial review. In rate cases, it is frequently provided that the higher rate continue in effect while the order is at issue before the courts. The difference between the two disputed rates is deposited in a separate fund, so that it may be refunded to consumers in case the courts uphold the original order for lower rates. The effect is that the lower rates of the original order will have been in force even though the higher rates have been paid.

Administrative adjudication has been described as justice. without law. There is an increasing realization that technical "Bevis, "Administrative Commissions and the Administration of Justice," loc. cit., Vol. I, p. 250.

34 questions of modern society cannot be easily classified into legal grooves. The ancient formulae of the common law frequently fail to submit to equitable application in an industrial age. 

More and more it is being realized that justice can be rendered only by investing administrative officers and tribunals with discretion to render justice in accordance with the needs of the situation, unbound by precedent and unfettered by technical legal procedure. For this reason administrative tribunals refuse to be bound by precedent. They publish no reasoned decisions upon which to predict future action. Such decisions as they do publish usually set forth a short statement of the facts supplemented by the decision reached. Members of the legal profession have sometimes criticized this lack of written opinions. They want some indication of future policy whereupon to base future briefs and arguments. Lawyers desire written opinions of decided cases so that they may have in permanent form the decision and the reasons therefor. These cases establish precedents, and it then becomes possible for the lawyer to formulate an opinion on a set of facts similar to those in the decided cases. He may thus predict the ruling of the administrative tribunal, and prepare his case for presentation as well as to give advice to his clients based on past rulings or decisions of the administrative authorities. Desirable as this may seem, there is much to be said in favor of allowing great flexibility for experimentation during this formative stage. As thought and action become crystallized in standard procedure, as the result of having weathered the tests of experience, there may emerge a new administrative law with the elements of certainty and predictability.

In the United States there is no legal limit upon the right of courts to review the decisions of administrative tribunals. Legislatures cannot insulate administration against judicial review by introducing into the statute clauses designed to thwart review.35

Even if a state constitution attempted to set up an administrative commission whose acts were not subject to review by the state courts, judicial review could be accomplished in the federal courts under the due process of law clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. 

The sum and substance of the situation is that the courts may review to the extent they deem desirable; that there is no method whereby one may know whether they will or will not review in individual cases; and that administrative decisions are final to some undefined extent, "and there seems to be a tendency at work to make them increasingly so. 

It is thought that on the whole the courts, especially the federal judiciary, welcome the relief afforded by the rapid growth of administrative adjudication in the last few years. Without this aid the dockets of the ordinary courts would have been so crowded that some other sort of relief would have been required.

Probably the reason most often given by the courts to justify review of administrative acts is an alleged distinction between questions of law and questions of fact. It is said that the court will review to correct errors of law, but will not interfere with administrative findings of fact. In findings of fact, however, the rule prevails that there must be evidence sufficient to support the decision. It is this latter rule which vitiates the entire hypothesis. In pronouncing judgment as to whether a given set of facts constitutes evidence sufficient to support administrative findings, the court is establishing a precedent which will act as a guide in future cases. In so doing it is formulating a given set of facts into a legal norm or measure of the sufficiency of evidence. Under such conditions, the distinction between questions of law and questions of fact breaks down. One is forced to agree with Dickinson that matters "of law grow downward into roots of fact, and matters of fact reach upward, without a break, into matters of law." 40

The distinction between fact and law will be no guide to the inquirer who is desirous of formulating a rule as to when a court will or will not review. This is amply illustrated in a recent federal case involving the Radio Commission. Time was taken from a station to which it was previously allotted and given to another. A federal court granted the original station full-time operation, thus permitting a certain amount of interference. 41

Here questions of fact were inseparably tied up with considerations of public interest and convenience. A similar situation is involved where a California court overruled the 

Industrial Accident Commission in a hernia case, 2 on grounds. that the findings of the Commission were not supported by the 39 42

Jurisdictional Fact 

The decision in a recent United States Supreme Court case45 presents the doctrine of "jurisdictional fact," also referred to as basic or fundamental fact. A federal statute provides that the United States Employees' Compensation Commission shall have the authority to make compensation awards to certain persons coming under the statute. However, the relation of employer and employee, among other things, must exist before the commission shall have jurisdiction to make an award. Since the fact of the employer-employee relation is the one which determines the jurisdiction or power of the commission to act in this type of case, it is referred to as a jurisdictional fact, which presents a question of law.

In this case, the Commission decided that the relation of employer-employee existed, and made an award of compensation to the injured employee. The employer appealed to the courts, and the Supreme Court held that the Commission had no authority to make an award unless the injured party actually was an employee. Since this fact was a jurisdictional one, the 

Commission should not be permitted to decide it for itself. The question of the existence of the jurisdictional fact must be determined by evidence presented in a court of law. The court

The practical result of the doctrine of jurisdictional fact is to permit a complete re-examination in a court of law of facts which otherwise would have been conclusively determined by the administrative agency. A decision of the Interstate Commerce Commission made after a formal hearing and protected by procedural safeguards, should be considered differently from a decision of fact made by a meat inspector relative to summary destruction of food. In the former case, the doctrine of jurisdictional fact does not have strong reasons for its application. 

Where a case can be tried again on new evidence before another tribunal and thus delay the final settlement, the result is to deprive the administrative authority of its advantage of speed. It also tends to make the administrative agency appear ineffectual.

Toward the end of the nineteenth century, the Supreme Court of the United States began to use this clause to nullify administrative acts and legislation which seemed to them to be contrary to good social, economic, and political policy.50 Consequently, judicial review under this clause has had an extremely widespread effect on administrative practice and findings.51

There are several ways whereby an administrative action may get before a court for review. An aggrieved party may bring an action for damages. Sometimes, as in the case of the 

Interstate Commerce Commission, the administrative agency must resort to the courts to enforce its orders. The so-called extraordinary writs serve to bring administrative acts before the regular courts. These include habeas corpus, mandamus, certiorari, quo warranto, and injunction. Then there are express provisions in statutes for appeal; for instance, the provision allowing appeal from the California Railroad Commission direct to the state supreme court. Another opportunity for judicial review is afforded where an administrative agency is permitted by statute to sue for the expense of executing an order after its non-observance. The question of the validity of the order may be raised in such a suit.52

Under our system of law, the courts have it within their power to review administrative acts to the extent that they deem desirable. There are no ironclad rules which will enable one to forecast with accuracy how far a court will review in a given. case.

There are two classes of cases in which the question of contempt of an administrative body may arise. Most of the cases have arisen in instances where the defendant has refused to testify; and there have been some decisions upholding the administrative exercise of the contempt power under these circumstances. French Droit Administratif 

England developed a centralzed system of courts centuries. before the same was true in France. The Norman conquerors sent the king's circuit judges over the realm almost at once. 

While the King's Courts did not immediately drive out feudal justice, they did establish their supremacy by the thirteenth century. In France, however, the feudal courts administered a large field of ordinary jurisdiction up to the time of the revolution. They were independent of the king, and each administered its own body of law. In other words, France did not have a unified judicial system on the eve of the revolution of 1789. For many years there was conflict between the king's administration and the feudal courts. Not having a judicial system of his own, the king was required to resort to the parlements, as the regional tribunals were called, to enforce his own regulations. The parlements were reactionary and opposed many needed reforms. As the royal authority gathered

During the last century of the Bourbon monarchy, suits in which the authority of the crown was directly interested were tried in special courts more responsive to the royal desire.

Under such conditions there was no doubt but that the government dominated this field of justice. These courts of the king were, however, the forerunners of the modern French administrative courts. The revolution swept away the feudal judiciary and set up a national system of ordinary courts. But it also retained the administrative courts as a separate and independent judicial régime. The Dual System of Courts 

61 It is necessary to realize that France has two mutually independent systems of courts, one the ordinary judiciary and the other administrative. Any action at law must come under the jurisdiction of one or the other. An independent Tribunal of 

Conflicts settles all matters of conflicting jurisdiction. For example, suppose a gendarme injures a citizen. If it is a personal wrong not related to duty, the officer is liable and trial is in the ordinary courts; if it is a fault of the service, the government is liable and trial is in the administrative courts. The 

Tribunal of Conflicts determines jurisdiction in this as well as all other cases. French writers have resented the implication of 

Dicey, which has probably represented the Anglo-American view, that French administrative courts are dominated by the government and that the droit administratif represents an effort to give the governmental officer a privileged position by trying him in his own court. Englishmen are beginning to change their ideas in this respect. 

Lord Hewart points out that the droit administratif has the virtue of being a system of law, while the administrative determinations of England are not at all juridical in nature.63 All writers today agree that the administrative courts of France are sufficiently free from governmental dominance to be classified as courts in the English sense.

The Council of State is the supreme administrative court of France. The method of selection operates in practice to secure a judicial personnel which combines those educated in the law with experts in the various administrative functions. The legal personnel has entered through competitive examinations open to licenciés en droit. A certain number of the personnel are appointed by the ministry from high administrative officials (directeurs or prefets). While these appointments may be to a certain extent political in nature the confidence inspired by the Council of State in the French people is such that a bad appointment would cause a scandal. While members of the 

Council of State are removable by the government in theory, they have in practice attained an independence which is comparable to that of British or American federal judges.**

This combination of legal training and technical experience in the judges of an administrative court is thought to be highly desirable. Hauriou claims that each administrative operation is both technical and juridical in nature. The authority which makes decisions in the judicial field should have legal training, but in the technical field the competence of the expert is required. 

Furthermore, each technical field differs, thus necessitating several types of technical competency. This assortment of expert qualifications is not met by the ordinary judiciary whose professional background is confined purely to commerce and private affairs.65 In the structure of the Council of State, the French 63

It is not based upon successful practice at the bar. The young law graduates prepare by training for this examination and career. Personnel of this type is supplemented by specialists who have had practical experience in the various fields of administration. In this manner is constituted the tribunal which is custodian of that branch of jurisprudence known as the droit administratif.

The prefectural councils, or lower administrative courts, were composed formerly of personnel not well trained, but a law of 1926 established in their stead twenty-two interdepartmental prefectural councils, each composed of a president and four councillors named by decree of the Minister of the Interior. A competent personnel is assured by the requirement that a certain percentage of appointees must be trained in the law. A professional outlook is assured by requiring at least half of the membership of the prefectural council of the Seine to be appointed by promotion from the other councils.66 These interdepartmental prefectural councils are administrative courts of the first instance, before which a citizen in modest circumstances can cite a government officer or agency at practically no cost. 

Justice is summarily rendered, without an expensive suit in the ordinary courts, to the person who holds a grievance against the government.

The droit administratif is case law. Furthermore, most of its major concepts have developed in the last half century. We are accustomed to look at France as a nation with a rather loosely written constitution, highly centralized, and with an absence of a check on legislative and executive action. The Council of 

State has developed, however, juristic concepts which enable it to nullify acts of the government. While it cannot declare statutes unconstitutional, it can accomplish a very similar purpose by nullifying an administrative ordinance which is legislative in nature. It does this under the principle that the administrative act was in excess of power and hence void. All 

Hauriou, op. cit., p. 981.

administrative actions can be questioned on the grounds that they are ultra vires; even the President's decrees may be nullified, with the exception of his purely political dealings with parliament.

This power to nullify administrative acts in excess of power was once the major action before administrative courts, but there are some newer developments which have vastly expanded the administrative jurisdiction. The first is an action which questions the misapplication of power. It makes discretionary acts subject to judicial review. Port gives the following example: 

The Council of State quashed a decision of the War Minister which excluded a grain dealer from competing for contracts under the War Office because the grain dealer held political and religious opinions of which the Minister disapproved. Held, that the motives which determined this grain dealer's exclusion were improper, as they had no relation either to the contract or to the dealer's professional capacity.67

Another example of judge-made law is the liability of the government for money damages. A liability for property damage has existed for some time, although it is not absolute, differing with each service. Liability on contracts has been long admitted. It is but very recently, however, that an individual could recover money damages from the state for injuries resulting from faulty operation of a public service. In 1910, damages were allowed against the state when a policeman, in pursuing a criminal, knocked down and broke the leg of a bystander.68 In the United States, the only remedy an innocent bystander would have had in this instance would be a suit against the officer, with slight chance of recovery, even if a judgment were secured. This principle of liability for personal damages has since been expanded by the Council of State, thus nullifying to a large extent the formerly universal principle which made the sovereign immune from suit.

ADMINISTRATIVE ADJUDICATION The Future of Administrative Adjudication 

There is really very little to fear in the development of administrative justice. All of the Anglo-American scruples relative to maintaining the supremacy of the law are well safeguarded so long as the law courts retain their present power to review administrative acts. Indeed, many of those friends of social justice who have regarded the growth of administrative agencies as a means of adapting a slowly changing law to a new society will say that the real causes for anxiety lie in the other direction. They see in the tendency of some courts to overthrow technical findings of fact by commissions a positive menace to the orderly development of social concepts in the law. 

There is also evident a growing lack of confidence in judicial remedies as insurers of good government. At most they are purely negative in nature, and it is easily understandable that they should have bulked large in the negative political philosophy underlying the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries inception of our institutions. Today we are beginning to realize that good government is not the product of laws. Judicial office, especially in the states, cannot rise much higher than the political system of nominations and elections from which it springs. 

Furthermore, the field of litigation today is just as highly technical as it is juridical. It is believed that the traditional type of judge brings no special fitness to the solution of the technical questions of fact which arise under an industrial society."⁹ 

Administrative Courts in America 

Are we developing a system of administrative courts? Referring to the Interstate Commerce Commission and the State Public Service Commissions, Dickinson states that, more and more these are becoming assimilated to courts, employing truly judicial processes and hedged about with proper judicial safeguards. The same development may be expected to take place in other administrative tribunals if they succeed in maintaining themselves and winning a firm place in our

governmental system. The result will be the formation of a great system of courts of specialized jurisdiction, each with its own rules and its own practice, but truly judicial in character and methods, and all subject in matters of general law to the ultimate control of the traditional courts.70

History has successively demonstrated that administrative discretion tends to become crystallized into a body of known, ascertainable, and consistently applied law." The traditional example is found in the development of that body of Anglo- American jurisprudence known as Equity. In the beginning it was a purely administrative means of relieving miscarriage of justice in the ordinary courts. Litigants adversely affected would appeal to the conscience of the king to set aside the judgment or give other relief in those cases where the rigorous application of the letter of the law would fail to render justice. 

Gradually, as appeals of this kind increased in volume, the king delegated this power to his chancellor. As time went on, the chancellor was unable to personally handle all such matters, so a number of assistants were added for that specific purpose. 

In time they acquired judicial status and their chamber became known as the Chancery Bench. Common-law courts are today administering throughout the English speaking world the rules of equity, which had their origin in administrative fiat. 

A practitioner at the federal bar recently stated that it is "clear that the courts of general jurisdiction are not sufficiently familiar with the intricacies of governmental law and regulation and the antecedent history thereof to make their reviews entirely satisfactory to both the government and the aggrieved plaintiff or defendant." 72 McGuire's proposed solution would be a specialized federal court sitting alternately as business demanded in each of the nine circuits of the existing Circuit 

Courts of Appeals and at Washington. Jurisdiction would be comparable with that of the French Council of State and would include at least all of that authority which federal courts now have over administrative acts. Review would be by certiorari

CHAPTER XX ADMINISTRATIVE LEGISLATION 

The lawmaking bodies of this country include the Congress and the state legislatures, the executive departments, and the judiciary. But there is another lawmaking agency which is becoming increasingly important. In recent years, government has responded to the needs of our modern society by creating many administrative agencies for the regulation of the innumerable activities engaged in by the inhabitants of this populous country. These boards and commissions, or administrative agencies, possess limited legislative and judicial powers. 

They promulgate rules, regulations, and orders which have the effect of laws enacted by legislatures. Hence, these administrative tribunals are lawmaking bodies, and the rules, regulations, and orders which they issue constitute what are referred to as "Administrative Legislation."

Administrative legislation is not new. All through our national history Congress has delegated to others the power to complete in their details grants of statutory power given in general terms.¹ The fact remains, however, that to the host of new administrative agencies, created by the states and Congress in the twentieth century, have been delegated the power to make rules restricting individual freedom and liberty to a degree probably not contemplated by our constitutional forefathers. 

Legislation is general or special. The distinguishing feature of the former is that it is general in application affecting all persons who come within its purview. Instead of being directed at a particular set of circumstances or at a particular act of an individual at a given time, it applies to all individuals who meet 

¹J. P. Comer, Legislative Functions of National Administrative Author ities (Columbia University Press, 1927), p. 50; James Hart, The Ordinance

Making Power of the President of the United States, Johns Hopkins Uni versity Studies in Historical and Political Science, Series XLIII, No. 3, 1925, pp. 17-23. 415

[Pt. IV 

ADMINISTRATIVE LAW 

its conditions. However, special legislation is not general in application; it makes exemptions from the application of the general rule of law. Usually, legislation contemplates continuity of time. Instead of applying to a particular situation which will expire when the order is carried out, legislation continues to establish a rule of conduct for similar situations in the future. 

In this respect it differs from an administrative order which applies only to particular cases. As indicated in the previous chapter, however, there are border line cases where it is difficult to distinguish between an administrative order, administrative legislation, and administrative adjudication. 

Nature of Administrative Legislation

The student might search the laws and legal literature in vain for the term "administrative legislation." Instead he would hear of rules, regulations, instructions, general orders, circulars, bulletins, notices, and memoranda. There is no uniformity in nomenclature, nor is there clear distinction as to the meaning of these terms. Thus, the legislative power of the 

President of the United States is commonly referred to as the ordinance-making power. He is said to have both an independent and a delegated lawmaking power. The former is derived from the expressed or clearly implied terms of the Constitution itself. He exercises it as the result of being commander-in-chief of the army and navy, and through his control over foreign affairs, his pardon and amnesty power, and as a result of his obligation faithfully to execute the laws of the United States. Then there are the powers to make rules and regulations granted by Congress to the President, to department heads, commissions, and other administrative officers. "What distinguishes legislation from adjudication is that the former affects the right of individuals in the abstract and must be applied in a further proceeding before the legal position of any particular individual will be definitely touched by it; while adjudication operates concretely upon individuals in their individual capacity." John Dickinson, Administrative Justice and the Supremacy of Law (Harvard University Press, 1927), p. 21. 

J. A. Fairlie. "Administrative Legislation," Michigan Law Review (January, 1920), Vol. XVIII, No. 3, pp. 181, 199. 

Hart, op. cit., note title. 

Comer, op. cit., pp. 22-23.

ADMINISTRATIVE LEGISLATION 

There are in general two types of federal administrative legislation, supplementary and contingent. The former is the power given to administrative officers to fill in the details of laws passed in general terms. This practice has been much more widespread in Europe than in the United States, where legislatures have sought to foresee the future contingencies and embody them in detailed statutes. Continental European countries have always sanctioned a more liberal use of the executive ordinance than has been the case in Anglo-American states. The other class of administrative legislation is that which makes a law effective only upon the President's finding and declaring a certain set of facts to exist. It has been extensively used in foreign affairs, especially in commercial and tariff matters. A leading example is the power given the President to make modifications of existing tariff regulations in consideration of reciprocal trade privileges granted by another power. 

The courts have recognized administrative rules and regulations as having the force of law. For instance, all valid federal rules and regulations that come into conflict with state laws take precedence over such laws, and in some cases a penalty for a crime can be inflicted as the result of an administrative order. Much of the current administrative legislation is in the nature of restrictions upon the liberty and property of individuals made in pursuance of the police power. Examples are the rules of boards of health, building and safety codes, and rules of public utility commissions setting standards of service.

The Industrial Commission of the State of Wisconsin formulates, promulgates, and enforces a number of codes containing police power regulations having the force of law. Among these are a boiler code, a building code, a heating and ventilation code, a building and construction code, an elevator code, and a fire prevention code. Each of these contains provisions which place very decided restrictions upon the use of private property in the interests of the safety of society as a whole, yet they are purely administrative in inception and promulgation. In the dicta of State v. Whitman, Justice Rosenberry states that these powers have been sustained. He goes on to state that here "is a field in which the necessity of an administrative agency is apparent to the most superficial observer. While the Legislature might by act prescribe the same rules as are prescribed by the Industrial Commission, when prescribed they would remain rigid, inflexible, subject to alteration only by amendment by subsequent Legislatures.' 99 10 Courts take judicial notice of administrative rules. By this is meant that the judges will give them their true weight and effect, even though they are not cited by either the plaintiff or defendant.

The courts, high and low, hold themselves bound to accept them as authoritative acts, just as they would accept the complete enactments of Congress. They are interpreted as though they were statutes. They bind the departments that promulgate them, as well as persons coming within their terms, and cannot be made retroactive where the interest of an individual is placed in jeopardy.11 "F. M. The power of both state and local boards and departments of health to draft rules and sanitary codes to carry out the health laws of the states has been upheld many times.¹² It has been adjudged a lawful delegation of the police power to deprive owners of property, along a lake from which a city receives its water supply, of the right to swim therein.13 A physician may be convicted of a misdemeanor under a statute providing a penalty for violating the rules of the state board of health, where he failed to abide by such a rule which required the reporting of a scarlet fever case.14 Sanitary regulations must be reasonable, however. A rule of a State Board of Embalmers was not reasonable when it resulted in the revocation of an undertaker's license for transporting home a dead body over about fifteen miles of rural territory in violation of a rule requiring him to embalm it, and allow twelve hours to elapse before such transportation. 15 

Delegation in Municipalities 

The general rule is that the legislative powers of a municipal corporation cannot be delegated to a committee of the council or to an administrative officer.16 For instance, an inspector of buildings cannot be authorized by ordinance to zone the city into residence, business, and industrial areas." Indeed, the digests are teeming with cases giving lip service to the principle that city councils cannot delegate their legislative power.

The fact remains that such delegations are nevertheless authorized, frequently by the very self same cases that so emphatically announce the general principle opposed to delegation. 

The legal reasoning by which delegation is justified in the face of outright prohibition, may take one of two or three courses. In the first place, it is stated that a city council may delegate to an administrative official the "power to determine some fact or state of things upon which the law makes or intends to make its own action depend." 18 The distinction involved here is not so easy to ascertain in practice. As stated in the previous chapter, matters of law and fact are difficult to separate. 

This power to declare that a certain state of things exists may be a very subjective determination, involving the exercise of considerable discretion.

Another rule followed by the courts in cases involving the delegation of power by ordinance, is that it is legal to delegate to administrative officers the discretionary authority necessary to make an ordinance effective, but that the legislature must lay down rules, norms, or standards to guide the exercise of administrative discretion.19 Here again, the courts are given considerable opportunity to pay due obeisance to legal proprieties and at the same time reach a conclusion in keeping with the necessities of an urban, industrial society. The court permits considerable leeway in determining whether the guide or standard established in the law is sufficient. 

It is legal to delegate to a bridge committee of a municipality the power to make rules regulating a public bridge, even though a city council cannot delegate its legislative power; for "it may authorize others to do those things which it might properly but cannot understandingly do."20 An ordinance giving the city manager power to prescribe the conditions and terms under which a garbage removal permit should be issued is not an illegal delegation of legislative power, even though he in-

In a recent case, the United States Supreme Court held that a certain delegation of legislative power by Congress to the President was unconstitutional. Section 9 (c) of the National 

Industrial Recovery Act of June 16, 1933, purports to authorize the President to pass a prohibitory law. The subject to which this authority relates is defined. It is the transportation in interstate and foreign commerce of petroleum and petroleum products which are produced or withdrawn from storage in excess of the amount permitted by state authority. The President issued an executive order carrying this power into effect, and delegated to the Secretary of the Interior authority to exercise power under the act and order. The Secretary of the Interior promulgatd certain orders and regulations in pursuance of the authority vested in him. The plaintiffs attacked the validity of Section 9 (c) as an unconstitutional delegation to the President of legislative power and as transcending the authority of the Congress under the commerce clause. The regulations and the attempts to enforce them by coming upon the properties of the plaintiffs were assailed under the Fourth and Fifth Amendments of the Constitution. The plaintiffs sought permanent injunctions restraining the federal officials from enforcing the orders and regulations. 25 26

The court in its decision stated that there are limits of delegation which there is no constitutional authority to transcend, and that Section 9 (c) goes beyond those limits. As to the transportation of oil produced in excess of state permission, the Congress has declared no policy, has established no standard, has laid down no rule. There is no requirement or definition of circumstances and conditions in which the transportation is to be allowed or prohibited. The court stated that the President is not immune from the application of the "general principles of constitutional government." When the President is invested with legislative authority as the delegate of Congress in carrying out a declared policy, he necessarily acts under the constitutional restriction applicable to such a delegation. The court decided that Section 9 (c) was invalid and that the Executive Orders and the regulations issued by the Secretary of the Interior thereunder were without constitutional authority. The court granted the permanent injunctions restraining the defendants. from enforcing the aforementioned orders and regulations.27 

Delegation of legislative power is unconstitutional, according to the letter of the law, and the courts have announced that this is their understanding of the law. Then the courts proceed to adopt subterfuges, such as the doctrines of quasi-judicial and quasi-legislative powers, which will permit them to harmonize such an interpretation with what any reasonable person will understand to be a practical necessity for such delegation. Some courts are today even frankly acknowledging that certain kinds of legislative power can be delegated. The result is that courts are free to approve or disapprove the delegation of legislative power to the extent that they desire. Just as in the case of administrative justice, however, the courts are gradually permitting an ever increasing domain of administrative discretion and final determination. Safeguards

There are many who feel that the delegation of legislative power is unavoidable, even if undesirable, in the midst of the complex social conditions under which we live. Realizing the 

Panama Refining Company v. Ryan, Amazon Petroleum Corporation v.

urgency of the situation, they demand that certain safeguards be established in order to avoid the arbitrary exercise of administrative legislative power. Of course, judicial remedies against arbitrary administrative power are always available, but they are neither summary nor adequate for all exigencies. For instance, the President of the United States, in the exercise of his ordinance power, is neither civilly liable in a suit for damages nor criminally liable except by impeachment. Because legislative acts are discretionary in nature, they are free from the operation of writs enjoining their issue. Those responsible for administrative legislation are not criminally liable, and their liability for damages is remote.28 Instead of this negative safeguard, which requires resort to judicial action, it is proposed that political and administrative precautions be taken to prevent the making of arbitrary regulations. Among the suggested safety measures has been compulsory publication, “laying before the legislature" for a certain number of days, approval by the chief executive, and approval by advisory committees. 

Some of these will be discussed in the following paragraphs. 

At present there is no uniformity, or order in the publication of administrative rules and regulations by either the federal, state, or city governments. As a matter of fact, city ordinances are commonly left unpublished, in a collective sense, for years. 

In the larger cities they are published individually in an official paper which only a few lawyers and officials read. In Great Britain, the power to make rules which modify the statutes has been delegated to the ministries. For instance, the 

Rating and Valuation Act of 1925 says that if any difficulty arises in connection with the application of the act to any exceptional area, or the preparation of the first valuation list for any area, or "otherwise in bringing into operation any of the provisions of this Act," the Minister "may by order remove the difficulty." It is further provided that "any such order may modify the provisions of this Act so far as may appear to the Minister necessary or expedient for carrying the order into effect." 33 The House of Lords has ruled that the courts are precluded from scrutinizing an order or regulation made under a statutory formula to the effect that "rules made under this Act shall have the same effect as if enacted in this Act."34 It is this that Lord Hewart refers to as The New Despotism. 

It is probably reasonable to expect that in normal times the courts of the United States would not permit such a far-reaching delegation of legislative power. In Great Britain, where Parliament is supreme, the courts dare not question a parliamentary enactment. They may review a rule or order to determine whether it is ultra vires or not, that is, whether the administrative officers acted within the powers delegated by Parliament, but no court can question Parliament's right to delegate. Under our doctrine of constitutional limitations, however, the courts could question the legality of delegation by the legislature. 

There has, nevertheless, been at least one notorious instance, prior to 1933, of delegation by Congress to the President of the power to change existing statutes. This was an emergency measure, during the World War, giving the President the authority to alter temporarily the laws of Congress establishing and organizing the administrative agencies of the national government.35 The New Deal legislation seems to offer many precedents for such delegation during peace time. 

Some statutory rules and orders must be laid before Parliament a certain number of days before they become effective.

Just how large a percentage of British administrative legislation is subject to this requirement is not apparent, but Lord Hewart says it is exceedingly small. 36 Such a provision is not very prevalent in the United States, although not entirely unheard of. At least one industrial commissioner has voiced his disapproval of proposals requiring the approval of the legislature or governor before the commission's rules become effective. It is claimed that these political agencies could not possibly attain the knowledge and understanding necessary to pass intelligently on the technical codes; that such approval would degenerate into mere perfunctory sanction which would in turn lead to a shifting of responsibility for commission mistakes to the governor, or political interference with the technical regulative functions. There is the further possibility of orders piling up on legislative or gubernatorial desks for lack of time for consideration, with resultant damage to the effectiveness of the commission's work. There is real reason to doubt that approval by the political agencies of government would offer much protection against arbitrary administrative legislation. 

European and American legislatures use two different means of bringing the white light of publicity to bear on administrative practice. In the parliamentary governments of Europe it is the question hour, the effort of the opposition to embarrass the minister by harassing questions in open session. This is possible where the leaders of the administration are at the same time members of the legislature. In the United States, however, administrative officers are constitutionally prevented from becoming members of the legislature, nor have lawmaking bodies taken kindly to the suggestion that they be permitted to attend sessions without power to vote. The American Congress has placed primary reliance upon special legislative investigating committees, and it cannot be said that they have not been effective.38 On many occasions undesirable regulations have been uncovered, leading to their abolition.

Where Does It Take Us?

It is obvious by this time that the whole system of administrative regulation is contrary to the eighteenth and nineteenth century concepts of constitutional government. There are many, both in England and the United States, who cannot bring themselves to believe that the changes involved in this trend are at all necessary. For purposes of illustration let us refer to Oscar 

W. Underwood, a Democratic majority leader of Congress during the years when the Federal Trade Commission was being established and when the Interstate Commerce Commission was being endowed with effective authority. He regarded delegation to these commissions with grave apprehension and questioned whether it accomplished the purposes for which intended.12 His reasoning was based on the tenets of Jeffer-

He placed great store in a "government of laws and not of men." 

Nor can it be said that the party of Alexander Hamilton has been any more receptive to the growth of administration in fact.43 Most Republicans are just as much opposed to governmental interference with individual liberty, especially in the economic field, as the followers of Thomas Jefferson." The point is that delegation has been a sort of desperate last resort, compelled by the force of circumstance and contrary to the underlying wishes and inclinations of all concerned. The delegation has been necessary, irrespective of what one might wish. 

A new social, economic, and political world is upon us and we are trying to run it with outworn steering apparatus. 

Laski aptly points this out in discussing the contemporary dissatisfaction with the workings of the British Parliament.45 

Parliament functioned well in the nineteenth century because it dealt chiefly with those large governmental problems to which its type of deliberation is well adapted: the franchise; religious toleration; the establishment of a national educational system -"or with economic problems like the limitation of hours of labor and the control of factory conditions, which lent themselves by their very nature to analysis by party discussion." Some American scholars are inclined to see merit in those very aspects of the system which the British are beginning to regard with alarm. Beard is inclined to see virtue in Parliament's shifting of a large part of its burdens to administrative authorities. 

As a result, the few great measures which it does pass are formulated more explicitly than most acts of Congress and are debated with more thoroughness and illumination. When it is dealing with legislation of great national significance it draws the lines on administrative authorities with a precision often wanting in federal statutes; it has leisure to give to the matter and invites the best talents of both houses to take part in deliberations.47

Beard's chief criticism of Congress is that it follows no uniform standards as to what legislative powers it will and will not delegate. It will give the Federal Trade Commission power to regulate great businesses and then spend a half-hour of its own time debating whether to pay a claim for a cow. A total realignment of delegated powers on a rational basis would relieve Congress of four-fifths of its business, and some of the powers now vested in other agencies might go back to Congress.48

ters is regarded by at least one British writer as an evidence of too much delegation. We are accustomed to hear a great deal about the tremendous burden of contemporary legislatures as compared with those of the past. The number of Public General Acts passed by Parliament in the years from 1866 to 1875 has been compared with those passed from 1920 to 1929both periods containing a total of ten years. In the earlier era, there was a total of 1,125, with an average of 112 per year; in the later period, the total was 578 and the average 58-the latter about half the rate of the nineteenth century decade.** 

The inference is that Parliament is shirking its duty by delegating much of its former work to the departments to be performed through statutory rules and orders. It is by no means certain that such an inference can be drawn from these figures, yet it must be admitted that they may have tremendous significance. The tendency is to regard legislatures as vastly overworked in spite of the delegation to administrative authorities. 

The only very definite conclusion that can be drawn relative to the future course of administrative legislation is that delegation will continue, not because any one wants it to, but because it seems to be the only way to deal with various situations which arise. American courts probably will abandon subterfuge more and more in dealing with such delegation and frankly recognize its legal status as in State v. Whitman. A more orderly means of drafting and publishing rules and regulations may be expected to develop. As the older generation of lawyers, statesmen, and scholars passes on there will arise a new one which will not look upon administrative legislation as a strange and hostile alien. Then will administrative legislation achieve its normal and healthy place in the legal firmament; then also will it be a useful servant, well disciplined and worthy of respect, and not an intruder suspected of designs on personal liberty.

CHAPTER XXI  

American public law distinguishes between an officer and an employee. While this distinction may seem to be at times rather far-fetched, the fact remains that it is very important in practice. For on it may depend whether a widow receives workmen's compensation for her husband's death; whether a city. manager must be a resident when chosen;2 or whether consulting engineers must pay a federal income tax on fees received from state or local governments.³ 

Who is a Public Officer? 

What, then, are the requisites, qualifications, attributes, or properties which distinguish an office from an employment? 

It is not possible to make such a distinction with great preciseness. The most common attribute of an officer would seem to be that to him is delegated responsibility for the exercise of some portion of the sovereign power. Thus, one whose duty it is to regulate traffic upon public streets is exercising a part of the sovereign power, and hence is an officer. The term "office" ordinarily, but not invariably, embraces the idea of tenure, duration, emolument, and duties fixed by law. Sometimes the exaction of a public oath of office and an official bond are referred to as distinguishing features of a public office. 1 2

The law recognizes both de jure and de facto officers. A de jure officer is one whose title to office is valid, while a de facto officer is one who has no right or title to the office he holds, even though he is the physical incumbent performing the duties of the office. Examples of a de facto officer are: one who was appointed to take the place of an officer under civil service who was illegally removed and later restored; a board of supervisors of a county elected under an unconstitutional act; or one who performed the duties of policeman even though his appointment was irregular.¹2 

Even though a de facto officer's title to office may be bad, his acts are valid so far as the public or third parties are affected. 

The reasonableness of this rule will be realized when it is understood that the de facto officer assumes office in good faith with the understanding that he is acting properly and according to law. At the same time, the public and third parties have learned to regard him as the one duly and legally constituted to carry on the functions and duties of that particular office. 

Confusion would result from impeaching his acts performed in accordance with law. Thus, a contract between a school board and teacher is valid even though one member of the board was a de facto officer.13 The public and third parties may deal with a public officer without making special inquiry into the validity of his title, and in doing so they will be fully protected as to transactions within the scope and authority of such an officer.¹4 

A common-law principle which has been carried over into modern American public law is that the same person cannot hold two incompatible offices at the same time. Offices are incompatible when their respective functions are inconsistent or conflicting, and when their performance by a single person would result in such great contrariety and antagonism as to interfere with faithful and impartial performance of the duties of each. The mere physical inability of a single individual to perform the functions of more than one office does not constitute incompatibility. The decisions of the courts in each jurisdiction will constitute the most reliable guide as to whether specific offices are incompatible. 

The acceptance of an office which is incompatible with that previously held results in the vacation of the first office. This is true even though the second office is inferior to the first. If an officer accepts an incompatible office and fails to establish title to it, as when an election is declared void, he cannot regain the former office to which another person has been appointed or elected.16

If an office is a new one, or unknown to the common law, its powers, duties, functions, and the scope of its authority must be set down in some express enactment of law, which should speak with sufficient clarity and fullness to enable it to be interpreted with a reasonable degree of certainty. For instance, a policeman is not an "officer" of an Illinois city until an ordinance is adopted creating the office of policeman as such, for the office of policeman was unknown at common law." Certain present-day offices, such as sheriff, coroner and constable, existed at common law several centuries ago. If such offices are created by name only, without specifying the functions to be performed, it is presumed that the office is to be conducted as at common law. The rule of international law that a sovereign state cannot be sued without its consent has effectively blocked direct suit against the government in both England and America. The alternative is a suit against the officer or employee, a judgment against whom is seldom of much worth, except in those instances where the legislature makes a practice of paying judgments against individuals. The truth is, as Carleton Kemp Allen has so aptly stated, that "the remedies of the subject against the State in France are easier, speedier, and infinitely cheaper than they are in England today." 21 The droit administratif has developed a right of direct suit, and recovery of money damages, against the state. In 

England and America, one may sue the officer and maybe the state will pay the judgment. To be sure, both the federal and state governments are gradually developing administrative procedures such as the Courts of Claims of the United States and of New York-for settling equitable claims, but these are far from being based on principles of legal right as is the case with the droit administratif. One of the surest and easiest means of securing money damages from the government is to know an influential legislator who will secure the passage of a special bill authorizing payment. 

Freund inferred that actions against officers are rare because the legal digests contained meager sections under this heading.22 

Today students are beginning to realize that the digests are very inadequate guides to almost any branch of administrative law, chiefly because there is no classification of administrative law in the principal digests. The fact is that actions and judgments against officers are by no means rare. The cases are scattered throughout the digests instead of being collected under the appropriate heading.

A public officer is, however, liable for violation or neglect of a ministerial duty, and he is not excused because of a mistake of judgment. An exception to this rule exists, however, when the superior directed, encouraged, or ratified the acts of the subordinate, or personally co-operated therein.23 

The citizen is not without relief against federal officers. In the beginning it was not possible to sue federal officers in federal courts because the common-law procedures were not available, except to the extent that they had been embodied in federal statutes and the Constitution. The result was that the common law remedies did not automatically apply. This resulted, in the early years of the Constitution, in no formally recognized mode of action against customs officers. The remedy which was evolved provided for a suit against the officer in the state courts, using the action of trover or assumpsit. The defendant would then set up a defense of federal jurisdiction and the case would be transferred to the federal courts, the government indemnifying the officer for the amount of the judgment. A statutory method of review has now been substituted for actions against the collector of the customs. The old form of action still applies to internal revenue and postal cases. The point is that actions against these federal officers are merely formalities for holding the government to account, for it reimburses all judgments. 24 The federal government and the states are not legally liable for the torts of their agents. In the case of municipal corporations, the rule is otherwise. 

There the right of legal damages has long been recognized for certain classes of cases. In so-called governmental functions there is no liability. These include those governmental operations which the city conducts as a local arm of the state. In thus administering state functions, it partakes of the state's sovereignty to the extent that it is immune from damage liability. Governmental functions include primary operations of the city such as police, fire, and education. On the other hand, liability is well established in those cases where the city is engaged in enterprises which are commercial in nature, or which commonly are or can be engaged in by private capital. These will include the generation and distribution of electricity, the operation of a street railway, or water supply. Of course, controversy frequently arises as to whether a given function is governmental or corporate, as in the case of sewer operation or garbage disposal. Hence, there will be a number of activities classified one way by some courts and the opposite by others.25 

The present tendency is undoubtedly in the direction of extending municipal liability. A California statute recently created such liability in cases where municipal motor vehicles injure citizens. The reasoning was based on the concept that the adoption of the council-manager form of government makes the city predominantly corporate in nature, its ministerial and commercial operations overshadowing its governmental functions.26

Extraordinary Remedies 

It is necessary and desirable that there be some means of control over the administration in the carrying on of governmental functions, so that efficiency be maintained and private rights of individuals be protected. The administrative law encompasses three methods of control: the administrative, the legislative, and the judicial. Ordinary judicial machinery is employed in providing a judicial control over administrative action. The ordinary rules of the private and criminal law are applied to the administration and its officers. However, in a large number of cases the activities of the administration are not subject to the control of the courts of law by the use of ordinary remedies and by the application of the ordinary private or criminal law. Further, the rule as to the finality of administrative action in certain proceedings makes it necessary to provide extraordinary legal remedies against such action. In these cases, then, special remedies must be employed if the judicial control is to be effective. Therefore, in addition to the ordinary legal remedies the special or extraordinary legal remedies are provided.

The purpose of these extraordinary remedies is to provide judicial control over the administration in the exercise of its governmental functions, and to furnish the means and manner in which the individual citizen can protect his personal and property rights from illegal and oppressive interference by the government in action. These peculiar writs are used to protect the rights of the individual against the erroneous or illegal orders of administrative agencies which may enforce its decrees without the sanction of law courts, and where no adequate 

28 Kaufman v. City of Tallahassee, 84 Fla. 634, 94 So. 697 (1922).

Ch. 21] 443 

remedy is provided by a private suit against the offending administrative officer.

Most of the powers of administrative tribunals are created by statute, although the common law and equity have provided a large part of the remedies against the non-exercise or illegal use of those powers. The statute creating the administrative power may provide a remedy; it may expressly exclude or recognize, or even modify the common law remedy; or no provision whatever may be provided by legislation. These extraordinary remedies are a part of the common-law system of remedies. In some jurisdictions these writs have been abolished, and statutory orders have been substituted for them. The extraordinary legal remedies are certiorari, mandamus, injunction, habeas corpus, quo warranto, and prohibition. These remedies are also referred to as prerogative writs. The word "writ," in Latin, breve, means a formal letter of a business character. 

A writ, as hereinafter used, is a formal writing issued by authority of law and is employed for the purpose of acquiring jurisdiction of a person or his property, or compelling him to appear in a court of law.

Certiorari 

The writs of certiorari, injunction, and mandamus are the most generally used administrative law remedies. The writ of certiorari is also referred to as the writ of review. The writ of certiorari, or review, functions from a procedural standpoint as its name indicates. When a superior court, as contrasted with an inferior one, issues the writ, it directs the inferior court or administrative tribunal to certify or prepare and forward the entire record of the proceedings including all the evidence presented in the inferior tribunal for purposes of review. The reviewing superior court will then examine the evidence and proceedings which are before it, and determine whether the ad- 39

Thus, the writ affords a means of judicial control over the actions of the administrative commission, board, or officer and corrects administrative error and illegality. It is generally stated that a writ of certiorari is a writ issued by a judicial body to an inferior tribunal or officer exercising judicial functions, ordering the one to whom it is directed to "certify" to the issuing superior court a transcript of the proceedings and of the record of the inferior tribunal which is to be reviewed. For the purposes of issuing the writ, it has been repeatedly determined by courts of law that functions of certain commissions, boards, and officers are "judicial functions," although these administrative authorities are not courts of law.33

It is usually provided by statute (in some states the writs have been abolished and statutory orders substituted) that the writ is to be issued only when an inferior tribunal, board, or officer exercising judicial functions has exceeded the jurisdiction of such tribunal, board, or officer and there is no appeal, nor in the judgment of the court any plain, speedy, and adequate remedy. Thus, three concurring requisites are essential before the writ will be issued: (1) the administrative tribunal must have acted in a manner not within its designated power and authority; (2) there must be no right of appeal by the complaining party to a higher administrative tribunal or to a court; (3) there must be no ordinary remedy available. The writ of certiorari, then, lies to an administrative agency exercising judicial power, commanding it to certify the record of a given case to a superior court for review. A writ of certiorari was sought to review the action of the Industrial Accident Commission in making its findings and award against the petitioners and discharging the defendant company and its insurance carrier from all liability. The petitioners are the widow and son of a salesman in the employ of the defendant company, who was fatally injured when struck by an automobile. The petitioners are seeking to recover compensation under the Workmen's Compensation Act. From the testimony presented at the hearing, the commission found that the deceased salesman had reported for work on the day he was killed and had been directed to proceed to another plant of the defendant employer. In accordance with a custom approved by the employer, he stopped at a restaurant for coffee. 

Then he announced his intention to go for his overcoat which he had left at the office of the employer the night before. Before proceeding he went across the street to leave his brief case, which was a part of his equipment. In returning across the street he was struck by an automobile, receiving injuries from which he died.

The commission found that the evidence did not establish that the deceased was performing services arising out of and occurring in the course of his employment at the time of the accident, and issued its order denying compensation to the petitioners. On a writ of certiorari, the state supreme court reviewed and examined the proceedings and evidence as presented at the hearing before the commission. The court decided that under the circumstances and facts of this case the injuries of deceased were received in the course of employment and they are compensable. The court annulled the order of the commission denying compensation to the petitioners. 34 Leffert et al., Petitioners v. In a proceeding instituted before the Board of Medical Examiners, the license of the appellant (plaintiff) to practice medicine and surgery in the state was revoked. Thereafter he filed in the superior court a petition for a writ of certiorari in which it was prayed that the proceedings before the board which resulted in the order for the revocation of his license, be reviewed and the order annulled. The appellant contended that one of the members of the board was prejudiced against him and since the vote of that member was necessary for a legal order of revocation, a qualified quorum was not present, and the board was without jurisdiction to act. He further contended that none of the evidence received by the board on the hearing of the charges against him was properly admissible. 

On a writ of certiorari, the court reviewed and examined the proceedings and evidence as presented before the board at the hearing which resulted in the revocation of his license. The court concluded that a member of the board who is biased or prejudiced, as evidenced by his activities in the matter preceding or during the hearing, is not for such reason disqualified to sit in such matter as a member of the board. The court further decided that from an examination of the record of the proceedings before the board, it appeared that none of the evidence received by the board on the hearing of the charges against the appellant was properly admissible. Therefore, the court concluded, the board was without jurisdiction to make its order revoking the license of appellant to practice medicine and surgery in the state. The order of the board revoking the license was annulled.3

Mandamus 

35 By means of the writ of certiorari a complete review by a judicial body of the exercise or non-exercise of powers of an administrative tribunal is effected. Where a complete review or re-examination of administrative action is unnecessary or not desired, the writ of mandamus is usually employed. Certiorari will lie if the act of an administrative tribunal is “judicial,” 25 Dyment, Appellant v. Board of Medical Examiners et al., 93 Cal. App. 

65, 268 Pac. 1073 (1928).

Ch. 21] 449 

and mandamus may be used if the act is "administrative." The remedies of certiorari and mandamus are mutually exclusive. 

The writs are issued in the discretion of the court. The writ of mandamus is used to compel the performance of a purely ministerial duty which the law especially enjoins as a duty resulting from an office, trust, or station. A ministerial duty is one in respect to which nothing is left to discretion. Ministerial functions are routine in nature and involve no judgment relative to a selection between alternatives in reaching conclusions of importance. The function of the writ is to compel an officer to do something which he is required by law to do. Although mandamus cases are usually entitled "People ex rel. (by the relation of) . . .," the action is by a private individual, and the official duty involved is one owed that person. The purpose of mandamus is not to establish a legal right but to enforce one already established. The duty sought to be enforced must be ministerial only, and not within the defendant's discretion. If a defendant refuses to respond to a writ of mandamus, he may be compelled to obey by contempt proceedings, and he is generally liable in damages to the injured party.

In a proceeding in mandamus, it was sought to compel the secretary of state to accept for filing a certificate of amendment to articles of incorporation of the petitioner corporation. As originally incorporated the corporation had seven directors. 

Thereafter and in compliance with the statute, the corporation filed with the secretary of state a certificate purporting to increase the number of directors to nine. The secretary of state refused to accept the certificate of amendment for filing. The company petitioned the court for a writ of mandamus to compel the acceptance of the certificate for filing. The court granted the petition for a writ of mandamus and decided that the duty to file amended articles of incorporation is one which the company can compel the secretary of state to perform by means of a writ of mandamus.36 

Pratt-Low Preserving Company, Petitioner v. Jordan, Secretary of 

State, 218 Cal. 577, 24 Pac. (2d) 457 (1933). See Tate v. North Pacific College, 70 Ore. 160, 140 Pac. 743 (1914); Warren v. Ickes, 1 S. C. D. C. (N. S.)

I (Supreme Court, D. of C.) (1934).

A writ of mandamus was sought to compel the civil service commissioners to change the answers to certain questions in an examination and to advance the petitioner's rating. The plaintiff, or petitioner, and other members of the police department were examined for the purpose of establishing a list of persons eligible for appointment to the position of captain of police. 

A "key" for rating the answers was prepared by examiners appointed by the civil service commission, and after the examination was held all participants therein were invited to inspect it. 

After such inspection, petitioner objected to the answers of three questions as fixed by the rating key. The commission changed one of the answers in accordance with petitioner's contention, but declined to make a change in the other two answers. 

Petitioner was placed number twelve on the list of those eligible for appointment to the position of captain. The petitioner then applied to the court for a writ of mandate to compel the commission and its members to change the answers complained of and to alter petitioner's position on the eligible list. 

The court examined the questions and answers and concluded that there was sufficient basis for the decision of the commission, and that the petitioner had suffered no legal injury from the action of the commission. The tendency on the part of courts is to leave examinations in the hands of members of boards to whom they have been entrusted. The general control of civil service examinations, including the making of rules considered advisable by the commissioners for conducting such examinations, was vested in the commission. Rules so made within the provisions of the law are binding, and the decision of the commission relative to the examination in question is final. Therefore, mandamus will not lie to compel the commissioners to change the answers to the questions or to advance the petitioner's rating. However, mandamus would lie to give the proper place on the eligible list after the result of the examination is established, for the list definitely follows the markings or grades given those examined.³7
