Injunction

A writ of injunction is an order from a court of equity enjoining an administrative tribunal or officer from taking action. 

The remedy functions in a negative manner as contrasted with the positive characteristics of mandamus. It is a general principle of equity jurisdiction that equity will not grant relief where there is a plain, speedy, and adequate remedy at law. The Supreme Court of the District of Columbia can issue writs of injunction restraining heads of federal departments who illegally cause damage to personal or property rights of the individual citizen. This power has not been conferred by Congress upon the United States district courts. It belongs to the Supreme 

Court of the District of Columbia by reason of its common law and equity powers, and because these administrative officials are in the District of Columbia within the jurisdiction of the court.

In an injunction case involving a city ordinance providing that whenever the city electrician should find any electrical wiring or apparatus defective, or work installed which endangered life or property, he should notify the owner of the premises in writing to cease using electric current and to repair the defects within ten days. If the property owner did not comply, the service of electric current was to be discontinued. The city electrician examined the plaintiff's premises and determined that the electric wiring therein was defective. The plaintiff claimed otherwise and refused to repair the alleged defects, whereupon the city proceeded to have plaintiff's supply of electric current discontinued. The plaintiff sought an injunction restraining the city from enforcing the ordinance against him, claiming that the wiring in his house was in proper condition and that the ordinance was void.

The trial court found that the wiring in plaintiff's house was in proper condition, and that the ordinance was void in so far as it conferred arbitrary power upon the city electrician to determine whether the electric wiring was proper. The arbitrary, oppressive, and illegal exercise of power was found to lie in the fact that the city electrician was permitted, as the au-

[Pt. IV 

ADMINISTRATIVE LAW 

thorized agent of the city council, to pass his judgment and make his determination upon the question. Further, in passing his judgment and in making his determination he was inadequately controlled by specifications limiting his power. The specifications did not particularize what he must find before he could declare that the electrical appliances were dangerous to life or property. The determinations as to whether or not in a given instance they were dangerous to life or property were left to the exercise of his discretion. The court concluded that the plaintiff was within his rights in resorting to the court for a determination of this question, and the court found that in this particular instance the power of the city electrician was unjustly and oppressively used. The injunction was granted, and the plaintiff was relieved from the necessity of complying with the directions of the city electrician relative to necessary changes and repairs.38 

Habeas Corpus

The extraordinary legal remedy of habeas corpus is used for the purpose of testing the legality of the detention of a person. 

Since the power to commit is considered judicial, one who is detained by administrative authorities may have the matter of his detention brought before a court of law where the legality of the detention is reviewed. The chief object of the writ is to secure the liberation of one who has been imprisoned without legal cause. Habeas corpus is available in the federal district courts as well as in the state courts. It has gained special prominence as a remedy in cases before the United States Department of Labor involving the detention and deportation of aliens. The writ can be granted by inferior as well as appellate courts, and it is more easily obtainable than certiorari and mandamus. 

In a habeas corpus case, a city council adopted two ordinances imposing a penalty upon anyone who solicited contribu- 38

PART V PUBLIC RELATIONS

CHAPTER XXII  

When the citizen discusses public administration, the first thing that comes into his mind is the public official—and to the average citizen this means a political officer. He is prone to believe that anyone who works for the government is bound to be either a politician or a political worker, and hence a self-seeker in the baser sense. If the distinction between politics and administration is to mean anything in practice, administration must receive a certain amount of wholesome publicity divorced from the political fortunes of those in power. The administrative branches should be so organized and operated that they would carry on regardless of what political faction might be in power. 

There is a vast amount of information about administration, as distinct from politics which many citizens would like to know. 

One group of farmers might want to be kept advised of the progress that government entomologists are making against the corn borer, whereas a metropolitan dweller might desire the public library to notify him of rare books coming to its notice. This type of information, non-political and unaffected by electoral vicissitudes, should be presented to the citizen for what it is worth. If government entomologists are competent scientists, their findings should be presented to the farmers through an intelligible and readable medium. The bibliographical facilities of a public library should most certainly be made available to specialists in a wide variety of cultural and scientific pursuits. 

The administrative branch is not only justified, but should actually be required, to place itself before the public with its best foot forward. In other words, it should be constantly striving to ascertain what the public thinks about its procedures and then correct those procedures to suit popular convenience, if this can be done without violating the tenets of science and technology. 

Thus, administration should resist being stampeded by unreas- 457

[Pt. V 

PUBLIC RELATIONS 

oning popular passion into ignoring the lessons taught by scientific progress. Flood contaminated waters should be dosed with chlorine even if the taste offends those not fearful of germs.

But there are a legion of contacts which non-political administrators make with the public and which could be turned into prolific sources of goodwill by a little attention and study. This could be accomplished with restraint and good taste, and without attaching a Hollywood publicity office to every major governmental agency. What is required is the gradual growth of friendly, mutual confidence between lay citizens and the bureaus. 

Such a cordial liaison, entirely divorced from politics, is sometimes referred to as public relations. 

What Does the Public Think? 

William Bennett Munro is authority for the statement that, striking an average, "it would probably be within bounds to say that the American city does not get more than sixty cents on the dollar for its payroll expenditure." ¹ Without vouching for the validity of this estimate, one can at least accept it as the mature judgment of a noted scholar. When it comes to ascertaining what the man on the street thinks of public employment as a career, it is possible to obtain a small cross-section of public opinion. During 1927 and 1928, Leonard D. White was able to secure the opinion of 4,680 residents of the city of Chicago as to their preference for employment either by the city or a private employer. Indicating overwhelmingly adverse attitudes toward city employment, the results indicated that city employees were less courteous, less competent, and less industrious than those in fields of private endeavor. It was quite generally thought that merit was more fully recognized in private than in city employment, and that private employment was on the whole much to be preferred.2 

White continued the investigation in 1930 and 1931 by securing the opinions, on substantially the same subject matter, of W. B. Munro, Municipal Government and Administration (The Macmillan Co., 1925), Vol. II, p. 27. 

2 L. D. White, The Prestige Value of Public Employment in Chicago (Uni versity of Chicago Press, 1929), p. 37.

Ch. 22] 459 

7,168 persons at eleven widely scattered points. The results again showed attitudes adverse to public employment, although the reactions were slightly less marked in several instances. Federal employment was regarded most favorably as compared to state and municipal employment, which were preferred in the order named. Of the total responses on a questionnaire containing several items, there were almost twice as many responses favorable to industrial employment as to public employment. It was thought that private employees were four times as courteous, three times as efficient, and twice as honest. Women regarded city employment with more favor than men, while younger people tended to have a higher regard for municipal service than did older folks. The answers to the questionnaire indicated that the highly educated person looked unfavorably upon employment in the public service. The foreign born thought more of public employment than natives, probably due to the much higher prestige attached to public service in the old world.³ 

A closer examination of conditions in those governmental units enjoying reasonably good personnel administration will tend to indicate that the popular estimate of public employment has been too low. In general, the compensation for the positions paying less than $2,000 per annum in the years 1928-1929 compared very favorably with private employment, although governmental workers in the professional, technical, and executive positions have always fared worse in salary matters than their brethren receiving salaries from industry. If it is kept in mind that the great mass of workers are in the low salaried groups, the conclusion is that the average routine worker would be better off with a government job. This conclusion is amplified by the fact

The Public Must be Administration Conscious 

The public attitude toward governmental employment is low because the ordinary person is prone to judge all public business by the impression created by professional politicians. The public must become administration-minded if it is to understand its government. For every mayor or councilman involved in a political scandal, there are hundreds of administrative officers and employees who have won their positions by some special fitness or preparation brought out in competitive examination. They are rendering a dollar's worth of effort for a dollar's worth of pay over a drafting board, over the accounting ledgers, reading meters, apprehending criminals, or preparing legal opinions. 

They are honorable and upright individuals untouched by crookedness and corruption. Many of them are persons endowed with qualities of leadership and executive capacity. Politics may be crooked, as the man of the street will undoubtedly volunteer, but the days of politics in that sense are being rapidly eclipsed by the new administration whose finer personnel is even now creating a higher respect for governmental employment in general.

The public must be made administration minded or administration conscious. The traditions of American public life have been all to the contrary. The word "administration" has entered the American political science vocabulary only in the twentieth century. If the citizen, the chamber of commerce, or the farmers' league wanted something from the government, no time was wasted with "government clerks." The councilman, mayor, or congressman was approached and he did whatever

Maybe it would be a special bill to pay a pension to Mary Roe; it might be a call on the secretary of so-and-so to urge the appointment of Richard Doe, or to protest the dismissal of Samuel Moe. The number of individual bills settling claims against the government is appalling." 

A recent study of federal personnel administration found that pressure on departments by individual congressmen seriously hampered effective personnel work. The curse of American city administration has been the practice of boards and councils in taking administration into their own hands. 

The cure for this situation lies in educating the public to the real functions and worth of the administrative branch of government, so that there will develop a tradition of legislative hands-off the administrative domain. Some fatalistic critics of the American political scene will doubtlessly regard political rapacity too firmly imbedded to succumb to any such movement. 

Nevertheless, such a tradition does exist in England and is developing in the United States. In the last decade, the old congressional pork barrel for public buildings and rivers and harbors has been largely brought under administrative control. At 

Berkeley, Manager Edy had an agreement with his council that citizen complaints involving pure administration should be referred to him. The new budget staff agencies are gaining a powerful influence over governmental appropriations, not because they have final determinative powers, but because they are the only ones who have an adequate understanding of the financial problems of the city, state, or nation. The growth of technical knowledge is compelling the public and the politician to defer to the technically competent administrator. A real estate subdivider once influenced a city council to uncover a city water reservoir and install an ornamental fountain adjacent to the subdivision. The city water superintendent, the county health officer, and the state health department, all protested vigorously, saying that the growth of algae would discolor the water and make it undrinkable. The subsequent protests from consumers

confirmed the position of the administrators, and the reservoir was eventually covered over at an outlay of thousands of dollars in public moneys. The laws of science cannot be ignored or defied, either by self-seeking politicians of by privilege-seeking citizens. The repetition of incidents like that just related is slowly convincing the American public that fire burns, and that defying the laws of technology is playing with fire. 

The public should be educated to demand the facts direct from unbiased sources whenever administrative officers are under criticism. For this purpose the development of research agencies, both within and without the government, should be encouraged. The strides made by professional administration during the last ten years have been largely due to the fact-finding efforts of bureaus of governmental research, institutes for administrative investigation, taxpayers' associations, and budget bureaus. Fact finding, coupled with an effective method of reporting to the public, could eventually force sensational journalism to cease creating unjustified public attitudes toward the public service; and it could furthermore create more favorable publicity at the source by forcing the wayward official to mend his ways. Research is a double-edged sword—a wide dissemination of facts will compel adequate administrative performance, and it will readily disprove the lie when false information is circulated by interests with ulterior motives. Laymen concerned about the problems of citizenship would do well to give every possible support to governmental research agencies. 

What Can the Official Do? 

The entry of the technologist into the governmental field has raised the problem of harmonizing the interests of technology with those of the politician. The latter has very largely had his way, but decreasingly so. He has been so jealous of his ancient prerogatives that it would probably be fair to say, on the whole, that the best technologists have not been willing to enter governmental service. There have been conspicuous exceptions, of course; notably in the professional and scientific branches of certain federal departments, such as Agriculture. The admin-

Ch. 22] 463 

istration of Franklin D. Roosevelt brought to Washington an unusually large number of persons whose qualifications were technical rather than political, many from academic walks of life -the "brain trust." 

The administrator himself can do a great deal to direct public attention away from the sensationalism of politics toward a sound appreciation of, and interest in, administrative achievement. A certain British commentator has even declared this to be "the problem of the twentieth century: the relationship of officials and the public." Succeeding chapters will indicate how the development of standards and measurements of administrative achievement may be expected to instill public confidence, and what may develop from more efficient methods of reporting. The fostering of an esprit de corps, a professional pride in governmental service, will do a great deal to raise popular esteem; but with it will have to go a security of tenure not always existing at the present time. While many splendid officials and employees now take an honest pride in their calling, others berate and refer slightingly to their governmental connection. Prior to the depression years beginning in 1929, many federal workers looked forward to the day when private employment would beckon them out of the government fold. 

In the higher grades this is largely a matter of inferior prestige and a sense of frustration in attempts at personal betterment-a situation not inherent in public service as evidenced by the high prestige of European civil services. Public servants can hardly expect the public to regard them with deference so long as they do not conduct themselves with professional dignity. Formerly, group gatherings of officials consisted of the popularly-elected administrative officers of local governments. Frequent elections and their resultant turnovers interfered with that continuity necessary to the creation of a professional consciousness. Annual meetings were dominated by papers and speeches telling "How we do it at Podunk.” "Herman Finer, "Officials and the Public," Public Administration (Jan uary, 1931), Vol. IX, No. 1, p. 23. M. E. With the increasing professionalization of the public service this is gradually changing. No one could ask for a more professional attitude toward their calling than that manifested in the national conferences of the International City Managers' Association. The state leagues of municipalities are developing research and training programs with staffs chosen solely on the basis of technical competence. That splendid new group of national organizations located in Chicago is having a profound influence in professionalizing the state and local governments. 

The university man with his scientific approach toward government is achieving an ever increasing prestige in the various fields of public administration. 

The Technique of Public Relations 

The public service suffers because it is the only business service which does not advertise. To correct this alleged defect, it has sometimes been suggested that a bureau of public relations be established in each department. In smaller cities one could probably function for all.10 The idea would be that the contacts of administration with the public would be handled by persons who were skilled and experienced in public relations. 

These men would not be political appointees; they would be purely professional workers. They would not be subservient to the political machine in power, and they need not become embroiled in controversial matters. They would merely try to study and direct the day-by-day prosaic contacts of officials with citizens, so that the least possible friction would arise, and so that maximum favorable impressions would result. 

The natural reaction of the "man on the street" to such a proposal would undoubtedly be one of profound skepticism. Such a bureau would inevitably be expected to become the publicity organ for the politicians in power. It would be suspected of a conscious endeavor to cover up administrative scandals and inefficiency, and to exert every effort to place political incumbents "Herman Finer, The British Civil Service (The Fabian Society, London, 1927), p. 71. 

10 See Stephen B. Story's suggestions for a "Service Bureau," Public Management (March, 1930), Vol. XII, No. 3, p. 117.

Ch. 22] 465 

in a favorable light. There is room to believe that this estimate would not be far from wrong in a great number of cases. Yet the idea should not be wholly condemned. Could there not be in the city manager's staff, for instance, a person whose duty it would be to prepare formal reports for the press, inspect premises for general sightliness, inspire a public contact morale in the personnel, instruct in the elements of counter contacts, conduct a speakers' bureau, and prepare reports for the public? Suppose he does strain himself to place the city in a good light with its citizens. If his representations constitute gross exaggerations, he will be discovered soon enough. If they represent essential truths, as will usually be the case, the public will be on the road toward becoming administration conscious. The idea has possibilities. 

Handling Complaints 

City managers have been particularly effective in settling dayby-day grievances that citizens feel they have against the municipal service. "As a matter of fact the average citizen without political influence is likely to get quicker service in a city manager municipality than elsewhere, especially if it be a small municipality. The reason for this is because the city manager has sufficient authority to enable him to settle most complaints without procrastination, whereas the complainant in mayor-council municipalities has to travel the circuitous route of council appointee, council committee chairman, other members of the committee, entire council. Along this route he encounters endless delays because there is no one who cares to take the responsibility of making a decision or has authority to do so." 11 foregoing quotation from a previous study by the author is not intended to create the impression that complaints are well settled only in council-manager cities. It simply happens that the manager has been the first professional general administrator to appear upon the scene. He has demonstrated that professional administration is not averse to listening to the woes of the common man.

"J. M. Pfiffner, The City Manager Plan in Iowa (State Historical So ciety of Iowa, Iowa City, 1929), p. 151.

A recent symposium showed that the city manager spends from 15 to 60 per cent of his time interviewing citizens who call at his office. Probably a fair estimate would place the average for this type of duty at one-fifth of the manager's time.¹² In 

Auburn, New York, a complaint bureau in connection with the city manager's office, handled by a secretary and confidential clerk, disposes of about 90 per cent of the callers.13 Most managers seem to feel that this constant palaver with citizens is a necessary part of the day's routine. Manager Hume K. Nowlan of Hinton, West Virginia, grants interviews only when his secretary deems the occasion sufficiently important to summon him by secret buzzer. [The] city manager is either "out" or sees callers in the public office, standing throughout the interview, whether it be with a councilman, salesman, visitor, or taxpayer. Those who have business so private in nature that they are not willing to discuss it publicly with a public official are requested to present their propositions in writing. Eight out of ten realize that what they thought important is really inconsequential, smile and forget; one tries and gives up in disgust; the tenth writes it out-sometimes on asbestos paper-and is answered firmly but courteously. This plan saves 75 per cent in the amount of time the city manager would have to spend with interviews, discourages requests for special favors, and eliminates social, sales, and idle talk.14

The degree to which the administrator makes himself available for casual interviews with aggrieved citizens will necessarily vary with individuals and communities. Experience has indicated that the city manager is frequently of necessity much more of a pacifier than an administrator. As soon as our cities are willing to allow their administrators to release their time from arbitrating petty community strife, just so soon can managers start to avoid this burden of interviews without danger of criticism. At present it seems to be a necessary evil. Probably the proposed bureau of public relations can develop a technique of handling complaints that will inspire public confidence and thus release the chief administrative officer's time.

There is no question that every organization will reflect the spirit of the man at the head. So it may be said that the public contact discipline in any given group will be largely determined by the morale engendered from the top down. It is not too broad a statement to say that one can usually sense the morale, esprit de corps, or discipline of a given unit by its public contacts. "Tone" in an organization is largely an intangible which is felt rather than seen; it springs from leadership which inspires by the imprint of example. Only when public departments are headed by such leaders will the spirit of the organization generate good public relations.

Public Contact Discipline 

The new public administration must develop a public contact discipline-an organization esprit de corps which aims at fostering good will. There are various ways to work toward this end. 

In the first place, public employees can be drilled in using the principles of common courtesy in their counter contacts. 

White's study showed that over three times as many people thought private employees were more courteous than city workers.15 There may be considerable injustice in this popular estimate, yet the fact that it is fairly prevalent points toward the necessity for developing in the public service a super-courtesy. 

Along with it will go insistence on personal cleanliness, fresh linen, and the daily shave in those positions where the regular routine involves constant contact with citizens. Drill in the ordinary decencies of speech and greeting will not be amiss; gruffness, curtness, and bluntness in any form will be taboo. 

Smoking in offices where the public calls regularly will be controlled, as will also be the case with the unsightly cuspidor. 

Emphasis will be placed upon the care of the premises. 

White found that the city hall of Chicago, while not an unsightly building itself, leaves an unwholesome impression. The corridors are filled with loafers who inspire anything but confidence. 

They are untidy. "Cigarette stubs, half-smoked cigars, ashes, bits of paper, and debris collect faster than the corps of janitors 

15 White, Further Contributions to the Prestige Value of Public Employ ment, p. 24.

[Pt. V 

PUBLIC RELATIONS 

can remove them. The ubiquitous and essential cuspidors suggest an uncouth company." 16 White admits that not all city halls present an impression so unsavory as that of Chicago. The loafers are largely absent in Cleveland. It is undoubtedly the general reaction that public buildings are not as well cared for as private buildings, especially as their newness wears off. Political choice and direction of custodians and janitors is largely responsible for this. The general professionalization of the public service will eventually correct the situation. In the meantime some pressure can be brought to bear to adapt to city or county use those arts and sciences of building management which are so aptly exploited by department stores, hotels, and theaters in making the public conscious of a pleasing environment. Constant attention to the sanitation of rest rooms will be a tremendous factor.

It is frequently stated that the major point of contact with government on the part of most citizens of the poorer classes is through the policeman and police courts. Although there has been a vast improvement in the last decade, it can hardly be said that the police have had the good will of the populace to which they are entitled by virtue of their extremely important trust. 

For this the policeman has been partially responsible. Certain factors are bringing about a change in this respect, not the least of which is the confidence generated in school children by the exemplary conduct of traffic officers stationed at schools. It is a pleasing sight to see a burly policeman smilingly take a diminutive miss of seven by the hand and escort her across the street through traffic. This breeds confidence in the representatives of the law, even though police executives feel that the men are badly needed for patrol duty. It is believed that more of this type of friendly contact with the public can be cultivated by policemen without compromising their major objective of apprehending criminals.

The underprivileged classes tend to contact government only when they are in trouble. This inevitably takes them to the building in which police court is held. The physical surround- 

18 White, The Prestige Value of Public Employment in Chicago, pp. 154-155.

Ch. 22] 469 

ings of the average police court are very often far from attractive. Hence, a considerable section of humanity retains its impression of government as the result of inherently unfortunate contacts. Adjacent to the police court is probably a filthy jail where innocents and first offenders are forced to spend the night in direct contact with the diseased, the mentally deficient, the vagrant, and the seasoned criminal. The reorganization of the entire criminal justice and penological systems, placing professional judges and administrators in charge, will vastly ease the public relations problem on all levels of government. 

It is necessary to realize that certain intangibles in personality tend to promote pleasant relationships in all human contacts. 

Call it what one may, "soft soap," "hot air," flattery, or emulation, there is a way that certain folks have of creating a kindly regard in all hearts. The public administrator should not try to be all things to all people, for it is his duty to take a firm stand at times. Yet there is a certain happy medium which can be achieved without compromise. Former City Manager Story of 

Rochester claims that blarney "never hurt anyone and it is dearly loved by even the most hard shelled old reprobate who ever voted in five different precincts on election day. I would classify the kind of blarney which I am suggesting as the anesthetic which should be applied to painful acts of government. 

If you can make it easier to pay tax bills, easier to register complaints, easier to obtain permits or licenses, easier to get information, you can blarney your way to increased citizen support.' 

Story further feels that mail should be answered promptly by the manager himself, even if it is only to say that further time will be needed for a report. The manager should sign his own letters, avoiding stereotyped forms. Employees who "act superior to any citizen or stranger or talk down to them... should be invited to take a vacation without pay.'

CHAPTER XXIII  

Reporting is making available facts relative to the operations of government. It may take great diversity of form or manifestation: bimonthly letters with the garbage bill; ¹ radio talks;² municipal exhibits; notice of promulgation of administrative rules and regulations; results of scientific researches in the bureau of standards; releases to the press; and formal annual reports. 

For convenience in consideration, governmental reports can be classified into three general categories. (1) Administrative reports are those which are prepared as a matter of course to inform the administration. (2) A second class of reports are technical or professional in nature, an example being the printed decisions of a public service commission. (3) The type which is of immediate concern to this discussion, however, consists of a rather wide variety of mediums for informing the busy citizen of governmental results with a minimum of time and pain. 

Before proceeding to a consideration of these popular forms of disseminating information, it is advisable to inquire into the means of gathering the basic information which goes into them. 

One of the defects of existing reporting, the lack of vital information, results from perfunctory preparation, for frequently reports are prepared apparently for no reason other than to fulfill a statutory or charter requirement. At the close of the year, the job may be delegated to someone who has a light load irrespective of his qualifications. He may be an accountant, general clerk, or engineer. Looking through past annual reports, and calling on division heads to furnish pertinent information, 

¹J. H. Jamison, "Effective Publicity Appreciated at Berkeley," City Manager Magazine (February, 1926), Vol. VIII, No. 2, pp. 27-28. "Civic Education in Cincinnati Through the Radio," National Municipal 

Review (November, 1928), Vol. XVII, No. 11, p. 717. 472

he proceeds to formulate the annual report in just the manner it should not be prepared.3

Administrative Reports 

A series of administrative reports should be a matter of steady, methodical, and periodical accumulation. They should be based on original records in each division and department arranged in such uniformity and progression that accumulation will automatically be carried forward into a consolidated statement for all units. The preparation of these original records need not be an onerous extra task imposed upon already harassed line operators. They should consist of the day-by-day record of operations that would have to be made out in any case. Examples are offered by the policeman's report on the investigation of a crime, a timekeeper's record of work on a street repair gang, a mileage and tonnage report from a garbage truck, a record of a completed purchase, and a payroll. There are countless others, all of which are kept on standard forms, centrally accumulated and consolidated. The original documents remain in the lower stratum of the hierarchical order, but the consolidated results are recorded on uniform report forms and forwarded on toward the apex.* 

Perhaps a realistic statement of how this is actually carried into practice in a given council-manager city will be more illustrative. At Lynchburg, Virginia, monthly reports are compiled by the heads of bureaus and departments. The various bureaus keep their records on standard forms from which they draft monthly reports to the departmental directors, who, in turn, compile the reports for the departments and forward them to the City Manager's office for checking and revision. The monthly reports form a chronological record of various city activities in sufficient detail so that subsequently they furnish an authoritative reference work of all administrative action. Each month the reports are mimeographed in a 

Herman C. Beyle, Governmental Reporting in Chicago (University of 

Chicago Press, 1928), pp. 74-80. * An excellent discussion of this principle is contained in W. F. Willoughby, Principles of Public Administration (Johns Hopkins Press, 1927), pp. 609620.

limited number of copies bound for ready access to the city officials. The steadily growing number of volumes of the administrative record are supplemented by adequate maps, kept up to date, revealing the character and location of all physical properties and utility plants, separate maps being maintained for each system.5

While such a plan of administrative reporting undoubtedly sets standards far in advance of the prevailing average, it is difficult to see how vital information can be distributed to the public without it. A study recently made of the reporting situation in Chicago has the merits of giving scientific corroboration to defects of which students had been to a certain extent aware. It was found that over half of the local government authorities were not reporting to the public in any form, and that such reports as did emerge came with extreme irregularity. They consisted of puzzling and monotonous arrays of uninterpreted statistical tables; judgment was not exercised in the distribution of space to the various classes of material; and the reports came out much too late to attain much publicity value. The substance of the reports possessed low informative value, consisting largely of inconsequential minutiae, such as the pounds of spinach raised on the municipal farm. There was marked neglect of what might be considered standard or important matters, and even on the transactions covered the information offered was not really vital. While it may not be fair to condemn a nation on the basis of findings in a single city, it is obvious that the individual defects referred to are quite prevalent either singly or in combination.

Suggested Remedies 

It seems to be quite generally agreed that these defects could be overcome by the establishment of a central reporting agency which would supervise the printing and publication of reports, 5 National Committee on Municipal Reporting, Public Reporting (Munici pal Administration Service No. 19, New York, 1931), p. 8. "Beyle, op. cit., pp. 52-54.

supervise the various departmental reporters with respect to "methods of reportorial investigation, preparation of material for the reports, reportorial writing, distributing of formal reports, and the use of informal media for reporting." 10 The 

National Committee on Municipal Reporting reached the conclusion that reporting should be independent of "partisan influences that may destroy it as well as from administrative control that may misconstrue or pervert its purpose." This was to be accomplished by creating a report director or editor under a nonpartisan civic commission. This latter body was to be "representative both of all branches and departments of the city government and of civic leaders holding no office. Each newspaper in the city should be represented by its editor or a special appointee." In certain cases, the report editor could be the assistant city manager, municipal librarian, or city clerk. 99 11 There are several obvious advantages of such a plan. The control exercised over departmental reporting would assure prompt publication. Because of a balanced selection of material, printing costs could be reduced. A central clearing house of governmental information would be of no small advantage. 

It has also been suggested that such a central office could study in detail reporting needs. For instance, certain reports become permanent records and should be published on durable paper, while others could be printed on cheaper stock. A considerable saving in paper costs might result from such considerations. 

Moreover, a study could be made of obsolete legal provisions relative to reporting, with a view toward recommending corrective legislation. These and many other useful functions could be performed by a Bureau of Information and Publicity. Possibly it could be combined with the Public Relations Bureau suggested in a previous chapter. 

One of the functions of such a bureau would be to furnish releases for the press. The periodical reports that are being accumulated from day to day can be placed in handy form for newspaper use. Of course there is the omnipresent newspaperman's fetish for "news value" which has to be satisfied. This

At least one study has indicated that newsmen are not infallible judges of what the public wants to read about its government. 

An investigation of the reactions of school patrons to school news shows that of the total amount of space devoted to that purpose, approximately 25 per cent was devoted to subjects of greater reader interest, while 75 per cent was used for printing stories of lesser interest to readers.12 Reporters are not always as well informed on public administration as they imagine themselves to be. As a matter of fact, many of them are prejudiced against administration because of their intimate knowledge of the seamier side of politics, especially police contact with the underworld. They develop a sort of cynicism toward governmental agents in general. 

A distinguished feature writer of one of America's most famous dailies, speaking before a group composed mostly of university professors of political science, stressed the fact that the modern newspaper is essentially a commercial institution. It is not particularly interested in uplift or moral leadership, if such a course interferes with the declaration of dividends. Experienced newspaper men have found from experience what kind of copy will build circulation, and hence advertising. As a result, most newspapers are written down to the mass mind, just as are motion pictures. The governmental reportorial staff needs a keener sense of the newspaperman's news values, and the latter needs a fuller appreciation of the significance of the new administration-a correction of that distortion which views the council chamber and political underworld as the alpha and omega of reader interest in government. 

A Washington correspondent recently complained of the dullness of the ten pounds of federal departmental publicity which accumulates on his desk daily, coming from what is characterized as a great body of press agents who combine to form the "greatest propaganda establishment in the world." 13 They

It is an unwritten law that they will keep your confidence." 15 The higher tone of the city hall in council-manager cities probably tends to establish the confidence of reporters in city affairs in general.

Everything possible should be done to visualize the story which one is trying to tell. Pictures, cartoons, and sketches are to be used freely. Maps and diagrams always have their proper places in any report. Special emphasis is usually placed on the necessity for an organization chart showing sources of official authority and lines of responsibility.16 The important point about this whole question of visual presentation is solving the question of how much can safely be put into a chart. A chart made for popular consumption is worthless unless an average reader can grasp its intent at a glance. A huge proportion of the population has an anti-mathematical complex which throws up artificial mental hurdles in the path of comprehending anything involving numbers. Many others refuse to exert mental effort even when capable. Consequently a chart should be so simple that it will compel mental comprehension.

Financial Reports 

If there is one phase of municipal reporting that has failed to give the citizen a simple and accurate picture, it is that dealing with financial transactions. This is largely due to the faulty accounting systems that have generally prevailed in governmental circles. Without proper accounting procedure, it is impossible to prepare adequate financial reports. When accounting is such as actually to hide the true state of affairs to the officials themselves, how can they be expected to tell the public that which they do not know? Hence, the first step in fiscal reporting involves the installation of modern accounting procedure. 

In doing so, too much credence should not be given to the traditional procedures of commercial accountants who have not had governmental experience.

The National Committee has suggested the following nine questions that the citizen will be likely to ask about the financial transactions of his city: 

1. Who runs the finances of the municipality? 

2. What part is played by the taxpayer in the process? 

10 On graphical presentation see National Committee on Municipal Reporting, op. cit., pp. 27-30.

Ch. 

479 

3. Where does the municipality get its money? 

4. What is the economic capacity of the municipality? 

5. Where does the money go? 

6. What services does the municipality get for its money? 

7. What is the present financial condition? 

8. Was the money spent honestly and efficiently? 

9. What is the future financial program?

One of the most important demands at present seems to be the development of mediums which will accurately inform the public as to who is responsible for additional tax burdens. 

There should be adequate publicity given to the share of increase or decrease attributable to each of the overlapping taxing areas: general city, school district, county, state, and others. The citizen should know how much of the tax burden he has voluntarily assumed himself and over which the officials have no control. 

Such would include bond issues approved by popular vote and referenda authorizing increased levies. For instance, the only increase in taxes for the city of Los Angeles in 1931-32 was occasioned by a charter amendment which required a periodical actuarial examination of the police and fireman's pension fund. 

If the actuaries said the present levy was insufficient to maintain the fund, the city authorities had no alternative but to make a new levy. There is no objection to the people's voting for these things if they so desire, but they should know the truth that will restrain them from venting unjustified wrath on innocent officials. More "than one city administration has been defeated (and a few re-elected) because either of the public's failure to distinguish responsibility for tax increases, or the officials' failure to explain it to the taxpayers" 17 The next matter of interest is the tax base-the ability of the people to pay taxes. It will be advisable to show, graphically and otherwise, the assessed valuation of real estate, tangible personal property, and intangible personal property. This data should be presented over a period of years long enough to show trends. Available comparative statistics of tax burdens, while not 100 per cent valid, can be shown with interpretative remarks. 

17 National Committee on Municipal Reporting, op. cit., p. 63.

[Pt. V 

PUBLIC RELATIONS 

Examples are the per capita cost of city government published annually by the Federal Bureau of the Census, and the tables of tax rates and bonded indebtedness by C. E. Rightor, published annually in the National Municipal Review. A fairly valid comparison can sometimes be obtained by adjusting the assessed valuation of several cities in the same class to a 100 per cent basis through ascertaining the percentage of assessed value to true value. A really accurate judgment of ability to pay cannot be secured, however, until personal income data are more widely available.18

The one essential consideration in financial reporting, at least from the technical standpoint-and the citizen should be educated to look for it-is whether or not good budget procedure prevails. The best index to this is the extent to which a government is living within its income. If a city, state, or nation must consistently borrow for current expenses over a term of years, its budget procedure is usually faulty. While such borrowing may ease the tax burden temporarily, it will soon enough tend to make it unbearable. We see evidence of this everywhere during the depression of the 1930's. The cities with good budget procedure are in general immensely better off than their neighbors who are now suffering from the poor budgetary control of former years. One of the most realistic means of portraying such a trend is contained in the annual controller's reports of Rochester, New York. A bar chart very plainly shows the trend in current expense deficiency borrowing from 1919 to 1930.19 In every one of these years there has been borrowing for current expense, reaching a peak in 1927 and immediately dropping with the better budgeting methods under council-manager government. In 1930 there was an upward trend again, probably due to tax delinquencies during the depression. It would have been well to give the reason for this in a few short sentences. 

If every governmental area published such a uniform deficiency chart, the public would inevitably learn the follies of living on

Means of Attracting Citizen Attention 

Some of the most effective reporting has been carried on through the privately supported research bureaus. An example is Just A Minute, a weekly printed circular of the Detroit Bureau of Governmental Research. It aims to challenge the busy reader's attention as he goes through his mail, luring him to get the gist of some local governmental problem in four or five minutes of reading. In private conversation Lent D. Upson, Director of the Bureau, states that he has received many indications that it is read, and he regards the venture as highly worth while and justified. Other bureaus are maintaining a similar service. The taxpayer's associations usually employ some means of reaching their members as well as a varying proportion of the public. Probably the most dignified and ambitious venture of this kind is the Tax Digest, a well edited monthly periodical of the California Taxpayers' Association. In addition to being mailed to all members it is quite generally available in public libraries of the state. The chief difficulty of reporting through these private agencies lies in the fact that they touch, for the most part, only those members of the upper economic groups from which they must necessarily receive their support. 

Where their publications form the basis for frequent news stories in the daily press, as Upson says is the case in Detroit, this defect is, of course, to a certain extent obviated. 

Several cities have resorted to a municipal exhibit to arouse citizen interest and disseminate information about the government.

Much success was achieved with this project under the council-manager régime in Cincinnati. 20 The Dayton Bureau of Municipal Research held such an exhibit in 1915, attracting 50,000 citizens and 9,000 school children. It is said to have aided in securing the passage of a much needed bond issue.21 

20 "Stimulating Citizen Interest in Cincinnati," Public Management (November, 1928), Vol. X, pp. 719-720. 

21 C. E. Rightor, City Manager in Dayton (The Macmillan Co., 1919), p. 240.

[Pt. V 

PUBLIC RELATIONS 

Such an exhibit was held in the corridors of the Los Angeles City Hall in 1929. These exhibitions usually aim to pictorialize and dramatize the administrative side of city government through booths, displays, wall charts, maps, and replicas. For instance, the Los Angeles exhibit showed a model of the municipal airport, a graphic history of budget operations, eighteen "pictorial illustrations and graphs emphasizing the effect of lack of zoning, too much business zoning and the absence of business lines," and similar presentations for each department.22 The municipal exhibit doesn't seem to work out as an annual proposition. It costs from $1,500 to $2,500, and this amount is not always easy to secure. Furthermore, it comes into existence to meet some specific current public need and under zealous leadership. When another year comes around and both of these are lacking, the municipal exhibit fails to appear. Or a new political control of the city hall may frown upon such a venture at that time as being politically inopportune. None of these considerations, however, is an indictment of the exhibit as a means of reporting. 

Radio Reporting

There does not seem to be any example of outstanding success in reporting administrative activities regularly by radio. 

There have been spasmodic successful ventures, such as those of Colonel Sherrill in Cincinnati, but studied and continuous efforts are practically non-existent. The discussion of the situation is too often linked with political speeches of the President or governors. These ordinarily can not be included in the category of administrative reporting. A high broadcasting official recently suggested that a great deal could be accomplished by prevailing on local broadcasters to allot certain periods for administrative broadcasting. The mistake should not be made of asking for the most popular hours, the periods which produce the revenue for the station. Study and experience will reveal that special types of audiences can be developed for various offhours. For instance, housewives may like to turn on the radio

and rest at 10:30 A. M. Presentations should be brief and interesting; so it is thought that the proposal to broadcast council meetings would often prove dull and uninteresting, but a regular and short digest of these meetings could win a large and growing audience. Other matters of interest might include the problems of the city schools, public works, playgrounds, and parks.23 Why could not the bureau of public relations conduct investigations and researches into the proper methods of gaining and maintaining radio audiences? 

Probably stimulated by the spontaneous and far-reaching success of the dramatization of the news through the nationwide broadcast of the "March of Time," recent experiments have been made in radio dramatization of administrative activities. While this means of reporting has demonstrated its ability to hold an audience, it seems to be subject to certain very practical limitations. To be successful the work must ordinarily be done by professionals; this means professional script writers, professional directors, and professional radio performers. 

Only the most prosperous stations seem willing to bear this expense by themselves, and tax-levying agencies can hardly be expected to do so. 

It has been determined that in the average city of 25,000 there would be 139 organizations representing 16,000 individual and active members. Some managers have found certain of these citizen organizations quite receptive to addresses by administrative officers on public questions. One city manager recommends the drawing up of a program for such speakers for submission to the clubs in advance of the season. In this manner the administrators have their time scheduled and budgeted, the speeches are well planned and organized, and certain individuals are not overworked.24 Motion pictures of municipal operations have been used with considerable success in Rochester. One film is said to have accomplished much toward urging people to keep paper and metal out of garbage. The pictures

Now and then one discovers some unorthodox procedure in the field of reporting. At Berkeley, City Manager Edy hired a newspaper man to get up the annual report in the form of newspaper stories, headlines and all. One headline read: "Useless to

Lose Anything in Berkeley." Reading on one learns that the police recovered 92.8 per cent of property lost. At Dallas, Manager Edy reported on his first three years by means of an illustrated report resembling a weekly news magazine in format. As manager of Filmore, a small city of California, Mr. Arrasmith has attempted to pictorialize the mimeographed report. A local artist furnished the ideas for presenting the prosaic facts with accompanying cartoons, all of which is said by Mr. Arrasmith to have caused widespread interest in the annual report.

A most unique and effective reporting system has been developed by Manager Nowlan of Hinton, West Virginia. A mimeographed letter is sent to the council members as a call to the monthly meeting. They are also mailed to each department head, each civic association, each large business establishment, and to both local newspapers. The report usually outlines some important project or question that is due to come up at the next meeting. Frequently the mimeograph's adaptation to sketching is effectively used. One newspaper publishes every letter in full, claiming that it is a regularly anticipated feature. Mr.

 Clarence E. Ridley, Secretary of the International City Man agers' Association, has for several successive years published an appraisal of various city manager annual reports in the National Municipal Review." He has allotted a weight of five points as perfect score for each of twenty criteria. One of these is promptness, requiring publication not later than six weeks after the close of the period covered. Others are size, paper and type, important facts, and attractiveness. The length should not exceed fifty pages. Propaganda and pictures of officials are out of place. The cities whose reports have been appraised for three successive years have shown a tendency to secure progressively higher ratings. The reports that are issued are unquestionably becoming better, but it is doubtful whether the number of reports issued in different cities is increasing. Mr. 

Ridley says that it "is quite likely that other means of acquainting the public with facts about the government are playing a more important part, such, for example, as the radio, the short periodic report, and other more modern and perhaps less laborious methods." 28

At a budget hearing a mayor once assumed an attitude of skepticism toward a departmental request for a larger annual report. He maintained that it was a useless expenditure because no one ever reads them. This is largely true of the traditional reports prepared as an onerous extra task to fulfill a legal requirement. There are two types of public report. One is to form a record for administrators, researchers, and students, and the other is to inform the lay public. The difficulty is that in the past we have been expecting the busy citizen to read such uninteresting and technical matter. Why not print just enough of these reports to fill departmental files and library requirements and then try to state the essential facts and results of administration so that the busy lay citizen can be informed without undue effort on his part? CHAPTER XXIV STANDARDS FOR MEASURING ADMINISTRATIVE PERFORMANCE 

Of recent years there has been an increasingly insistent demand on the part of students of government for definite criteria, standards, or measurements to be used in judging the effectiveness of governmental operation.' The inspiration of the quest is obvious, for how is one to know whether government is administered well unless one knows what constitutes good administration? Without reliable yardsticks the citizen is unable to inform himself accurately and the public administrator lacks means to gain popular support for the proper development of his various services. 

One of the most valuable uses of the proper type of standards and measurements should be in reporting the results of administrative operation to the public. At present governmental reports are chaotic in this respect, for if they do not consist of an unintelligible mass of statistical tables they contain columns of propaganda aimed to place the administration favorably in the public eye. If it should prove possible to reduce measurements to simple units easily understood by the layman, it should be a relatively simple matter to lift the reporting situation out of this morass. A statement of achievements placed side by side with what is considered to be standard performance should enable the citizen to gain at a glance some comprehension of what his governmental administration is accomplishing. The development of such criteria would usher in the new day in gov- 

1 Lent D. Upson, "The Other Side of the Budget," National Municipal

XIII, No. 3, pp. 152-157; E. A. Cottrell, “Development of a Method of Rating the Relative Efficiency of Cities," American Political Science Review (Feb ruary, 1925), Vol. XIX, No. 1, pp. 149-155; Charles A. Beard, The Administration and Politics of Tokyo (The Macmillan Co., 1923), pp. 19-25. 488

ernment, for administrative history shows with certainty that widespread publicity of understandable facts is the deadliest enemy of the self-seeking politician. The installation of modern accounting practice is largely responsible for the clean-up of our cities during the last two decades, because those systems have required the making of a record of every significant transaction. 

Men hesitate to loot when the story must be made a part of the record, especially when the public is given the keys with which to interpret the records. 

A noteworthy modern classic in American government has brought to light with practical vividness the part that an evaluation of administrative processes can play in turning the tide of public opinion against a corrupt political machine.² In 1923, a group of prominent citizens of Cincinnati engaged Lent D. 

Upson of the Detroit Bureau of Governmental Research to survey and report on the local government situation in Cincinnati and Hamilton County. The resulting "Upson Report" was unique in that it set up administrative standards in accordance with which it evaluated the existing local governments. While many of the so-called "standards" set forth were mere guides rather than objective measurements, they gave the report a scientific flavor which bred confidence. There is no question that it constituted the factual background for a civic renaissance which has amazed the nation. Cincinnati has shown what citizens armed with facts can accomplish. 

Types of Standards 

The term "standard" has different meanings. For present purposes, a standard is an administrative achievement which has

comparative or measuring value. It may be stated in terms of quantity, quality, money cost, and (or) time—any one of these or several in combination.5 A standard need not be stated in terms of utmost achievement or excellence. For instance, a certain truck might find it possible to collect twelve tons of garbage per day, whereas experience might show that it is reasonable to expect the average truck to collect but seven tons. 

In some cases a standard will mean achievement par excellence, whereas in others it will mean a performance somewhat above mediocrity, which may be expected in the form of substantial sustained effort from ordinary human beings over prolonged periods of time. The main consideration is that it should have comparative or measurement usefulness. 

Probably the most reliable standards are the industrial, engineering, and technological standards developed by the American Standards Association and the Bureau of Standards of the federal government. To a very large degree these have to do with precise and exact engineering measurements which touch governmental operations at those numerous points where public works utilize industrial materials and processes. The governmental purchasing agent is using them when he lays down standard specifications for the materials which he buys. While students of public administration are greatly interested in the development of such standards, they are very much more vitally concerned with measuring administrative performance, which is quite a different thing. One also finds that one cannot ignore such local differences as latitude and longitude, weather, climate, topography, cultural background, and civilized status. These difficulties have been so real and insistent as to discourage most attempts to develop standards. Repeatedly enthusiasts have approached the task, but their ardor has been dampened by the formidable obstacles in the way. PUBLIC RELATIONS Model Laws 

Another source of standardization is to be found in model codes or laws proposed by special interest groups to serve as a basis for the drafting of laws to be enacted by legislative bodies. 

In the field of state and local government, the National Municipal League has done pioneer work with its Model City Charter, Model State Constitution, Model Registration System, and 

Model Budget Law." Prepared by committees of those thoroughly familiar with the subject matter, these publications present a valuable consensus on the important matter of administrative organization, but they do not pretend to set up measures of administrative performance. Significant contributions to the standardization of traffic regulations have been made by the National Conference on Street and Highway Safety sponsored by the United States Department of Commerce.12 The American 

Public Health Association has made, perhaps, the most conscientious effort of any of the functional groups to standardize its procedures, one of its notable achievements being the setting up of a model organization for city health departments.¹³ 

The significant feature of all these efforts is that they emphasize methods rather than achievements; they measure procedures but not results. This, however, does not mean that there is no value in establishing model procedures, for methods must by the very nature of things have some rather intimate relation to achievement. If several of the forty cities in a metropolitan area permitted drivers to "go" on the yellow light and others required them to wait for the green, the resulting confusion. certainly would have adverse effects on traffic results. Students are also well aware of the fact that pre-audit of proposed obligations by the chief accounting officer tends toward economy.

Unit Costs 

Unit costs are work units stated in terms of money. Sample work units are the cost per inmate per day in a hospital, the cost of removing a ton of garbage, or the cost of sweeping a mile of street. While certain types of standards will always be inseparable from unit costs, grave error will be encountered if it is attempted to put all measurements on a unit cost basis. The accountant alone will never solve the problem of how well an administrative department is operated. The question of how many policemen a community should have will certainly be related to how many it can afford, but the whole matter of the proper allocation and supply of police personnel will be based on considerations only remotely related to unit costs. A halfdozen state insane asylums may have extreme variations in cost per inmate, yet society might be receiving the greatest dividend from the highest or the lowest cost institution. The variation should cause the budget-makers to inquire into the reasons for the discrepancy, and it should also make the superintendents of the higher cost institutions tighten their administrative control where it is possible to do so without impairing the effectiveness of operation. It would be utter folly, however, for the budgetmakers arbitrarily to assume that the lowest cost institution should set the standard. This is a danger inherent in too great an emphasis on unit costs in establishing standards and measurements.

For many years various efforts have been made to compile comparative costs as between cities and states. One of the better known series is that issued by the Bureau of the Census, one presenting annual financial statistics on cities and another on states.1 The National Municipal Review has published C. Current Variables as Standards 

23 In many activities it is within the power of the administrator to establish his own standards as he goes along. An example is the police use of the spot map to indicate areas with high delinquency or traffic hazards. A map of the administrative area receives a special colored pin at the point of each crime or traffic accident. These maps may accumulate their pins for a year, with the monthly records transferred to smaller maps for filing purposes. By studying these maps the administrator is able to transfer his patrols to where they are needed, to present effective arguments for additional personnel and equipment, and to distribute effectively the facilities at his command. Unit costs of individual administrative departments can be used in the same manner, independently of comparison with similar costs in other governmental areas. A given set of costs may be far out of line for a given year, yet they constitute starting points for the determination of useful norms. They furnish criteria for the administrator who wants to know what constitutes good performance. It is only by some such procedure that adequate measurements can be ultimately produced. 

Standards of Individual Performance 

Very little attention has been given in the public service to the question of standardizing operations from the standpoint of the day-to-day work done by individuals. In other words, the thing which Frederick W. Taylor did for industry a quarter century ago has not become the practice in government. It will be remembered that Mr. Taylor revolutionized labor operations 

23 See reprints from Chattanooga Times, December 17, 1933, and December 

31, 1933.

in the manufacture of steel by standardizing the movements, loads, and positions of workmen as they went about their daily tasks. There is no doubt but what many of the operations in public administration are susceptible to the Taylor type of standardization, were it not for the resistance that would come from employees and spoils politicians. There also arises the question of the desirability of such a step from the social standpoint, in view of the great extent of unemployment during these 1930's. 

Taylorism could very well be introduced into government with a startling reduction of forces, but to do so would require an arrangement of society wherein men would fight for the right to leisure rather than the right to work. 

While Taylorism aimed primarily at a greater physical output at a smaller outlay of labor, there are many governmental branches wherein the objective is not physical output at all. Police, fire, justice, library, parks, recreation, all render services which are more or less intangible from a physical measurement standpoint. Nevertheless, they all embody procedures which are physical in nature if not directly concerned with some ultimate objective of output. August Vollmer has recently produced evidence to show that the work done by a police officer on patrol duty can be standardized.25 The literature in the field of education contains more and more references to performance standards.20

Functional Standards 

While police work is far from being standardized, the amazing technical progress made in that field in the last fifteen years makes it possible to draw certain important inferences, generally accepted by professional administrators.31 Among these are: a single head is better than a commission; the rank and file should be under civil service; entry should be confined to low ages, say twenty-one to thirty; educational requirements for entry should be at least two years high school, preferably a high school diploma; and that a certain minimum in the Alpha test should be achieved by all applicants.

Technical and professional development, such as that which has been made in police science, points the way toward greater standardization. 

It forms the basis from which a rating scale can be made. 

A long expressed desire for uniform crime statistics began to take form in 1927, with the appointment of a Committee on Uniform Crime Records under the auspices of the International Association of Chiefs of Police. As a result there appeared in 

1929 a volume entitled Uniform Crime Reporting designed as a guide for police departments in reporting crimes to a national agency. The major obstacle in carrying out such a scheme was the reconciling of divergent definitions of the various crimes in the several states. Two ways were open: enacting uniform crime laws or establishing formulæ for eliminating the divergencies as a part of the process of reporting. For obvious reasons, the latter course was adopted. A classification of the major crimes for each individual state, with the code reference, guides the local department in reaching class totals "which will be reasonably comparable with those of other jurisdictions." A monthly return sets forth the number of offenses known or reported to the police from which are subtracted those known to be unfounded. Two annual reports record the number of crimes known to the police and the number of persons charged respectively. Up to that time they had contained comparative tables of crime rates in individual cities. 37 Although the bulletin does not say so, the discontinuance of statistics on individual cities was undoubtedly due to what many considered to be distorted and untrue comparisons. In other cases, the directions for reporting were misinterpreted in such a manner as to be thrown out of line for comparative purposes. As important departments ceased to make reports, owing to what they considered to be unfair comparisons with statistics faultily compiled, and as sincere friends of the movement began to point out the weaknesses of any crime reporting system, the original enthusiasm for the project cooled to the point of sheer disillusion in some quarters. At the present writing, a saner outlook seems to be forming. It is realized that British official crime statistics have been published for decades, but always with caution as to their reliability and interpretation. Thus, the

Sanitation and Public Works 

In 1929 a joint co-operative venture was inaugurated and carried on by the research staff of the International City Managers' Association and other groups of officials through the Committee on Uniform Street and Sanitation Records.39 A cost accounting system based on complete records for controlling and analyzing labor, materials and supplies, and equipment was devised. To street sanitation activities, to which the project was originally delimited, were added street repairs, sewer cleaning and repairs, property maintenance, traffic and street signs, and other activities commonly found in a public works department. Demonstration installations were made in Brunswick, Georgia; Kenosha, Wisconsin; Troy, New York; Winona, Minnesota; Cincinnati, Ohio; and Lexington, Kentucky. Through them public works officials are enabled to obtain a record of every significant transaction through a series of periodical reports from the individual operator up to the director himself. 

Ultimate results express work units in terms of money costs, such as cost per ton of garbage removed, per mile of street cleaned, or per catch-basin cleaned.

The Public School System 

The scientific method of approaching the problems of public administration has probably had a wider application in the public schools than in any other branch of government. The National 

Education Association, the colleges of education in the great universities, the Federal Office of Education, state departments, and research agencies in city school systems have been applying themselves to the development of standards for many years.

Higher professional standards undoubtedly prevail in the selection of educational personnel than in any other field. The prevailing method of state certification of teachers on the basis of professional attainment is at least a half century ahead of what generally prevails in the general city government. No school board dares to employ a superintendent who does not possess a high minimum of professional qualification. When a similar state certification for city managers was suggested recently, the reaction was less than 50 per cent favorable. This is taken to illustrate amply that the idea of technical training for the job has taken much deeper root among the educators than elsewhere.

The treatment here accorded to educational standards is not that of the specialist. It is only intended to indicate to the general student of public administration some of the developments that are taking place. For instance, quite definite principles of business management have been set forth in the monumental work by Engelhardt and Engelhardt entitled Public School Busi ness Administration. As one specific example of the conclusions reached therein, let us select quotations from a study of high school cafeterias made by W. S. Ford. In addition to evolving a model bookkeeping system for cafeterias, Ford lays down more than a score of definite criteria, some of which are selected at random as follows:

Student help is used profitably in food service. This work should be on a pay basis. . . . The use of student help in the preparation of food for the cafeteria is not satisfactory. . . . 

The expenditure for food supplies should be between 60 and 65 per cent of the total current expense when heat, light, and rent are furnished by the board of education. . . . The ex- penditure for employees' salaries should not exceed 24 per cent of the total cost for the cafeteria current expenses.42

Public Health 

Probably no administrative field has gone farther than public health in developing criteria to judge the effectiveness of its work. Since public health administration in its present form is so young, this fact becomes especially significant. The standards and measurement referred to are the results of experiences growing out of a number of public health surveys covering a period of years. From these have been evolved by the American 

Public Health Association the Appraisal Form for City Health Work and the Appraisal Form for Rural Health Work." These are designed for the use of the health officer in the self-appraisal of his work. The standards are said to be equalled or exceeded by about one-fourth of the cities from which data are available. The criteria are so objective that little is left to the opinion of the appraiser. Very thoroughgoing and rigorous proofs of the form's validity have been made. Fire Fighting and Protection 

52 The National Board of Fire Underwriters has for a number of years rated the cities of the United States for the purpose of determining fire insurance rates. The price charged for insurance is based on two considerations: (1) the basic rate for the municipality, and (2) the individual rate for the specific risk, taking into account such factors as type of construction, wiring, and exposure. From the standpoint of measuring administration, only the first or basic rate need be considered. All of the factors entering into a city's fire protection are assigned a total of 5,000 points allocated as follows: water supply, 1,700; fire department, 1,500; fire alarm, 550; police, 50; building laws, 200; hazards, 300; and structural conditions, 700. In determining the rating of any city, the numbers given above express the total possible deficiency points in any category. In other words, the larger the number in the final rating the lower the rank. 

Cities are divided into classes on the basis of total scores as follows: 0-500 points, class 1; 501-1,000, class 2; 1,001-1,500, class 3; 1,501-2,000, class 4; 2,001-2,500, class 5; 2,501-3,000, class 6; 3,001-3,500, class 7; 3,501-4,000, class 8; 4,001-4,500, class 9; 4,501 and over, class 10.53

Some of the criteria used in rating the fire department include: officers, operators, qualifications of chief officers, chief's tenure of office, appointment and promotion of officers, enlist-

53 The ratings attained by the larger cities of the United States are pub lished in Harold A. Stone, Fire Insurance Classification of Cities and Fire

ment and promotion, retirement, apparatus, organization and distribution of companies, condition of equipment, reserve resources, fire station, discipline, and training. It is interesting to note that stress is placed upon permanent tenure of personnel selected by competitive examination with adequate retirement allowances. There is no question but that the National Board of Fire Underwriters has set up objective standards of operation which have had their effect in forcing higher performance in fire protection. As Ridley points out, however, it is necessary to measure results as well as operation. 

Ridley conducted several analyses in an effort to ascertain what, if any, measures of results might be attempted with any reasonable degree of success. He immediately dismisses fire loss per capita as unreliable because the larger cities contain almost twice as much material per capita subject to destruction by fire as the smaller ones. He goes on to conclude that the best available factor is the ratio of fire loss to the total assessed valuation of real property, corrected to its estimated true value. This is true because available data seems to point to the fact that the total value of the improvements on land bears a fairly constant ratio to the total value of land itselfthey are practically equal. Furthermore, personal property bears a fairly constant relation to the value of real property. It is, therefore, proposed that three criteria be used in measuring the results of fire protection: (1) number of fires per million valuation; (2) loss in dollars per million valuation (to have double weight); and (3) average loss per fire expressed in dollars. It is claimed that these criteria can be used for comparative purposes when done with caution and wisdom. They will indicate in a general way what other cities are accomplishing, but they will not discover the source of a high fire loss.55

A recent study of the National Board of Fire Underwriters' rating scale tends to show, after eighteen years of experience with it, that there is little if any correlation between a rating which a city attains and its fire loss. It is suggested that the scale be revised to include four factors which are now omitted.
